en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Text of the Two Matrices:
The Text of the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha.
The Preliminary Duties—4:
The broom, the lamp, water, and the seat;
these are called the "preliminary duties" for the Uposatha.
The Five Preliminary Duties:
Zeal, purity, determination regarding the season, the counting of monks, and the exhortation—
these are called the "preliminary duties" of the Uposatha.
Pattakalla-aṅga 4:
The Uposatha has been performed; as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the formal act are present;
and no common offenses exist.
And since there are no persons to be excluded from that assembly, it is said to be "fitting" (*pattakalla*).

Having completed the preliminary duties and preliminary tasks, we shall perform the act of propitiation by reciting the Pātimokkha with the consent of the harmonious Saṅgha of bhikkhus who have confessed their offenses. The Recitation of the Introduction (*Nidānuddesa*).
"Let the Saṅgha listen to me, venerable sirs. Today is the Uposatha day of the fifteenth. If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha.
What is the preliminary duty for the Saṅgha? Venerable sirs, declare your purity; I shall recite the Pātimokkha.
All of you who are present, listen closely and attend well. Whoever has committed an offense should disclose it."
If there is no offense, one should remain silent; by your silence, I shall know that you, venerable sirs, are pure.
Just as an individual answer is given when asked individually, so too is it proclaimed a third time in such an assembly.
And whichever monk, while it is being proclaimed a third time, remembers [an offense]...
If one does not disclose an existing offense, it constitutes a deliberate lie. Now, friends, a deliberate lie has been called a hindrance by the Blessed One.
Therefore, a monk who remembers an offense he has committed and desires purification must disclose that existing offense; for once disclosed, he finds ease.
Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited. Therefore, I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask:
Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? The venerable ones are pure in this matter;
therefore they are silent. Thus do I understand it.
The Introduction is finished.
Herein, these four rules entailing defeat come up for recitation. The Exposition of the Rules on Defeat. Herein, these four rules entailing defeat come up for recitation.
The Training Rule on Sexual Intercourse (1).

Whatever monk, having undertaken the training and the way of life of the monks, should, without renouncing the training and without disclosing his weakness, engage in sexual intercourse—even with an animal—is defeated and no longer in communion.
The Training Rule on Taking What Is Not Given.

2. Whatever monk, whether from a village or from a forest, should take what is not given, constituting theft, in such a manner of taking what is not given that kings, having seized a thief, would execute him, imprison him, or banish him, saying, "You are a thief! You are a fool!
You are deluded! You are a robber!"—a monk who takes what is not given in such a manner is also one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.
The Training Rule on Human Beings (Manussaviggaha-sikkhāpada) 3:

Whatever monk should intentionally deprive a human being of life, or should seek out a weapon for him, or should praise the beauty of death, or should incite him toward death, saying: "O man, what [is the use]?"

"Enough with this evil, wretched life; death is better for you than life"—if, with such a mind, intention, and resolve, one should in many ways praise the beauty of death or incite another toward death, he too is defeated and no longer in communion.
This is the training rule concerning superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
4. Whatever monk, not having direct knowledge, should claim for himself a superhuman state, a state of noble knowledge and vision worthy of the Ariyans, saying, "Thus I know;
thus I see," and who, at a later time—whether being questioned or not being questioned—being found guilty and desiring purification, should say: "Friends, I said that while not knowing it."
“I know,” “I see what I have not seen,” or “I am speaking empty falsehood”—except in the case of overestimation—this too is a *pārājika* offense, one by which a monk is no longer in communion.

Venerable sirs, the four *pārājika* rules have been recited. Having committed any one or another of these, a monk does not obtain communion with the monks as he did before; thus, after [the offense], he is *pārājika*.
There is no living together. Therefore, I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask:
Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? The venerable ones are pure in this matter;
therefore they are silent. Thus do I understand it.
The Pārājikas are finished.
The Recitation of the Saṅghādisesas:
Venerable sirs, these thirteen Saṅghādisesas are as follows.
The Dhammas come up for recitation.
The training rule on the emission of semen, 1:
Intentional emission of semen, except during a dream, is an offense entailing suspension from the Sangha (saṅghādisesa).
The Training Rule on Physical Contact 2. Whatever monk,
with a lustful mind and perverted thoughts, should engage in physical contact with a woman—
whether by taking her hand, or taking her hair, or touching any other part of her body— it is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
The Training Rule on Lewd Speech (3).

Whatever monk, overcome by lust and with a perverted mind, should address a woman with lewd words, such as a young man would address a young woman, relating to sexual intercourse, it is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
The Training Rule on Service to One’s Own Desire.
4. Whatever monk, overcome by lust and with a perverted mind, should in the presence of a woman speak in praise of his own sexual service, saying:

"Sister, this is the foremost of services—that one should serve a person like me, who is virtuous, of good character, and living the holy life, with this kind of service," provided it is connected with sexual intercourse, this is a *saṅghādisesa*.
The Training Rule on Acting as a Matchmaker (Sañcaritta-sikkhāpada) 5:

Whatever monk should act as a matchmaker, conveying a man’s intent to a woman, or a woman’s intent to a man, whether for the state of a husband or for the state of a lover, even if only for a momentary occasion, this is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
The Training Rule on Building a Hut (Kuṭikāra-sikkhāpada)
6. Furthermore, when a monk is having a hut built by means of a personal request, it should be built for himself without an owner and within the prescribed measurements.
These are the measurements: twelve spans of the Sugata’s span in length, and seven internal spans in width.
Monks must be brought along for the inspection of the site; those monks must designate a site that is free from harm and has space for a walkway around it.
If a monk should have a hut built by means of a personal request on a site that is crowded and lacks space for retreat, or if he should fail to have other monks designate the site,
or if he should exceed the prescribed measurements, it is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
This is the training rule concerning the construction of a dwelling (vihārakāra-sikkhāpada).
7. Furthermore, when a monk is having a large dwelling built for himself that has an owner, he must bring monks forward for the inspection of the site.
Those monks must designate a site that is free from harm and has space on all sides.
If a monk should have a large dwelling built on a site that involves harm and lacks space on all sides, or if he does not bring monks forward, [he commits an offense].
In the case of pointing out a location, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
The training rule concerning malice: 8.
Whatever monk, being malicious, hateful, and displeased, should groundlessly accuse another monk with a *pārājika* offense—
“Perhaps he might cause him to fall away from this holy life.

Later, whether being pressed for an explanation or not being pressed, that legal issue turns out to be groundless, yet the monk persists in his accusation; this is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
This is the training rule concerning matters belonging to another case (aññabhāgiya-sikkhāpada).
9. Whatever bhikkhu, being angry, ill-willed, and displeased with another bhikkhu, should, on account of some minor or trifling matter connected with a legal issue belonging to one category,
accuse him of an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*), thinking,
"Perhaps I might cause him to fall away from this holy life," and if at a later time, whether he is questioned about it or not, that legal issue is found to belong to a different category—
If there is a legal issue in which even a slight portion has been taken up, and a monk persists in his fault, it is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
The training rule on schism in the Sangha (10):
"Whosoever, however, a monk should strive for the schism of a harmonious Sangha, [or] should persist in a course that leads to schism..."
If a monk should take up and persist in a legal issue that leads to schism, that monk should be addressed by the monks thus:
"Venerable sir, do not strive for the schism of a harmonious Saṅgha, nor stand taking up and persisting in a legal issue that leads to schism;
let the Venerable one be reconciled with the Saṅgha, for the Saṅgha is harmonious, living in mutual agreement and without dispute."

“‘Living alone, one dwells in comfort. If that monk, being thus addressed by the monks, should persist as before, that monk is to be formally admonished by the monks up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that [position].
If, being admonished up to three times, he relinquishes it, that is good; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.”
The Training Rule on Following in Division 11.
Now, if there are one, two, or three monks who follow that very monk and speak in faction, and they should say:
"Venerable sirs, do not say anything at all to this monk; he is one who speaks according to the Dhamma."
“If these monks say, ‘This monk is a speaker on the Vinaya; this monk speaks having taken up our own desire and preference;
he knows but does not speak [otherwise]; this is acceptable to us,’ then those monks should be addressed by the other monks thus:
‘Venerable sirs, do not speak thus. This monk is not a speaker on the Dhamma; this monk is not a speaker on the Vinaya.’”

“Venerable sirs, may it not please you to cause a schism in the Saṅgha; let the venerable ones be at one with the Saṅgha, for the Saṅgha is at peace when it is united, living in harmony, without dispute, and following a single recitation.

If those bhikkhus, being thus addressed by the bhikkhus, should still persist as before, those bhikkhus are to be formally admonished by the bhikkhus up to three times so that they may relinquish their position.
If, being exhorted up to three times, they should relinquish that, it is well; if they do not relinquish it, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
The twelfth training rule on being difficult to admonish:
If a monk is of a difficult-to-admonish nature regarding the training rules included in the recitation by the monks...
When being spoken to according to the Dhamma, he makes himself unadmonishable, saying:
"Venerable sirs, do not say anything to me, whether good or bad; nor will I say anything to the venerable sirs, whether good or bad;
desist, venerable sirs, from speaking to me. That bhikkhu should be addressed by the bhikkhus thus: "Venerable sir, do not..."
“He has made himself unadmonishable; let the venerable one make himself admonishable.
Let the venerable one speak to the bhikkhus in accordance with the Dhamma, and the bhikkhus will speak to the venerable one in accordance with the Dhamma.
For the Saṅgha of that Blessed One is thus trained: namely, by mutual exhortation and mutual correction. And so that bhikkhu...
If, being spoken to by the monks, he should persist in that same way, that monk is to be formally admonished by the monks up to three times for the sake of relinquishing it.
If, being admonished up to three times, he relinquishes it, that is good; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
The Training Rule on Corrupters of Families (Kuladūsaka-sikkhāpada) 13:
Should any bhikkhu, being a corrupter of families and of evil conduct, dwell in dependence upon a certain village or town;
and his evil conduct is both seen and heard of, and families corrupted by him are seen—
and are heard, that bhikkhu should be addressed by the bhikkhus thus: "Venerable sir, you are a corrupter of families and one of evil conduct;
the venerable one’s evil practices are both seen and heard of, and the families corrupted by the venerable one are both seen and heard of.
Depart from this residence, Venerable Sir; enough of your staying here. And if [he should say] thus:
If that bhikkhu, being spoken to by the bhikkhus, should say to those bhikkhus:

"The bhikkhus are partial through favoritism; the bhikkhus are partial through hatred; the bhikkhus are partial through delusion; the bhikkhus are partial through fear; for such an offense they banish some, while they do not banish others," then that bhikkhu should be addressed by the bhikkhus as follows:
“Venerable sir, do not speak thus; the bhikkhus do not act out of favoritism, nor do they act out of hatred, nor do they act out of delusion, nor do they act out of fear.
It is you, venerable sir, who are a corrupter of families and of evil conduct; your evil conduct is both seen and heard, and families have been ruined by you.”
"They are seen and heard [engaging in such conduct]; venerable sir, depart from this residence; enough of your staying here.

If that bhikkhu, being thus addressed by the bhikkhus, should still persist as before, that bhikkhu is to be formally admonished by the bhikkhus up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that behavior. If, being admonished up to three times, he should relinquish it, [it is well].
This is wholesome; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
Venerable sirs, the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* rules have been recited: nine are offenses upon the first commission, and four are offenses upon the third admonition.
Should a monk commit any one of these, for as long as he knowingly conceals it, for that long...
That bhikkhu must undergo the probation against his will. When the bhikkhu has completed the probation, he must further undergo the six-night *mānatta* penance for bhikkhus.
Once the *mānatta* has been performed, that bhikkhu is to be rehabilitated (*abbheta*) wherever there is a Saṅgha of at least twenty bhikkhus.
Even if the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is short of one by a single member...
It should not be contradicted; that monk is not to be contradicted, and those monks are to be blamed. This is the proper course in this matter. In this regard, I ask the venerable ones:
Are you pure in this? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this?
The venerable ones are pure in this, therefore they are silent; thus do I understand it.
The Saṅghādisesa section is finished.
The recitation of the Aniyata rules:
Venerable sirs, these two Aniyata rules are as follows.
They come to the summary.
The first undetermined training rule:
1. Whatever monk, together with a woman, alone with one, in private, on a concealed seat suitable for action—
He might sit down. Then a female lay follower whose word is trustworthy, having seen him, might charge him with one of three offenses:

either a *pārājika*, a *saṅghādisesa*, or a *pācittiya*. If the monk admits to sitting down, he is to be dealt with according to one of those three offenses: either a *pārājika*, a *saṅghādisesa*, or a *pācittiya*.
Or, whatever that female lay follower of trustworthy speech might say, by that the monk is to be dealt with; this rule is undetermined.
The second undetermined training rule:
Furthermore, it is not the case that the seat is concealed or unfit for action, but it is indeed fit for a woman [to sit upon].

Regarding speaking with indecent words: if a bhikkhu should sit alone with a woman in secret on such a seat, and a female lay follower whose word is trustworthy, having seen him, should charge him with one of two offenses—either a *saṅghādisesa* or a *pācittiya*—and the bhikkhu admits to the sitting; [he is guilty of a *saṅghādisesa*].
He is to be dealt with according to one of two rules: either a *saṅghādisesa* or a *pācittiya*;
or he is to be dealt with according to whatever that trustworthy female lay follower (*upāsikā*) may say. This rule, too, is undetermined (*aniyata*).
Venerable sirs, the two undetermined rules have been recited. Therefore, I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter?
A second time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this matter?
You are pure in this matter, venerable sirs, since you are silent; thus do I understand it.
The *aniyata* (undetermined) rule is concluded.
The Nissaggiya Pācittiya Rules:
Now, Venerable sirs, these thirty Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules come up for recitation.
The Kathina Training Rule 1:

When a robe has been finished and the Kathina period has ended, a monk may keep an extra robe for a maximum of ten days; for one who exceeds that limit, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
The Udosita Training Rule.

2. When a robe has been finished and the kaṭhina has been suspended, if a monk should be separated from his three robes for even a single night, except by the consent of the monks, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Out-of-Season Robes: 3.
When a robe has been finished and the kaṭhina has been suspended, if an out-of-season robe should come to a monk...
If a robe-cloth should arise for a monk who desires it, he may accept it; having accepted it, he must have it made up quickly.
If it is not sufficient, that monk may keep that robe aside for at most one month, provided there is hope for its completion.
If he should keep it longer than that, even if there is still hope for its completion, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
The Training Rule on Old Robes (Purāṇacīvarasikkhāpada) 4:
Should any bhikkhu have an unrelated bhikkhunī wash, dye, or beat an old robe, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Receiving Robes (Cīvarapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpada)
5. Whatever monk, however, should receive a robe from the hand of an unrelated nun, except in exchange, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and expiation (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
This is the training rule regarding requesting from an unrelated person. 6.
Whatever monk, however, should request a robe from an unrelated householder or housewife, except [in specific circumstances], [it is an offense].
This is the rule; it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya). In this regard, the exception is as follows:
when a monk’s robe has been stolen or his robe has been lost—this is the exception in that case.
Hereafter follows the training rule (sikkhāpada) concerning the excess.
7. If an unrelated householder or housewife should invite a monk to accept many robes, that monk may accept from them robes up to the limit of one inner robe and one upper robe.
If he should accept more than that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
The First Training Rule on What Has Been Set Aside:
Should cloth-money for a robe have been set aside by an unrelated householder or housewife for a particular monk,
thinking, "Having purchased a robe with this cloth-money, [let us give it] to the monk named so-and-so..."
‘I shall clothe myself. If that monk, having previously been uninvited, should approach and make a specific request regarding the robe,
saying, ‘It would be good indeed if the venerable one, having purchased such or such a robe with these robe-funds,
would clothe me,’ out of a desire for excellence, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Second Training Rule on What Is Set Aside:
Should anyone, with reference to a bhikkhu, have separate cīvara-funds set aside by two unrelated householders or housewives,
[thinking], "With these separate cīvara-funds, having purchased separate cīvaras..."
“...we shall clothe the bhikkhu named so-and-so with robes. If that bhikkhu, having previously been uninvited,
should approach them and make a choice regarding the robes, saying, “It would be well if the venerable ones,
having purchased such and such a robe with these individual robe-funds, would clothe both of us together with one,” out of a desire for something fine—
If, having accepted it, he makes use of it, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Tenth Training Rule on Kings:
If a king, a royal official, a brahmin, or a householder, with reference to a certain bhikkhu, sends a messenger...

If one should send a robe-fund with the message: "Having purchased a robe with this robe-fund, clothe the bhikkhu named so-and-so with that robe," and if that messenger, having approached that bhikkhu, should speak thus:
"Venerable sir, this robe-fund has been brought for the sake of the venerable one; may the venerable one accept it."
“a cloth purchase. That monk should say this to the messenger:
“Friends, we do not accept cloth purchases; however, we accept robes at the proper time, provided they are allowable.
If that messenger should say to that monk, “But does the Venerable One have anyone who acts as his agent? [the monk seeking a robe]...
“Monks, a monk should point out a service-provider—either a monastery attendant or a lay follower—saying:
‘This, friends, is the service-provider for the monks. If that messenger, having informed that service-provider, approaches the monk and says:
‘Venerable sir, regarding the service-provider whom the venerable one pointed out,’”
"He has been requested by me; let the venerable one approach at the proper time, and he will clothe you with a robe.
Monks, a monk who needs a robe should approach the attendant and, after two or three times, should remind and urge him, saying, "I have need of a robe, friend.
If, after reminding and urging him two or three times, he succeeds in obtaining that robe, [it is well].
If this succeeds, it is well; if it does not succeed, he should stand silently for the purpose [of obtaining] that robe for four, five, or at most six times.
If, while standing silently for the purpose for four, five, or at most six times, he succeeds in obtaining that robe, it is well; but if, striving beyond that, he obtains it...
If he should cause that robe to be produced, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
If he does not cause it to be produced, he must either go there himself or send a messenger regarding the robe-fund that was brought for him, saying:
"Venerable sirs, that robe-fund which you sent for the sake of a certain monk has not become anything for that monk."
“One experiences benefit; let the venerable ones apply themselves to their own [task], lest your own [task] be lost. This is the proper course in this matter.
The first section on the Kathina, the training rule on silk.
11. Whatever monk should have a rug made mixed with silk, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Pure Black Wool: 12.
Whatever monk should have a rug made of pure black sheep’s wool, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
The Training Rule on Two Parts (Dvebhāgasikkhāpada) 13:
When a monk is having a new rug made, two parts of pure black wool must be taken;
the third part of white wool; and the fourth part of brown wool. If a monk does not take two parts of pure black wool...
If one should have a new rug made from sheep’s wool— with one-third consisting of white wool, one-fourth consisting of dark wool, and the remainder of the natural color—
it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
This is the training rule concerning the six-year period.
14. Furthermore, when a monk has had a new rug made, it must be kept for six years.

If, before the end of six years, he should have another new rug made—whether he has disposed of the former rug or not—except by the formal authorization of the monks, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Sitting Mats (Nisīdana-saṇṭhata-sikkhāpada) 15:
Furthermore, when a monk is having a sitting mat made, he must take from the border of the old mat a piece the size of a Sugata-span for the purpose of disfiguring it.
If a monk does not take from the border of the old mat a piece the size of a Sugata-span, [he commits an offense].
If one should have a new sitting mat made, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
This is the sixteenth training rule concerning sheep’s wool.
Furthermore, if sheep’s wool should accrue to a monk while he is traveling on a journey, he who desires [to keep it]...
These may be accepted by a monk; having accepted them, they may be carried by hand for a maximum distance of three *yojanas* if there is no one else to carry them.
If he should carry them beyond that distance, even if there is no one else to carry them, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
This is the training rule concerning the washing of wool.
17. Whatever monk should have wool washed, dyed, or carded by an unrelated nun, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Rule on Gold and Silver: 18.
Whatever monk should pick up gold or silver, or cause it to be picked up, or consent to its being deposited for him, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Trading in Money (Rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpada) 19:
Whatever monk should engage in various kinds of trading in money, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Buying and Selling (Kayavikkayasikkhāpada).
20. Whatever monk should engage in various kinds of buying and selling, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The second section on silk is concluded.
The training rule on bowls.
21. An extra alms-bowl may be kept for a maximum of ten days; for one who exceeds this period, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
22. The training rule concerning bowls with less than five mends:
Whatever monk should have another new bowl made by exchange when his own bowl has fewer than five mends, [there is] an offense entailing relinquishment.
It is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya). That monk must surrender that bowl to the assembly of monks;
and whatever is the least bowl among that assembly of monks, that should be given back to that monk with the words: "Monk, this is your bowl; it is to be kept until it breaks.
This is the proper procedure in this matter.
The Twenty-third Training Rule on Medicines:
Whatever medicines are suitable for sick bhikkhus, namely— ghee,
fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses— having accepted them, one may keep them in store for a maximum of seven days.
[These] may be used; for one who exceeds that [time], it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The training rule on the rain-cloak (vassikasāṭika): 24.
“When one month of the hot season remains,” a bhikkhu should seek a rain-cloak; “when half a month [remains]...”

Thinking, "Less than one month of the hot season remains," he should put it on. If he should seek a rain-season robe thinking, "Less than one month of the hot season remains," and should put it on thinking, "Less than half a month of the hot season remains," there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
This is the training rule concerning the confiscation of robes.

25. Whatever monk, having personally given a robe to another monk, being angry and displeased, should take it back or cause it to be taken back, commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Requesting Thread: 26.
Whatever monk, having himself requested thread, should have a robe woven by weavers, commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Great Weavers’ Training Rule (Mahāpesakārasikkhāpada) 27.
If an unrelated householder or housewife, having had a robe woven by weavers for the sake of a certain monk,
should approach those weavers beforehand— without being invited— and express a specific preference regarding the robe;
He might say, "Friends, this robe-cloth is being woven for me; please make it long, wide, well-woven, well-stretched, well-scrubbed, and well-combed.
Perhaps we too might give something small to the Venerable Ones. And having spoken thus, that bhikkhu—
If one should give even a small amount, down to just a portion of alms-food, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The training rule on urgent robes (accekacīvara-sikkhāpada) 28:
When ten days remain before the full moon of the month of Kattika, if an urgent robe-offering should arise for a monk...
A monk who considers it to be an emergency may accept [food]; having accepted it, he may store it until the time for robes.
If he should store it beyond that period, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
This is the training rule concerning apprehension.
29. Now, during the rains retreat on the full moon of Kattika, if a monk is dwelling in forest lodgings that are considered risky and dangerous,
he may, if he so desires, leave one of his three robes behind in an inhabited area, provided there is some specific reason for that monk to do so.
If he should be separated from that robe-cloth, that monk may be separated from it for a maximum of six nights.
If he should remain separated from it longer than that, except by the consent of the Saṅgha, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
This is the training rule concerning what has been assigned.
30. Whatever monk, knowing that a gain intended for the Saṅgha has been dedicated, should dedicate it to himself, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The third section on bowls is concluded.
Venerable sirs, the thirty rules entailing relinquishment and confession have been recited. In this regard, I ask the venerable ones: [Are you pure in this matter?]
"Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask:
Are you pure in this matter? The venerable ones are pure in this matter; therefore they are silent. Thus do I understand it.
The offenses entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya) are concluded.
Pure Pācittiya Offenses:
Venerable sirs, these ninety-two Pācittiya rules now come up for recitation.
The Training Rule on False Speech: 1.
In speaking a deliberate lie, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Insulting Speech.
2. In regard to malicious speech, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
3. The training rule on slander:
in regard to slandering monks, there is an offense of expiation.
The Training Rule on Reciting Word-by-Word (Padasodhamma-sikkhāpada) 4:
Whichever bhikkhu, however, should cause one who is not fully ordained to recite the Dhamma word-by-word, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The First Training Rule on Sharing a Bed (Paṭhamasahaseyya-sikkhāpada).
5. Whatever monk should share a sleeping place for more than two or three nights with one who is not fully ordained, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This is the second training rule concerning sharing a sleeping place. 6.
Whatever monk should share a sleeping place with a woman, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Teaching the Dhamma (Dhammadesanā-sikkhāpada) 7:
Whatever monk should teach the Dhamma to a woman with more than five or six words, except in the presence of a discerning man, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Reporting What Has Occurred (Bhūtārocana-sikkhāpada)
8. Whatever monk should announce a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*) to one who is not fully ordained, when it is true, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This is the training rule concerning the announcement of a grave matter (*duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpada*). 9.
Whatever monk should announce a grave offense (*duṭṭhulla-āpatti*) of a monk to one who is not fully ordained, except by the authorization of the monks, there is an offense of expiation.
The Training Rule on Digging the Earth (Pathavīkhaṇana-sikkhāpada) 10:
Whatever monk should dig the earth or cause it to be dug, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The first section: On False Speech.
The Training Rule on Plant Life 11.
An offense entailing expiation for the destruction of plant life.
The Training Rule on Speaking Deceitfully.
12. In the case of one who speaks otherwise or one who harasses, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Reviling: 13.
In the case of one who reviles or one who finds fault, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The First Training Rule on Lodgings 14. Whatever monk,
having spread out or caused to be spread out a bed, a bench, a mattress, or a stool belonging to the Saṅgha in the open air,
when departing, neither puts it away nor causes it to be put away—
If he should depart without asking permission, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Fifteenth Training Rule on Lodgings:

Whichever monk, having spread out a bed or having had one spread out in a dwelling belonging to the Sangha, when departing, neither puts it away nor has it put away, or departs without asking permission, commits an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Pushing In (Anupakhajja-sikkhāpada) 16:
Whatever monk, knowing that another monk has already entered a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha,
should push his way in and make his bed there, thinking, "He who finds it crowded will depart," making this very thing his sole motive;
If it is otherwise, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The training rule on ejecting (17):
Whatever monk, being angry and displeased, should eject a monk from a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, or should cause him to be ejected, it is an offense of expiation.
The Training Rule on the Upper Story Chamber (Vehāsakuṭi-sikkhāpada) 18:
Whatever monk, in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, should sit down or lie down on a bed or bench with detachable legs on an upper story chamber, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Large Dwellings (Mahallaka-vihāra-sikkhāpada).

19. When a bhikkhu is having a large dwelling built, he must determine its extent while standing on ground that is not yet cleared, up to the door-frames, the installation of the bolts, the preparation of the window openings, and the allowance for two or three layers of roofing;
if he should determine it beyond that, even while standing on ground that is not yet cleared, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Water with Living Beings 20.
Whatever monk, knowing that water contains living beings, should pour it out or cause it to be poured out upon grass or clay, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The second section: The Chapter on Plants.
The Training Rule on Exhortation (Ovādasikkhāpada) 21:
Whatever monk, not being authorized, should exhort the nuns, it is an offense entailing expiation.
The Training Rule on Sunset (Atthaṅgatasikkhāpada).
22. If a monk, even if authorized, should exhort the bhikkhunīs after the sun has set, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

23. Whatever monk, having approached the dwelling place of the bhikkhunīs, should exhort the bhikkhunīs except on an appropriate occasion, it is an offense of expiation. Herein, this is the appropriate occasion: when a bhikkhunī is ill; this is the occasion therein.
The Training Rule on Material Gain 24:
Whatever monk should say, "The elder monks give exhortation to the nuns for the sake of material gain," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on the Giving of Robes.
25. Whatever monk should give a robe to an unrelated nun, except in exchange, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Sewing Robes: 26.
Whatever monk should sew a robe for an unrelated nun, or have it sewn, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Arrangements (Saṃvidhāna-sikkhāpada) 27:

Whatever monk, having made an arrangement with a nun, should set out on a journey along a highway, even if only as far as the next village, except at the proper time, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Herein, this is the proper time: when the road is one that must be traveled by caravan.
It is considered dangerous and fearful; this is the occasion for it.
28. Training Rule on Boarding a Boat:

Whatever monk, having made an appointment with a nun, should board the same boat—whether going upstream or downstream—with the exception of crossing over [the river] transversely, commits an offense entailing confession (*pācittiya*).
The Training Rule on What is Prepared by a Nun 29.
Whatever monk, knowing that almsfood has been prepared by a nun, should eat it—except in the case of an initial undertaking by a householder—commits an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Secluded Sitting.
30. Whatever monk should sit down in private, one-on-one, with a nun, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The third section: The Chapter on Exhortation.
The Training Rule on Lodging Alms-food.
31. A monk who is not ill may eat one meal at a public rest-house. If he should eat more than that, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

32. In eating in a group, except on an appropriate occasion, it is an offense of expiation. Herein, this is the appropriate occasion: the occasion of illness, the occasion of the distribution of robes.
The time for making robes, the time for traveling on a journey, the time for boarding a boat, the time of a great festival, and the time when alms are given to ascetics—this is the occasion there.
33. The training rule on eating in succession:

"If one eats in succession, except at the proper time, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Herein, this is the proper time: the time of illness, the time of giving robes, and the time of making robes—this is the occasion there."
The Training Rule for Kāṇamātā, 34.
If a family should invite a monk who has approached them to accept cakes or flour-mash, a monk who so desires may accept two or three bowlfuls.
If he should accept more than that, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Having accepted two or three bowlfuls, he should take them out from there and share them with the other monks; this is the proper course of action in such a case.
35. The First Invitation Training Rule:
Whatever monk, having finished his meal and being invited to stop, should eat or consume fresh or cooked food that is not left over, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Second Training Rule on Invitation (Pavāraṇā-sikkhāpada) 36:
Whatever monk should invite another monk who has already finished his meal and been invited to stop, by offering him fresh food or soft food that is not left over,
saying, "Come, monk, eat or enjoy this," knowing [the other's state] and desiring to cause offense— [this is an offense of wrong-doing].
If one has eaten, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Eating at the Wrong Time (Vikālabhojana-sikkhāpada) 37:
Whatever bhikkhu should chew or eat solid or soft food at the wrong time, it is an offense of expiation.
The Training Rule on Storing Up (Sannidhikāraka-sikkhāpada) 38.
Whatever monk should eat or consume fresh or cooked food that has been stored up, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Luxurious Food (Paṇītabhojana-sikkhāpada).

39. Now, as for those fine foods, namely: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, fish, meat, milk, and curd—whatever monk, not being ill, should have such fine foods requested for his own sake and eat them, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Tooth-Sticks (Dantapona-sikkhāpada) 40:
Whatever monk should put into his mouth as food what has not been given, except for water and tooth-sticks, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The fourth section on eating is concluded.
The Training Rule on the Naked Ascetics (Acelaka-sikkhāpada) 41:
Whatever monk should, with his own hand, give fresh or cooked food to a naked ascetic, or to a male wanderer, or to a female wanderer, it is an offense entailing expiation.
The Training Rule on Sending Away (Uyyojana-sikkhāpada).
42. Whatever monk, having said to another monk, "Come, friend, let us enter a village or town for alms," should then dismiss him—whether he has had food given to him or not—saying, "Go, friend;
conversation or sitting with you is not comfortable for me; conversation or sitting alone is comfortable for me," making this very reason his pretext: [this is an offense of expiation].
If it is otherwise, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
43. The Training Rule on Families with Food:
Whatever monk should intrude and sit down in a family where food is being served, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Secluded Concealment 44.
Whatever monk should sit down in a secluded, concealed place together with a woman, it is an offense of expiation.
The Training Rule on Sitting in Seclusion.
45. Whatever monk should sit down in private with a woman, one-on-one, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Conduct: 46.
Whatever monk, having been invited and having partaken of a meal, should go before the meal [for further food] without informing a monk who is present...
Or if she should enter among families for alms after the meal, except at the proper time, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Herein, this is the proper time: the time for giving robes and the time for making robes; this is the proper time therein.
This is the Mahānāma training rule.

47. A monk who is not ill may accept an invitation for requisites for four months, except for a renewed invitation and except for a permanent invitation. Should he accept it for longer than that, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Troops on March (Uyyutta-senā-sikkhāpada): 48.
Whatever monk should go to see an army on march, except for a legitimate reason, it is an offense entailing expiation.
The Training Rule on Military Camps (Senāvāsa-sikkhāpada) 49.

If there should arise for that bhikkhu some reason to go to the army, he may stay with the army for two or three nights. If he should stay longer than that, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Battles (Uyyodhika-sikkhāpada)

50. If a bhikkhu, while staying with an army for two or three nights, should go to a military review, a mustering of troops, a battle array, or to see a regiment, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The fifth section, on the Naked Ascetics.
The training rule on drinking fermented liquor.
51. In drinking fermented liquor and spirits, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
52. The training rule concerning poking with the finger:
in poking with the finger, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Joking in Water (No. 53):
An offense entailing confession for joking in water.
The Training Rule on Disrespect.
54. In case of disrespect, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
55. The training rule on frightening:
Whatever monk should frighten another monk, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Fire (Jotisikkhāpada) 56:
Whatever monk, not being ill, should kindle a fire or have one kindled for the purpose of warming himself, except when there is a legitimate reason, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Bathing (Nahānasikkhāpada).
57. Whatever monk should bathe within half a month, except at the proper time, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya). Herein, this is the proper time:

"One month and a half remains of the hot season," and "the first month of the rainy season"—these two and a half months are the time of heat, the time of feverish distress, the time of illness, the time of work, the time of traveling on a journey, and the time of wind and rain; this is the proper time therein.
The Training Rule on Making Discolored: 58.
When a monk obtains a new robe, he must apply one of the three methods for making it discolored:
either blue, mud-color, or dark brown. If a monk does not apply one of the three methods for making it discolored...
If one should use a new robe that has been made discolored [by dye], it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Designation (Vikappana-sikkhāpada) 59:

Whatever monk, having personally designated a robe to a monk, a nun, a trainee nun (sikkhamānā), a male novice (sāmaṇera), or a female novice (sāmaṇerī), should use it without having had the designation rescinded, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Taking Away (Apanidhāna-sikkhāpada) 60:

Whatever monk should take away, or cause to be taken away, from a monk his bowl, or robe, or sitting mat, or needle case, or waistband—even if only in jest—it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The sixth section, the Chapter on Drinking Alcohol (Surāpāna-vagga), is concluded.
The Training Rule on Intentional Killing (Sañcicca-sikkhāpada) 61:
Whatever monk should intentionally deprive a living being of life, there is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Water Containing Living Beings (Sappāṇaka-sikkhāpada).
62. Whatever monk, knowing that water contains living beings, should consume it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

63. Whatever monk, knowing that a legal case has been settled in accordance with the Dhamma, should reopen it for a further formal act, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). This is the training rule on reopening (ukkoṭana-sikkhāpada).
The Training Rule on Grave Offenses 64:
Whatever bhikkhu should knowingly conceal a grave offense of another bhikkhu, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Those Under Twenty Years of Age.

65. Whatever monk, knowing that a person is less than twenty years of age, should ordain him, that person is not ordained and those monks are to be censured; this is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) in that case.
The Training Rule on Traveling with a Band of Thieves: 66.
Whatever monk, knowing it to be a band of thieves, should travel along a highway in their company by appointment, even as far as the interval between villages, there is an offense of expiation.
The Training Rule on Arranging Travel (Saṃvidhāna-sikkhāpada) 67:
Whatever monk, having made an arrangement with a woman, should set out on a journey along a highway, even if only for as far as the next village, incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Ariṭṭha.

68. Furthermore, if a bhikkhu should speak thus: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called ‘obstructive states’ by the Blessed One are not sufficient to obstruct one who indulges in them,” that bhikkhu should be addressed by the bhikkhus thus:
“Do not, Venerable Sir, speak thus; do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not so.”
"It is a slander against the Blessed One; for the Blessed One would not speak thus.
In many ways, friends, the Blessed One has stated that obstructive things are indeed obstructive, and they are sufficient to create an obstacle for one who indulges in them.
If, when being addressed by the monks in this way, that monk should persist as before, that monk [should be dealt with] by the monks up to the third time...
He should be exhorted to relinquish it. If, being exhorted up to three times, he should relinquish it, that is good.
If he does not relinquish it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This is the training rule concerning association with one who has been suspended (ukkhitto).

69. Whatever monk, knowing that a monk speaks thus, has not acted in accordance with the Dhamma, and has not relinquished that view, should eat together with him, live in association with him, or share a sleeping place with him, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This is the Kaṇṭaka training rule. 70.
If even a novice (samaṇuddesa) should speak thus: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, just as...”

"Those things declared by the Blessed One to be obstructive are not actually obstructive for one who indulges in them"—that novice monk should be addressed by the monks as follows: "Friend, novice, do not speak thus;
do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not speak in such a way. Friend, in many ways..."
“Novice, the obstructive states have been declared by the Blessed One to be obstructive; they are indeed sufficient to constitute an obstruction for one who indulges in them.
If that novice, being thus addressed by the monks, should still persist in the same way, that novice is to be addressed by the monks as follows:
“From this day forward, friend novice, you are no longer [to be considered a member of our community].”
"Thus that Blessed One, the Teacher, should be pointed out to you:
'Even that which other novice monks receive—namely, sharing a sleeping place with the bhikkhus for two or three nights—that you do not have; go away, fare along, and perish!
Furthermore, whichever bhikkhu, knowing that a novice has been thus dismissed, should support him, attend to him, or eat together with him...
Or if he should lie down together with him, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The seventh section: On Water Containing Living Beings.
The Training Rule on Fellow Practitioners.
71. Whatever monk, being addressed with what is in accordance with the Dhamma by other monks, should say:
"Friends, I will not train in this training rule until I have consulted another monk who is experienced and a master of the Vinaya," incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Monks, a monk who is training must understand, consult, and inquire; this is the proper course in such a case.
The Training Rule on Carping (Vilekhana-sikkhāpada) 72:
Whatever monk, while the Pātimokkha is being recited, should speak thus: “What is the use of these minor and lesser training rules being recited?
They lead only to remorse, vexation, and carping,” he commits an offense of expiation for disparaging the training rules.
The Training Rule on Delusion 73.
Whatever monk, while the Pātimokkha is being recited every half-month, should speak thus:
"Only now do I know that this rule, it seems, has come down in the Sutta, is included in the Sutta, and is recited every half-month."

“If other monks should know that this monk has previously sat [in the assembly] two or three times while the Pātimokkha was being recited— not to mention more than that— there can be no exemption for that monk on the grounds of ignorance;
and whatever offense he has committed therein, he must be dealt with according to the Dhamma.”
Furthermore, he should be made to acknowledge his delusion by saying: "It is a loss for you, friend;
it is ill-gotten for you, that when the Pātimokkha is being recited, you do not pay careful attention with thorough intentness. This is the offense of expiation (pācittiya) regarding that deluding.
The training rule on striking.
74. Whatever monk, being angry and displeased with another monk, should give him a blow, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
This is the training rule concerning the palm-strike. 75.
Whatever monk, being angry and displeased with another monk, should raise his hand as if to strike him, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Rootless Training Rule 76:
Whatever monk should groundlessly charge another monk with a *saṅghādisesa* offense, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
The Intentional Training Rule.

77. Whatever monk should intentionally cause remorse in a monk, thinking, "Let him be uncomfortable for even a moment," making this alone the reason and no other, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Eavesdropping (Upassuti-sikkhāpada): 78.

Whatever monk should stand eavesdropping upon monks who have fallen into quarreling, brawling, or dispute, thinking, "I will hear what they say," making this alone the reason and no other, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Obstructing Formal Acts (Kammappaṭibāhana-sikkhāpada) 79.
Whatever monk, having given his consent for formal acts that are in accordance with the Dhamma, should afterwards engage in criticism, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Not Going After Having Given Consent.

80. Whatever monk, while a formal discussion of a legal matter is being conducted in the Saṅgha, should rise from his seat and depart without having given his consent, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This is the rule concerning weakness. 81.

Whatever monk, after a robe has been assigned by a unanimous Saṅgha, should subsequently fall into a state of disparagement, saying, "The monks are diverting the gains belonging to the Saṅgha according to their personal friendships," it is an offense of expiation.
The Training Rule on Diversion, 82:
Whatever monk, knowing that a gain intended for the Saṅgha has been diverted, should divert it to an individual, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The eighth section: On Those in Accordance with the Dhamma.
The Training Rule on the Inner Palace (Antepura-sikkhāpada) 83:

Should any bhikkhu, without prior notification, cross the threshold (indakhīla) of a consecrated Khattiya king while the king has not yet departed and the regalia have not yet been removed, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on the Regalia (Ratana-sikkhāpada).
84. Whatever monk should pick up or cause to be picked up a jewel or what is considered a jewel, except within a monastery or within a dwelling, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

Furthermore, whatever jewel or what is considered a jewel has been picked up or caused to be picked up by a monk within a monastery or within a dwelling, it should be deposited [with the thought]: "To whom..."
"He will be there; he will take it"—this is the proper course in that regard.

85. As for any bhikkhu who, without having asked permission from a bhikkhu who is present, enters a village at an improper time, except when there is such an urgent business to be done, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on the Needle Case (Sūcighara-sikkhāpada) 86:
Whichever bhikkhu should have a needle case made of bone, ivory, or horn, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya) involving breaking [the object].
The Training Rule on Beds and Chairs (Mañcapīṭha-sikkhāpada).

87. When a monk is having a new bed or bench made, it should be made with legs eight finger-breadths long according to the Sugata-finger, except for the lower crossbar. For one who exceeds this measurement, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting down. 88.
Whatever monk should have a bed or a bench made upholstered with cotton-wool, there is an offense of expiation involving tearing it out.
The Training Rule on the Sitting Mat (Nisīdana-sikkhāpada) 89.
Furthermore, when a monk is having a sitting mat made, it should be made according to the proper measure. Herein, this is the measure:
two spans of the Sugata-span in length, one and a half spans across, and a fringe of one span. For one who exceeds these [measurements], there is an offense.
The offense of expiation involving cutting off.
The training rule on the itch-covering cloth (90):
Now, when a monk is having an itch-covering cloth made, it must be made according to the proper measure; this is the measure:
It is four spans long by two spans wide according to the Sugata’s span. For one who exceeds these measurements, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting.
This is the training rule concerning the rain-cloak.
91. Furthermore, when a monk is having a rain-cloak made, it must be made according to the proper measure. Herein, this is the measure:
six spans of the Sugata-span in length, and two and a half spans across. For one who exceeds this, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting down.
This is the training rule concerning Nanda.
92. Whatever monk should have a robe made to the measure of the Sugata’s robe, or exceeding it, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting down.
Herein, this is the measure of the Sugata’s robe for the Sugata: nine spans of the Sugata’s span in length, and six spans across; this is the measure of the Sugata’s robe for the Sugata.
The ninth chapter, on Jewels, is concluded.
Venerable sirs, the ninety-two *pācittiya* rules have been recited. Therefore, I ask the venerable ones:
Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this matter?
"You are pure; the venerable ones here are pure, therefore they are silent. Thus do I understand this.
The offenses entailing expiation (pācittiya) are concluded. The offenses entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
Venerable sirs, these four rules on offenses entailing confession now come up for recitation.
The first rule on training regarding offenses entailing confession:

1. Whatever bhikkhu, having with his own hand accepted fresh or cooked food from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī who has entered an inhabited area, should eat or consume it, that bhikkhu must confess:
"Friend, I have fallen into a blameworthy state, unbecoming and to be confessed; I confess it."
The Second Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule:
When monks are eating after being invited into families, if that nun stands there seeking an opportunity,
saying, “Give curry here, give rice there,” those monks should dismiss that nun.
“Step aside for a moment, sister, until the monks have finished eating.
If not even a single monk should feel inclined to dismiss that nun by saying, “Step aside for a moment, sister, until the monks have finished eating,” then those monks must confess:
“Friends, we have committed an offense that is blameworthy, unsuitable, and entailing confession; we confess it.”
The Third Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule: Now,
regarding those families designated as "trainee" (sekkha), whichever monk,
being not ill and not previously invited, should with his own hand accept either fresh food or soft food from such families designated as "trainee"— [he commits an offense].
If he should chew it or eat it, that bhikkhu must confess: "Friend, I have fallen into a blameworthy, unsuitable offense entailing confession; I confess it.
This is the fourth training rule on offenses entailing confession.
4. Furthermore, regarding those forest lodgings that are considered risky and dangerous:

if a monk, in such lodgings, having previously received no invitation, should with his own hand accept fresh or cooked food within the monastery and, being not ill, eat or consume it, he must confess it.
That monk should say: "Friends, I have committed an offense that is censurable, unseemly, and one requiring confession;
I confess it. Venerable sirs, the four rules requiring confession have been recited. Therefore, I ask the venerable ones:
Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this matter?
"Venerable sirs, you are pure in this matter; therefore, you are silent. Thus do I understand it.
The *Pāṭidesanīya* rules are concluded. Now, the *Sekhiya* rules.
Venerable sirs, these rules of training (sekhiya-dhamma) now come up for recitation.
1. The training rule on being well-rounded: "I shall wear my lower robe so as to be well-rounded"—this is the training to be observed.
2. "I shall wear my upper robe evenly all around"—this training is to be observed.
3. The training rule on being well-covered:
"I shall walk in inhabited areas well-covered"—this training is to be observed.
4. The training is to be observed: "I shall sit well-covered within an inhabited area.
5. The training rule on being well-restrained:
The training is to be observed: "I shall walk well-restrained within an inhabited area."
6. "I shall sit well-restrained in inhabited areas"—this training is to be observed.
7. The training rule on downcast eyes:
"I shall walk with downcast eyes in inhabited areas"—this training is to be observed.
8. "I shall sit with eyes cast down within an inhabited area"—this training is to be observed. 9.
"I shall not walk with my body held high within an inhabited area"—this training is to be observed.
10. The training is to be observed: "I shall not sit with my body raised up inside an inhabited area.
This concludes the first section on the full circle, the training rule concerning loud laughter.
11. "I shall not go among the houses laughing loudly"—this training is to be observed. 12.
"I shall not sit among the houses laughing loudly"—this training is to be observed.
[The Training Rule on Loud Noise.]
13. The training is to be observed: "I will go among the houses making little noise. 14.
The training is to be observed: "I will sit among the houses making little noise.
The training rule concerning the swaying of the body.
15. The training is to be observed: "I will not walk about shaking my body while inside a house. 16.
The training is to be observed: "I will not sit down shaking my body while inside a house.
The training rule concerning shaking the arms.
17. The training is to be observed: "I will not walk about inside a dwelling while swinging my arms.
18. The training is to be observed: "I will not sit down inside a dwelling while swinging my arms. The training rule concerning the swaying of the head.
19. "I shall not walk about inside a dwelling shaking my head"—this training is to be observed.
20. "I shall not sit down inside a dwelling shaking my head"—this training is to be observed.
The second section: On Laughing Loudly.
21. The training rule concerning leaning on a hand:
"I shall not walk through an inhabited area leaning on a hand"—this training is to be observed. 22.
The training rule concerning leaning on a hand: "I shall not sit down in an inhabited area leaning on a hand"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on the Veiled Head: 23.
"I will not go among the houses with my head veiled"—this training rule is to be observed. 24.
"I will not sit among the houses with my head veiled"—this training rule is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Crouching: 25.
"I shall not walk with crouched posture among the houses," this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on the Crossed Ankles.
26. "I shall not sit down in an inhabited area in a squatting posture," this training is to be observed.
27. "I shall receive almsfood attentively," this training is to be observed. This is the training rule on receiving with care.
The Training Rule on Being Mindful of the Alms Bowl (28):
"I shall receive alms food being mindful of the bowl"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Receiving an Equal Amount of Curry.
29. The training is to be observed: "I will receive almsfood with equal amounts of curry.
30. The training rule on the level brim:
The training is to be observed: "I will receive almsfood up to the level of the brim."
The third chapter, on the Section on Propping Up [the Bowl]. Training Rule 31:
"I shall eat almsfood attentively"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Being Mindful of the Alms Bowl (32):
"I shall eat almsfood being mindful of the bowl"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Successive Order.
33. The training is to be observed: "I shall eat almsfood by going from house to house in regular order.
34. The training rule on equal curry:
The training is to be observed: "I shall eat almsfood with equal curry."
The Training Rule on Mounds: 35.
The training is to be observed: "I shall not eat almsfood by pressing it down from a mound.
The Training Rule on Covering the Rice.
36. "I shall not cover curry or sauce with rice out of a desire for more," this is a training to be observed.
This is the training rule regarding the solicitation of curry and rice. 37.
"Being not ill, I shall not eat curry or rice that I have had requested for my own sake," this is a training to be observed.
The Training Rule on Perceiving Fault: 38.
The training is to be observed thus: "I shall not look at the alms-bowl of others with a critical mind.
The Training Rule on Mouthfuls.
39. The training is to be observed: "I shall make the mouthful not too large. This is the training rule on mouthfuls (ālopa).
40. The training is to be observed:
"I shall make the mouthful round. This is the training rule on mouthfuls.
The fourth chapter, on Thoroughness, is concluded.
Training Rule 41:
The training is to be observed thus: "I shall not open my mouth while a morsel of food has not yet been brought to it."
The Training Rule on Eating (Sikkhāpada 42):
While eating, one should observe the training rule: "I will not put my whole hand into my mouth. The Training Rule on Having a Mouthful (Sakabaḷa-sikkhāpada).
43. The training is to be observed: "I shall not speak with food in my mouth.
The Training Rule on Throwing Lumps of Food: 44.
The training is to be observed: "I shall not eat by throwing lumps of food."
The Training Rule on Breaking Up Mouthfuls (45):
"I shall not eat by breaking up mouthfuls"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Cheek-Filling.
46. The training is to be observed: "I shall not eat stuffing out my cheeks.
The Training Rule on Shaking the Hand: 47.
The training is to be observed: "I shall not eat shaking my hand."
The Training Rule on Scattering Grains: 48.
The training is to be observed: "I shall not eat scattering grains.
The Training Rule on Protruding the Tongue.
49. The training is to be observed: "I shall not eat with the tongue protruding.
The training rule on making the *capucapu* sound: 50.
The training is to be observed: "I shall not eat making the *capucapu* sound."
The fifth chapter on mouthfuls.
Training rule 51: "I shall not eat making a 'suru-suru' sound"—this training is to be observed.
Training Rule 52: "I shall not lick my hands"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Licking the Bowl.
53. The training is to be observed: "I shall not eat licking the bowl.
54. The training rule on licking the lips:
The training is to be observed: "I shall not eat licking the lips."
The Training Rule on What is Contaminated with Food (Sāmiṣa-sikkhāpada) 55: "I shall not receive a water vessel with a hand that has food on it"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Having Rice (Sasitthaka-sikkhāpada).
56. The training is to be observed: "I shall not discard bowl-washing water containing rice within an inhabited area.
The Training Rule on the Umbrella-Bearer: 57.
The training is to be observed: "I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who holds an umbrella in their hand, unless they are ill."
The Training Rule on One Carrying a Staff (58):
"I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who is not ill and is carrying a staff"—this is the training to be observed.
The Training Rule on One Carrying a Sword.
59. "I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who has a weapon in hand, unless they are ill"—this training is to be observed.
60. "I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who has a weapon in hand, unless they are ill"—this training is to be observed. (The Training Rule on One with a Weapon in Hand)
The Sixth Chapter:
The Surusuru Group. Training Rule 61:
"I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who has put on sandals and is not ill"—this is a training to be observed.
The Training Rule on Sandals (Upāhana-sikkhāpada) 62:
"I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who is wearing sandals and is not ill"—this is the training to be observed.
The Training Rule on Vehicles (Yāna-sikkhāpada).
63. The training is to be observed: "I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who is seated in a vehicle and is not ill.
64. The training rule on reclining:
The training is to be observed: "I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who is reclining and is not ill."
Training Rule 65:
"I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who is sitting with their arms wrapped around their knees unless they are ill"—this is the training to be observed.
The Training Rule on the Veiled Head.
66. "I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who has their head wrapped up, unless they are ill"—this training is to be observed. 67.
"I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who has their head covered, unless they are ill"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on the Ground (Chamāsikkhāpada) 68:
"I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who is seated on a seat while I am sitting on the ground, unless I am ill"—this is the training to be observed.
The Training Rule on Low Seats (Nīcāsanasikkhāpada).
69. "I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who is seated on a high seat while I am seated on a low seat, unless I am ill"—this training is to be observed.
70. Standing Precept:
"I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who is seated while I am standing, unless I am ill"—this training is to be observed.
The training rule on walking behind:
"I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who is not ill while walking behind them as they walk in front"—this is the training to be observed.
The training rule on walking on a bypath.
72. "I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who is walking on the path while I am walking off the path, unless I am ill"—this training is to be observed. 73.
"I shall not, while standing and not being ill, discharge feces or urine"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Excrement in Green Vegetation 74.
"I shall not discharge feces, urine, or spittle upon green vegetation unless I am ill"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Excrement in Water.
75. "I shall not, when not ill, defecate, urinate, or spit in water"—this training is to be observed.
This is the seventh section on sandals.
Venerable friends, the rules of training (sekhiya-dhamma) have been recited. Therefore, I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter?
A second time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this matter?
You are pure in this matter, friends, therefore you are silent; thus do I understand it.
The training rules (sekhiyas) are concluded.
The Settling of Legal Matters:
Venerable sirs, these seven principles for the settling of legal matters now come up for recitation.
For the settling and pacification of legal issues as they arise, the resolution face-to-face (sammukhāvinaya) should be granted;
the resolution through mindfulness (sativinaya) should be granted; the resolution for one who is no longer deluded (amūḷhavinaya) should be granted.
It should be dealt with by confession;
by a majority decision;
by a formal act of further penalty.
"Covering over as with grass":
Venerable sirs, the seven principles for the settlement of legal issues have been recited. Regarding these, I ask the venerable ones:
Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this matter?
"You are pure, venerable sirs; you are pure in this matter, therefore you are silent. Thus do I understand it.
The methods for settling legal issues are concluded.
Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited.
The four Pārājika rules have been recited;
the thirteen Saṅghādisesa rules have been recited;
the two Aniyata rules have been recited.
The thirty *nissaggiya pācittiya* rules have been recited;
the ninety-two *pācittiya* rules have been recited;
the four *pāṭidesanīya* rules have been recited.
The rules of training (sekhiya-dhamma) have been recited;

the seven principles for settling legal issues (adhikaraṇa-samatha-dhamma) have been recited. This much of the Blessed One’s teaching, which has come down in the Suttas and is included within the Suttas, comes up for recitation every half-month.
In this regard, all should train together, being harmonious, friendly, and without dispute.
The fifth section, the detailed exposition, is concluded.
The Bhikkhu Pātimokkha is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha Text:
Preliminary Duties—
4 A broom, a lamp, water, and a seat;
These are called the "preliminary duties" (*pubbakaraṇa*) for the uposatha.
The preliminary tasks (*pubbakicca*) are:
the motion for consent (*chanda*), the declaration of purity (*pārisuddhi*), the announcement of the season (*utukkhaṇa*), the counting of the number of bhikkhus, and the exhortation (*ovāda*).
These are called the "preliminary duties" for the Uposatha.
Regarding the factors of the proper time:
the Uposatha and as many bhikkhunīs as have attained the status for formal acts (kamma).
There are no common offenses present, nor are there persons who ought to be excluded; therefore, it is said to be "the proper time.
Having completed the preliminary duties and preliminary tasks, with the consent of the harmonious community of nuns whose offenses have been confessed, we perform the act of reciting the Pātimokkha.

The Recitation of the Introduction: Let the Noble Saṅgha listen to me. Today is the Uposatha of the fifteenth day. If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha.
What is the preliminary duty for the Saṅgha? Noble ladies, announce your purity; I shall recite the Pātimokkha.
Let all of us, being present, listen well and attend closely. Whatever offense any of you may have, let her disclose it;
for one who has no offense, silence must be maintained. By your silence, friends, I shall know that you are pure.
Just as there is an answer when one is questioned individually, so too, in an assembly such as this, [the matter is established] up to the third time.
It has been announced. Now, whatever nun, when it has been announced up to the third time, should knowingly fail to disclose an existing offense, she commits an intentional falsehood.

Sisters, intentional falsehood has been called by the Blessed One an obstructive state; therefore, for a nun who remembers [an offense], having fallen into it and desiring purification, there being an existing...
An offense must be disclosed; for once it is disclosed, she finds ease.
Sisters, the introduction has been recited. Therefore, sisters, I ask you: Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask:
Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? You are pure in this matter, sisters.
"Therefore, be silent; thus do I hold this.
The Introduction is concluded.
The Exposition of the Defeats (Pārājika).
Therein, these eight *pārājika* rules come up for recitation.
The training rule on sexual intercourse (1):
Whatever nun should intentionally engage in sexual intercourse, even with an animal, she is *pārājika*, one who is no longer in communion.
The Training Rule on Taking What Is Not Given (2):

Whatever bhikkhunī should take from a village or from a forest what is not given, in such a manner of taking what is not given that kings, having seized a thief, would execute him, imprison him, or banish him, saying, "You are a thief! You are a fool! [that bhikkhunī is also to be dealt with according to the rule].
“You were deluded at that time,” [if she says this], a bhikkhunī who takes what is not given in such a manner is also defeated and no longer in communion.
3. The Training Rule on Human Beings:
Whatever bhikkhunī should intentionally deprive a human being of life, or provide him with a weapon—
If she should seek [to kill him], or praise the beauty of death, or incite him toward death, saying, "O man,
what is the use of this wretched, miserable life for you? Death is better for you than life," and thus, with a mind that is displeased and a thought of death,
should in many ways praise the beauty of death or incite him toward death— this too is a *pārājika* offense, and she is no longer in communion.
The Training Rule on Superhuman States (Uttarimanussadhamma-sikkhāpada) 4:
Whatever nun, however, being without direct knowledge, should claim for herself a superhuman state— a noble knowledge and vision worthy of the Ariyans—
saying, "Thus I know, thus I see," and who, at a later time, being questioned about it...
Or, if she has committed an offense and, when being interrogated or not being interrogated, while desiring purification, should say: "Venerable lady, not knowing, I said that I know;
not seeing, I said that I see; I have spoken what is empty and false," except out of overestimation, she too is defeated and no longer in communion.
This is the training rule concerning those who sit with their knees raised above the ground.

5. Whatever nun, being lustful, should consent to being touched, stroked, grasped, contacted, or pressed against below the collarbone and above the knees by a lustful man—she too is defeated and no longer in communion;
this is the offense regarding what is above the knees.
The Training Rule on Concealing a Transgression (Vajjappaṭicchādikā-sikkhāpada) 6:
Whatever nun, knowing that another nun has committed an offense entailing defeat (pārājika),

neither confesses it herself nor reports it to the community, and subsequently— when that nun has been suspended, deceased, expelled, or has left the order— [is found to have concealed it], [she commits an offense].

If she should say: "Noble lady, even before, I already knew of this bhikkhunī that 'this sister is such-and-such and such-and-such,' yet I did not reproach her myself nor inform the Saṅgha," she too is one who has committed a pārājika offense,
one who is no longer in communion, a concealer of a fault.
The Training Rule on Following One Who Has Been Suspended (Ukkhittānuvattikā-sikkhāpada) 7:
Whatever bhikkhunī should follow a bhikkhu who has been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction—
being disrespectful, unrepentant, and having failed to seek assistance— that bhikkhunī should be addressed thus by the bhikkhunīs:
She should be told: "Venerable lady, this bhikkhu has been expelled by a united Saṅgha in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction;
he is disrespectful, unrepentant, and has not made amends. Venerable lady, do not follow this bhikkhu.
If that bhikkhunī, being thus addressed by the bhikkhunīs, should persist as before, that bhikkhunī is to be formally admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times.
