If she should relinquish it upon being exhorted up to the third time, that is good;
if she should not relinquish it, she too is defeated and excluded from the community as one who follows a suspended nun.
This is the training rule concerning the eight points.
8. Whatever nun, being lustful, should consent to taking hold of the hand of a lustful man,
or should consent to taking hold of the corner of his outer robe, or should stand together with him, or converse with him, or go to a rendezvous,
or should consent to a man coming to her, or should enter a concealed place, or [expose] her body for that purpose— [this is an offense entailing a formal meeting of the Saṅgha].
If she should provide [anything] for the purpose of practicing this unrighteousness, she too is defeated (pārājika) and excluded from the community;
these are the eight grounds. Sisters, the eight pārājika rules have been recited.
Having committed any one of them, a bhikkhunī does not obtain communion with the bhikkhunīs as she did before; thus she is, after that, defeated (pārājika).
"He is one with whom there is no communal living. In this matter, venerable ladies, I ask you: Are you pure in this? A second time I ask:
Are you pure in this? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this? You are pure in this, venerable ladies, therefore you are silent;
thus do I understand it."
The Pārājika section is finished.
The recitation of the Saṅghādisesa rules:
Venerable ladies, these seventeen Saṅghādisesa rules are as follows.
The Dhamma comes up for recitation.
The training rule on litigiousness, number one:
Whatever bhikkhunī should live litigiously with a householder, a householder’s son, or a slave...

Whether by a slave, a servant, or even by a wandering ascetic or a paribbājaka— if she ordains such a person, this nun too has committed an offense that entails immediate defeat, a *saṅghādisesa* offense involving banishment.
This is the training rule concerning one who ordains a thief.
2. Whatever nun, knowing that a female thief has been sentenced to death and is publicly known, should ordain her— without having obtained permission from the king,
or the Saṅgha, or a group, or a guild, or a clan— except in a case of incapacity, this nun too has committed an offense that is an immediate offense,
a *saṅghādisesa*, which entails being sent away.
The Training Rule on Going to Another Village Alone (3).
Whatever bhikkhunī should go to another village alone, or should go to the other side of a river alone,
or should stay apart at night alone, or should be left behind from the group alone— this bhikkhunī also incurs an offense entailing immediate confession.
[This is] an offense involving a legal issue that must be brought to an end, a *saṅghādisesa*.
The training rule on reinstating one who has been suspended: 4.
Whatever nun, however, [should knowingly] associate with a nun who has been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction...
If she should ordain a woman without having obtained the consent of the Sangha of nuns who performed the formal act, and without knowing the will of the assembly,
this nun too has committed an offense that is an immediate transgression,
a *saṅghādisesa* involving expulsion. This is the first training rule concerning the acceptance of food.

5. Whatever bhikkhunī, being lustful, should with her own hand accept fresh or cooked food from the hand of a lustful man and then eat it or consume it, this bhikkhunī too has committed an offense that is an immediate offense,
a *saṅghādisesa*, which entails formal meeting and removal.
The Second Training Rule on Receiving Food: 6.

Whatever nun should speak thus: "What will this man do for you, noble lady, whether he be lustful or free from lust, since you yourself are free from lust? Come now, noble lady, accept whatever this man gives you."
“Whether it be solid food or soft food, having accepted it with your own hand, eat or consume it”—
this too is an offense for a bhikkhunī that is an immediate offense, a *saṅghādisesa* involving expulsion.
This is the training rule on matchmaking (*sañcaritta*).
7. Whatever bhikkhunī should act as a go-between— conveying a man’s intention to a woman, or a woman’s intention to a man,
whether for marriage or for a lover, even if only for a moment— that bhikkhunī too has committed an offense that is an immediate offense, a *saṅghādisesa* involving expulsion.
The Training Rule on Malice (Duṭṭhadosasikkhāpada) 8:
Whatever nun, being malicious, hateful, and displeased, should groundlessly accuse another nun of an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika),
thinking, "Perhaps I might cause her to fall away from this holy life," and if at a later time—
Whether she is being interrogated or not being interrogated, if that legal issue is found to be groundless and the nun maintains her fault,
this nun too has committed an offense that is an immediate offense, a *saṅghādisesa* involving expulsion.
This is the training rule concerning matters belonging to another case.
9. Whatever nun, being angry, resentful, and displeased with another nun, should— on account of some minor matter or mere pretext arising from a legal issue belonging to a different category—
accuse her of an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*), thinking,
"Perhaps I might cause her to fall away from this holy life," and if, at a later time, she is either questioned or not questioned about it:
Or if that legal issue belongs to a different category, yet some slight portion of it has been taken up,
and the nun maintains her position of fault— this nun too has committed an offense that is an immediate transgression,
a *saṅghādisesa* involving expulsion. This is the training rule concerning the renunciation of the training.
10. Whatever nun, being angry and displeased, should speak thus: “I renounce the Buddha; I renounce the Dhamma; I renounce the Saṅgha;
I renounce the training. What indeed have these nuns to do with the Sakyan daughters?
There are other nuns who are modest, conscientious, and desirous of training; to them I [shall go].”
“I shall lead the holy life in his presence. That bhikkhunī should be addressed by the other bhikkhunīs thus:
“Noble lady, do not speak thus in anger and displeasure, saying: ‘I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dhamma, I renounce the Saṅgha, I renounce the training;
what indeed are these ascetics, these daughters of the Sakyans?’”
‘There are other nuns who are peaceful, modest, conscientious, and desirous of training; in their presence I shall lead the holy life.
‘Rejoice, sister; the Dhamma is well-expounded. Lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.
If that nun, being thus addressed by the nuns, should persist as before, that nun [is to be dealt with] by the nuns...
She is to be admonished up to three times for the relinquishing of that [action].

If, being admonished up to three times, she relinquishes it, that is good; if she does not relinquish it, this nun too has committed an offense that is to be confessed after the third time, a *saṅghādisesa* which entails formal meeting and sending away from the community.
The Training Rule concerning Anger over a Legal Case (Adhikaraṇakupita-sikkhāpada): 11.
Whatever nun, being accused in any legal matter, being angry and displeased, should speak thus:
"The nuns act out of favoritism; the nuns act out of hatred; the nuns act out of delusion."

‘The bhikkhunīs act out of favoritism; the bhikkhunīs act out of ill will; the bhikkhunīs act out of delusion; the bhikkhunīs act out of fear. If that bhikkhunī has been rebuked by the bhikkhunīs in this way, she should be addressed by them thus:
‘Venerable lady, do not speak thus when you have been dealt with in some legal matter, being angry, displeased, and resentful:
“The bhikkhunīs act out of favoritism; the bhikkhunīs act out of ill will; the bhikkhunīs act out of delusion; the bhikkhunīs act out of fear.”’”
“...and the bhikkhunīs,” [she says]. “Noble ladies, she might go out of favoritism, she might go out of ill-will, she might go out of delusion, or she might go out of fear.

If that bhikkhunī, being thus addressed by the bhikkhunīs, should persist as before, that bhikkhunī is to be formally admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that [position]. And if, up to three times...
If, being thus admonished, she should relinquish it, that is well;
if she should not relinquish it, this nun also has committed an offense that is to be dealt with at the third [admonition], a *saṅghādisesa* offense involving expulsion.
This is the first training rule regarding evil conduct.

12. Now, if bhikkhunīs live in association, of evil conduct, of evil reputation, of evil fame, causing vexation to the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs, and concealing each other’s faults, those bhikkhunīs should be addressed by the bhikkhunīs thus:
“Sisters, you indeed live in association, of evil conduct, of evil reputation, of evil fame, causing vexation to the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs...”
“O Noble Ladies, you are quarrelsome and conceal each other’s faults; separate yourselves! The Saṅgha praises seclusion for sisters.

If those bhikkhunīs, being thus addressed by the bhikkhunīs, should persist in that very same way, those bhikkhunīs are to be formally admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that behavior. And if, up to three times...
If, being thus admonished, they should relinquish it, that is well;
but if they do not relinquish it, these bhikkhunīs too have committed an offense entailing a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), which involves expulsion, after a third [admonition].
This is the second training rule concerning evil conduct.
13. Whatever nun should speak thus: "Venerable ladies, you should live in association;

do not live apart. There are other nuns in the Saṅgha who are of such conduct, such speech, and such behavior, who harass the community of nuns and conceal each other’s faults, yet the Saṅgha says nothing to them;
it is only to you that the Saṅgha [says something]. [She commits an offense.]
Out of contempt, disdain, impatience, talkativeness, and weakness, she spoke thus: “Sisters, you live in close association;
you are of evil conduct, of evil reputation, and of evil fame; you harass the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs and conceal each other’s faults.
Separate yourselves, noble ladies! The Saṅgha praises seclusion for the sisters. She—
A bhikkhunī should be addressed by the bhikkhunīs thus: "Venerable lady, do not speak thus;

Venerable lady, you should dwell in association, do not dwell apart. There are other bhikkhunīs in the Saṅgha who are of such conduct, such speech, and such behavior, who cause trouble for the bhikkhunī-saṅgha and conceal each other’s faults; the Saṅgha [deals with] them..."
She said nothing; it was you yourselves whom the Saṅgha spoke thus out of contempt, disparagement, impatience, gossip, and weakness:
“Sisters, you live in close association, of evil conduct, of evil reputation, of evil fame, harassers of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, and concealers of each other’s faults.
Withdraw, noble ladies; the Saṅgha requires seclusion for the sisters.”

‘...praises it. And if that bhikkhunī, being thus addressed by the bhikkhunīs, should still persist in her position, that bhikkhunī is to be formally admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that [position].

If, being admonished up to three times, she relinquishes it, that is good; if she does not relinquish it, this bhikkhunī also [commits] an offense involving formal meeting up to the third time (yāvatatiyaka).
An offense entailing a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa) that must be confessed and removed from which one has fallen.
Rule 14 on causing a schism in the Saṅgha:
Whatever nun should strive for the sake of a schism in a harmonious Saṅgha, or should act in a way conducive to a schism...
If she should persist in taking up and maintaining a legal issue that leads to schism in the Saṅgha, that bhikkhunī should be addressed by the bhikkhunīs thus:
"Noble lady, do not strive for the schism of a harmonious Saṅgha, nor persist in taking up and maintaining a legal issue that leads to schism.
Let the noble lady be reconciled with the Saṅgha; for the Saṅgha is harmonious when it is in concord, rejoicing together, and free from dispute."

“Living alone, one dwells in comfort. If that bhikkhunī, being thus addressed by the bhikkhunīs, should persist as before, that bhikkhunī is to be formally admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that [position].
If, being admonished up to three times, she relinquishes it, that is good. If she does not relinquish it, this too—
A nun who has committed an offense that is a *saṅghādisesa*, which involves being sent away after a third admonition.
The training rule concerning those who follow and support schism (15).
Now, there are other nuns who are her followers and supporters of a faction, whether they be one or more.
If two or three [laywomen] should say this: "Sisters, do not say anything to this bhikkhunī;
this bhikkhunī speaks according to the Dhamma, this bhikkhunī speaks according to the Vinaya; this bhikkhunī speaks having taken up our will and preference;
she knows but does not speak; this is acceptable to us," those bhikkhunīs [should be addressed] by the bhikkhunīs...
They should be addressed thus: "Venerable ladies, do not speak in this way; this nun does not speak according to the Dhamma, nor does she speak according to the Vinaya.
Venerable ladies, do not approve of a schism in the Saṅgha. Let the venerable ones be reconciled with the Saṅgha;
for when the Saṅgha is united, living in harmony, without dispute, and in common recitation, it dwells in comfort. And so those nuns...

If, when being spoken to by the bhikkhunīs, they should persist in that same way, those bhikkhunīs are to be formally admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that [behavior]. If, being admonished up to three times, they should relinquish it, that is good.
If they do not relinquish it, these bhikkhunīs also [have committed] an offense entailing a formal meeting up to the third time (yāvatatiyaka-dhamma).
She has committed an offense entailing suspension, a *saṅghādisesa*.
The Sixteenth Training Rule on Being Difficult to Correct:
If a nun is of a difficult-to-correct nature, regarding the training rules included in the recitation, by the nuns...
When she is being spoken to in accordance with the Dhamma, she makes herself unaccountable, saying:
"Noble ladies, do not say anything to me, whether good or bad; nor will I say anything to you, noble ladies, whether good or bad. Desist, noble ladies, from speaking to me!
That bhikkhunī should be addressed by the bhikkhunīs thus: "Venerable lady, do not make yourself unaccountable."

"Venerable lady, you have indeed spoken what ought to be said; let the Venerable Lady herself take her own part, and let the Venerable Lady speak to the bhikkhunīs in accordance with the Dhamma, and the bhikkhunīs shall likewise speak to the Venerable Lady in accordance with the Dhamma. For the Saṅgha of that Blessed One has been thus trained:
namely, by mutual exhortation and mutual correction. And so that bhikkhunī was addressed by the bhikkhunīs.
If she should persist in that very way even when being spoken to, that bhikkhunī is to be formally admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times for the sake of relinquishing it.

If, being admonished up to three times, she relinquishes it, that is good. If she does not relinquish it, this bhikkhunī too has committed an offense entailing a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), which involves expulsion and is to be dealt with on the third admonition.
The Seventeenth Training Rule on Corrupting Families:
Now if a bhikkhunī, being a corrupter of families and of evil conduct, dwells in dependence upon a certain village or town,
and her evil conduct is both seen and heard of, and families are [ruined] by her—
If her corrupt conduct is both seen and heard, that bhikkhunī should be addressed by the bhikkhunīs thus:
"Venerable lady, you are a corrupter of families and of evil conduct; indeed, the evil conduct of the venerable lady is both seen and heard.
Families have been corrupted by the venerable lady, and this corruption is both seen and heard. Depart, venerable lady, from this residence; enough!"
"By staying here. And if that bhikkhunī, being thus addressed by the bhikkhunīs, should say to those bhikkhunīs:
"The bhikkhunīs act out of favoritism; the bhikkhunīs act out of hatred;
the bhikkhunīs act out of delusion; the bhikkhunīs act out of fear; they expel some for such an offense [while others are not]."
“...some do not grant the going-forth,” that bhikkhunī should be addressed by the bhikkhunīs thus: “Do not say so, Noble Lady;
the bhikkhunīs do not act out of favoritism, nor do they act out of ill will, nor do they act out of delusion, nor do they act out of fear;
rather, Noble Lady, you are a corrupter of families and one of evil conduct.”
“Venerable lady, evil conduct is both seen and heard in you; families corrupted by you are both seen and heard of.
Depart, venerable lady; enough of your staying here in this residence.
If that bhikkhunī, being thus addressed by the bhikkhunīs, should persist in her behavior as before, that bhikkhunī is to be formally admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times.
If she should relinquish it upon being pressed up to three times for the sake of relinquishing it, that is good.
If she does not relinquish it, this nun also has committed an offense that is a *saṅghādisesa*, which involves formal meeting of the Saṅgha and entails expulsion, occurring upon the third admonition.
Venerable ladies, the seventeen *saṅghādisesa* rules have been recited: nine that constitute an offense at the very first instance, and eight that occur upon the third admonition.
Whichever of these offenses a bhikkhunī commits, that bhikkhunī must undergo the penance of *mānatta* for a fortnight before both Saṅghas.
Once she has completed the *mānatta*, that bhikkhunī is to be rehabilitated (*abbhetabbā*) wherever there is a community of twenty bhikkhunīs.
Even if the community of bhikkhunīs is short of one from the number twenty, [that bhikkhunī...]
It is irreproachable; that bhikkhunī is not at fault, and those bhikkhunīs are beyond reproach—this is the proper course in this matter.
Herein, noble ladies, I ask you: Are you pure in this? A second time I ask:
Are you pure in this? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this? You are pure in this, noble ladies, therefore you are silent. Thus do I understand it.
The Saṅghādisesa section is finished.
The Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules:
Now, venerable ladies, these thirty Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules—
The Dhamma comes down in brief:
The training rule on the accumulation of almsbowls. 1.
Whatever bhikkhunī should make an accumulation of almsbowls, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Out-of-Season Robes (Akālacīvarabhājana-sikkhāpada) 2:
Whatever nun, having determined an out-of-season robe to be an "in-season robe," should cause it to be distributed, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Training Rule on the Exchange of Robes (Cīvaraparivattana-sikkhāpada).
3. Whatever nun, however, having exchanged a robe with another nun, should later say:
"Come, sister, here is your robe; bring back this robe for me; what is yours is yours alone, and what is mine is mine alone;
bring back this robe; give me back my own," and should either take it away herself or cause it to be taken away—[this is an offense].
or [if she does so], it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The training rule on requesting something else: 4.
Whatever nun, having requested one thing, should request another, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Exchanging for Something Else (Aññacetāpana Sikkhāpada) 5:
Whatever nun, having requested one thing, should request something else, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The First Training Rule on Exchanging for the Saṅgha’s Property.

6. Whatever nun should have another thing exchanged for a requisite belonging to the Saṅgha that was intended for a specific purpose and designated for that purpose, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
This is the second training rule concerning the exchange of requisites belonging to the Saṅgha. 7.

Whatever nun should have another thing exchanged for a requisite belonging to the Saṅgha that was intended for a specific purpose, designated for that purpose, and [obtained] through solicitation, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The First Training Rule on Exchanging for a Group [of Goods]: 8.

Whatever bhikkhunī should exchange for something else a communal requisite intended for another purpose and dedicated to another, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Second Training Rule on Exchanging for a Group [of Goods].

9. Whatever nun should have another thing bartered for in exchange by means of a requisite intended for another purpose, designated for another, belonging to a group, and obtained through solicitation, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
This is the training rule regarding bartering for personal items. 10.

Whatever nun should have another thing bartered for in exchange by means of a requisite intended for another purpose, designated for another, belonging to an individual, and obtained through solicitation, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The First Chapter on Robes.
The Training Rule on Heavy Cloaks (11):

When a nun is having a heavy cloak made, it should be made with a maximum of four *kākaṇa* coins' worth of material. If she should have it made for more than that, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
The Training Rule on Light Outer Garments 12.

When a bhikkhunī is having a light outer garment made, it may be made for a maximum value of two and a half kaṃsas. If she should have it made for more than that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
The Training Rule on Stiff Materials.

13. When a robe has been finished and the kaṭhina period has been suspended, a nun may keep an extra robe for at most ten days. For her who exceeds that limit, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Storing (Udosita-sikkhāpada): 14.

When a robe has been finished and the kaṭhina period has been suspended, if a nun should be separated from her three robes even for a single night, except by formal authorization from the community of nuns, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.

The Training Rule on Out-of-Season Robes (Akālacīvara-sikkhāpada): 15. When a robe has been finished and the kaṭhina period has been suspended, if an out-of-season robe should accrue to a bhikkhunī, it may be accepted by that bhikkhunī if she so desires;
having accepted it, she must have it made up quickly.
There shall be no fulfillment [of the required amount]. That nun must set aside that robe for at most one month, provided there is an expectation of fulfilling what is deficient.
If she should set it aside for longer than that, even if there is an expectation [of fulfillment], it is an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
This is the training rule concerning requesting from one who is unrelated.

16. Whatever nun should request a robe from an unrelated householder or housewife, except on an appropriate occasion, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya). Herein, this is the appropriate occasion: when a nun’s robe has been stolen or her robe has been lost;
this is the occasion in that case.
The Subsequent Training Rule 17:

If an unrelated householder or housewife should invite her to accept many robes, that bhikkhunī may accept robes from them at most as an inner and outer robe. If she should accept more than that, [she commits an offense].
An offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The first training rule concerning what has been set aside:
If, for the sake of a nun, a robe-fund is [prepared] by an unrelated householder or housewife...
The means for purchasing the robe has been prepared with the thought: "Having purchased a robe with this robe-fund, I shall clothe the bhikkhunī named so-and-so with that robe.
In this case, if that bhikkhunī, not having been previously invited, approaches [the donor] and makes a specific request regarding the robe, saying:
"It would be good indeed if the venerable one, with this robe-fund, were to purchase such and such a robe for me..."
Or, having caused a robe to be purchased [for her], if one says, "Clothe her," out of a desire for something fine, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The second training rule concerning what has been set aside: 19.
Now, with reference to a bhikkhunī, if two unrelated householders or housewives...
When funds for the purchase of individual robes have been set aside with the thought,
"Having purchased individual robes with these funds for the purchase of individual robes, we shall clothe the bhikkhunī named so-and-so with robes," and if that bhikkhunī,
not having been previously invited, should go there and make a specific request regarding the robes, saying, "It would be good indeed..."
If, out of a desire for something more excellent, one says, “Venerable sirs, having purchased such and such a robe with these funds for individual robes,
clothe both of us together with one,” it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
This is the training rule concerning kings.
20. Now, if a king, a royal official, a brahmin, or a householder, for the sake of a certain bhikkhunī,
should send a messenger with a robe-fund, saying, "Having purchased a robe with this robe-fund,
clothe the bhikkhunī named so-and-so with a robe," and if that messenger, having approached that bhikkhunī, should speak thus:
“Venerable lady, this robe-fund has been brought for the sake of the venerable one;
may the venerable one accept the robe-fund. That nun should say to that messenger:
“Friends, we do not accept robe-funds; rather, we accept a robe at the proper time, provided it is allowable. If that messenger—
If one should say to a bhikkhunī, "Does your ladyship have anyone to perform services for you?"—
for a bhikkhunī who needs robes, monks, a service-provider should be pointed out, whether a monastery attendant or a lay follower,
saying, "This, friend, is a service-provider for the bhikkhunīs. If that messenger, having informed that service-provider...
Having approached that nun, he should say: "Venerable lady, the person appointed by you as your attendant has been engaged by me;
please approach him at the proper time, and he will clothe you with the robe-cloth.
Monks, a nun who needs robe-cloth should approach her attendant and urge and remind him two or three times.
“If [the donor says], ‘Friend, I need a robe,’ and she, being urged and reminded two or three times, should procure that robe, it is well;
if she should not procure it, she should stand silently for the purpose of that [robe] four, five, or at most six times; having stood silently four, five, or at most six times...”
If they should procure that robe while it is being kept in reserve for them, that is well.
But if, by striving beyond that, they should procure that robe, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
If they do not procure it, she should either go there herself or send a messenger to the place from which the robe-fund was brought, saying: "That which you..."
"Venerable sirs, you have sent a cloth-fund for the sake of a bhikkhunī; that brings no benefit whatsoever to that bhikkhunī.
Venerable sirs, apply yourselves to your own [affairs]; let not your own property go to waste. This is the proper course in such a case.
The second chapter on robes is concluded.
The Training Rule on Gold and Silver (Rūpiyasikkhāpada) 21:

Whatever nun should herself take gold or silver, or cause it to be taken, or consent to its being deposited for her, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Trading with Money (Rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpada)
22. Whatever bhikkhunī should engage in various kinds of transactions involving money, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Buying and Selling: 23.
Whatever bhikkhunī should engage in various kinds of buying and selling, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
The Training Rule on the Bowl with Fewer than Five Repairs (Ūnapañcabandhana-sikkhāpada) 24:

Whatever nun should have another new bowl made when her own bowl has fewer than five repairs, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya). That nun must relinquish that bowl to the assembly of nuns, and whoever...
The edge of the bowl belonging to the assembly of bhikkhunīs should be given to that bhikkhunī with the words:
"Bhikkhunī, this bowl is yours; it should be kept until it breaks. This is the proper procedure in this matter.
The training rule on medicine.

25. Now, whatever medicines for sick bhikkhunīs there may be that are to be used as tonics—namely, ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses—having accepted them, they may be used after being stored for a maximum of seven days.
For one who exceeds this limit, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Taking Back a Robe (Cīvaraacchindana-sikkhāpada) 26:

Whatever bhikkhunī, having herself given a robe to another bhikkhunī, being angry and displeased, should take it back or cause it to be taken back, commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Requesting Thread (Suttaviññatti-sikkhāpada).
27. Whatever nun, having herself requested thread, should have robe-cloth woven by weavers, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
This is the training rule concerning the great weaver. 28.
If, with reference to a nun, an unrelated householder or housewife should have robe-cloth woven by weavers...
If she should cause [the weaver] to weave, and if that nun, having previously been uninvited, should approach the weavers and express a preference regarding the robe-cloth, saying:
"Friends, this robe-cloth is being woven for me; make it long, make it wide, make it well-stretched, well-woven, well-beaten, well-scratched, and well-combed; let it be so..."

“Let us also give even a small amount to the venerable ones. If that bhikkhunī, having spoken thus, should give even a small amount, even as much as a mere alms-food gift, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
This is the training rule concerning urgent robes (accekacīvara-sikkhāpada).

29. When ten days remain until the full moon of the month of Kattika (the end of the rainy season), if a robe intended for a nun should arise, it may be accepted by the nun, thinking it to be urgent; having accepted it, it may be kept until the time for robes.
If she should keep it beyond that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
The Training Rule on What Has Been Dedicated 30.
Whatever nun, knowing that a gain dedicated to the Saṅgha has been dedicated, should dedicate it to herself, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
The third section on bowls is concluded.
"Ladies, the thirty rules on offenses entailing relinquishment and confession have been recited. Therefore, ladies, I ask you:
Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this matter?
You are pure in this matter, ladies, therefore you are silent; thus do I understand it."
The offenses involving forfeiture and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya) are concluded. Now,
venerable ladies, these are the one hundred and sixty-six simple offenses of confession (pācittiya).
The Dhamma comes down in brief.
The Training Rule on Garlic 1:
Whatever bhikkhunī should eat garlic, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Removing Hair from the Intimate Parts 2.
Whatever bhikkhunī should have hair removed from the intimate parts, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Slapping with the Palm.
3. In the case of striking with the palm of the hand, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The training rule on the "powdered-antimony" [application]. 4.
In the case of the powdered-antimony [application], there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Purification by Water (Udakasuddhika-sikkhāpada) 5.
Furthermore, when a bhikkhunī is taking up water for purification, she must take no more than two finger-joints' depth. For one who exceeds that limit, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Attending Upon (Upatiṭṭhana-sikkhāpada).
6. Whatever nun should stand by a monk while he is eating, offering him water or a fan, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
7. The Training Rule on Raw Grain:

Whatever nun, having requested raw grain, or having had it requested; or having roasted it, or having had it roasted; or having pounded it, or having had it pounded; or having cooked it, or having had it cooked—should eat it, there is an offense of expiation.
The First Training Rule on Disposing of Excrement: 8.
Whatever nun should dispose of, or cause to be disposed of, excrement, urine, rubbish, or food scraps over a wall or over a fence, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Second Training Rule on Disposing of Excrement.
9. Whatever bhikkhunī should discard or cause to be discarded excrement, urine, rubbish, or food scraps on green vegetation, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Dancing and Singing: 10.
Whatever bhikkhunī should go to see dancing, singing, or instrumental music, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The First Chapter on Garlic.
The Training Rule on Darkness at Night, 11:
Whatever nun, in the darkness of night and without a lamp, should stand or converse alone with a man, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Secluded Places 12.
Whatever nun should stand or converse alone with a man in a secluded place, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Conversing in the Open Air.
13. Whatever nun, however, should stand or converse alone with a man in an open space, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Sending Away a Second Nun (Dutiyikauyyojana-sikkhāpada): 14.
Whatever nun, however, [should stand or converse] alone with a man on a carriage road, in a cul-de-sac, or at a crossroads...
If she should stand together with her, converse with her, whisper into her ear, or dismiss a companion nun, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
15. The Training Rule on Departing Without Informing:
Whatever nun, having approached families before the meal and sat down on a seat, should depart without informing the owners, it is an offense of expiation.
The Training Rule on Sitting Down Without Asking Permission (16).
Whatever nun, having approached families after the meal, should sit down or lie down on a seat without asking permission from the owners, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
The Training Rule on Spreading [a Seat] Without Asking Permission.

17. Whatever bhikkhunī, having approached families at an improper time, should spread out a bed or have one spread out, or sit down or lie down upon it without having asked the owner’s permission, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
18. Whatever bhikkhunī, on account of what is wrongly grasped or wrongly understood, should cause another to be censured, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Nineteenth Training Rule on Cursing:
Whatever nun should curse herself or another with reference to hell or the holy life, it is an offense of expiation.
The Training Rule on Weeping.
20. Whatever nun should weep, striking herself again and again, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The second section on the dark of night.
The training rule on nakedness.
21. Whatever nun should bathe naked, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on the Bathing Robe (Udakasāṭika-sikkhāpada): 22.
When a nun is having a bathing robe made, it must be made according to the proper measure. This is the measure:
It is four spans of the Sugata-span in length and two spans across. For one who exceeds these measurements, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting.
This is the training rule concerning the sewing of robes.

23. Whatever bhikkhunī, having had a bhikkhunī’s robe unsewn or having had it unsewn by another, does not subsequently sew it herself when there is no obstacle, nor makes an effort to have it sewn, except within four or five days, incurs a pācittiya.
This is the training rule concerning the movement of the outer robe (saṅghāṭicāra). 24.
Whatever bhikkhunī should exceed the five-day limit for the movement of the outer robe, incurs a pācittiya.
The Training Rule on the Exchange of Robes 25.
Whatever nun should wear a robe intended for exchange, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Group Robes.
26. Whatever bhikkhunī should create an obstacle to the community’s acquisition of robe-cloth, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This is the training rule concerning obstruction. 27.
Whatever bhikkhunī should obstruct a legitimate distribution of robe-cloth, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Giving Robes (Cīvaradāna-sikkhāpada) 28:
Whatever bhikkhunī should give a robe belonging to a recluse to a householder, or to a male wanderer, or to a female wanderer, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Exceeding the Proper Time (Kālaatikkamana-sikkhāpada)
29. Whatever bhikkhunī, however, should let the robe-season pass by because of a weak expectation of robe-material, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
30. The training rule on the suspension of the kaṭhina:
Whatever bhikkhunī should obstruct a lawful suspension of the kaṭhina, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Third Chapter on Nakedness.
The Thirty-First Training Rule on Sharing a Single Bed:
Should any two bhikkhunīs lie down on a single bed, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Sharing a Single Blanket and Covering Cloth (32):
Whatever two bhikkhunīs should lie down together sharing a single blanket and covering cloth, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Causing Discomfort.
33. Whatever bhikkhunī should intentionally cause discomfort to another bhikkhunī, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This is the training rule concerning not attending to [the sick]. 34.
Whatever bhikkhunī, when a co-resident sister is suffering, neither attends to her nor makes an effort to have her attended to, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Expelling (Nikkaḍḍhanasikkhāpada) 35:
Whatever nun, having given a dwelling place to another nun, being angry and displeased, should expel her or cause her to be expelled, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Intercourse (Saṃsaṭṭhasikkhāpada).

36. Whatever nun should live in association with a householder or a householder’s son, that nun should be addressed by the nuns thus: “Venerable lady, do not live in association with a householder or a householder’s son;
separate yourself, venerable lady, for the Saṅgha praises seclusion for a sister. And if that nun, by the nuns...
If she should persist in that very same way even when being spoken to, that bhikkhunī is to be formally admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times for the sake of relinquishing it.
If, being admonished up to three times, she relinquishes it, that is good.
If she does not relinquish it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Within One’s Own Country (Antoraṭṭha-sikkhāpada) 37:
Whatever nun should travel on a journey within her own country when it is considered dangerous and fearful, and she is without a caravan, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Beyond One’s Own Country (Tiroraṭṭha-sikkhāpada)

38. Whatever bhikkhunī should travel on a journey through a foreign country that is considered dangerous and perilous, without being accompanied by a caravan, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). 39.
Whatever bhikkhunī should go on a journey during the rains retreat, there is an offense of expiation.
The Training Rule on Setting Out on a Wander (Cārikā-pakkamana-sikkhāpada) 40:
Whatever bhikkhunī, having completed the rains residence, should not set out on a wander, even for as little as five or six yojanas, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The fourth section, the Chapter on Promptness (Tuvaṭṭavagga).
The Training Rule on Royal Palaces (Rājāgāra-sikkhāpada) 41:
Whatever bhikkhunī should go to see a royal palace, a painted hall, a monastery, a pleasure grove, or a lotus pond, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Using High Seats (Āsandi-paribhuñjana-sikkhāpada)
42. Whatever bhikkhunī should use a high couch or a luxurious couch, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Spinning Thread 43.
Whatever bhikkhunī should spin thread, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Domestic Service, 44:
Whatever bhikkhunī should perform domestic service, there is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Legal Proceedings.
45. Whatever nun, being addressed by another nun with the words, “Come, venerable lady,
settle this legal case,” and having consented by saying “Very well,” subsequently neither settles it— despite there being no obstacle— nor makes an effort to settle it,
incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Giving Food (Bhojanadāna-sikkhāpada) 46:
Whatever nun should, with her own hand, give either solid food or soft food to a householder, or to a male wanderer, or to a female wanderer, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Lodging-Clothing (Āvasathacīvara-sikkhāpada)
47. Whatever nun, however, should use a lodging-robe without having relinquished it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This is the training rule concerning lodging-places. 48.
Whatever nun, however, should set out on a journey without having relinquished her lodging, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Mastering Animal Sciences 49.
Whatever bhikkhunī should master an animal science, there is an offense of expiation.
The Training Rule on Reciting Animal Sciences.
50. Whatever nun should teach worldly lore, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The fifth section on picture galleries.
The training rule on entering a monastery.
51. Whatever bhikkhunī, knowing that a monastery has resident bhikkhus, should enter it without having asked permission, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). 52.
Whatever bhikkhunī should revile or abuse a bhikkhu, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Reviling a Group (Gaṇaparibhāsana-sikkhāpada) 53.
Whatever bhikkhunī, being angry, should revile a group, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Being Invited (Pavārita-sikkhāpada).
54. Whatever bhikkhunī, having been invited or having been offered food, should eat or consume either solid food or soft food, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
55. Whatever bhikkhunī should be one who is stingy regarding families, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). This is the training rule concerning those who are stingy regarding families.
The Training Rule on Residing in a Monastery Without Bhikkhus 56.
Whatever bhikkhunī should spend the rains residence in a monastery where there are no bhikkhus, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on the Invitation Ceremony (Apavāraṇā).

57. Whatever nun, having completed the rains residence, does not invite correction from both Saṅghas on three grounds—either by what is seen, or by what is heard, or by suspicion—commits an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
58. Whatever nun does not go for the exhortation or for the communal living, commits an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Approaching for Exhortation (Ovādūpasaṅkamanasikkhāpada) 59.

Every half-month, two things should be expected from the community of monks by a bhikkhunī: the inquiry regarding the Uposatha day and the approaching for exhortation. For one who lets this [time] pass, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on What Grows in the Groin (Pasākhejātasikkhāpada).
60. Whatever nun, however, should have a boil or a wound arising in the groin lanced,
incised, washed, smeared, bound, or released by a man, alone with one person, without having obtained leave from the Saṅgha or a group,
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The sixth chapter: The Chapter on Monasteries.
Training Rule 61: Regarding Pregnant Women.
Whatever nun should ordain a pregnant woman, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Nursing Mothers 62.
Whatever nun should give the full admission to a nursing woman, there is an offense of expiation.
The First Training Rule on Trainee Nuns.
63. Whatever bhikkhunī should give the full admission to a *sikkhamānā* who has not trained for two years in the six rules, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This is the second training rule for *sikkhamānās*. 64.

Whatever bhikkhunī should give the full admission to a *sikkhamānā* who has trained for two years in the six rules but has not been approved by the Saṅgha, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
The First Training Rule on Married Women: 65.
Whatever bhikkhunī should give the full admission to a married woman who is less than twelve years old, there is an offense of expiation.
The Second Training Rule on Married Women.

66. Whatever nun should give the full admission to a married girl who is more than twelve years old, but who has not trained for two years in the six rules, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This is the third training rule concerning married girls. 67.

Whatever nun should give the full admission to a married girl who is more than twelve years old and who has trained for two years in the six rules, but who has not been authorized by the Saṅgha, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The First Training Rule on Co-residents (Sahajīvinī): 68.
Whatever bhikkhunī, having given the full admission to a co-resident, neither herself assists her nor causes another to assist her for two years, commits an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Following the Preceptor (Pavattinī).
69. Whatever nun, however, does not follow her preceptor (pavattinī) for two years after she has been ordained [by her], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This is the second training rule concerning co-residents. 70.
Whatever nun, having ordained a co-resident, neither dismisses her nor causes her to be dismissed, even if she is as far as five or six yojanas away, there is an offense of expiation.
The Seventh Chapter on Pregnant Women.
The First Training Rule Concerning a Maiden: 71.
Whatever nun should give the full admission to a maiden who is less than twenty years of age, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Second Training Rule for a Maiden: 72.
Whatever nun should give the full admission to a maiden who has reached twenty years of age, but who has not trained in the six rules for two years, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Third Training Rule for a Maiden: [To follow]

73. Whatever nun should give the full admission to a maiden who is twenty years of age, who has trained for two years in the six rules, but who has not been approved by the Saṅgha, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Being Less Than Twelve Years [of Ordination]: 74.
Whatever nun, being less than twelve years [of ordination], should give the full admission, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Being Fully Twelve Years [of Ordination] (75).
Whatever nun, though fully twelve years [of ordination], should give the full admission without being authorized by the Saṅgha, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on the Matter of Censuring.

76. Whatever nun, when addressed with the words, “Enough, noble lady, let your ordination wait for now,” should respond, “Very well,” and later engage in disparaging speech, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This is the first training rule concerning the ordination of a trainee nun (sikkhamānā). 77.
Whatever nun should say to a trainee nun, “If you, noble lady, will give me a robe, then I will [ordain you]...”
Having said, "I will give the full admission," if she subsequently does not give the full admission because there is no obstacle, nor does she make an effort to have her given the full admission,
it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This is the second training rule concerning the failure to give the full admission to a female trainee (sikkhamānā).
78. Whatever nun, however, having said to a trainee nun, “If you, noble lady, will follow me for two years, I will ordain you,” should afterwards—
despite there being no obstacles— not ordain her nor make an effort toward ordaining her,
it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Dwelling in Sorrow, 79.

Whatever bhikkhunī should give full admission to a trainee nun (sikkhamānā) who is associated with men, associated with boys, fierce, and dwelling in sorrow, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Not Being Authorized.
80. Whatever nun should ordain a trainee (sikkhamānā) who has not been authorized by her mother and father or by her husband, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Rule on Those Undergoing Probation (Pārivāsika-sikkhāpada): 81.
Whatever nun should ordain a trainee through the giving of consent by one who is undergoing probation, there is an offense of expiation.
The Rule on Ordination Every Year (Anuvassa-sikkhāpada) 82.
Whatever nun should ordain [a girl] every year, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The Rule on One Year [of Training].
83. Whatever nun, however, should ordain two [nuns] in one year, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The eighth section, the Chapter on Maidens.
The Training Rule on Umbrellas and Footwear.
84. Whatever nun, not being ill, should use a sunshade and sandals, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Vehicles: 85.
Whatever nun, not being ill, should travel by vehicle, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Saṅghāṇi Training Rule 86:
Whatever nun should wear a hip-cord, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Female Ornaments.
87. Whatever bhikkhunī should wear female ornaments, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Perfumes and Cosmetics: 88.
Whatever bhikkhunī should bathe with perfumes and cosmetics, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Perfumed Mustard Seed (Vāsitaka-sikkhāpada) 89:
Whatever nun should bathe with perfumed mustard seed, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Having a Nun Rub [the Body] (Bhikkhuniummaddāpana-sikkhāpada).
90. Whatever bhikkhunī should have herself massaged or rubbed by another bhikkhunī, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
This is the training rule regarding having a trainee nun (sikkhamānā) massage her. 91.
Whatever bhikkhunī should have herself massaged or rubbed by a trainee nun, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Having a Novice Nun Massage (92):
Whatever nun should have herself massaged or rubbed by a novice nun, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). The Training Rule on Having a Laywoman Massage:
[93] Whatever nun should have herself massaged or rubbed by a laywoman, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
93. Whatever nun should have herself massaged or rubbed by a female householder, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Not Asking Permission: 94.
Whatever nun should sit down on a seat in front of a monk without asking permission, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Asking Questions (Pañhāpucchanasikkhāpada) 95:
Whatever bhikkhunī should ask a question of a bhikkhu who has not granted her leave, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on the Uncovered (Asaṃkaccikasikkhāpada).
96. Whatever nun should enter a village without wearing her breast-cloth, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The ninth section on the parasol and sandals.
The training rule on false speech.
97. In the case of intentional lying, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The training rule on disparaging speech (omasavāda-sikkhāpada): 98.
In the case of disparaging speech, there is an offense entailing expiation.
The Training Rule on Slander (Pesuñña-sikkhāpada) 99:
In slandering bhikkhunīs, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Reciting Together (Padasodhamma-sikkhāpada).
100. Whatever bhikkhunī should teach the Dhamma word by word to one who is not fully ordained, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This is the first training rule concerning sleeping together. 101.
Whatever bhikkhunī should share a sleeping place for more than two or three nights with one who is not fully ordained, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Second Training Rule on Sharing a Bed with a Man 102.
Whatever bhikkhunī should share a bed with a man, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Teaching the Dhamma.
103. Whatever nun should teach the Dhamma to a man with more than five or six words, except in the presence of a discerning woman, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
104. Whatever nun should announce superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) to one who is not fully ordained, when such states have actually occurred, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Disclosing Grave Offenses 105.
Whatever nun should disclose a grave offense of another nun to one who is not fully ordained, except by authorization of the nuns, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Digging the Earth.
106. Whatever nun should dig the earth or cause it to be dug, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The tenth section, on False Speech;
the training rule concerning living plants (bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada).
107. To cause damage to vegetation is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
108. Regarding one who speaks otherwise [than the truth] and one who harasses: it is an offense entailing expiation.
The Training Rule on Rebuking (Ujjhāpanaka-sikkhāpada) 109:
In the case of rebuking or disparaging, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The First Training Rule on Lodgings (Senāsana-sikkhāpada).
110. Whatever nun, having spread out or caused to be spread out in the open air a couch, a bench, a mattress, or a rug belonging to the Saṅgha,
departs without either putting it away herself or causing it to be put away, or goes away without asking permission,
commits an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The Second Training Rule on Lodgings 111.

Whatever nun, having spread out a bed or having had one spread out in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, when departing, neither puts it away herself nor has it put away by another, or departs without informing [another], commits a *pācittiya*.
The Training Rule on Encroaching.
112. Whatever nun, in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, knowingly intrudes upon a nun who has already entered first and makes her bed there,
thinking, "She who finds it crowded will depart," making this alone the reason and no other,
commits an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Expelling (Nikkaḍḍhanasikkhāpada) 113:
Whatever nun, being angry and displeased, should expel or cause another nun to be expelled from a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on the Upper Story (Vehāsakuṭisikkhāpada).

114. Whatever nun, however, should sit down or lie down on a bed or bench with detachable legs in an upper chamber of a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
115. When a nun is having a large dwelling built for herself, [the measurement] up to the door-frame and the installation of the bolt...
For the purpose of preparing the opening for the light, one standing on ground free of green vegetation may resolve [to build] up to two or three layers of roofing.
If she should resolve to build more than that, even if standing on ground free of green vegetation, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The training rule concerning water containing living beings.
116. Whatever nun, knowing that water contains living beings, should sprinkle it on grass or clay, or cause it to be sprinkled, incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The eleventh section: The Chapter on Living Beings.
The Training Rule on Lodging Alms-food.
117. A non-ill bhikkhunī may eat one meal at a public rest-house. If she should eat more than that, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

118. In eating in a group, except on an appropriate occasion, it is an offense of expiation. Herein, this is the appropriate occasion: the occasion of illness, the occasion of the distribution of robes.
The time for making robes, the time of traveling on a journey, the time of boarding a boat, the time of a great assembly, and the time of a meal for ascetics—this is the occasion there.
The Training Rule of Kāṇamātā 119:
If one should invite a bhikkhunī who has entered a family with cakes or with dough-cakes to bring them [to her], [it is an offense].
A bhikkhunī who desires [to receive food] may accept two or three bowlfuls. If she should accept more than that, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Having accepted two or three bowlfuls, she should take them out and share them with the other bhikkhunīs; this is the proper course of action in this matter.
The training rule on eating at the improper time.
120. Whatever bhikkhunī should eat or consume either solid food or soft food at an improper time, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Storing Up: 121.
Whatever bhikkhunī should eat or consume either solid food or soft food that has been stored up, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Tooth-Cleansers 122.
Whatever nun should put food into her mouth that has not been given, except for water and tooth-cleansers, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Sending Away.

123. Whatever nun, however, should dismiss another nun—having first said to her, "Come, noble lady, let us enter a village or town for alms"—whether she has caused food to be given to her or not, saying:
"Go, noble lady; conversation or sitting together with you is not comfortable for me;
conversation or sitting alone is comfortable for me," provided this is the only reason she gives.
If it is otherwise, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
124. The Training Rule on Families with Food:
Whatever nun should sit down intruding upon a family where food is being served, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Being Secluded with a Man 125.
Whatever nun should sit down in a secluded, concealed place together with a man, it is an offense of expiation.
The Training Rule on Sitting in Seclusion.
126. Whatever bhikkhunī should sit down in private, one-on-one, with a man, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The twelfth section on eating is concluded.
The training rule on wandering.

127. Whatever nun, being invited with food, should visit families before or after the meal without having informed a nun who is present, except on an appropriate occasion, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
Herein, this is the appropriate occasion: the time for giving robes, the time for making robes; this is the occasion therein.
The Mahānāma Training Rule 128:

A nun who is not ill may accept an invitation for requisites for four months, except for a renewed invitation and except for a permanent invitation. Should she accept it for longer than that, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Troops on March.
129. Whatever nun should go to see an army on march, except for a legitimate reason of that kind, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
This is the training rule concerning staying with an army. 130.

If there should be some legitimate reason for that nun to go to the army, she may stay with the army for two or three nights. If she should stay longer than that, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
131. The Training Rule on Combat:

If a bhikkhunī, while staying with an army for two or three nights, should go to see a combat, a military review, an array of troops, or a troop formation, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Drinking Alcohol.
132. In drinking fermented liquor and spirits, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
133. The training rule on poking with the fingers:
In poking with the fingers, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Joking in Water (Hasadhamma-sikkhāpada) 134:
In water, if one jokes, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Disrespect (Anādariya-sikkhāpada).
135. In case of disrespect, there is an offense of expiation.
The training rule on frightening: 136.
Whatever nun should frighten another nun, there is an offense of expiation.
The Thirteenth Chapter on Conduct.
Rule 137: On Fire.
Whatever nun, not being ill and desiring to warm herself, should kindle a fire or have one kindled, except for a legitimate reason of that sort, commits an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The 138th Training Rule on Bathing:
Whatever nun should bathe less than once every half-month, except at the proper time, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
Herein, the proper time is these two and a half months: namely, "one month and a half remaining of the hot season" and "the first month of the rainy season."
The time of heat, the time of feverish distress, the time of illness, the time of work, the time of traveling on a journey, and the time of wind and rain—this is the occasion there.
The Training Rule on Making Discolored (No. 139):
Now, when a nun has obtained a new robe, she must apply one of the three methods for making it discolored.
It should be taken up as blue, or mud-colored, or blackish-brown.
If a bhikkhunī should use a new robe without taking up one of these three disfigurements, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Designation (Vikappaṇa-sikkhāpada).

140. Whatever nun, having assigned a robe to a monk, a nun, a trainee nun, a male novice, or a female novice, should use it herself without it being formally relinquished, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Concealing: 141.
Whatever nun should conceal, or cause another to conceal, the bowl, robe, sitting mat, needle case, or waistband of a nun—even if only for the sake of a joke—there is an offense of expiation.
The 142nd Training Rule on Intentional Killing:
Whatever nun should intentionally deprive a living being of life, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Water Containing Living Beings.
143. Whatever bhikkhunī, knowing that water contains living beings, should use it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Rule on Reopening [a Case]: 144.
Whatever bhikkhunī, knowing that a legal issue has been settled in accordance with the Dhamma, should reopen it for a formal act (kamma), there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
145. The Training Rule on Traveling with a Robber Band:

Whatever nun, knowing that she is traveling with a robber band, should set out on a journey together with them, even if only as far as the next village, commits an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Ariṭṭha.

146. Whatever bhikkhunī should speak thus: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called ‘obstructive states’ by the Blessed One are not actually sufficient to constitute an obstruction for one who indulges in them,” that bhikkhunī should be addressed by the bhikkhunīs as follows:
“Do not, noble lady, speak thus; do not misrepresent the Blessed One.”
"It is not right to misrepresent the Blessed One; the Blessed One would not speak thus.
Noble lady, in many ways the Blessed One has stated that obstructive things are indeed obstructive, and they are sufficient to create an obstacle for one who indulges in them.
If that bhikkhunī, being thus addressed by the bhikkhunīs, should still persist in her position, that bhikkhunī [should be dealt with by the bhikkhunīs].
She should be admonished up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that [behavior].
If, being admonished up to three times, she relinquishes it, that is good. If she does not relinquish it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The fourteenth chapter, the Chapter on Fire (Jotivagga), is concluded.
147. The Training Rule on Sharing Possessions with One Who Has Been Suspended:

Whatever nun, knowing that a nun who speaks in such a manner has not performed the *anuddhamma* (act of reconciliation), has not made amends for her offense, and has not relinquished that view, should share possessions with her, live together with her, or sleep in the same bed as her, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
The Training Rule on the Thorn.

148. If a female novice should speak thus: "As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called 'obstructive states' by the Blessed One are not sufficient to obstruct one who indulges in them," that female novice should be addressed by the bhikkhunīs as follows:
"Do not, noble lady, speak thus to the female novice; do not misrepresent the Blessed One."
"It is not right to misrepresent the Blessed One; the Blessed One would not speak thus.
Noble lady, in many ways the Blessed One has stated that things which are obstructive for a novice are indeed obstructive, and they are sufficient to create an obstacle for one who indulges in them.
If, when being addressed by the bhikkhunīs in this way, that novice should still persist in her position, she—
The female novices should be addressed by the nuns thus: “From this day forward, noble lady, you must no longer point to that Blessed One as your teacher;
nor do you have the privilege shared by other female novices of sharing a sleeping place with the nuns for two or three nights. Go away, depart, and disappear! Whosoever nun...
If, knowing that a novice has been so expelled, one should converse with him, or attend upon him, or eat together with him,
or share a sleeping place with him, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This is the training rule concerning those in common with the Dhamma.
149. Whatever nun, when being addressed by nuns in accordance with the Dhamma, should say:

"Venerable ladies, I will not train in this training rule until I have questioned another nun who is experienced and a bearer of the Vinaya," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Monks, a training nun must understand and must question others.

This is the proper course in that regard. The training rule on remorse (vilekhana-sikkhāpada): 150. Whatever bhikkhunī, while the Pātimokkha is being recited, should speak thus: "What is the use of these minor and lesser rules?"... [text continues] ...this is a pācittiya. This is the training rule on remorse. 151. Whatever bhikkhunī, while the Pātimokkha is being recited, should speak thus: "Why do you recite these rules over and over again? They have already been heard before. If she says this with the intent to cause annoyance, this is a pācittiya. This is the training rule on causing annoyance. 152. Whatever bhikkhunī should say to another bhikkhunī: "Come, sister, let us go to the village or town for alms," and having gone there, should not give her any food, whether hard or soft; if she does so intentionally, this is a pācittiya. This is the training rule on not giving food. 153. Whatever bhikkhunī should say to another bhikkhunī: "Come, sister, let us go to the village or town for alms," and having gone there, should eat herself while not giving any food to that bhikkhunī, whether hard or soft; if she does so intentionally, this is a pācittiya. This is the training rule on eating alone. 154. Whatever bhikkhunī should say to another bhikkhunī: "Come, sister, let us go to the village or town for alms," and having gone there, should eat herself and give food to that bhikkhunī, whether hard or soft, and then, after they have finished eating, should say: "Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you"; if she does so intentionally, this is a pācittiya. This is the training rule on departing after eating together. 155. Whatever bhikkhunī should say to another bhikkhunī: "Come, sister, let us go to the village or town for alms," and having gone there, should eat herself and give food to that bhikkhunī, whether hard or soft, and then, after they have finished eating, should say: "Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you"; if she does so intentionally, and that bhikkhunī, being pressured by her, goes out of the village or town, this is a pācittiya. This is the training rule on departing under pressure. 156. Whatever bhikkhunī should say to another bhikkhunī: "Come, sister, let us go to the village or town for alms," and having gone there, should eat herself and give food to that bhikkhunī, whether hard or soft, and then, after they have finished eating, should say: "Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you"; if she does so intentionally, and that bhikkhunī, being pressured by her, goes out of the village or town, and while going, should say: "I am not going; why did you say, 'Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you'? If she says this, this is a pācittiya. This is the training rule on going against one's will. 157. Whatever bhikkhunī should say to another bhikkhunī: "Come, sister, let us go to the village or town for alms," and having gone there, should eat herself and give food to that bhikkhunī, whether hard or soft, and then, after they have finished eating, should say: "Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you"; if she does so intentionally, and that bhikkhunī, being pressured by her, goes out of the village or town, and while going, should say: "I am not going; why did you say, 'Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you'? If she says this, and that bhikkhunī, being pressured by her, returns to the village or town, this is a pācittiya. This is the training rule on returning under pressure. 158. Whatever bhikkhunī should say to another bhikkhunī: "Come, sister, let us go to the village or town for alms," and having gone there, should eat herself and give food to that bhikkhunī, whether hard or soft, and then, after they have finished eating, should say: "Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you"; if she does so intentionally, and that bhikkhunī, being pressured by her, returns to the village or town, and while returning, should say: "I am not going; why did you say, 'Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you'? If she says this, this is a pācittiya. This is the training rule on returning against one's will. 159. Whatever bhikkhunī should say to another bhikkhunī: "Come, sister, let us go to the village or town for alms," and having gone there, should eat herself and give food to that bhikkhunī, whether hard or soft, and then, after they have finished eating, should say: "Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you"; if she does so intentionally, and that bhikkhunī, being pressured by her, returns to the village or town, and while returning, should say: "I am not going; why did you say, 'Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you'? If she says this, and that bhikkhunī, being pressured by her, goes out of the village or town once more, this is a pācittiya. This is the training rule on going out again under pressure. 160. Whatever bhikkhunī should say to another bhikkhunī: "Come, sister, let us go to the village or town for alms," and having gone there, should eat herself and give food to that bhikkhunī, whether hard or soft, and then, after they have finished eating, should say: "Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you"; if she does so intentionally, and that bhikkhunī, being pressured by her, returns to the village or town, and while returning, should say: "I am not going; why did you say, 'Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you'? If she says this, and that bhikkhunī, being pressured by her, goes out of the village or town once more, this is a pācittiya. This is the training rule on going out again against one's will. 161. Whatever bhikkhunī should say to another bhikkhunī: "Come, sister, let us go to the village or town for alms," and having gone there, should eat herself and give food to that bhikkhunī, whether hard or soft, and then, after they have finished eating, should say: "Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you"; if she does so intentionally, and that bhikkhunī, being pressured by her, returns to the village or town, and while returning, should say: "I am not going; why did you say, 'Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you'? If she says this, and that bhikkhunī, being pressured by her, goes out of the village or town once more, and while going, should say: "I am not going; why did you say, 'Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you'? If she says this, this is a pācittiya. This is the training rule on going out again under pressure. 162. Whatever bhikkhunī should say to another bhikkhunī: "Come, sister, let us go to the village or town for alms," and having gone there, should eat herself and give food to that bhikkhunī, whether hard or soft, and then, after they have finished eating, should say: "Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you"; if she does so intentionally, and that bhikkhunī, being pressured by her, returns to the village or town, and while returning, should say: "I am not going; why did you say, 'Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you'?
