If she says this, this is a pācittiya. This is the training rule on going out again against one's will. 163. Whatever bhikkhunī should say to another bhikkhunī: "Come, sister, let us go to the village or town for alms," and having gone there, should eat herself and give food to that bhikkhunī, whether hard or soft, and then, after they have finished eating, should say: "Go away, sister; I do not wish to see you"; if she does so intentionally, and that bhikkhunī, being pressured by her, returns to the village or town
“‘The training rules that have been recited lead only to remorse, vexation, and distress’—if she disparages the training rules, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
151. The Training Rule on Concealment:
Whatever nun, when the Pātimokkha is being recited every half-month, should speak thus: “Only now...”
“I know this, noble lady: ‘This rule, it seems, is included in the Sutta, contained in the Sutta, and comes up for recitation every half-month.
If other bhikkhunīs should know that this bhikkhunī has previously sat through the Pātimokkha being recited two or three times, let alone more than that, and yet she... [does not acknowledge it].

There is release for a bhikkhunī through ignorance; whatever offense she has committed therein, she must be dealt with according to the Dhamma, and furthermore, delusion must be imposed upon her: "It is a loss for you, noble lady;
it is ill-gotten for you, that when the Pātimokkha is being recited, you do not apply yourself with thorough attention. This [is the rule] in that case.
In the case of causing delusion, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Striking (Pahārasikkhāpada) 152:
Whatever nun, being angry and displeased with another nun, should give her a blow, there is an offense of expiation.
153. The Training Rule on the Slap:
Whatever bhikkhunī, being angry and displeased with another bhikkhunī, should raise her hand to strike her, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Training Rule on Groundless Accusation.
154. Whatever bhikkhunī should groundlessly charge another bhikkhunī with a *saṅghādisesa* offense, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

155. Whatever bhikkhunī should intentionally cause anxiety in a bhikkhunī, thinking, “In this way she will be uncomfortable for even a moment,” making this alone the reason and no other, it is an offense of expiation.
156. The Training Rule on Eavesdropping:

Whatever nun should stand eavesdropping upon nuns who have become quarrelsome, contentious, and fallen into dispute, thinking, "I will hear what these women say," making that very thing her motive; [this is an offense of expiation].
If it is otherwise, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The fifteenth section, the Chapter on Views.
The training rule on obstructing formal acts (kamma).
157. Whatever nun, having given her consent for legal proceedings that are in accordance with the Dhamma, should afterwards engage in criticism, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).

158. Whatever nun, while a formal discussion of a legal matter is taking place in the Saṅgha, should rise from her seat and depart without having given her consent, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
159. The Rule on the Weak (Dubbalasikkhāpada):

Whatever bhikkhunī, after a robe has been given by a unanimous Saṅgha, should subsequently engage in criticism, saying, “The bhikkhunīs are diverting communal gains according to their personal friendships,” there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This is the Rule on Diverting (Pariṇāmanasikkhāpada).
160. Whatever nun, knowing that a gain intended for the Saṅgha has been diverted to an individual, should divert it to an individual, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The Jewel Precept (Ratana-sikkhāpada) 161.
Whatever nun should pick up a jewel or what is considered a jewel, except within a monastery (ajjhārāma) or within a dwelling (ajjhāvasatha), [there is an offense of expiation].
If she should herself take it up or cause it to be taken up, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

However, if a nun takes up or causes to be taken up a jewel or what is considered a jewel within a monastery or a dwelling, it should be deposited with the thought: "He to whom it belongs shall take it away.
This is the proper course of action in such a case.
The Training Rule on the Needle Case (Sūcighara-sikkhāpada) 162.
Whatever nun should have a needle case made of bone, or of ivory, or of horn, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya) involving breaking [the object].
The Training Rule on Beds and Chairs (Mañcapīṭha-sikkhāpada).

163. When a bhikkhunī is having a new bed or chair made, it should be made with legs eight finger-breadths long according to the Sugata’s finger-breadth, except for the lower crossbar. For one who exceeds this measurement, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting down. 164.
Whatever bhikkhunī should have a bed or chair upholstered with cotton-wool, there is an offense of expiation involving tearing it out.
165. The Training Rule on the Itch-Covering Cloth:
When a bhikkhunī has an itch-covering cloth made, it should be made according to the proper measure.
Herein, this is the measure: four spans of the Sugata-span in length, and two spans across. That...
For one who exceeds [the measure], there is an offense of expiation involving cutting down.
The Nanda Training Rule 166:
Whatever nun should have a robe made to the measure of the Sugata’s robe, or exceeding it, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting down.
It is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya). Herein, this is the measure of the Sugata’s robe for the Sugata:
nine spans of the Sugata’s span in length, and six spans across; this is the measure of the Sugata’s robe for the Sugata.
The sixteenth section, the Dhammika-vagga.
Venerable ladies, the one hundred and sixty-six rules on expiation have been recited. Therefore, I ask you, venerable ladies:
Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask:
Are you pure in this matter? You are pure in this matter, venerable ladies; therefore you are silent. Thus do I understand it.
The Pācittiyas are finished.
The Pāṭidesanīyas:
Now, venerable ladies, these eight Pāṭidesanīyas—
The rules come up for recitation.
The training rule on requesting ghee (1):
Whatever nun, not being ill, should request ghee and eat it, that nun must confess: "Venerable ladies, I have fallen into a blameworthy, unbecoming, offense entailing confession; I confess it."
The Training Rule on Requesting Oil (2):
Whatever nun, not being ill, should request oil and consume it... [as before] ...I confess that.
The Training Rule on Requesting Honey.
3. Whatever nun, not being ill, having requested honey, should eat it... [as before] ...I confess that.
This is the training rule regarding the request for molasses. 4.
Whatever nun, not being ill, having requested molasses, should eat it... [as before] ...I confess that.
The Training Rule on Requesting Fish 5.
Whatever nun, not being ill, having requested fish, should eat it... [etc. ...I confess that.
The Training Rule on Requesting Meat.
6. Whatever nun, not being ill, having requested meat, should eat it... [as before] ...I confess that.
The training rule on requesting milk: 7.
Whatever nun, not being ill, having requested milk, should eat it... [as before] ...I confess that.
The Training Rule on Requesting Curd (Dadhivijñāpana-śikṣāpada) 8.

Whatever nun, not being ill, should request curd and eat it, that nun must confess: "Venerable ladies, I have fallen into a blameworthy state, an unsuitable offense entailing confession; I confess it.
Venerable ladies, the eight rules entailing confession have been recited. Regarding this, I ask you: Are you pure in this matter?
"You are pure in this matter. A second time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask:
Are you pure in this matter? You are pure in this matter, sisters; therefore you are silent. Thus do I understand it.
The *pāṭidesanīya* rules are concluded.
The Sekhiyas:
Now, sisters, these Sekhiya rules come up for recitation.
The training rule on being well-rounded.
1. "I shall wear my lower robe evenly all around"—this training is to be observed. 2.
"I shall wear my upper robe evenly all around"—this training is to be observed.
The training rule on being well-covered.
3. "I shall go well-covered in inhabited areas"—this training is to be observed. 4.
"I shall sit well-covered in inhabited areas"—this training is to be observed.
This is the training rule on being well-restrained.
5. "I shall go well-restrained among the houses," this training is to be observed. 6.
"I shall sit down well-restrained among the houses," this training is to be observed.
The training rule on downcast eyes.
7. "I shall go with downcast eyes among the houses," this training is to be observed. 8.
"I shall sit with downcast eyes among the houses," this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Raised Eyes.
9. "I shall not walk with my upper robe tucked up in inhabited areas"—this training is to be observed. 10.
"I shall not sit down with my upper robe tucked up in inhabited areas"—this training is to be observed.
The first section, on the Circular Robe.
The Training Rule on Excessive Laughter 11.
“I will not go among the houses laughing excessively,” this training is to be observed. 12.
“I will not sit among the houses laughing excessively,” this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Loud Voices 13:
"I shall walk with little sound in inhabited areas"—this training is to be observed. 14:
"I shall sit with little sound in inhabited areas"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Swinging the Body 15.
The training is to be observed: "I will not go among the houses of the laity swinging my body. 16.
The training is to be observed: "I will not sit among the houses of the laity swinging my body."
The Training Rule on Swinging the Arms: 17.
“I shall not go among the houses swinging my arms,” this training is to be observed. 18.
“I shall not sit among the houses swinging my arms,” this training is to be observed.
19. The training rule concerning swaying the head:
"I shall not go among the houses of others swaying my head"—this training is to be observed. 20.
The training rule concerning swaying the head: "I shall not sit among the houses of others swaying my head"—this training is to be observed.
The Second Chapter on Excessive Laughter.
Training Rule 21: "I shall not walk with hands on hips in inhabited areas"—this training is to be observed.
22. The training is to be observed: "I shall not sit with hands on hips among the houses.
23. The training rule concerning the veiled head:
The training is to be observed: "I shall not go among the houses with my head covered."
24. "I shall not sit with my head covered in an inhabited area," this training is to be observed. 25.
"I shall not walk on tiptoe in an inhabited area," this training is to be observed.
Training Rule 26:
"I shall not sit cross-legged in an inhabited area"—this training is to be observed.
Training Rule on Receiving with Care.
27. The training is to be observed: "I shall receive almsfood respectfully.
This is the training rule on receiving with awareness of the bowl. 28.
The training is to be observed: "I shall receive almsfood with awareness of the bowl."
The Training Rule on Receiving Alms-food with Equal Amounts of Curry (No. 29):
The training is to be observed thus: "I shall receive alms-food with equal amounts of curry.
The Training Rule on [Receiving] Up to the Brim.
30. The training is to be observed: "I shall receive almsfood with my bowl level.
This is the third section, on the one who stands with hands on hips.
The training rule on eating with care.
31. The training is to be observed: "I shall eat almsfood with careful attention.
This is the training rule on eating with mindfulness of the bowl. 32.
The training is to be observed: "I shall eat almsfood with mindfulness of the bowl."
The Training Rule on Successive Alms (Sapadāna-sikkhāpada) 33:
"I shall eat almsfood by going from house to house in succession"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Equal Soup (Samasūpaka-sikkhāpada).
34. The training is to be observed: "I shall eat almsfood with an even amount of sauce. 35.
The training is to be observed: "I shall not eat almsfood by pressing it down from a heap."
The Training Rule on Covering Rice with Curry: 36.
"I shall not cover curry or sauce with rice out of a desire for more"—this is the training to be observed.
The Training Rule on Requesting Curry and Rice.
37. The training is to be observed: "I shall not, when not ill, request curry or boiled rice for my own sake and then eat it.
38. The training is to be observed: "Perceiving with a sense of reproach, I shall not look into the bowl of others."
The Training Rule on Mouthfuls 39.
The training is to be observed: "I shall not make a mouthful that is too large.
The Training Rule on Bites.
40. The training is to be observed: "I shall form the morsel into a round shape.
This is the fourth section on "With Care.
The training rule concerning not having [food] brought.
41. The training is to be observed: "I shall not open my mouth until a morsel has been brought to it.
The training rule on eating: 42.
The training is to be observed: "While eating, I shall not insert my entire hand into the mouth."
The Training Rule on Having Food in the Mouth (Sakabaḷasikkhāpada) 43: "I shall not speak with food in my mouth"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Dropping Lumps of Food (Piṇḍukkhepakasikkhāpada).
44. The training is to be observed: “I shall not eat by tossing up morsels.
45. The training rule concerning the cutting off of morsels:
The training is to be observed: “I shall not eat by cutting off morsels.”
The Training Rule on Cheek-Bulging:
"I shall not eat with cheek-bulging"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Hand-Waving.
47. The training is to be observed: "I shall not eat shaking my hand.
48. The training rule on scattering rice:
The training is to be observed: "I shall not eat scattering rice."
The Training Rule on Not Licking the Tongue (49):
"I shall not eat licking the tongue"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Making the *capu-capu* Sound.
50. The training is to be observed: "I shall not eat making a 'capucapu' sound.
This concludes the fifth section on mouthfuls.
The training rule concerning making a "surusuru" sound.
51. The training is to be observed: "I shall not eat making a *surusuru* sound.
52. The training rule on licking the hands:
The training is to be observed: "I shall not eat licking my hands."
The Training Rule on Licking the Alms Bowl (Pattanillehakasikkhāpada) 53:
The training is to be observed thus: "I shall not eat while licking the alms bowl.
The Training Rule on Licking the Lips (Oṭṭhanillehakasikkhāpada).
54. The training is to be observed: "I shall not eat licking the lips. 55.
The training is to be observed: "I shall not accept a water vessel with a hand soiled by food."
Training Rule 56:
"I shall not discard bowl-washing water containing rice-grains within an inhabited area"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule concerning one holding a sunshade in hand.
57. "I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who has a parasol in hand, unless they are ill"—this training is to be observed. 58.
"I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who has a staff in hand, unless they are ill"—this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on Having a Weapon in Hand (No. 59):
"I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who has a weapon in hand and is not ill"—this is the training to be observed.
The Training Rule on Having a Weapon in Hand.
60. "I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who has a weapon in hand and is not ill"—this training is to be observed.
The sixth chapter, the Surusuru-vagga.
The training rule on sandals.
61. “I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who has put on sandals and is not ill,” this training is to be observed.
This is the training rule concerning sandals (upāhana-sikkhāpada). 62. “I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who has put on shoes and is not ill,” this training is to be observed.
Training Rule 63:
"I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who is in a vehicle and is not ill"—this training is to be observed.
Training Rule on Reclining.
64. “I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who has gone to bed and is not ill,” this training is to be observed. 65.
“I shall not teach the Dhamma to one sitting with legs crossed (pallatthikā) and who is not ill,” this training is to be observed.
The Training Rule on the Veiled Head (No. 66):
"I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who has a veiled head unless they are ill"—this is the training to be observed.
The Training Rule on the Covered Head.
67. “I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who has not covered their head, unless they are ill,” this is a training to be observed. 68.
“I shall not teach the Dhamma while sitting on the ground to one who is seated on a seat, unless they are ill,” this is a training to be observed.
Training Rule 69: One should train oneself thus:
"I shall not teach the Dhamma while sitting on a low seat to one who is sitting on a high seat and is not ill.
Training Rule on Standing.
70. "I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who is sitting while I am standing, unless he is ill"—this training is to be observed. 71.
"I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who is walking in front while I am walking behind, unless he is ill"—this training is to be observed.

The Training Rule on Not Walking Along the Path: 72. "I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who is walking along the path while I am walking off the path, unless I am ill"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Standing While Voiding Excrement: [73] "I shall not void excrement or urine while standing"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Lying Down While Voiding Excrement: [74] "I shall not void excrement or urine while lying down"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Voiding Excrement or Urine in Water: [75] "I shall not void excrement or urine in water"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Voiding Excrement or Urine on Cultivated Land: [76] "I shall not void excrement or urine on cultivated land where crops are growing or on green grass"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Voiding Excrement or Urine on a Rock: [77] "I shall not void excrement or urine on a rock that is frequented by people or animals"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Voiding Excrement or Urine on a Tree: [78] "I shall not void excrement or urine on a tree trunk that is frequented by people or animals"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Voiding Excrement or Urine on a Conspicuous Spot: [79] "I shall not void excrement or urine on a conspicuous spot such as a mountain peak, a mountain cave, a cliff edge, a riverbank, or a well"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Ascending a Tree: [80] "I shall not ascend a tree higher than the height of a man, except in case of illness"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Sitting on a Raised Seat: [81] "I shall not sit on a raised seat such as a couch, a chair, a long bench, a bed, or a high seat, except in case of illness"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Sitting on a Seat Covered with Spreads: [82] "I shall not sit on a seat covered with spreads such as woolen cloth, cotton cloth, silk cloth, or embroidered cloth, except in case of illness"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Sitting on a Seat with Fringes: [83] "I shall not sit on a seat with fringes such as those made of animal hair, wool, or yak-tail hair, except in case of illness"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Sitting on a Seat with Cushions: [84] "I shall not sit on a seat with cushions such as those stuffed with cotton, wool, or kapok, except in case of illness"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Sitting on a Seat with Stuffed Cushions: [85] "I shall not sit on a seat with stuffed cushions such as those stuffed with cotton, wool, or kapok, except in case of illness"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Sitting on a Seat Covered with Animal Skins: [86] "I shall not sit on a seat covered with animal skins such as those of lions, tigers, leopards, or black antelopes, except in case of illness"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Using a Bedstead with High Posts: [87] "I shall not use a bedstead with high posts or a bedstead with carved legs, except in case of illness"—this is the training to be observed.

The Training Rule on Using a Bedstead with Canopies: [88] "I shall not use a bedstead with canopies or curtains, except in case of illness"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Using a Bedstead with Red Covers: [89] "I shall not use a bedstead with red covers or red bedspreads, except in case of illness"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Using a Bedstead with White Covers: [90] "I shall not use a bedstead with white covers or white bedspreads, except in case of illness"—this is the training to be observed. The Training Rule on Using a Bedstead with Blue Covers: [91] "I shall not use a bedstead with blue covers or blue bedspreads, except in case of illness"—this is the training to be observed. 73. “I will not, when not ill, defecate or urinate while standing”—this training is to be observed.

The seventh chapter, the Section on Sandals, is concluded.
Venerable ladies, the training rules have been recited. Therefore, I ask you, venerable ladies:
Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this matter?
You are pure in this matter, for that reason you are silent; thus do I understand it.
The Sekhiya rules are finished.
Regarding the settling of legal issues:
Venerable ladies, these are the seven methods for the settlement of legal issues.
The Dhamma comes up for recitation.
For the settling and pacification of legal issues as they arise, face-to-face resolution (sammukhāvinaya) should be granted;
resolution through mindfulness (sativinaya) should be granted.
The verdict of past insanity should be granted.
It should be dealt with according to admission.
By a majority decision.
The *tassapāpiyasika* (decision by further penalty).
The *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass).
Venerable ladies, the seven principles for the settling of legal issues have been recited. Therefore, I ask you, venerable ladies: Is it so?
"Pure? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this matter?
You are pure here, venerable sirs, therefore you are silent; thus do I understand it.
The methods for settling legal issues are concluded.
Venerable ladies, the introduction has been recited;
the eight rules on defeat have been recited;
the seventeen rules on formal meetings of the Saṅgha have been recited.
The thirty *nissaggiya pācittiya* rules have been recited;
the one hundred and sixty-six *pācittiya* rules have been recited;
the eight *pāṭidesanīya* rules have been recited.
The rules of training (sekhiya-dhammā) have been recited;

the seven principles for settling legal issues (adhikaraṇa-samatha-dhammā) have been recited. This much of the Blessed One’s word, which has come down in the Suttas and is included in the Suttas, comes up for recitation every half-month.
In this regard, all should train together, being harmonious, friendly, and free from dispute.
The fourth section, the detailed recitation, is finished. The Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha is concluded.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The Commentary on the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*:
The Introduction to the Work.
With a mind of clear confidence, [I pay homage] to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
Having paid homage to those who are worthy of worship, the recipients of honor and respect,
the lamps of the lineage of elders, steadfast in the discipline of the Vinaya,
and lions among the ancient teachers— I bow with palms joined in reverence.
The Pātimokkha has been proclaimed by the Great Seer as the foremost of blameless states,
the gateway for entering into liberation. By one who is gentle,
free from agitation, and whose conduct is pure and austere;
Requested by the Elder Soṇa, who was endowed with discipline and conduct,
this commentary on him— complete in its analysis— is for the purpose of resolving the doubts of those monks who have conceived uncertainty therein.
I shall recite, by name, the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*, the beautiful [work] based on the oral tradition of the Mahāvihāravāsins.
Commentary on the Introduction.
In this context, *pātimokkha* means that which is foremost (*paatimokkha*), most excellent (*atipamokkha*), most superior (*atisettha*), and most sublime (*atiuttama*).
Thus, according to this etymological meaning, although it is of one kind, it is twofold when classified according to the types of training rules (*sīla*).

For it is said: "He dwells restrained by the restraint of the *pātimokkha*" and "This is the beginning, this is the mouth, this is the pre-eminent [source] of wholesome states; therefore it is called..."

In such passages as "the Pātimokkha," virtue is called the Pātimokkha; whereas in such passages as "both his Pātimokkhas were thoroughly mastered in detail," the text is called the Pātimokkha. Therein, virtue is that which protects (pāti);
it liberates (mokkheti)—that is, it releases—one who guards it from the sufferings of the woeful states and so forth, or from self-reproach and the like.
It is called *pātimokkha* because it protects from fears. Furthermore, the book is also called *pātimokkha* because it illuminates that *pātimokkha*.
The meaning of the word stated at the beginning is common to both.
In this regard, the following commentary applies to both the *sīla-pātimokkha* (the precepts) and the *gantha-pātimokkha* (the book), for when the book is explained...
Its meaning has already been explained. Furthermore, this Pātimokkha of the Text is twofold: the Bhikkhu-pātimokkha and the Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha.
Therein, the Bhikkhu-pātimokkha—beginning with “Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me”—is established by five sections of recitation;
while [the Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha]—beginning with “Let the Saṅgha, noble ladies, hear me”—is established by four sections of recitation.
The Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha is established. Therein, in the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha, there are five recitations (uddesa), namely:

the recitation of the introduction (nidāna-uddesa), the recitation of the Pārājikas, the recitation of the Saṅghādisesas, the recitation of the Aniyatas, and the detailed recitation (vitthāra-uddesa). Therein, first, the recitation of the introduction is as follows:
"Let the Sangha, venerable sirs, hear me... [omission] ...for when it has been revealed, there is ease for him; therein I ask the venerable ones..."
"Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask:
Are you pure in this matter? The venerable ones are pure in this matter; therefore they are silent. Thus do I understand it.
Having said this, and after the rest of the Sutta had been recited according to the method beginning with "The introduction, venerable ones, has been recited," it was declared: "It has been recited."

It exists. The sections for the recitation of the *pārājika* rules and so forth should be joined by reciting the *pārājika* rules and others starting from the beginning of the introduction (*nidāna*).

The detailed exposition is indeed extensive. However, because of the statement, "The remainder should be announced by means of hearing," in the case of the recitation of the *pārājika* rules and so forth, when an obstacle arises while a certain portion has been performed, the remainder should be announced together with that [portion] by means of hearing. Regarding the recitation of the introduction (*nidānuddesa*):
However, there is no such thing as "announcing" [the Pātimokkha] when the hearing has not yet been completed.

In the case of the Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha, however, the recitation of the *aniyata* rules is omitted; the rest is exactly as previously stated. Thus, this will be the commentary on both these Pātimokkhas, which are established by five and four sections of recitation respectively. Now, as for the Bhikkhu-pātimokkha herein:
First, therefore, this is stated for the purpose of explaining that [phrase]:
"Let the bhikkhus, endowed with virtue and desiring training, hear from me the determination of the meaning of the words beginning with 'Let my words be heard.'"
For here, "let him hear" is a statement of the command to listen; "me" is a term of self-reference by the one who proclaims it;
"venerable sir" is a term of respect and deference; and "the Saṅgha" is a term for a collection of individuals.
All of this is the speech that must first be uttered by the reciter of the Pātimokkha; for when the Blessed One was permitting the recitation of the Pātimokkha, he [gave these instructions].
It was stated at Rājagaha; therefore, whoever recites the Pātimokkha must address the Sangha-thera as "Venerable friend" (āvaso) if he is the senior member.
If he is junior, he should address him as "Venerable sir" (bhante), according to the method set forth in the Canon.
For either the Sangha-thera may recite the Pātimokkha—on account of the expression "the Pātimokkha headed by the Thera"—or the junior member may do so. "I authorize..."
“Monks, the Pātimokkha is to be entrusted to whichever monk there is who is competent and capable,” because of this statement.
Now, although the word “Saṅgha” refers generally to a collection of individuals, it is nevertheless twofold:

the Saṅgha worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya-saṅgha*) and the conventional Saṅgha (*sammuti-saṅgha*). Therein, the Saṅgha worthy of offerings is the collection of the eight noble persons (*ariya-puggala*).
It is called the "conventional Saṅgha. This refers generally to the assembly of monks; that is what is intended here.
Furthermore, this [Saṅgha] is fivefold according to its formal acts (*kamma*): a group of four, a group of five, a group of ten, a group of twenty, and a group of more than twenty.
Among these, by means of a group of four, one may perform all formal acts of the Saṅgha except for ordination (*upasampadā*), the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), and rehabilitation (*abbhāna*).
It is permissible. In the Middle Countries, it is permissible for a group of five to perform all sangha-kamma except for ordination (*upasampadā*) and the act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna*).
With a group of ten, it is permissible to perform all sangha-kamma except for the act of rehabilitation alone.
With a group of twenty, it is not permissible to perform any sangha-kamma whatsoever.

Likewise, [it is stated] "by a group of more than twenty. This, however, is stated for the purpose of showing that an act (*kamma*) which must be performed by a Saṅgha consisting of four members or more may not be performed by one with fewer members, but it is permissible when there are more.
In this context, however, the term "Saṅgha" refers to any conventional assembly (*sammuti-saṅgha*), beginning with those consisting of four members.
"Ajjuposatho" means "today is the Uposatha day"; by this, he excludes other Uposatha days. "Pannaraso" (the fifteenth) excludes any other Uposatha day.

For according to the days, three Uposathas are mentioned: the fourteenth-day, the fifteenth-day, and the Uposatha for reconciliation (*sāmaggi-uposatha*). Among these, [of the] winter, summer, and rainy seasons...
By counting two fortnights each for the third and seventh fortnights of the three seasons, there are six fourteenth-day Uposatha days; the remaining eighteen are fifteenth-day ones.
Thus, there are twenty-four Uposatha days in one year; this, first of all, is the normal practice. [The Buddha said:
"Monks, I allow you to recite the Pātimokkha once a fortnight, either on the fourteenth or the fifteenth day."

Furthermore, according to the statement, "The resident monks must comply with the visiting monks," and other such injunctions, it is permissible to perform the Uposatha on another fourteenth day when such conditions exist. However, for those who have completed the previous rains-residence, the full moon of the month of Kattika is the [proper time];
yet, if they are harassed by quarrelsome individuals and consequently postpone their Pavāraṇā, then [the time is] that of the month of Kattika.

The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the full moon of the latter Kattika, and the full moon of the latter Kattika for those who have completed the rains residence—these three are also the days for the Pavāraṇā ceremony; this too is the normal practice.
However, when such circumstances exist, it is permissible to perform the Pavāraṇā on the two preceding fourteenth days of the two Kattika full moons as well.
But when the Saṅgha has been split according to the method described in the Kosambaka Khandhaka, and that monk has been reinstated,
and the Saṅgha effects its unity for the sake of settling that matter— at that time, because of the statement, "The Uposatha should be performed immediately;
the Pātimokkha should be recited," any other [Uposatha] besides those on the fourteenth and fifteenth days [is also valid].

Any day whatsoever is called a "unanimity Uposatha day"; however, for those who have completed the previous rains-residence, within the month of Kattika, this very day is called the "unanimity Pavāraṇā day.
Thus, by the term "the fifteenth," he excludes other Uposatha days from these three [possible] days.
Therefore, by the statement "Today is the Uposatha," [he indicates] that it is not any other Uposatha day.
When [the Uposatha] is prohibited, the Uposatha must not be performed on that day at all. However, on whichever other day is the Uposatha day, the Uposatha may be performed.
When performing it, if it is the fourteenth-day [Uposatha], one should say: "Today is the fourteenth-day Uposatha.
If it is the fifteenth-day [Uposatha], one should say: "Today is the fifteenth-day Uposatha. If it is a Uposatha for the sake of concord...
It is said: "Today is the Uposatha; there is concord. Regarding the phrase "If it seems timely to the Saṅgha":

here, "timely" (*pattakāla*) means that the time has arrived for this formal act (*kamma*); "timely" (*pattakāla*) itself is "proper" (*pattakalla*). This [phrase] is comprised here of four factors, as the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā have said:
"The Uposatha, as many bhikkhus as are competent for the formal act..."
“Shared offenses do not exist,
and there are no persons to be avoided in that case;
therefore it is said, ‘It is the right time.’”
In this context, "Uposatha" refers to any one of the three Uposatha days.
For when that day exists, this formal act (kamma) of the Saṅgha is said to be "timely" (pattakalla), but not when it does not exist. As it is said:
"Monks, the Uposatha should not be performed on a non-Uposatha day; whoever should perform it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."

"As many bhikkhus as are eligible for the formal act" means as many bhikkhus as are eligible, appropriate, and fit for that Uposatha act—at the very least, four regular bhikkhus—and they must stand within a single boundary (*sīmā*) without departing from arm's reach of one another.

Now, this boundary is of two kinds: the formally established boundary (*baddha-sīmā*) and the naturally established boundary (*abaddha-sīmā*). Among these, there are eleven types of deficient boundaries (*vipatti-sīmā*).

Having passed beyond [the boundary], a formally authorized boundary (*sammatā sīmā*)— which is endowed with the threefold perfection, connects sign with sign, and is established— is called a "bound boundary" (*baddhasīmā*).
[It is invalid if it is] too small, too large, has broken signs, has signs consisting of shadows, has no signs,
is authorized while standing outside the boundary, is authorized across a river, is authorized across the ocean, is authorized across a lake, or if one boundary is made to intersect another boundary.
“Formally authorized,” meaning it was authorized by one who has completely encompassed the boundary with another boundary.
For these are called the eleven defective boundaries (*vipatti-sīmā*), based on the statement: “In eleven ways, formal acts (*kamma*) fail due to the boundary.

Among these, the "too small" (*atikhuddaka*) is where twenty-one monks cannot sit. The "too large" (*atimahatī*) is that which—even by as little as a hair’s breadth—[does not encompass the entire area].
It is authorized after having exceeded three *yojanas*. A "broken sign" (*khaṇḍanimitta*) is said to be an unconnected sign;

after designating a sign in the eastern direction, it is permissible to designate them in sequence in the southern, western, and northern directions, and then to designate back again toward the previously designated sign in the eastern direction and establish [the boundary]. Thus it is an "unbroken sign."

[This] occurs. However, if one brings [an object] gradually and, having defined the sign (*nimitta*) in the northern direction, places it right there, it is called a "broken sign" (*khaṇḍanimitta*). There is another kind of broken sign as well:
that which is designated by making a single sign between a tree with no heartwood (a "signless" tree), a stump, or a heap of dust or sand.

"Shadow-sign" (chāyānimittā) means that which is agreed upon by making any kind of shadow, such as the shadow of a mountain, as the sign. "Signless" (animittā) means that which is agreed upon without describing any signs whatsoever.
"Agreed upon while standing outside the boundary" (bahisīme ṭhitasammatā) means that which is agreed upon by one standing outside the signs after the signs have been described.
"Agreed upon in a river, the ocean, or a lake" means in these [locations].

[Boundaries] such as rivers and the like are considered [natural boundaries]. For even though that [river] is thus considered [a boundary], it is indeed not considered [as a formal boundary] because of the statement:
"Bhikkhus, every river is without a boundary; every ocean is without a boundary; every lake is without a boundary.
When one merges a boundary with another boundary, it is called "considered" when one merges the boundary of others with one's own boundary. For if [the case of] the ancient...
To the east of the monastery, there were two trees, a mango tree and a rose-apple tree, whose branches were intertwined with one another;
among them, the rose-apple tree was on the western side, and the boundary of the monastery was established by including the rose-apple tree within it and excluding the mango tree.
Later, when a monastery was built to the east of that [original] monastery...
When monks are binding a boundary, they bind it by including that mango tree within and excluding the rose-apple tree; thus the boundary becomes intermingled with the other boundary.
By "overlapping the boundary with the boundary" is meant: by one who has formally established his own boundary so as to overlap the boundaries of others.
For if he [overlaps] the entire boundary already bound by others, or even a portion of it...
Or, having made [a certain point] the limit, one establishes one’s own boundary; this is called "overlapping the boundary with the boundary.
Thus, these eleven types of defective boundaries have been established by transcending them.
They are endowed with the threefold perfection: perfection of the signs, perfection of the assembly, and perfection of the formal act (kammavācā).
"Appropriate. In this context, "appropriate by way of the excellence of the sign" refers to the eight signs mentioned as follows:

the mountain sign, the rock sign, the forest sign, the tree sign, the path sign, the anthill sign, the river sign, and the water sign—namely, those signs suitable for meditation that have been obtained in their respective directions and locations.
“‘What is the sign in the eastern direction? Venerable sir, this mountain is the sign,’ and so on;
having praised it correctly in such a manner, they are agreed upon. In this regard, the one who has reached the sign (*nimittūpaga*) should be understood briefly as follows:
a mountain—whether consisting of pure earth, pure rock, or a mixture of both—is a ‘sign-reacher’ when it is larger than the size of an elephant, while anything smaller than that is not.”
It is not permitted. Even an iron ball on a stone landmark is considered a stone;

therefore, any stone that, by way of maximum size, begins from something smaller than the measure of an elephant and, as a minimum limit, is the size of a lump of thirty-two palas of clay, qualifies as a landmark, but nothing smaller than that.
However, a flat stone (piṭṭhipāsāṇa) is permitted even if it is very large. Regarding a forest landmark:
A forest consisting of even four or five trees that have heartwood or are mixed with heartwood is sufficient for the purpose of the sign;

less than that is not permitted. A tree that still has heartwood and is established in the ground—even if it is only eight finger-breadths in height and as thin as the shaft of a needle—is sufficient for the purpose of the sign; anything smaller than that is not.

It is not permissible. Whether it be a path for walking or a cart road, if it passes through two or three village fields, such a path is considered a "sign-source" (*nimittupaga*) only when it is actually used by foot-travelers or carts; if it is not so used, it is not permissible.
As for an anthill, even one as small as a cow's horn, provided it has been produced that very day, is permissible down to a minimum height of eight finger-breadths.

An anthill that has become a landmark is not permitted if it is smaller than that. Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of an unbound boundary (*abaddhasīmā*), the river we shall describe is a landmark; any other is not permitted.

As for water—that which stands still in pits, lotus ponds, tanks, natural lakes, salt marshes, the ocean, and so forth—starting from that, even down to a pit dug in the earth at that very moment and filled with jars:
Even when filled, that which reaches up to the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*) is "standing still" (*saṇṭhamānaka*) and possesses the characteristic mark;
anything else—whether flowing, not remaining for the duration of the stated limit, or contained in a vessel—is not permissible.
Regarding the perfection of the assembly, it is said to be "properly endowed" when, at the very least, four monks have gathered together.

As many monks as are standing within that village boundary—whether it be a fixed boundary, or one defined by a river, the ocean, or a lake—without having stepped outside [the boundary], they are all considered duly authorized either by being within arm’s reach of one another or by having brought their consent (*chanda*).
They are said to be "fit for the perfection of the formal act" (*kammavācā*) when [the proclamation begins]: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me; as far as the surrounding signs..."

It is to be understood as a "bound boundary" (*baddhasīmā*) when it has been established by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakammavācā*) that is pure according to the method stated in the passage beginning with "proclaimed," and which,
having transcended the eleven boundaries of failure, is endowed with the threefold success and connects one landmark with another.
Its subdivisions are the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*), the boundary of common affiliation (*samānasaṃvāsasīmā*), and the boundary of non-separation (*avippavāsasīmā*).

The unbonded boundary (*abaddhasīmā*), however, is threefold: the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*), the seven-abhyantara boundary (*sattabbhantarasīmā*), and the water-splash boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*).

Among these, as far as a single village field extends, this is called the village boundary. In a forest devoid of villages, the area extending seven *abbhantaras* all around is called the seven-abhyantara boundary.
Therein, "devoid of villages" refers to a forest such as the Viñjhāṭavi or the like, or in the midst of the ocean.
Or it is found among fishermen on lamp-posts along paths where no one travels.

"Seven *abbhantara*s all around" means that for those standing in the center, there are seven *abbhantara*s in every direction, which amounts to fourteen by calculation. Therein, one *abbhantara* measures twenty-eight cubits;
and this boundary increases according to the size of the assembly, therefore [it extends] all around.

The internal boundary must be established starting from the edge of the assembly. However, if two separate Saṅghas perform the Uposatha separately, one *sattabbhantara* (the distance of seven fathoms) should be set aside between the two *sattabbhantaras* for the purpose of a buffer zone (*upacāra*).
Furthermore, regarding the status of rivers and such as boundaries, according to the method stated in the passage beginning, "Monks, all rivers are not boundaries," etc., [the following applies].

Having rejected that, it was further stated: "Monks, whether in a river, in the ocean, or in a lake, the area within the distance of a splash of water from a man of medium height—this is the boundary for common affiliation and a single *uposatha* ceremony therein.
This is what is called a water-splash boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*). Within that, during the time of righteous kings, every half-month and every ten days...
If, after five days have passed, the rain falls from the clouds and the flow ceases as soon as the clouds have vanished,
this does not count as a river. However, that river whose flow does not cease during the four months of the rainy season—
even during such a period of good rainfall— and where, by way of a ford or a non-ford, one arrives at the point of training (sikkhākaraṇīya) according to the established characteristic...

If, while covering the circle of the navel and without having tucked up the inner robe, even a single finger’s breadth of the inner robe becomes wet for a nun who is crossing over, she may enter either the ocean or a pond; from its source onwards, it is called a river.
The ocean is indeed well known. However, a pool that has not been made by anyone digging, but has arisen naturally, on all sides—
It remains filled with water brought from elsewhere; that place where water collects in a river during the aforementioned rainy season is called a "natural lake" (*jātassara*).
Furthermore, a pool excavated by water that has emerged after breaking through a river or the ocean also attains this characteristic; this too is indeed a natural lake.
"Within the range of a water-splash of a man of medium strength" means: that area which is delimited on all sides by the water-splash of a man of medium physical strength;
there, just as dice-players throw a wooden ball, so too, having taken either water or sand in the hand, it should be thrown with full force by a man of medium strength.
In that regard, wherever water or sand thrown thus falls, this is called a "water-boundary" (*udakukkhepa*).
This is a boundary delimited by the throwing of water in those rivers and so forth, which is both of common affiliation (*samānasaṃvāsa*) and of a single observance day (*ekūposatha*);
however, this [boundary] is obtained only within the interior of these rivers and so forth.

Not outside. Therefore, from whatever area of a river or lake is flooded by water during the four months of the normal rainy season, or from whatever place in the ocean the natural waves roll in and settle, that is the *kappiya-bhūmi* (permissible ground).
Standing there, it is allowable to perform the Uposatha and other rituals. During times of drought...
Whether in winter or in summer, even when the rivers and lakes have dried up, that very place remains a *kappiyabhūmi* (a ground where food may be prepared).
However, if they dig a well or a pond in a dried-up lake or reservoir, or if they cultivate crops there, that spot becomes village-field territory (*gāmakkhetta*).

Furthermore, the *udakukkhepasīmā* (the boundary determined by the range of a water-splash) does not extend beyond what is called the *kappiyabhūmi*; it extends only within it. Therefore, [whatever is] inside those [boundaries]—
Starting from the edge of the assembly, a boundary defined by the throwing of water should be established all around.

However, if two Saṅghas perform separate Uposatha and other formal acts, another single "throwing of water" boundary should be placed between the two water-boundaries for the purpose of defining their respective precincts.
For this is both the seven-fathom boundary and the water-throwing boundary for the bhikkhus.
It is obtained starting from the point where one stands within the boundary.
Even if one stands outside the boundary, provided one does not step beyond another boundary of exactly that same extent, one still invalidates the act;
this is the settled conclusion in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). Thus should the unbonded boundary be understood. In this way, by way of the bonded and unbonded boundaries—
This was said with reference to two kinds of boundaries: “And they must remain within arm’s reach, standing within a single boundary.

For when those four bhikkhus are standing within a single boundary without having left arm’s reach, this Uposatha ceremony of the Saṅgha is said to be “fit” (pattakalla); not otherwise. As it is said: “I allow you, bhikkhus...”
"...to recite the Pātimokkha for the four [assemblies].

Regarding the phrase "and there are no common offenses" (*sabhāgāpattiyo*): here, when the entire Saṅgha incurs a light offense through a common basis such as eating at the improper time (*vikālabhojana*), such a similarity of basis is called "common" (*sabhāga*). Due to the cause of eating at the improper time...
However, it is permissible to confess an offense that has been incurred—which is of a similar nature—to one who has also incurred an offense on account of eating non-leftover food.
But when there is a common offense, those monks should immediately dispatch a single monk from a neighboring residence, saying:
"Go, friend; having dealt with that offense, return, and we shall deal with our own offenses in your presence."
If this can be obtained, that is good; if it cannot be obtained, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This entire Saṅgha has fallen into a common offense.
When it sees another monk who is pure and free from offense, then [it shall confess] that offense in his presence."
Having said, "I will make amends for it," the Uposatha should be performed. But if he is uncertain, he should say, "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me:
this entire Saṅgha is uncertain regarding a shared offense;
when I become certain, I will then make amends for that offense," and having said this, the Uposatha should be performed. But if anyone there...
If one confesses an offense to another person, thinking that it is permissible to confess a *sabhāga* (similar) offense [to someone of the same class], the confession is indeed well-confessed.

However, because the one who confesses does so on account of the act of confessing, and the one who receives it does so on account of the act of receiving, both incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Since that offense arises from different bases, they must confess to one another; at this point, those two are free from offense.
They exist; in their presence, the remaining similar offenses should be confessed or announced.

If they perform the Uposatha without doing so—by following the procedure beginning with "Venerable sirs, announce your purity"—they incur the dukkaṭa offense prescribed for performing the Uposatha while possessing an offense.
If the entire Saṅgha [is likewise affected] when a similar offense exists...
If one performs the Uposatha without following the prescribed procedure, the entire Saṅgha incurs an offense according to that very method;
therefore, when there is a common offense (sabhāgāpatti), it is said that it is not "fitting for the Saṅgha" (pattakalla). For this reason, it is stated:
"And common offenses do not exist. This is because, even when these common offenses are absent, though dissimilar offenses (visabhāgāpatti) may be present—
It is indeed appropriate.
Since there are no persons who should be excluded present there, [it is said]: "Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited in an assembly that includes householders;
whoever should recite it incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). From this statement, a householder... "Monks, [it should not be recited]..."

A nun, a trainee nun (sikkhamānā), a male novice (sāmaṇera), a female novice (sāmaṇerī), one who has renounced the training, one who has committed an offense involving defeat (antimavatthu), one suspended for not seeing an offense, one suspended for not making amends for an offense, and one who does not relinquish a pernicious view— these are the persons mentioned by way of the method beginning with: "The Pātimokkha should be recited in an assembly where a nun is seated."

The twenty-one persons who are to be avoided— namely, one who has been suspended (ukkhitto), a eunuch (paṇḍako), one living in communion by theft (theyyasaṃvāsako), one who has gone over to another sect (titthiyapakkantako),
an animal (tiracchānagato), a matricide (mātughātako), a patricide (pitughātako), a murderer of an arahant (arahantaghātako), a defiler of a bhikkhunī (bhikkhunidūsako), a schismatic (saṅghabhedako),
one who has shed the blood of a Buddha (lohituppādako), and one with both sexual organs (ubhatobyañjanako)— are to be excluded by being kept outside the reach of one’s hand.
They are to be avoided. For if the Saṅgha performs the Uposatha while these three types of suspended persons (ukkhitaka) are present, it incurs a Pācittiya offense;
in the remaining cases, a Dukkaṭa offense. And here, "an animal" refers to one for whom full ordination is prohibited;
the members of other sects (titthiya) are included among householders. These too are indeed called "persons to be avoided. Thus, [the assembly is] fit [to perform the ceremony] by means of these.
It should be understood that [the Uposatha] is comprised of four factors.

By the phrase "the Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha," those other three types of Uposatha mentioned according to the performing agent—the Uposatha in the Saṅgha, the Uposatha in a group (gaṇa), and the Uposatha for an individual (puggala)—are referred to; among these, the other two...
Having rejected [the other forms], he explains the Uposatha in the Saṅgha as the recitation of the Sutta itself.

By the phrase "one should recite the Pātimokkha," he excludes the other three types of Uposatha—the Suttuddesa, the Pārisuddhi-uposatha, and the Adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha—which were mentioned as the three ways in which the Uposatha is to be performed;
among these, he specifies only the Suttuddesa. This is the Suttuddesa.
What is called the recitation of the Pātimokkha is twofold: the recitation of the Pātimokkha as exhortation and the recitation of the Pātimokkha as injunction. Therein, [the former begins]:
"Patience is the supreme austerity; forbearance...
and "...the non-doing of all evil... and so forth.
The three verses beginning with “No reviling, no harming” are called the *ovāda-pātimokkha* (the exhortation precept); these are recited by Buddhas alone, not by disciples.
That which is spoken in the manner beginning with “Let the Saṅgha listen to me, venerable sirs” is called the *āṇā-pātimokkha* (the command precept).
The disciples alone recite this, not the Buddhas; and it is precisely this that is intended by the term "Pātimokkha" in this context.
As for the other two types of Uposatha, first, the Uposatha of purification (pārisuddhi-uposatha) is twofold: that performed in the presence of others and that performed through mutual announcement.
Regarding these, that which is performed in the presence of others applies also to those who have already performed the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā).

It is twofold by way of performing it in the presence of those who have not been invited [to the invitation ceremony]. Therein, having granted bodily concord (*kāyasāmaggi*) in the presence of those who have been invited at the Great Invitation (*mahāpavāraṇā*)—

whether one has entered the later rains-residence (*pacchimikā*), whether one has not entered it, or whether one’s rains-residence has been interrupted— and in the presence of those who have been invited at the four-monthly invitation (*cātumāsiniyā*),
whether one has entered the earlier rains-residence (*purimikā*), whether one has not entered it, or whether one’s rains-residence has been interrupted...
Having said three times, "Venerable sir, I am pure; let you remember me as 'pure,'" it should be performed.

However, except on the day of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), at other times, when the *pātimokkha* has been recited by the resident monks, whether the assembly has not yet risen, or some have risen, or all have risen, those others who are equal...
Or if fewer than that number arrive, they should announce their purity in the presence of those who are there, according to the method already stated.
Furthermore, this procedure performed by means of mutual announcement is twofold: it is carried out either by means of a formal motion (*ñatti*) being established or not being established.
In that regard, when three monks dwell in a certain monastery, on the Uposatha day—
When they have assembled, one monk, having said, "Venerable sirs, listen to me; today is the Uposatha of the fourteenth" or "the fifteenth," and having established the motion with the words,

"If it seems appropriate to the venerable ones, let us perform the Uposatha of mutual purification," the senior monk should arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, sit in the kneeling posture, and...
Having raised his hands in reverential salutation (*añjali*), he should say three times: "Friends, I am pure; may you consider me to be 'pure'.
The others, having said "Venerable Sir," should speak in the same manner. Having thus laid down the motion (*ñatti*), it should be performed.
However, where two monks reside, the purity should be declared according to the stated method without laying down a motion.
"It should be announced" refers to this *pārisuddhi-uposatha* (uposatha by means of a declaration of purity).
However, if there is only one monk, he should perform all the preliminary duties,
ascertain that no others have arrived, and having said, "Today is my Uposatha on the fourteenth" or "on the fifteenth," he should say, "I resolve [it]."
"This is the Uposatha by formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha*). Thus, it should be understood that there are three kinds of Uposatha according to the manner in which they are to be performed.

At this point, nine types of Uposatha have been illustrated. Among these, the Uposatha characterized by three features—namely, by way of the day as the fifteenth, by way of the agent as the Saṅgha-Uposatha, and by way of the manner of performance as the recitation of the Sutta—is what is explained here.
It should be understood as follows: while that [state] is occurring, if one does not observe the Uposatha and, on that Uposatha day, goes for the purpose of staying—
except with a Saṅgha or except due to obstacles— to another monastery that is without monks, or to a residence or non-residence belonging to those of a different communion,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
What is the prior duty of the Saṅgha? It refers to that which has been handed down in the Canon by way of such passages as,

“I allow you, monks, to sweep the Uposatha hall,” and so forth, concerning what is to be done by the Saṅgha when the Uposatha is to be performed— this being stated in connection with the performance of the Uposatha itself,
namely, “The Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha”— as well as that which appears in the Commentaries.
“The broom, the lamp, water, and the seat—
these are called the ‘preliminary duties’ (pubbakaraṇa) for the Uposatha. The declaration of consent,
the purity of the monks, the announcement of the season, the counting of the monks, and the exhortation.”
“These are called the ‘preliminary duties’ (pubbakicca) for the Uposatha.
Thus, the ninefold preliminary duty has been shown by two names. One asks: “What is that which must be done?
For it is not permissible to perform the Uposatha without having performed that; therefore, a monk who is not ill and has been instructed by the Elder [should go] to the Uposatha hall.
The floor must be swept, drinking water and washing water must be set out, a seat must be prepared, and a lamp must be lit;
one who fails to do so incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Even the senior monk (*thera*), having recognized what is appropriate, must give the instruction.

Regarding "confession of consent and purity" (*chandapārisuddhi*): here, when the Saṅgha has assembled for the purpose of performing the Uposatha, [one may perform] the Uposatha outside [the boundary].
Having arrived, one who has gone to the place of assembly but does not grant physical presence must give consent (*chanda*).
Even one who is ill or occupied with duties must also give consent by granting formal purity (*pārisuddhi*). How is it to be given?
In the presence of another monk, saying: "I give consent; take my consent; announce my consent. This...
The meaning must be communicated by body, by speech, or by both; in this way, consent (*chanda*) is given.
However, one who has not observed the Uposatha, or is ill, or is preoccupied with duties, must give their purity (*pārisuddhi*). How is it to be given? In the presence of another monk, saying:
“I give my purity; take my purity; announce my purity”—this is the meaning.
It must be communicated either by body, by speech, or by both; in this way, the *pārisuddhi* (declaration of purity) is given.

Furthermore, when giving it, one's consent (*chanda*) must also be given. For this was said by the Blessed One: "I allow you, monks, on that very Uposatha day, while giving *pārisuddhi*, to also give consent, for there may be business for the Saṅgha. In this context, the giving of *pārisuddhi*...
One accomplishes the observance day (uposatha) for both the Saṅgha and oneself, but not the remaining duties of the Saṅgha.
By giving consent (chandadāna), one accomplishes the observance day for the Saṅgha as well as its other duties, yet one's own observance day remains unperformed.
Therefore, by one who gives formal purity (pārisuddhi), consent must also be given. As for the "pure consent" (suddhikacchanda) mentioned previously:
Or, it is permissible for one person to bring back the consent (*chanda*) or the purity (*pārisuddhi*) of many people.

However, if that person, while on the way, sees another monk and gives his own consent and purity to both those monks to whom he had received theirs and to himself, then the consent and purity belong to him alone;
the others' consent and purity, however, become like a cat’s chain (*biḷālasaṅkhalikā*).
If she is present by name but does not come, he himself must go to the place where they have assembled and announce it.

If, however, he intentionally fails to announce it, he incurs a dukkaṭa offense. As for the consent and purity (chandapārisuddhi), these are considered conveyed as soon as he has merely entered the reach of their hands.
"Announcement of the season" means the proclamation of the seasons, such as "so much of the winter season and so forth has passed, so much remains.
"Counting the bhikkhus" means the counting of the bhikkhus, such as "this many bhikkhus have assembled in the Uposatha hall.
Indeed, the Uposatha must be performed only after both of these have been done. "Exhortation" refers to the exhortation of the bhikkhunīs; for [without it], it is not [valid].
It is permissible to perform the Uposatha without announcing the exhortation requested by the bhikkhunīs.

For the bhikkhunīs, having arrived [on the previous day] thinking, "Tomorrow is the Uposatha," and having asked, "Is this the Uposatha of the fourteenth or the fifteenth?", they return again on the Uposatha day [to say]:
"Venerable sirs, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha pays homage at the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and requests the approach for the exhortation."
"Venerable sir, may the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha receive the invitation to attend the exhortation"—thus do they request the exhortation.
Apart from one who is ignorant, ill, or pregnant, no other person—even if he is a forest-dweller—is permitted to refuse it;
therefore, by the monk who has accepted it, at the Uposatha hall, the monk who recites the Pātimokkha should be addressed as follows:
He should say: "Venerable sirs, the community of bhikkhunīs pays homage at the feet of the community of bhikkhus and requests the approach for exhortation;
may the community of bhikkhunīs, venerable sirs, receive the approach for exhortation. The reciter of the Pātimokkha should ask:
"Is there any bhikkhu appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs? If there is such a bhikkhu...
If one has been appointed as the instructor of the bhikkhunīs, he should then say to them: "The bhikkhu named so-and-so has been appointed as the instructor of the bhikkhunīs;
let the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs approach him. If there is no such person, he should ask:
"Which venerable one is able to instruct the bhikkhunīs? If someone is able, he too—provided he possesses the eight [qualities]—should be appointed.
Having authorized one who possesses these qualities right there, the recipient of the exhortation should be told:
"The monk named so-and-so has been authorized as the exhorter of the bhikkhunīs; let the community of bhikkhunīs approach him.
But if no one is willing, the reciter of the Pātimokkha should say: "There is no monk who has been authorized as the exhorter of the bhikkhunīs."
“May the community of bhikkhunīs be established in what is inspiring. For up to this point, the entire Dispensation, comprised within the three trainings, has been announced.
Having accepted with “Very well,” that bhikkhu should announce it to the bhikkhunīs on the first day of the fortnight (the *pāṭipada*).
The community of bhikkhunīs should also dispatch those bhikkhunīs, saying: “Go, noble ladies, and ask: ‘What, noble lady, [is the date]?’”

When [the messenger] asks, "Does the community of bhikkhunīs obtain the opportunity to approach for exhortation?", those [bhikkhunīs] should accept it by saying, "Very well, noble sir," and having approached that bhikkhu, they should speak thus: "What is it, noble sir, that the community of bhikkhunīs obtains regarding the approach for exhortation?
He should say, "There is no bhikkhu appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs; let the community of bhikkhunīs [approach] with inspiring confidence."
“May she prepare it,” they should accept with “Very well, Noble Lady. This is stated with reference to two or three who have come together.
Among them, however, one bhikkhunī must both speak and accept, while the others are her companions.
But if either the Saṅgha of bhikkhus or the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs is not complete, from both sides—
Or it may be merely a group or merely an individual. In this regard, the sequence of words is as follows:
“Noble sirs, the bhikkhunīs pay homage at the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and request the approach for the exhortation;
may the bhikkhunīs, noble sirs, receive the approach for the exhortation,” [and] “I, noble sir, [request] the Bhikkhu Saṅgha...”
“I pay homage at your feet, and I request the opportunity to approach for instruction; may I receive it, noble lady, the opportunity to approach for instruction.
“The community of bhikkhunīs, noble lady, pays homage at the feet of the noble ladies and requests the opportunity to approach for instruction;
may the community of bhikkhunīs indeed receive the opportunity to approach for instruction, noble lady. “The bhikkhunīs, noble lady, [pay homage] at the feet of the noble ladies...”
“They pay homage and request the approach for instruction, saying: ‘May the nuns, noble sirs, receive the approach for instruction. [The monk says:
‘I, noble sirs, pay homage at the feet of the noble ones and request the approach for instruction; may I, noble sirs, receive the approach for instruction. [The monk says:
‘The Saṅgha of nuns, noble sir, pays homage at the feet of the noble one and requests the approach for instruction.’”
“Venerable sir, let the community of bhikkhunīs receive the opportunity to approach for exhortation.
“Venerable sir, the bhikkhunīs pay homage at your feet and request the opportunity to approach for exhortation; let the bhikkhunīs, venerable sir, receive the opportunity to approach for exhortation.
“Venerable sir, I pay homage at your feet and request the opportunity to approach for exhortation.”
“Venerable sir, may we receive the opportunity to approach for instruction. That monk, at the time of the Uposatha, should speak thus:
“Venerable sir, the nuns pay homage at the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and request the opportunity to approach for instruction;
may the nuns, venerable sir, receive the opportunity to approach for instruction. “Venerable sir, the nun [requests] the Bhikkhu Saṅgha...”
She bows at his feet and requests permission to approach for instruction, saying: "Venerable sir, may the bhikkhunī receive permission to approach for instruction.
[The bhikkhunī says: "Venerable sir, the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs... Venerable sir, the bhikkhunīs... Venerable sir, the bhikkhunī bows at the feet of the venerable ones;
they bow, she bows. They request, she requests permission to approach for instruction; may she receive it."
“Venerable sir, let the community of bhikkhunīs [be informed]; venerable sir, let the bhikkhunīs receive [the instruction]; venerable sir, let the bhikkhunīs come for the exhortation.

At the uposatha hall as well, whether by the reciter of the Pātimokkha, the proponent of the motion, or another bhikkhu—if there is a bhikkhu who has been appointed—he should, in the same manner as before, say: “The community of bhikkhunīs...”
It should be said: "Let that bhikkhunī approach; let those bhikkhunīs approach; let that bhikkhunī approach. If there is no such person, it should be said:
"May the bhikkhunī-saṅgha, O bhikkhunīs, accomplish this with inspiring grace; may they accomplish it; may she accomplish it.
The one who receives the exhortation, having returned on the first day of the fortnight, should speak in exactly the same way.
This is the brief analysis of this matter. Having thus announced the exhortation requested by the bhikkhunīs, the Uposatha should be performed.
Therefore it was said:
“Consent, purity, the announcement of the season, the number of bhikkhus, and the exhortation;”
"These are called the 'preliminary duties' for the Uposatha.
"Venerable sirs, announce your purity" means: announce your state of being pure. "I shall recite the Pātimokkha"—this is the statement of the reason for announcing one's purity.
"And, monks, one who has an offense should not listen to the Pātimokkha..."

For it is said: "Whoever should listen [to the Pātimokkha] while it is impure incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Therefore, it is not permitted to listen to the Pātimokkha when it is not pure.
That is why it was said: "Venerable sirs, announce your purity; I shall recite the Pātimokkha. Here, one might ask:
since it has been stated that "the Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha and should recite the Pātimokkha," does this [recitation] here also...
It should be said, "it will be recited," for in this way what precedes and what follows are connected. It is replied: this is merely a matter of phrasing;

it is not actually connected [in that sense], but it accords in terms of its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*). Through the harmony of the Saṅgha, through the harmony of the group, and through the recitation by an individual, the Pātimokkha becomes recited for the Saṅgha—this is the characteristic here. Therefore, [the text says] "Pātimokkha..."
"I shall recite"—this alone is what should be said here.
"All of you who are present, listen well and attend closely" refers to the Pātimokkha.
"All of you who are present" means as many as there are in that assembly—elders, novices, and those of middle standing. "Listen well" means with focused attention.
Having brought it to mind, we should attend to it with our whole heart by way of the door of the ear.
"We bring it to mind" means that, having become one-pointed in mind, we should establish it in the mind.

And here, although it might seem appropriate to say "Listen and bring it to mind" because it was said, "I shall recite the Pātimokkha," nevertheless, by the words "The Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha,"...
It does not agree. For this performance of the Uposatha belongs to a united Saṅgha, and the reciter of the Pātimokkha is also included within the Saṅgha;
therefore, because he is included in the Saṅgha, it is appropriate for him to say only, "We listen, we attend.
Now, as for what was said, "Venerable sirs, announce your purity," regarding that announcement of purity: ...just as the announcement of purity [is made]...

In order to show that [this is the case], he said: "He who may have an offense should disclose it. In this context, "he who may have" means one who might have committed an offense by any one of the six ways.

For when committing an offense, it occurs through lack of shame, ignorance, being overcome by remorse, perceiving what is improper as proper, perceiving what is proper as improper, or through forgetfulness.
One commits [an offense] in these six ways.
How does one commit it through lack of shame? Even while knowing that something is unallowable, one crushes it and transgresses.
And this has been said:
“He intentionally commits an offense, he conceals his offense, and he goes upon a wrong path—such a person is called one devoid of shame. How does one commit an offense through ignorance?

For a person who is ignorant, dull-witted, and deluded, not knowing what should and should not be done, performs what should not be done and fails in what should be done; thus one commits an offense through ignorance.
How does one incur an offense through being dominated by remorse? When remorse has arisen concerning what is allowable and what is unallowable, one should consult a master of the Vinaya;
if it is allowable, it may be done, but if it is unallowable, it must not be done.
Yet, this person disregards this by thinking, "It is permissible," and simply transgresses. In this way, one incurs an offense through being dominated by remorse.

How does one incur [an offense] through the perception of what is allowable in regard to what is unallowable? One eats the flesh of a bear, thinking it is "the flesh of a pig"; one eats at an improper time, perceiving it as the proper time. In this way, one incurs [an offense] through the perception of what is allowable in regard to what is unallowable. How does one incur [an offense] through the perception of what is unallowable in regard to what is allowable?

One eats the flesh of a pig, thinking it is "the flesh of a bear"; one eats at an improper time, perceiving it as the proper time. In this way, one incurs [an offense] through the perception of what is unallowable in regard to what is allowable. How does one incur [an offense] through forgetfulness?
One incurs offenses such as sleeping together [with a woman], being separated from one's robe, and so forth, through forgetfulness. Thus...
"By any one of these six modes" means by whichever mode [the offense] has been committed;
"of whichever of the seven classes of offenses it may be"—this refers to whether it belongs to an elder, a novice, or one of middle standing.
"He should reveal it" means he should confess that offense or make it manifest. "In the absence of an offense" means...
But for one who has not thus fallen into an offense, or who, having fallen into an offense, has emerged from it, confessed it, or reported it—that offense is said to be "non-existent.
Regarding such a non-existent offense, one should remain silent.
Indeed, by means of silence, we shall know that the venerable ones are "pure"; for it is by the very reason of their silence [that this is understood].
"I shall know that the venerable ones are indeed pure. Now, "as is the response when asked individually" means as one person, being asked by another, would answer;
it is said that just as one person, being asked individually, would answer upon knowing, "This person is questioning me."
"Even so, it has been announced up to three times for such an assembly. Regarding this, some teachers say:
"In this very same way, for this assembly of monks, [the announcement is made]: 'Whoever has an offense, let him reveal it;
one who has no offense should remain silent. By your silence, we shall know that the venerable ones are pure.'"

Thus, the correct interpretation is that the word *yāvatatiyaṃ* is an adverbial accusative meaning "up to the third time," and it qualifies the act of announcing (*anusāvite*). It indicates that the announcement must be repeated until the third time. This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "some" (*keci*) mentioned above: some teachers hold the view that the word *yāvatatiyaṃ* refers to the announcement made by the *samanubhāsaka*; others hold the view that it refers to the announcement made by the *ñattikāraka*; and still others hold the view that it refers to the recitation performed by the *pātimokkhuddesaka*. Therefore, the interpretation that the word *yāvatatiyaṃ* refers to the subsequent inquiry at the end of the recitation—"Is this assembly pure...? A third time I ask"—is also not tenable. Consequently, the word *yāvatatiyaṃ* must be understood as an adverbial accusative meaning "up to the third time," qualifying the act of announcing. It signifies that the announcement must be repeated until the third time. This is the established meaning. 1. Commentary on the First Pārājika:
"Whoever" (yo pana) refers to anyone, distinguished by gender and so forth through variations such as short or long vowels.

"A bhikkhu" (bhikkhu) refers to one who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*) either by the "Come, bhikkhu" formula, by going for refuge, by accepting instruction, by answering questions, or by accepting the eight weighty rules (*aṭṭha garudhammā*).
Among these eight types of ordination— the ordination by messenger, the ordination by eight proclamations,

and the ordination by a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three announcements— one is ordained by means of a formal act of ordination consisting of a motion followed by three announcements (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*), which is irreversible and fit for its purpose. Furthermore,
