In this context, "the basis" refers to a person seeking full ordination (*upasampadā*). This should be understood as excluding eleven types of persons incapable of the path:

those under twenty years of age from the time of conception, those who have previously committed any of the ultimate offenses (*antimavatthu*), and the eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*) and others. Here, "under twenty years of age" means having not completed twenty years since the moment of conception.
"One who has previously committed an ultimate offense" refers to one who has committed any of the four *pārājika* [offenses].
He was previously one who had committed another [offense]. Eunuchs and others are mentioned in the discussion on persons to be avoided.

Among them, excluding the *āsittapaṇḍaka* (the drenched eunuch) and the *usūyapaṇḍaka* (the jealous eunuch), what is intended here is the *opakkamikapaṇḍaka* (the surgically-caused eunuch), the *napuṃsakapaṇḍaka* (the natural eunuch), and the *pakkhapaṇḍaka* (the occasional eunuch) who remains on the side of the eunuch-nature.
A "thievish co-resident" (theyyasaṃvāsaka), however, is of three kinds: one who takes the outward signs, one who takes the communal life, and one who takes both.

Among these, he who, having gone forth himself, does not count his years as a bhikkhu, does not accept salutation from bhikkhus or sāmaṇeras according to seniority, does not yield his seat, and does not appear at the Uposatha and other ceremonies—this person, due to impure intent, [is a thievish co-resident].

One who is merely wearing the marks [of a monk] because they have been stolen is called a *liṅgatthenaka*. However, one who was ordained by monks as a novice (*sāmaṇera*), but having removed his saffron robes,
engages in sexual intercourse with them while still intent upon doing so, and then puts on those robes again and claims the status of a novice—
this person is not a *liṅgatthenaka*, because the marks bestowed by the monks have not been relinquished.
He is neither one who has consented to co-residence corresponding to his gender, nor is he one who merely shares co-residence.

The same principle applies even to one who has committed an offense involving the ultimate category (*antimavatthu*). However, a novice (*sāmaṇera*) who, having gone abroad, counts his years as a monk, accepts salutations according to seniority, takes precedence over seats, and appears at the Uposatha and other ceremonies—this [novice] possesses only the mere fact of co-residence.

Therefore, it is called "co-residence" (*saṃvāsa*) in the sense of living together. Indeed, in this context, every variety of activity—beginning with the counting of a bhikkhu’s years since ordination—is to be understood as "co-residence.
The same principle applies even to one who, having renounced the training (*sikkhā*), acts again in such a manner [as a monk] thinking, "No one knows me.
However, for one who has gone forth himself and, having entered a monastery, performs the salutation according to seniority (*yathāvuḍḍha*), [this does not constitute co-residence].
He accepts [offerings], he refuses a seat, he counts the years of seniority for monks, and he appears at the Uposatha and other ceremonies;
because he has stolen both the outward mark and the communal life, he is called "one who steals both.
The same applies to one who, by way of abandoning his responsibility, removes his saffron robes, commits a final offense, and then puts them back on again, practicing in this manner.
This threefold person is what is intended here as one who dwells in communion through theft. However, setting aside these three types,
whoever here assumes the outward signs [of a monk] out of fear of the king, famine, wilderness, disease, or enemies, or for the sake of obtaining robes— [that person is also included].
“As long as one does not consent to co-residence, provided that his mind is pure,
for that long he is not called a ‘one who lives in theft’ (theyyasaṃvāsaka).
However, one who has been fully ordained and, desiring the state of a heretic, himself adopts the outward mark of a heretic such as a garment of kusa grass, etc., [is indeed a theyyasaṃvāsaka].

One who adopts [the practices] from them, or goes forth in their presence, or having gone naked to the Ājīvakas and adopts their vows—this is called one who has gone over to another sect (titthiyapakkantaka).

One who, like Devadatta, with a wicked mind and a murderous intent, [inflicts harm] upon the living body of the Tathāgata—even as much as the drinking of a tiny fly...

It is unshakable by way of the perfection of the subject matter (*vatthusampatti*). How is it unshakable by way of the perfection of the motion (*ñattisampatti*)?

First, there are five defects of the motion: the failure to avoid misconceptions regarding the subject matter, the Saṅgha, the individual, and the motion itself, and the subsequent formalizing of the motion. In that regard, [regarding the first defect], concerning one who seeks full ordination, [saying] "this person named so-and-so..."

The failure to mention the subject matter (*vatthu*) is called non-specification of the subject matter (*vatthu-aparāmasana*). In the phrase, “Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs,” to say “Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs” but fail to say “the Sangha” is called non-specification of the Sangha (*saṅgha-aparāmasana*).

To fail to mention the preceptor by saying, “He seeks ordination from such-and-such a person,” is called non-specification of the individual (*puggala-aparāmasana*). The complete failure to recite the formal motion (*ñatti*) in its entirety is [non-specification of the motion].

“Misapprehension regarding the motion” means as follows: having completed the first formal act (kammavācā) and said, “This is the motion,” to then proclaim the motion by saying, “It is pleasing to the Saṅgha,” is what is called “establishing the motion afterwards.
Thus, when a motion is free from these faults, it is unshakeable due to its perfection through the proper accomplishment of the motion.
There are five faults of the proclamation (*anussāvana*): non-adherence to the matter, the Saṅgha, and the individual for the sake of its being unshakeable; omitting the proclamation;
and proclaiming at an improper time. Among these, the non-adherence to the matter and so forth are exactly as described in relation to the motion (*ñatti*).
However, regarding the three proclamations, in any one of them, the failure to adhere to these [requirements] constitutes non-adherence.
However, failing to recite the formal act (*kammavācā*) in its entirety, but merely proclaiming the motion (*ñatti*) four times;
or, within the formal act itself, the non-recitation or faulty recitation of a syllable or a phrase, is what is meant by "omission of the proclamation" (*sāvanāya hāpana*).
To perform the subsequent proclamations without first establishing the motion at the proper time—that is, performing them out of place—is "acting at the wrong time" (*akāle*).
This is called the proclamation (*anussāvana*). Thus, for a proclamation that is free from these defects, it is unshakeable by virtue of the perfection of the proclamation.
Furthermore, for an act performed within a boundary that has transcended the previously mentioned characteristics of failure and limits, it is unshakeable by virtue of the perfection of the boundary.
[It is also unshakeable] when there is no arrival of as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the formal act (*kamma*), nor of those who are entitled to give their consent (*chanda*).
Non-acceptance [of the candidate] and the protestation of those present—these are the three defects of an assembly.

When an act is performed by an assembly free from these, it becomes unshakable by virtue of the excellence of the assembly. Furthermore, because it is worthy of the cause and worthy of the Teacher’s instruction, it is called "worthy of the occasion" (*ṭhānāraha*).
Thus, that which is performed by means of this unshakable, occasion-worthy formal act of ordination consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatuttha*)—
One who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*) is intended here by the term "monk" (*bhikkhu*). However, others besides those excluded by formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*) are also included.
"Having entered upon the training and the way of life of the monks" means:
that training of the monks known as higher virtue (*adhisīla*), and that wherein they live together—sharing a single livelihood and living in common—was prescribed by the Blessed One.

The "way of life" (*sājīva*) consists of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*); one who has entered into that by way of practicing the training is "one who has entered upon the training and way of life of the bhikkhus.
"Has entered" means that, while fulfilling the training and not transgressing the way of life, he has approached both of these.
"Without renouncing the training or disclosing weakness" means without rejecting the training upon which he has entered.

And regarding that one who has entered upon the way of livelihood (*sājīva*), it should be understood that there is no renunciation of the training (*sikkhā*) in the absence of weakness [in the intention], provided that one does not manifest such weakness therein.

In this regard, having understood the renunciation of the training by way of the mind, the field, the time, the application, and the person, its non-renunciation should be known through the absence of those factors. How so?

For the renunciation of the training occurs only with a mind desiring to fall away from the state of being fully ordained (*upasampanna*); it does not occur for one speaking in jest or in a loud voice.
Thus, the renunciation of the training occurs by way of the mind, not through the mere absence of those factors.
Likewise: "I renounce the Buddha; I renounce the Dhamma; I renounce the Saṅgha; the training; the Vinaya; the Pātimokkha; the recitation;
the preceptor; the teacher; the co-resident pupil; the pupil living under one's care; one who shares the same preceptor; one who shares the same teacher."
Of these twenty-two fields of merit (khettapada): namely, the fourteen beginning with the Buddha, who were addressed with the words, “I renounce my fellow-celibates” (sabrahmacāriṃ paccakkhāmi);

and the eight beginning with the householder, who were addressed with the words, “Regard me as a householder, a lay follower (upāsaka), a monastery attendant (ārāmika), a novice (sāmaṇera), a member of another sect (titthiya), a disciple of another sect (titthiyasāvaka), one who is not an ascetic (asamaṇa), or one who is not a son of the Sakyan (asakyaputtiya). By means of any expression whatsoever, for one who wishes to say anything among those [objects] and says anything at all, there is a renunciation of the training;
it does not occur for one who renounces by taking the name of a particular tree or the like. Thus, the renunciation occurs by way of the field, not by way of its absence.
In this context, there is the expression in the present tense, namely “I renounce” (*paccakkhāmī*) and “hold me” (*maṃ dhārehi*);

and there are those statements expressed by way of the verb without specifying time— such as “Enough for me with the Buddha,” “What need have I of the Buddha,” “I have no use for the Buddha,” and “I am well-liberated from the Buddha”—
which are joined with the preceding fourteen phrases.
The four phrases beginning with “Enough for me” constitute the renunciation itself by way of their synonyms;

it is not the case for one who utters past, future, or hypothetical expressions such as “He has renounced,” “He will renounce,” “Hold me [as his wife],” “He will hold me [as his wife],” or “What if I were to renounce? and so forth.
In this way, the renunciation occurs by means of both the present time and an unspecified time, and not by the absence of those [times].

Furthermore, the application is twofold: physical and verbal. Therein, by making a vocal utterance in any language whatsoever according to the method beginning with "I renounce the Buddha," the renunciation occurs through verbal application alone; it does not consist of writing down syllables.
or making a bodily exertion such as showing hand gestures and so forth—in this way, the renunciation occurs through verbal exertion alone, not in its absence.
Furthermore, the person is twofold: he who renounces and he to whom one renounces. Regarding these, he who renounces—
Thus, provided that he is not one who is insane, deranged, or overwhelmed by pain;

and provided that the person to whom he renounces is of human birth, is not one who is insane or otherwise disqualified, and is present in person for the renunciation of the training—since a declaration made to one who is not present, whether by messenger or by letter, is not valid. Thus, by way of the persons as described above...
There is a renunciation, not by way of their absence.
Consciousness (vijānana) is also twofold, according to whether it is determined or undetermined.

In that regard, when one determines for whom or for which [beings] and says, "I shall announce this to him" or "to these," if those people, having heard the words as they normally do in the world, at the moment of adverting—

If they understand—immediately after his speech, in whatever manner they recognize that "this person is dissatisfied" or "he aspires to the state of a householder"—that he has renounced the training, then the training is indeed renounced.

There is training. However, for one who declares it without specifying [the person], if anyone of human birth understands the meaning of the words in the manner described, the training is indeed renounced.
Thus, renunciation occurs by way of such understanding, not merely through the absence of that [understanding].

Either by way of the mind and so forth of the aforementioned types, or else by not renouncing the training in its entirety— that is,
having not renounced the training and without disclosing some degree of weakness that constitutes the actual state of having renounced the training—
one might "engage in sexual intercourse. Herein, "sexual intercourse" refers to those things similar [to it] through the obsession of lust.
"Both kinds of things. "Should practice" means he should practice or commit. "At the very least" means by the ultimate limit.

this is an additional rule (anupaññatti) here. "Is one who has committed a defeat" means he is defeated, he has fallen into defeat. "One who is no longer in communion" means [one who is no longer in communion] with those of natural status.

For in the formal acts of the Saṅgha, he does not even serve as one who completes the quorum. This, first of all, is the word-by-word commentary. As for the detailed analysis here:
there are three types of women, categorized as human, non-human, and animal. Of these...

However, for the sake of the common determination (*sādhāraṇa-vinicchaya*) of all training rules (*sikkhāpada*), there is this summary table (*mātikā*):
The source (*nidāna*), the person (*puggala*), the subject matter (*vatthu*), and the manner of the formulation (*paññatti-vidhi*).
The offense of being commanded, the non-offense, failure, and the factors [of the offense];
the method of origination, the distinctions regarding action, perception, and consciousness;

The sevenfold basis for formulation (*paññattiṭṭhāna*): this is indeed the source for all training rules (*sikkhāpada*).

"Person" (*puggala*) refers to whichever individual on account of whom each respective training rule was formulated. "Basis" (*vatthu*) refers to the transgression committed by that particular person. "Formulation method" (*paññattividhi*) consists of:

the original formulation (*paññatti*), the subsequent formulation (*anupaññatti*), the formulation for what has not yet arisen (*anuppannapaññatti*), the universal formulation (*sabbatthapaññatti*), the partial formulation (*padesapaññatti*), and the common formulation (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*).
There are nine kinds of designation (*paññatti*) by way of uncommon designation, designation from one side, and designation from both sides.
Among these, "designation of what has not yet arisen" (*anuppanna-paññatti*) refers to that which is designated when a fault has not yet occurred;

it is found only for bhikkhunīs by way of the acceptance of the eight weighty rules (*garudhamma*), and does not exist elsewhere. [Examples include: ordination by a group consisting of a quorum with a master of the Vinaya as the fifth member, sandals for groups of monks, and regular bathing.
"Leather spreadings"—by way of these, there are four kinds of what is called "local promulgation.
For it is only in the Middle Country that an offense occurs through these; and even among them, only the mere prohibition of regular bathing has come down in the Pātimokkha.
Beyond that, there is no other such thing as "local promulgation. All [other rules] are indeed "promulgations for all places," as are the two pairs of "common promulgations."

The pair concerning "proclamation on one side" (*ekatopaññatti*) is identical in meaning; therefore, setting aside the pair concerning "unarisen proclamation" (*anuppannapaññatti*), the pair concerning "universal proclamation" (*sabbatthapaññatti*), and the pair concerning "proclamation on one side," the detailed exposition for all [the remaining] four types of proclamations should be understood.

Regarding the terms *āṇattāpatti*, *nāpatti*, and *vipatti*: here, *āṇatti* refers to an injunction (*āṇāpanā*). *Āpatti* refers to [an offense] by way of prior application (*pubbappayoga*) and so forth.
The classification of offenses. "Non-offense" refers to non-offenses by way of ignorance and so forth. "Failure" (vipatti) refers to any one of the failures in virtue, conduct, view, or livelihood.
Thus, the detailed exposition should be understood in all instances by way of these [factors], such as the command and so forth.
"Factor" (aṅga): in all training rules, the factor for an offense should be understood.

Regarding the method of origination (*samuṭṭhāna-vidhi*): for all offenses, there are these—body, speech, body and speech, body and mind, speech and mind, and body, speech, and mind—which consist of one factor, two factors, and three factors respectively.
These are called the six origins (*cha samuṭṭhānāni*), which are also referred to as the "origins of the training rules" (*sikkhāpada-samuṭṭhānāni*).
Among them, the first three are without mental intention (*acittaka*), while the latter three involve mental intention (*sacittaka*). Of those, by means of one...
Offenses arise through two, three, four, or six origins; there are no offenses with five origins.
In this context, "originating from one" means that it arises through the fourth, fifth, or sixth origin, and not by any other.
"Originating from two" means [it arises] through the first and fourth, or the second and fifth.
It originates through the third and sixth origins, the fourth and sixth origins, and the fifth and sixth origins; it does not originate through others.
"Originating from three" means it originates through the first three origins and the last three origins; it does not originate through others.
"Originating from four" means [it originates] through the first, third, fourth, and sixth origins, and through the second, third, fifth, and sixth origins.
And it arises through its own origins, not through others. "Six origins" means that it arises through all six.
Thus:
Threefold, they have one origin; fivefold, they arise from two.
"Two ways for three and four bases; one way for six origins.
By way of origin, there are thirteen offenses in total; by way of origin according to the first formulated training rule, they receive thirteen names: those originating from the first *pārājika*,...

[The offenses] originating from taking what is not given, acting as a go-between, encouraging [another], the kaṭhina robe, sheep’s wool, the *padasodhamma* rule, traveling on a journey, a caravan of thieves, teaching the Dhamma, reporting what has occurred, causing a thief to rise up, and [acting] without permission.
Among these, that which originates from both body and mind is called "originating from the first pārājika.
That which originates from the three mental [factors] is called "originating from taking what is not given. That which originates from all six [factors]...
This is called "originating from wandering about. That which originates by the sixth [offense] alone is called "originating from formal admonition.
That which originates by the third and the sixth is called "originating from the kaṭhina.
That which originates by the first and the fourth is called "originating from sheep’s wool. That which originates by the second and the fifth is "originating from the recitation of the Pāṭimokkha."
[This is] the name. That which originates from the first, third, fourth, and sixth [factors] is called "originating from a journey" (*addhāna-samuṭṭhāna*).
That which originates from the fourth and sixth [factors] is called "originating from a caravan of thieves" (*theyyasattha-samuṭṭhāna*).

That which originates from the fifth alone is called "originating from the teaching of the Dhamma" (*dhammadesanā-samuṭṭhāna*). That which originates from the three origins that are without consciousness (*acittaka*)...

This is called the origin from the misrepresentation of reality (*bhūtārocanasamuṭṭhāna*). That which originates from the fifth and sixth [rules] is called the origin from the instigation of a thief (*corivuṭṭhāpanasamuṭṭhāna*).
That which originates from the second, third, fifth, and sixth [rules] is called the origin from what is not authorized (*ananuññātasamuṭṭhāna*).
Thus, the determination should be understood in all cases by way of this method of origin as well.

"By way of diversity through functional, perceptual, and volitional consciousness": having understood the diversity of all offenses by means of these—functional consciousness and so forth—the analysis should be understood in every instance.
For all offenses are fivefold according to the mode of their origination (*samuṭṭhāna*); namely:

there is an offense that originates from functional consciousness (*kiriyato*), there is one from non-functional (*akiriyato*), there is one from both functional and non-functional (*kiriyākiriyato*), and there is one that "might be... (*siyā*).
It may arise from action (*kiriyato*), it may arise from non-action (*akiriyato*), and it may arise from both action and non-action (*kiriyākiriyato*).
In this context, that which arises for one who commits a transgression through body or speech—such as digging the earth and so forth—is said to "originate from action.
That which arises for one who fails to perform what ought to be done by body or speech—such as the first *kathina* offense—is [said to originate] from non-action.

"Arising from" (samuṭṭhāti) means: that which occurs both for one who acts and for one who does not act, such as the offense of receiving a robe from the hand of a nun who is not a relative—this is said to arise from "action-and-non-action" (kiriya-akiriyato).
That which may occur for one who acts and may also occur for one who does not act, such as the offense of accepting money (rūpiya)—this [arises] sometimes from action...

It is said that [an offense] originates from non-action (*akiriya*). That which occurs both for one who is acting and for one who is neither acting nor not acting—such as the offense of building a hut (*kuṭikārāpatti*)—is said to originate sometimes from action (*kiriya*) and sometimes from both action and non-action (*kriyākiriya*).

Furthermore, all offenses are twofold by way of perception (*saññā*): those involving release from perception (*saññāvimokkha*) and those not involving release from perception (*no-saññāvimokkha*). In this regard:
Because one is released through the absence of the perception of transgression, this is "release by perception" (*saññāvimokkha*); the others are "not release by perception" (*nosaññāvimokkha*).
Furthermore, all [these offenses] are twofold according to the mind: those with mind (*sacittaka*) and those without mind (*acittaka*).
Among these, that which arises solely by way of origination from a state with mind is "with mind. That which arises either without mind or mixed with mind is "without mind."

Regarding the "classification according to blameworthy actions" (*vajjakammappabheda*): here, all offenses (*āpatti*) are twofold by way of being blameworthy—namely, those that are blameworthy by nature in the world (*lokavajja*) and those that are blameworthy by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*).
Among these, that offense for which the mind is exclusively unwholesome (*akusala*) on the side of being intentional is blameworthy by nature in the world;
the rest are blameworthy by rule. Furthermore, all are threefold by way of bodily action, verbal action, and both. Among these, in the door of the body...

That which is to be committed through the body is called bodily action (*kāyakamma*); that which is to be committed through the door of speech is called verbal action (*vacīkamma*); that which is to be committed through both is called both bodily and verbal action;

there is no such thing as an offense (*āpatti*) in the door of the mind. Thus, by this classification of blameworthy actions (*vajjakamma*), the determination [of offenses] is to be understood in all cases.

"Method for the two triads" means the method for the triad of wholesome states and the triad of feelings. For when one incurs an offense, one does so either with an unwholesome mind or with a wholesome or indeterminate mind;
likewise, one may be possessed of painful feeling or possessed of either of the other two feelings.
Even though this is so, in all training rules (sikkhāpada), there is one type of mind by way of the unwholesome mind, and [another] by way of the wholesome and indeterminate minds.

There are two types of consciousness; by way of all [types], there are three types of consciousness. By way of painful feeling, there is one feeling; by way of pleasant and equanimous feelings, there are two;
by way of all [feelings], there are three feelings. Only this classification is obtained, and no other.
"Having known the characteristic which stands in seventeen ways as common" refers to this section beginning with the introduction and ending with the fourfold analysis of feeling (*vedanāttika*).
Having understood the seventeenfold characteristic, the wise one should apply it.
The meaning is that in each respective case, according to what is appropriate, the learned bhikkhu should apply this characteristic in conformity with each training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
However, when not so applied, it is difficult to understand; therefore, [it will be explained] at the conclusion of the non-common analysis of all the training rules.
Without extracting this matrix (mātikā), we shall demonstrate it by way of application.
Herein, however, the application is as follows: This was laid down at Vesālī concerning the Elder Sudinna, in the case of the transgression of sexual intercourse.
“One should practice the sexual act”—this is the formal rule (paññatti) here; “without having renounced the training”—this is the qualification.

And there are two supplementary rules (*anupaññatti*): "even down to one who is an animal" and [the previous rule]. Now, this supplementary rule may be one that causes an offense, as in the training rule regarding speaking otherwise (*aññavādaka-sikkhāpada*) and so forth;
it may be one that does not cause an offense, as in the cases beginning with "except in a dream" (*aññatra supinā*);

and it may be one that supports an offense, as in the cases of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) and so forth. However, in this instance, it should be understood as one that supports [the offense].
From this point on, however, wherever there is a supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*), we shall indicate it merely as “this is a supplementary rule.
With the exception of the supplementary rules, the remainder in every instance should be understood as the original rules (*paññatti*). This is the method of analysis to be applied everywhere.
Regarding the very matter that arose concerning a monk, [it was stated]: “But whatever nun should intentionally engage in sexual intercourse...”

"one should partake"—since this was thus laid down for bhikkhunīs as well, it is a common rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*). Because one does not incur an offense through the mere command, it is "not by command" (*anāṇattika*).
However, one who commands a bhikkhu is not released from the offense of undertaking what is unallowable;

there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for bodily contact due to lust for sexual intercourse. Even if one [removes] the skin and so forth without remainder from a living body along the aforementioned path...
When [the organ] is completely severed, only the sign and the shape remain;
in that case, even for one who inserts as little as a swelling or a piece of calloused skin arising on the genitals—provided there is the intention of sexual intercourse—it is a *pārājika* offense.
For one who inserts a dry swelling, a dead piece of skin, or a hair where the bodily sensitivity has perished, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If the path has been torn out entirely, leaving not even the mere shape of the mark behind,
then there is a grave offense (thullaccaya) for the one who makes the effort, by way of the classification of the wound; likewise,

there is a grave offense for making a wound with a blade in the eyes, nostrils, ear-holes, or the sheaths of the prepuce of human beings, or in the sheaths of the prepuce and the nostril-cavities of animals such as elephants and horses.

In the case of animals, however, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) when the sign is minute—such as on the eyes, ears, nostrils, or anus of snakes, fish, and so forth—or when it lacks the dimension required for insertion, or in all other parts of the body such as the armpits.
When the sign is a dead body, from the point when it is half-decayed until it has not yet begun to putrefy, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
Once it has putrefied, there is an offense of wrong-doing; the same applies when it has been reduced to a skeleton.

For one who inserts the sexual organ while it is touching the mouth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If the tongue has protruded from the lips or [the organ] is on the teeth, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
For a piece of flesh that has fallen outside the [sexual] organ, there is an offense of wrong-doing; such is the classification of offenses here.
[There is no offense] for one who does not know, one who does not consent, one who is insane, one whose mind is deranged, one overwhelmed by pain, or for those who are first offenders.
There is no offense. Herein, one who does not know is one who, due to having fallen asleep, does not perceive even an effort made by another.
One who does not consent is one who, although knowing, does not give his approval. One who is insane is one who has reached an incurable state of madness due to bile.
One whose mind is deranged is one whose mental composure has been disturbed by yakkhas. And for both of these, [there is no offense].
The criterion for non-cognition is the state of equal engagement toward fire, gold, excrement, sandalwood, and so forth.

One who, due to being afflicted by intense pain, does not cognize anything at all is "one overcome by pain" (*vedanāṭṭa*). One who is the primary factor regarding each respective object is "the beginner" (*ādikammika*).
This, however, is not an offense. Among the four failures, this is failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*). It has two factors: the intention to engage and [the actual act].
And the practice of the path by means of the path. Regarding its origin and other characteristics, this training rule (sikkhāpada) originates from the first *pārājika*;

it is an action (*kiriya*), liberated through perception (*saññāvimokkha*), accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*), blameworthy according to worldly standards (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and associated with two types of feeling (*dvivedana*).
These characteristics—origin and so forth—apply to the offense (*āpatti*), not to the training rule itself. However, for the sake of convenience in terminology...
In all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), the teaching has been presented under the heading of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*);
therefore, in other such instances as well, one should not pay attention to the literal phrasing (*byañjana*), but should grasp only what is intended.
For the Protector (*nātha*) spoke of the refuge in terms of the meaning (*attha*).
The Great Sage, the benefactor of the world,
does not value mere phrasing. Therefore, the wise person,
having found no delight in the syllables, should fix their mind upon the meaning.
The commentary on the first *pārājika* is finished.
2. Commentary on the second *pārājika*:
Regarding the phrase "from a village or from a forest," here, every [type of dwelling], whether consisting of a single hut or otherwise, whether enclosed or unenclosed—
Whether it be inhabited by humans or non-humans, or even one settled for more than four months, any place whatsoever—even if it is merely a caravan—is to be understood as a "village.
With the exception of the village and its precincts, the remainder is called "forest. To avoid confusion therein, this distinction should be understood:
a house, the vicinity of a house, a village, and the precincts of a village. For within the space where water falls from the eaves of a roof is the interior of the precincts.
What is called "the house" (ghara): furthermore, the place where a woman standing at the door discards water used for washing vessels;
the place where a woman standing inside the house discards a broom or a dustpan that was previously thrown outside;
and the space connecting the two corners in front of the house with a tree-stump gate in the middle—[this is the house].
Excluding the enclosure built for the purpose of preventing cattle from entering, all of this is called the "vicinity of a house" (*gharūpacāra*).
Now, regarding that which is the very last house:
when a man of middle strength stands within such a vicinity of that house, young men, displaying their own strength, stretch out their arms—
They throw a clod of earth; the area within which that thrown clod falls is called the village (*gāma*).

Beyond that, the area within the range of another clod-throw is called the vicinity of the village (*gāmūpacāra*). However, the place where the clod, having fallen, rolls and comes to rest need not be included.
In the case of an enclosed village, however, the enclosure itself constitutes the boundary of the village. Of that...
If there are two boundary markers (*indakhila*), the village precinct (*gāmūpacāra*) is the distance of a stone’s throw from the inner marker for one standing there.
The meaning in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) should also be understood by this same method.
Therein, the offense regarding entering a village at an improper time and so forth must be delimited according to the precinct shown for an unenclosed village.
Thus, setting aside this village and its precincts, the remainder is what is called "the forest" (*arañña*) in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
This statement, "whether from a village or from the forest," is merely for the purpose of instruction.

However, even regarding those "houses and house-precincts" and "village precincts" mentioned for the sake of showing the boundaries of these two, if one steals an article belonging to a *pārājika* offense, it is indeed a *pārājika*.
*Adinnaṃ* means what belongs to another human being. *Theyyasaṅkhātaṃ*: here, *theno* is a thief;
the state of a thief is *theyya*, which is a name for the intention to steal. *Saṅkhā* and *saṅkhātaṃ* are identical in meaning;

it is a name for a portion, as in such passages as "for the proliferation of conceptualization (*papañcasaṅkhā*) has its source in perception" (*saññānidānā*). It is both theft (*theyya*) and a portion (*saṅkhātaṃ*).
The meaning is that "that which is reckoned as theft" refers to a single mental factor (cittakoṭṭhāsa) reckoned as the intention to steal.
This nominative case is used here in the sense of the instrumental; therefore, it should be understood in its actual sense as "by that which is reckoned as theft.
And since he who takes by means of what is reckoned as theft possesses the intention to steal, [the author] omits the literal phrasing and shows only the underlying meaning.
"It is to be understood that its word-commentary has been stated thus: ‘with a thieving mind, with a mind intent on taking away.
‘Should take’ means he should carry it off by means of one or another of the twenty-five modes of theft.
Those twenty-five modes of theft, however, should be carefully observed by combining five sets of five. The so-called five sets of five are: the set of five regarding various articles..."

The fivefold group concerning a single article, the fivefold group concerning taking with one's own hand, the fivefold group concerning prior preparation, and the fivefold group concerning theft by carrying away.

Among these, the first two fivefold groups are obtained by way of the phrases "should take up," "should carry off," "should steal," "should disturb the posture," and "should move from its place," which are stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) for this very term.

In this context, the group of five items consisting of various articles should be understood in terms of both animate and inanimate objects; the other [group] is to be understood only in terms of animate objects.
How so? "Should take" means he makes an assault upon the monastery; there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). He causes doubt to arise in the owner;
there is an offense of grave transgression (*thullaccaya*). When the owner, thinking "it will not be mine," relinquishes his responsibility, there is an offense...
Regarding the *pārājika* offense: "Should carry away"—if, while carrying another's goods, one touches the load on the head with a thieving intention, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If he moves it, it is a *thullaccaya*. If he lowers it from his shoulder, it is a *pārājika*.
"Should misappropriate"—if, when asked regarding goods deposited with him, "Give me the goods," he says, "I will not take them," it is a *dukkaṭa* for the owner.
If she gives rise to doubt, it is a *thullaccaya*. If the owner gives up the effort, thinking, "It shall not be mine," it is a *pārājika*.
"Should disturb her posture" means: if she steps forward with the first foot, thinking, "I will take the goods away together with the carrier," it is a *thullaccaya*.
If she steps forward with the second foot, it is a *pārājika*. "Should move her from her place" means: [if she moves] one who is standing on dry ground...
If one touches an article with the intention to steal, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one moves it, it is a *thullaccaya*. If one causes it to fall from its place, it is a *pārājika*.
In this way, first, the pentad of various articles is to be understood.

Furthermore, regarding the taking, seizing, stealing, the disturbance of postures, and the causing to fall from its place of a slave or an animal belonging to another, by means of the aforementioned method beginning with "application" (*abhiyoga*), etc.:
The fivefold group concerning single articles should be understood.
What is the fivefold group concerning taking by one's own hand? They are: taking by one's own hand, commanding, relinquishing, accomplishing the purpose, and abandoning the task.
Therein, "taking by one's own hand" means one steals another's article with one's own hand. "Commanding" means [commanding] "of such-and-such a person..."

"Command another, saying: 'Steal this merchandise. What is called "causing forfeiture" (nissaggiya) is the act of standing inside designated areas for evading customs duties and causing [the goods] to fall outside.

What is called "one who accomplishes the purpose" (atthasādhaka) is one who commands another, saying: "When you are able, steal such-and-such a person's merchandise. In that case, if the other person, being free from obstacles, steals it—
For the one who gives the order, it is a *pārājika* offense at the very moment the order is given.
Or, if one places oil worth a *pāda* from another’s oil-jar into sandals or other items that must necessarily be worn, it is a *pārājika* offense the mere moment they leave the hand.

Furthermore, the relinquishment of the burden (*dhuranikkhepa*) should be understood by way of the goods entrusted for the purpose of a monastery’s business. This applies even to one who does not return goods borrowed for a short time or goods that were to be given.
"This is the same method" refers to this fivefold set concerning direct physical action (*sāhatthika-pañcaka*).
What is the fivefold set concerning preliminary effort (*pubbapayoga-pañcaka*)? It consists of: preliminary effort, simultaneous effort, conveying by appointment, making a sign, and making a gesture.
Among these, "preliminary effort" is to be understood by way of giving an order. [The others are] by way of causing displacement from one's place, and [the rest regarding] barrenness and so forth.
And by means of transferring [ownership] and taking possession of fields and so forth, it should be understood as joint application (*sahapayoga*).
"Conspiracy" (*saṃvidhāvahāra*) means stealing after having made an agreement and consultation, thinking, "We shall steal such-and-such a commodity.
For when those who have made such an agreement have departed, if even one person moves that commodity from its place, there is theft for all of them. "Giving a signal" (*saṅketakamma*)...
*Ūhanā* (hinting) is the act of making known by means of a sign.

For if one is told at some time such as before the meal, "At such-and-such a time, steal such-and-such an object," and then steals it either later than or earlier than that agreed-upon time, the theft belongs to the one who made the hint at the very moment the hint was given.
*Nimittakamma* (sign-making) is for the purpose of producing recognition.

Making signs such as rubbing one’s eyes. For if, after making a sign in this way, one takes what was said to be taken "later" or "earlier," then for the maker of the sign, the theft occurs at the very moment the sign was made; this is the pentad of preliminary acts.
What is the pentad of theft by stealth? Theft by stealth, theft by force, theft by artifice, theft by concealment...

“Stealing by means of fraud” (*kusāvahāra*). In this context, when one steals after breaking into houses and so forth while remaining invisible, or when one takes [property] after deceiving others with false measures, false coins, and the like—the act of taking in such a manner is to be understood as “stealing by theft” (*theyyāvahāra*).
On the other hand, when one takes what belongs to others by force or through physical compulsion, such as village-robbers and the like, or by virtue of power obtained for oneself—
In the same manner as previously described, one takes what is extra, like a royal servant or the like; for one who takes in this way, it should be understood as "taking by force" (*pasayhāvahāra*).
Taking after having made a pretense, however, is called "taking by pretense" (*parikappāvahāra*). This is twofold, according to the object (*bhaṇḍa*) and the occasion (*okāsa*).
Herein, this is "pretense regarding the object": one desiring a cloth enters an inner room [and thinks], "If there is a cloth..."
Having reflected, "I will take it if it is thread, I will not take it if it is not," he takes a bag in the dark.
If there is a garment therein, there is an offense of defeat (pārājika) at the very moment of lifting it. If it is thread, he is protected.
Having taken it outside, released it, and knowing it is "thread," he brings it back and puts it away; he is indeed protected. Even though he knows it is "thread"...
If one goes thinking, “Whatever is obtained, that shall be taken,” he must be made to pay for every step. If he takes it after placing it on the ground, there is a *pārājika* offense upon lifting it.
If he pursues a thief crying out, “Thief! Thief! but the thief escapes by jumping over him, he is innocent.
If the owners see [the object] and take it, he is still innocent. If anyone else takes it, he must pay the value of the goods. Regarding the owners...
If, having seen [the robes] being returned, one takes them with the perception that they are refuse-rags (*paṃsukūla*), thinking, "I took this long ago;

it now belongs to me," even for one who takes them in this way, it is indeed a case of *bhaṇḍadeyya*. In this context, the mental construction (*parikappa*) that proceeds in the manner of, "If it will be a robe-cloth, I shall take it," and so forth, is called a "mental construction regarding the goods" (*bhaṇḍaparikkappa*).
The conceptualization of space, however, should be understood as follows:

someone who has entered another’s monastery grounds or similar places, seeing some object capable of arousing greed, delimits a boundary by way of a doorway, a porch, the base of a palace, a gatehouse, the foot of a tree, or the like, thinking:
"If they see me within this interval, they will take hold of me out of a desire to look at me and follow me about."

If one conceives the thought, "I will show it as if [I am giving it back], but if they do not see it, I will take it away," then as soon as he takes it and exceeds that conceived limit, there is theft.
Thus, this conception which proceeds in the manner just described is called "conception by occasion.
When one takes after having conceived in this way through both types of conception, it should be understood as "theft by conception" (*parikappāvahāra*).
But stealing after having concealed it is called "concealed-stealing. It should be understood as follows:

when a bhikkhu, seeing finger-rings or other items belonging to others that have been taken off and left in gardens or similar places, conceals them with dust or leaves, thinking, "I will take them later," then so long as he has not yet removed them, there is no theft.

...it exists. However, when the owners, searching for it and not seeing it, go away still longing for it with the thought, "We shall find out tomorrow," then there is theft (avahāra) for one who takes it out [of concealment].

This applies to one who takes it while it is still concealed, either with the perception of ownership, thinking, "This is my property," or with the perception that it is refuse, thinking, "They have gone now; this is discarded goods."

However, it is liable to restitution (*bhaṇḍadeyya*). Even if those [owners] return on the second or third day, search for it, and having failed to find it, depart after relinquishing their responsibility, what was taken remains liable to restitution.

If, later on, one who has learned of it refuses to give it back when being exhorted, there is theft (*avahāra*) because the owners have relinquished their responsibility. Why? Because they did not see it due to his effort. But as for whoever...

If one, with a thieving mind, steps on an object of such a kind while it remains exactly where it is and, without concealing it, pushes it into mud or sand by means of the foot, the theft is complete at the very moment it has been pushed in.
However, stealing by shifting [the object] with kusa grass is called "stealing by means of kusa grass" (kusāvahāra). That too should be understood as follows: whichever monk...
Or, having dropped some blade of *kusa* grass— whether made of *vilīva*, or made of palm leaf, or marked with a sign— upon whatever portion of the robe is being distributed,
one who wishes to take another’s portion (which may be less valuable, more valuable, or equal in value to his own) by placing it near his own portion,
out of a desire to transfer the *kusa* grass that fell on his own portion onto another’s portion;
He lifts it up and protects it for that long. Even when the other's portion has been dropped, he still protects it.
But when, after that [first portion] has fallen, he lifts a blade of *kusa* grass from the other's portion, at the mere act of lifting it, there is theft (*avahāra*).
If he first lifts a blade of *kusa* grass from the other's portion with the intention of dropping it into his own portion, he protects it during the act of lifting.
Even when throwing it down, one is protected [from the offense] as long as one is removing one’s own *kusa* grass from one’s own portion;
however, for one who, having removed it from their own portion, throws it into another’s portion, there is theft (*avahāra*) at the mere moment it leaves the hand.
This is the theft of *kusa* grass. Thus, the meaning of what was stated—“‘Should take’ means he should steal by way of one of the twenty-five modes of theft”—has been clarified.
"Of such a kind" means of whatever sort. "Taking what is not given" refers to the seizing of what belongs to another and has not been given.
"Kings" is said specifically with reference to Bimbisāra; as for others, whether they would act in that way or not, they are not the standard.
"They might kill" means they might strike with their hands and so forth, or cut with a weapon. "They might bind" means by means of rope-bindings and the like.
"Or they would bind him. "Or they would banish him" means they would expel him. They would revile him with these words: "You are a thief! You are a fool! You are deluded! You are a robber!
But for the taking of what kind of ungiven thing do kings act in this way? For a foot or for something worth a foot.
"A monk taking such an ungiven thing"—such a monk as was mentioned by the Ancients...
If one takes by any means whatsoever— whether it be a quarter of a kahāpaṇa or a value equivalent to a quarter—
any kind of property, whether animate or inanimate, that has not been given and is situated anywhere on the ground or elsewhere, among the types of theft already mentioned, one becomes defeated;
what need then to speak of taking more than that?
This was laid down at Rājagaha concerning the Elder Dhaniya, in the case of taking wood that had not been given by the king.
"From a village or from a forest"—this is the subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*) here; it is a common rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), and it involves three offenses.

For the preliminary effort, such as going for the purpose of carrying it away, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); for touching it, there is an offense of wrong-doing; and for causing the object subject to a *pārājika* offense to move, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
For one who acquires [it] for one māsaka or less than a māsaka, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for more than a māsaka or less than five māsakas, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya); for five māsakas or more than five māsakas, it is an offense involving defeat (pārājika).

In all cases, the determination should be understood according to the time of acquisition, the place of acquisition, and whether or not the object has been lost through use, as a vessel, or by being exchanged, and so forth.

There is no offense for one who perceives it as belonging to Sakka, for one taking with confidence, for temporary use, for what is possessed by a peta, for what is possessed by an animal, for one perceiving it as a rag-robe, and for those such as the insane. Regarding the failure of virtue (*sīlavipatti*):

it consists of [taking] what is possessed by another human being, the perception that it is possessed by another, heavy requisites, the intention to steal, and the acts of taking away of the kinds already mentioned.
And taking by means of [these]—these are the five factors here. It originates from taking what is not given; it is an action; it is liberated by perception;
it is accompanied by consciousness; it is a worldly offense; it is bodily action; it is verbal action; it is unwholesome consciousness; it has three feelings.
The commentary on the second *pārājika* is finished.

3. Commentary on the Third Pārājika In the third [offense], "intentionally" (*sañcicca*) means having formed an intention, having resolved together with that intention. It means having intended and planned with the murderous volition (*vadhakacetanā*), precisely with the perception (*saññā*) that it is a living being, thinking, "I shall kill.
"A human being" (*manussaviggaha*) refers to the body of one belonging to the human species while alive, starting from the stage of the embryo (*kalala*).

"Should deprive of life": one might separate [the being] from life even at the stage of the *kalala* (embryo) by means of heating or crushing, or by the administration of medicine, or by any other appropriate means beyond that.
To clarify this matter, one must understand what a living being is, what the taking of life is, what it is to be a taker of life, and the preliminary effort for the taking of life.
This is how it should be understood. In this context, "living being" (*pāṇa*) refers, in conventional usage, to a sentient being, but in the ultimate sense, to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
"Taking life" (*pāṇātipāta*) is that volition (*cetanā*) by which one instigates the physical or verbal effort that cuts off the life-faculty.

"One who takes life" is the person endowed with the aforementioned volition. "The effort for taking life" refers to the six types of effort for taking life, beginning with the manual effort (*sāhatthika*).
[The means of killing are: by one's own hand, by command, by a stationary [means], by means of knowledge, and by means of supernormal power (*iddhi*).

Therein, "by one's own hand" (*sāhatthika*) refers to striking with the body or with something connected to the body when one is killing personally. "By relinquishing" (*nissaggiya*) refers to the relinquishing of spears, arrows, mechanical devices, stones, and so forth, with the body or with something connected to the body, by one who wishes to kill someone standing at a distance. Therein, each one...

It is twofold, by way of the distinction between specific intent (*uddissa*) and non-specific intent (*anuddissa*). Regarding these, in the case of specific intent, one is bound by the karma through the death of that very person for whose sake one strikes.
In the case of non-specific intent—where one thinks, "Let whoever [be there] die"—one is bound by the karma through the death of anyone at all due to the cause of the blow.
In both cases, whether the victim dies immediately upon being struck or later from that same illness, it is at the very moment of being struck that [the offense occurs].
Bound by karma. Regarding "one who commands": this refers to the act of commanding another by saying, "Kill such-and-such a person.
In that regard:
The object, the time, the place, the weapon, and the posture;
"Specific action"—these are the six determinants of an instruction.
In this context, "the object" refers to the person. For if a person is instructed, "Kill him," and he kills that very person, there is an offense for the one who gave the order.
But if he kills another, or if he kills another while thinking it was someone else, the one who gave the order is released. [The instruction is: "Kill this person."
When [the order] has been given, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the one who gave the command. Regarding "time": this refers to times such as before the meal.
For if one is commanded, "Kill him before the meal," and kills him precisely before the meal, there is an offense for the one who gave the command.

But if he kills him either after or before that specific time designated as "before the meal," the one who gave the command is released. By this method, the legal determination is to be applied in all cases.

It should be understood as follows. "Permanent" (*thāvaro*) refers to such things as digging a pit for one who wishes to kill with immovable implements, preparing a trap, placing swords and other weapons, administering poison in ponds and the like, or offering physical charms (*rūpūpahāra*).
Here too, according to the method already stated, the distinction between "specified" (*uddissa*) and "unspecified" (*anuddissa*) should be understood.
"Consisting of science" (*vijjāmaya*) refers to the muttering of spells (*vijjā-parijappana*) for the purpose of killing.
"Consisting of psychic power" (*iddhimaya*) means the employment of psychic power born of the maturation of kamma.
"Or he might seek out one who carries a weapon": here, "carrier" (*hāraka*) means one who carries; what does he carry? Life.

Alternatively, "that which is to be carried" is "carrier," meaning that which is to be placed near [the victim]. It is a "weapon-carrier" (*satthahāraka*) because it is both a weapon (*sattha*) and a carrier (*hāraka*).
"Assa" means of a human being. "Pariyeseyya" (should seek) means he should act in such a way that he obtains it;

the meaning is "he should set it down. By this, he shows the method involving a stationary object (*thāvarapayoga*). For otherwise, one would become subject to a defeat offense (*pārājika*) merely by the act of seeking;

and that is not appropriate. However, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), disregarding the literal phrasing of this [text], that which is included here under the category of the method involving a stationary object—
“[He might take] a weapon”: this was said in order to demonstrate that very thing. “Or he might praise the beauty of death”:
either by means of speech or by writing on palm leaves and the like, he would proclaim the excellence of death in such a manner as, “Whoever dies in this way obtains wealth,” and so forth.
By this, it is shown that just as in the case of the statement, “he might take what is not given,” there is a figurative (pariyāya) explanation.
He is not exempted; for by the statement "he should thus praise," it should be understood that here he is not exempted even from figurative discourse (*pariyāyakathā*).
Or, "he should incite to death" means he should cause him to adopt the means for the sake of death, such as by saying, "Bring a weapon," and so forth.
By this, he shows the application of an instruction. "O man!"—this is a form of address. What?
“Tuyhimi nātiādi” is an illustration of the manner of commentary. “Iti cittamanoti” means “thus it is mind-consciousness”; thus it is *citta*, thus it is *manas*.
In the phrase “Death is better for you than life,” the meaning is “one whose mind is set on death” (*maraṇacitto*) or “one whose mind is death” (*maraṇamanas*).

And here, the word “mind” (*mano*) is stated for the purpose of illustrating the meaning of consciousness (*citta*). For that very reason, in its word-commentary (*padabhājana*), it says: “That which is consciousness, that is mind.”

“Cittasaṅkappo” means a varied intention (*vicittasaṅkappo*). Here too, the word “iti” should be supplied. Furthermore, “saṅkappo” is a name for mere deliberation (*saṃvidahana*), not for *vitakka* alone.
And in this context, that deliberation is comprised of perception (*saññā*), volition (*cetana*), and intention (*adhippāya*);
therefore, “thus with a mental intention” refers to one who perceives death, as stated in the passage: “Death is better for you than life.”
"Intention for death" means "the purpose of death"; this is how the meaning should be understood here.

For this same method is shown even in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*). By this, he shows that there is no such thing as "expounding the Dhamma" for one who speaks according to the method beginning with, "A single day of life is better for one who exerts firm energy," and so forth, without the thought of death and the like. "In many ways" means in various modes.

"By various reasons. The passage beginning with "Again, the praise of death," etc., is the concluding statement. "He becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense" means that even if [the victim] is a human being encountered at that very moment, one who deprives such a person of life according to the manner described becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
This was laid down concerning a number of monks at Vesālī, in the matter of their taking each other's lives.
“Or the praise of death”: this is an additional rule (anupaññatti) here; it is a common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti), and it is a formal act of censure (sāṇattika).

For digging a pit or similar acts for the purpose of killing, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Even if anyone falls into a pit dug without a specific target, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
And in the case of causing suffering to a spirit (yakkha), a hungry ghost (petta), an animal, or a human being—even if they are of the animal class—there is likewise only an offense of wrong-doing.

For one who is of human birth, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) when causing suffering; likewise for the death of a *yakkha* or similar being. However, for the death of an animal, there is a *pācittiya* (offense of expiation), whereas for the death of a human, it is a *pārājika* (defeat).
According to this method, the classification of offenses everywhere should be understood by way of the distinction in the preliminary effort (*payoga*).
This applies to one who kills unintentionally, one who does not know [the victim], one who has no intention for death, and those who are insane, and so forth.

There is no offense. In this context, "unintentionally" means that even if another dies through an effort performed without intending, "By this means I shall kill this person," there is no offense, as in the case of the incident involving the throwing of a pestle.

"Without knowing" means that even if another dies through an effort made by one who does not know, "This person will die by this [means]," there is no offense, as in the case of the incident involving the alms-food containing poison. "One whose intention was not for death" means...
If one who does not desire death uses a means [to bring it about], there is no offense even if the other person dies, just as in the case of the matter of medicine.

Thus should the analysis regarding "unintentionally" and so forth be understood. In this context, there are five factors: (1) a failure in virtue; (2) a living being of human kind; (3) the perception that it is a living being;
(4) the murderous intention; (5) the means employed; and (6) death by that means. This is the basis for the offense of taking what is not given.

It is a functional state, a liberation through perception, associated with consciousness, blameworthy by worldly convention, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and painful feeling.
The commentary on the third *pārājika* is finished.
4. Commentary on the fourth *pārājika*.
In the fourth [case], they do not recognize it because they do not know its existence within themselves, as it has not arisen in their own mental continuum (*sakasantāna*).
"Superhuman states" (*uttarimanussadhamma*) refers to the qualities (*dhamma*) of both those who meditate (*jhāyin*) and the Noble Ones (*ariya*).
"Referring to oneself" (*attupanāyika*) means either applying that [state] to oneself by asserting "it exists in me," or identifying oneself with it by thinking "I am seen therein."
"Practicing" means referring to oneself; that which refers to oneself. Having established it thus, the connection is:

"one should practice. Regarding "the noble knowledge and vision": here, sublime and supramundane wisdom is "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) in the sense of knowing, and it is "vision" (*dassana*) in the sense of seeing, because it makes the Dhamma directly manifest as if seen with the eye; thus it is "knowledge and vision. It is noble.
"Pure and supreme knowledge and vision" refers to noble knowledge and vision (*ariya-ñāṇadassana*). It is sufficient, adequate, and capable of destroying the defilements;
thus, it is "noble knowledge and vision" regarding these superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) distinguished by jhāna and so forth.

Alternatively, one who possesses such noble knowledge and vision is "one for whom noble knowledge and vision is sufficient" (*alamariyañāṇadassano*); that is "one possessing sufficient noble knowledge and vision. "One would practice" means this according to the manner described above.
Having claimed for oneself a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), one should announce it—either by body, by speech, or by both—to a person of human kind who is capable of understanding.
The phrase “thus I know, thus I see” is a demonstration of the manner of such proclamation;
for when one proclaims after having claimed it for oneself, doing so without any other pretext, one proclaims in this way. Therefore, as for this...
In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), the distinctions such as “I attained the first jhāna,” “I am attaining it,” and “I have attained it” are stated;
all of these should be understood as being included right here. For when one says, “Thus I know, thus I see,” he does not merely utter these words;
rather, he means that by this and that reason, this phenomenon...
By saying "I have [attained it]" one demonstrates its existence; and by saying "I have entered upon it" and so forth, its existence is demonstrated through the reasons of entering upon it and so on.

Therefore it was said: "Whatever distinction is stated in the word-commentary—'I entered upon the first jhāna,' 'I enter upon it,' 'I have entered upon it,' and so forth—all that is included right here. From that...
"At another time" means at some time other than the time when it was announced.
This is a demonstration of the time for confessing the offense; however, one incurs the offense at the very moment it is announced.
Since, once the offense has been incurred, one confesses whether urged by another or not urged, it is therefore said: "whether being pressed or not being pressed."
"Has fallen" means that at the very moment it was announced, he had fallen into a *pārājika* offense.
"Desiring purity" means looking toward or wishing for his own purification from the state of a householder and so forth.
For since he has fallen into a *pārājika*, he is incapable of attaining *jhāna* and the like while remaining in the status of a monk; thus, his status as a monk is no longer what is called "purity."

However, because one who is a householder, or one who is a lay follower (*upāsaka*), a nun (*ārāmikā*), or a novice (*sāmaṇera*) is capable of attaining the path to heaven through giving and so forth, or the path to liberation through meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and so forth, therefore his status as a householder and so on is called "purity" (*visuddhi*).
Hence it was said: "looking toward purity such as the state of being a householder. "He might speak thus" means: in this way.
How would one say it? "I did not know, friend," and so forth. In that context, "not knowing" means being without knowledge;
"not seeing" means being without vision. "I spoke empty falsehoods" means: because it was devoid of the actual meaning of my words, it was empty;
because it was intended as a deception, it was false—I spoke, that is, I uttered—this is what is meant. "Except for overestimation" refers to that which, having applied the three characteristics...

In one who is contemplating mental formations (*saṅkhāra*) and has begun insight (*vipassanā*), there arises overweening pride (*adhimāna*) consisting in the perception of having attained what has not been attained.
Apart from that overweening pride, if anyone should behave out of mere evil desire (*pāpicchatā*), he too is one who has committed a defeat (*pārājika*); this is the meaning.
This was laid down with reference to the monks on the banks of the Vaggumudā river at Vesālī, concerning the matter of their proclamation of superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
The rule laid down as “except in the case of overestimation” is here a subsequent rule (anupaññatti), a common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti), and not a formal injunction (anāṇattika).

If one proclaims non-existent states such as jhāna and so forth—described by such phrases as “I attained the first jhāna”—and if he proclaims this to anyone at all who is a human being, immediately thereafter [the thought arises]: “This person is an attainer of jhāna.”
Or if one knows that meaning in any way whatsoever, such as "he is noble," it is a *pārājika*. If one does not know it, it is a *thullaccaya*.
However, if one knows while someone is reporting by means of a false pretext in such a manner as, "The monk who stayed in your monastery attained the first *jhāna*," it is a *thullaccaya*.
If one does not know it, it is a *dukkaṭa*. [This applies] when done out of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

There is no offense for one who announces [the attainment] without the intention of boasting, nor for those who are insane and so forth. In this context, there are five factors: (1) failure in virtue; (2) the non-existence of superhuman states within oneself;
(3) the announcement of such states out of evil desire; (4) the use of a pretext other than the truth; (5) the fact that the person to whom it is announced is of human birth;
and (6) the person’s understanding at that very moment. The origins and other characteristics are exactly the same as those stated for the offense of taking what is not given.
The commentary on the fourth *pārājika* is finished.
"Venerable friends, the four *pārājika* rules have been recited"—this refers specifically to the *pārājikas* recited here.
However, when taken together, all twenty-four *pārājikas* should be understood. Which are the twenty-four?
First, there are the four offenses for monks and the four not shared with nuns mentioned in the Pāḷi—making eight;
these, together with the eleven pārājikas consisting of the incapacity of the eleven types of persons such as the *paṇḍaka* and so forth, amount to nineteen.
To this is added the pārājika of renunciation for a nun who desires the state of a householder.
Twenty, and furthermore, by way of these four— Lambī, Mudupiṭṭhika, one who takes another’s sexual organ with the mouth,
and one who sits upon another’s sexual organ— they say, “the four anuloma pārājikas. Thus,
combining these four with the previous twenty, there are twenty-four pārājikas in total.
These things are to be understood. "He does not obtain communal living with the bhikkhus" means he does not obtain communal living with the bhikkhus consisting of such acts as the Uposatha ceremony.

"As before, so after" means that just as previously—during his time as a householder and during his time as one not yet ordained—he was not in communion, even after having committed a *pārājika* offense, he remains likewise outside of communion; there is no communal living for him with the bhikkhus.
“Communal living” refers to the distinctions such as the Uposatha ceremony and so forth. Regarding that, when one says, “I ask the venerable ones,” it means:
among those four *pārājika* offenses, I ask the venerable ones, “Are you pure in this regard? The phrase “kaccittha” means “kacci ettha” (is there purity in this);
the meaning is: “In these four *pārājika* offenses, are you pure? Alternatively, “kaccittha parisuddhā” means “kacci parisuddhā attha” (are you indeed pure?).
The meaning is "be [thus]. The rest is entirely clear in every respect.
The commentary on the *Pārājika* section of the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Pātimokkhavaṇṇanā* is finished.
The Section on Saṅghādisesa:
"Now, moreover" (*ime kho pana*) is a phrase used to direct attention toward what is about to be stated. "Venerable sirs" (*āyasmanto*) is an affectionate address to those assembled.
"Thirteen" (*terasā*) is a limitation by number. "Saṅghādisesa" is their name. "Offenses" (*dhammā*) refers to the transgressions.

“They come to be mentioned in the summary” means they come to be mentioned by their specific form, not merely by a general statement such as “for whomsoever there may be an offense,” as is the case in the Nidāna. 1.
Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Emission of Semen.
"Volitional" (*sañcetanā*) means that volition (*cetanā*) exists therein; "volitional action" (*sañcetanikā*) is simply volition, or it is called "volitional" because volition exists as its object.
"Emission of semen" (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*) is the emission of semen.
When, due to lust, rigidity, or other such factors, the genitals have become functional, one—without citing any pretext such as illness or the like—[emits] within internal forms and so forth.

In some cases, for one who makes an effort toward a sign with the intention of relishing the pleasure of emission, there is the meaning of "causing the semen to fall from its place" among the ten kinds of semen—blue and so forth—due to the diversity of underlying dispositions and elements.
"Except in a dream" means setting aside that emission of semen which occurs in a dream. "Saṅghādisesa" refers to that [offense] which occurs except in a dream.
The intentional emission of semen: this is the meaning of the category of offenses called *saṅghādisesa*. As for the etymological meaning here:
it is called *saṅghādisesa* because the Saṅgha must be desired both at the beginning (*ādi*) and at the remainder (*sesa*). What is meant?
For one who, having committed this offense, desires to emerge from it, that emergence from the offense [requires] both at its beginning and...

The Saṅgha is required for the granting of the *parivāsa* probation at the beginning; for the granting of the *mānatta* penance in the middle—either by means of sending back to the beginning (*mūlāya paṭikassana*) or otherwise;

and for the rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) at the end. Since not even a single formal act (*kamma*) can be performed here without the Saṅgha, it is called a *saṅghādisesa* because the Saṅgha is required both at the beginning and at the end.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Seyyasaka, regarding the incident of discharging semen by means of an intentional effort, with the proviso: “except in a dream.
This is a subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*), a non-common rule (*asādhāraṇapaññatti*), and one without a formal instruction (*anāṇattika*).

However, if one causes another to perform an effort upon one’s own organ and thereby causes it to be discharged, one indeed incurs the offense—even if one has merely intended it, even if [the effort is performed] in the air.
If one makes an effort toward the sign by shaking the hips, but it does not issue forth, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

However, if it issues forth from its place even as much as what a single small fly could drink, there is a *saṅghādisesa* (offense entailing suspension), even if it has not yet entered the stream of water.
For that which has fallen from its place necessarily enters the stream of water; therefore, [the offense is complete] at the mere moment it has entered the stream of water.
"Whether he has gone outside or not, it is a *saṅghādisesa*," so it is stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
There is no offense for one who does not make an effort, for one who does not intend to cause emission, for one dreaming a dream, or for those who are insane and so forth, even if emission occurs.

In this case, there are three factors: failure of virtue, volition, and effort, as well as the emission itself. The origins and other characteristics are exactly the same as those stated for the first *pārājika*.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the emission of semen is finished.
2. Commentary on the second training rule concerning bodily contact:
"In the second [rule], *otiṇṇo* (fallen into) means either fallen into passion arising within, like beings [possessed] by yakkhas and so forth, or [fallen] into wells and such."

This is a designation for one who, without considering beings as they truly are, becomes attached to an object that provokes lust, or has himself descended into passion; it refers to one possessed by lust for physical contact.
"With a mind that has changed" means having abandoned its natural state, which consists of the continuum of the purified *bhavaṅga*, and proceeding otherwise;
or, it means changed in an ugly way, just as something undergoing transformation becomes ugly as it turns. Thus...

The meaning is: "with a mind that has been turned back by means of the stated [counteractive] passion. "Together with a woman" means together with any living human female, even one born on that very same day.
"Should engage in physical contact" means he should enter into bodily union, such as the joining of bodies through grasping the hand and so forth.
The passage beginning with "grasping the hand" is the detailed explanation of its meaning.
In this context, "hand" (*hattha*) refers to the area from the wrist down to the tips of the fingernails.

"Braid" (*veṇī*) is a designation for a mass of hair, whether it has been braided or not, and whether consisting of pure hair alone or mixed with blue and other colored threads, flowers, coins, garlands, golden leaf-patterns, strings of pearls, and so forth. Furthermore, by the mention of "braid," the hair itself is also included here.
It is taken together with the hair. Thus, the grasping of a hand as defined by the aforementioned characteristics is "grasping the hand" (*hatthaggāha*);

the grasping of the braid of hair is "grasping the braid" (*veṇiggāha*). The touching of the remaining body, or the touching of this or that particular limb, is called "touching. Whoever [performs] that grasping of the hand, or grasping of the braid, or [the touching] of this or that...
"Or if one should engage in the touching of a limb [of a woman], for him there is an offense class called *saṅghādisesa*.

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the Elder Udāyī regarding the matter of engaging in physical contact; it is a unique rule (*asādhāraṇapaññatti*), not subject to a formal instruction (*anāṇattika*).
It applies even to one who perceives a woman as a woman and touches her with hair to hair, or to a woman..."
For one who, with the intention of sexual intercourse, makes an effort and admits to the contact while being touched, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
However, for one who holds [the body] with one hand and touches it here and there with the other hand even for a whole day, it is only a single offense.
But for one who touches without holding [the body], provided he does not release his hand from the body from the head down to the feet, [it is a single offense].
If he touches [her], it is one offense; even if he grasps all five fingers together, it is still only one.

However, if he grasps the five fingers of both a man and a woman together, there are five offenses. For one who is in doubt about a woman, or who perceives her as a paṇḍaka, a male, or an animal, it is a thullaccaya.
The same applies when touching with the body or with something connected to the body, or in the case of non-human females, paṇḍakas, and males.

Also in the case of physical contact. However, regarding a human woman, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for touching her body with one’s own body or similar acts, as well as for touching a man’s body and so forth. Also for one who, while being touched by a woman, admits to the contact with his own body even though he had no intention of indulging;
for one who touches a woman with the intention of liberation; and for one who does so unintentionally, through lack of mindfulness, or unknowingly.
