An itch-covering cloth (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi*) must be determined as long as the affliction exists; when the affliction is gone...
When [the robe] has been relinquished once it has been laid aside, it must be formally assigned; that one [assignment] alone is sufficient.
A face-towel must indeed be determined [as one's own]; however, whether it be one or many, and even if large, it is certainly permissible.
There is no limit to the number of requisites-cloths; as many as one desires may be determined. A bag and a water-strainer are also subject to formal assignment according to the final measurement.

“Requisite cloth” (*parikkhāracola*) must indeed be determined; it is also permissible to determine even many [pieces] together by way of such a formula as, “I determine these robes as requisite cloths,” and so forth.
However, regarding the bed-covers, chair-covers, pillows, blankets, and rugs—namely, those spreadings given for the purpose of bedding equipment—there is no need for a formal determination.
There is indeed no [robe] at all. Furthermore, all this robe that has been determined (adhiṭṭhita) in the manner described loses its determination through these eight causes:
giving it to another, taking it back after having given it, receiving it in trust, returning to the lower state, renouncing the training, death, change of sex, and relinquishing it.
As for the triple robe (ticīvara), however, by the measure of the surface of the nail of the little finger...
Even if there is a hole, it is relinquished only by means of tearing it apart. For if even a single thread remains uncut within the hole, it is still protected.

In that regard, with respect to the outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*) and the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), a hole situated beyond a portion measuring one span in length and eight finger-breadths in width breaks the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*); the same applies to the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*).
In length, this is the very measure; however, in width, it should be understood as four finger-breadths. It does not exceed the stated dimensions even when all three [robes] are combined;
therefore, once a hole has formed, the triple robe remains in the category of an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), and after sewing it, it must be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) again.
As for the rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*), it may be kept even after the lapse of the rainy season months.
The itch-covering cloth also loses its determination when the ailment is cured. Therefore, it must be formally assigned [to another] after that.
However, we shall explain the characteristics of formal assignment for all robes in the training rule concerning the assignment of robes alone.
For, in this context, whatever is neither determined nor assigned should be understood as "extra robe-cloth."

"Exceeding that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture": the meaning is that for one who exceeds that aforementioned measure of cloth by more than ten days—provided that during this interval he does not act so as to prevent it from becoming "extra cloth"—there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture;
that is, the cloth becomes subject to forfeiture and he incurs an offense of expiation.
Alternatively, *nissaggiya* means "that which involves relinquishing" (*nissajjana*); it is the name for the disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) to be performed in its preliminary stage.

Or, it is called *nissaggiya* because "it has relinquishing as its characteristic. What is that? It is the *pācittiya*. The meaning here is this: for one who lets that [period] pass, there is a *pācittiya* offense together with the disciplinary act of relinquishment (*nissaggiyavinayakamma*). And that...
Now, regarding this robe-cloth: the dawn of the day on which it was acquired depends upon that day of acquisition.
Therefore, when the dawn breaks on the eleventh day together with the day the robe was acquired, it has exceeded the ten-day limit.
Having taken that [robe], it must be relinquished to the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual. Herein, this is the method—first, in regard to the Saṅgha:
It should be relinquished in this way: “Venerable sir, this robe-cloth of mine, which has exceeded ten days and is to be relinquished, I relinquish to the Saṅgha.
Having thus relinquished it, the offense should be confessed in this way: “Venerable sir, I have fallen into one offense entailing relinquishment and confession;
I confess it. If there are two, one should say “two,” and if...
Beyond that, it should be called "a large number. When relinquishing [the robes], if there are two or many, one should say:
"Venerable sir, these robes of mine, which have exceeded ten days and are subject to relinquishment, I relinquish to the Saṅgha.
One who is unable to recite the formal text may speak otherwise. [This should be done] by an experienced and competent monk.
The Saṅgha should be informed: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so remembers an offense;
he discloses it, makes it clear, and confesses it. If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, I shall accept the offense of the monk named so-and-so.
Having accepted the offense according to this characteristic, one should say to him: "Do you see it?"
“Yes, I see it,” “You should exercise restraint in the future,” “I shall certainly exercise restraint well.
But in the case of two or several [offenses], the distinction in wording should be made according to the previous method. Regarding the offense confessed:
“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs; this robe-cloth, which was subject to relinquishment for the monk so-and-so, has been relinquished to the Saṅgha.”

"If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this robe-cloth to the monk named so-and-so"—in this way should the relinquished robe-cloth be given. If there are two or many [monks], the phrasing should be adjusted accordingly.
However, when one is relinquishing it to a group, having said "these" or "these here," one should say, "I relinquish them to you, venerable sirs."
It should be said by the receiver of the offense: "Venerable sirs, let it be heard by me: this monk named so-and-so remembers an offense...
[as before] ...he confesses it; if it is the proper time for the venerable ones. Regarding the giving of the robe-cloth as well: "Venerable sirs, let it be heard by me:
this robe-cloth, which is subject to relinquishment for the monk named so-and-so, [is given] to the venerable ones..."
It should be said: "It has been relinquished; if it is appropriate for the venerable ones, may the venerable ones give this robe-cloth to the monk named so-and-so.

The rest is exactly as before. However, by one relinquishing it to an individual, after saying "this" or "these," he should say "I relinquish them to the venerable one"; having relinquished them, [he should say] "I..."
“Venerable sir, I have committed one offense entailing relinquishment and confession; I confess it. In this way the offense should be confessed.
But if the other person is junior, he should be addressed as “friend. When the senior monk says, “Do you see it?
or “Do you see them?”, he should reply, “Yes, venerable sir,” or “Yes, friend,” and then say, “I see it. Thereafter, regarding the future...
When it is said, "You should restrain yourself," or "You all should restrain yourselves," one should say, "Very well, I shall restrain myself thoroughly.
When an offense has been thus confessed, the robe should be given with the words, "I give this robe to the Venerable One.

The method for two or three [monks] should be understood in the same way as previously stated. However, for two [monks], the relinquishment should be performed in the same manner as for the community (gaṇa).
Then, both the acceptance of the offense and the giving away of the forfeited robe must be performed by one of them, just as it would be by a single individual;

this, however, is the procedure for all [cases of] things to be relinquished (*nissaggiya*). As for the items—the robe, the bowl, and the sitting mat—there is only a difference in the substance itself;
but when the substance is out of sight, it should be relinquished with the words, "This. If there are many, [it should be said], "These."
This must be stated. The same principle applies to giving away what has been relinquished (*nissaṭṭha*).

For one who does not return an object that has been relinquished with the perception, "This was given to me by him," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, if one, knowing it belongs to that person, seizes it by means of a pretext, he should be dealt with according to the value of the goods after the owner has relinquished his claim.
This was laid down at Vesālī concerning the group of six bhikkhus regarding the matter of wearing an extra robe;
"not exceeding ten days" is the subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*) here. It is a common rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), not a specific instruction (*anāṇattika*).

For one who uses [the robe] without having relinquished it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). And as it is here, so it is everywhere; therefore, we shall not explain it further below. Even when the ten days have not elapsed...
For one who perceives it as having been exceeded when it has not, or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
For one who perceives it as not having been exceeded when it has been exceeded, or for one who is in doubt, there is likewise an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).

The same applies to those who perceive as "formally determined" (*adhiṭṭhita*), etc., what is actually not formally determined, not assigned, not relinquished, lost, destroyed, ruined, burnt, or stolen. Within ten days, [there is no offense] regarding what is formally determined, assigned, relinquished, lost, or destroyed.
There is no offense in the case of those who have been burned, maimed, or taken on trust, nor in the case of those who are insane and so forth. Regarding failure in conduct (*ācāra-vipatti*):

just as this [Pārājika] is, so too are the subsequent offenses; for among both Pātimokkhas, the Pārājikas and Saṅghādisesas constitute failure in virtue (*sīla-vipatti*), while all remaining offenses constitute failure in conduct.
There is no offense whatsoever that is called failure in livelihood (*ājīva-vipatti*) or failure in view (*diṭṭhi-vipatti*).
Furthermore, on account of failure in livelihood (*ājīvavipatti*), six classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*) have been prescribed, excluding the offense of wrong speech (*dubbhāsita*);
and on account of failure in view (*diṭṭhivipatti*), two classes of offenses have been prescribed, namely the *pācittiya* and the *dukkaṭa*. This is the defining characteristic here;
thus, the discussion of failure is concluded right here, and we shall not examine it further. [Regarding] a robe that is complete in its birth and measure...
The five factors here are: being one's own property, not having reached the count [of ten], the state of having severed impediments, being an extra robe, and the passing of ten days.

It originates from the *kaṭhina* (robe-making ceremony), is non-intentional (*akiriyā*), is not a liberation through perception (*nosaññāvimokkha*), is without mental concomitants (*acittaka*), is an offense by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), is bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and verbal action (*vacīkamma*), consists of three types of consciousness (*ticitta*), and consists of three types of feeling (*tivedanā*).
The commentary on the Kathina training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the Udosita training rule:
Regarding the second [rule], "when a monk's robe is finished," one should not grasp the meaning here in the same way as in the previous training rule.

The meaning of the instrumental expression "by a bhikkhu" (*bhikkhunā*) when it occurs as "when the robe is finished by a bhikkhu" (*niṭṭhite cīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā*) should be understood in the sense of agency (*sāmivasena*).
For there is no such thing as an action that must be performed by a bhikkhu in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇavasena*); rather, in the sense of agency, it means:
when the robe is finished by a bhikkhu and the kaṭhina has been suspended—thus, by these two factors, the completion of the robe and the suspension of the kaṭhina.
The meaning is appropriate thus: "If a bhikkhu whose impediments have been severed should dwell apart from his three robes even for a single night.

In this context, "with the three robes" means with any one of the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) and so forth that has been determined according to the method of determining the three robes. "Should dwell apart" means he should dwell separated [from them];
the manner of this is explained in the Canon by such passages as: "A village may have a single precinct or multiple precincts," and so on.

Having deposited any of the fifteen types of items mentioned—namely, villages, market towns, dwellings, watchtowers, watchmen’s huts, upper chambers, palaces, attics, boats, carts, fields, granaries, monasteries, hermitages, the foot of a tree, or open spaces—at any one of these locations, if one should cause dawn to rise while remaining outside those villages and other places beyond the reach of hand-contact (*hatthapāsa*), this is the summary here;
the detailed explanation, however, is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*. Except for...

"By the consent of the Saṅgha" means: setting aside that which the Saṅgha grants to a sick bhikkhu as the authorization not to be separated from his three robes (*ticīvara*), it should be understood that for a bhikkhu who has not obtained such authorization, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) even for being separated from them for a single night, according to the method already stated.
Only here [is the formula]: "Venerable Sir, this robe of mine was spent away overnight..."

There is a difference in the phrasing [of the rules] by way of such expressions as, "except by the consent of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, it is an offense entailing relinquishment" (nissaggiya), and so forth; however, this is the distinction:
it was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhus regarding the occasion of setting out on a journey through the country wearing only the inner and upper robes.
"Except by the consent of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus"—this is the subsequent rule (anupaññatti) here, and it is a common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti).

There is no formal instruction (anāṇattika). For one who perceives that they have not been separated when they have not been separated, and for one who is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

For one who perceives that they have been separated when they have been separated, as well as for one who does not perceive it or is doubtful, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya);
likewise for those who perceive that something has been relinquished or given away when it has not been relinquished or given away, and so forth. When it has been relinquished before dawn...

Furthermore, there is no offense regarding the various types of relinquishment mentioned in the context of the first *kathina* ceremony; likewise, there is no offense for one who has received formal authorization (*sammuti*) when staying apart from his robe.
However, once the illness has subsided, he must return, or else, while remaining right there, he must formally relinquish the robe.

Even if that same illness or another illness should recur, it is still considered permissible (*kappiya*) as long as it was obtained in accordance with the rules. This constitutes the state of having determined the robe (*adhiṭṭhitacīvaratā*).
The four factors here are: the kaṭhina not having been spread, the formal authorization not having been obtained, and being separated by night.

The origin and other characteristics are exactly as described for the first *kaṭhina*. For indeed, while in that case there was non-determination and non-assignment—which are non-actions—here it is non-returning; this is the distinction.
The commentary on the Udosita training rule is finished.
3. Commentary on the Akālacīvara training rule:
Regarding the third [rule], "a bhikkhunī whose robe is finished," the sense of the instrumental case is to be understood as expressing the agent itself. "Out-of-season robe" (akālacīvara).

That which is called the "robe season"—namely, the last month of the rainy season when the kaṭhina has not been spread, and the five months when the kaṭhina has been spread—excluding that time, anything that arises at another time;

and whatever is given to the Saṅgha even at the proper time with the thought, "This is out-of-season robe-cloth (akālacīvara)," or to an individual in such a manner as, "I give this to you," and so forth—that is what is called "out-of-season robe-cloth. "Should arise" means...

Such a robe—whether obtained from the Saṅgha by way of one's own share, or from a group such as the Suttantikas, or from relatives, or from friends, or as a rag-robe, or with one’s own wealth; or else, as it is said:
"Monks, there are these eight headings for the arising of a robe: one gives within the boundary, one gives by agreement, one gives by the assignment of alms, one gives to the Saṅgha..."

It may arise from one of these eight headings: "he gives to the Saṅgha," "he gives to both Saṅghas," "he gives to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence," "he gives specifying [the recipient]," or "he gives to an individual. And here, when one gives by referring to the boundary, saying, "I give to the boundary," it is called "giving to the boundary";
this same method applies everywhere. And here, "boundary" refers to a delimited boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*).

The boundary is fifteenfold: the precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*), the common residence boundary (*samāna-saṃvāsa-sīmā*), the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*), the gains boundary (*lābha-sīmā*), the village boundary (*gāma-sīmā*), the town boundary (*nigama-sīmā*), the city boundary (*nagara-sīmā*), the inner boundary (*abbhantara-sīmā*), the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepa-sīmā*), the district boundary (*janapada-sīmā*), the kingdom boundary (*raṭṭha-sīmā*), the realm boundary (*rajja-sīmā*), the island boundary (*dīpa-sīmā*), and the world-system boundary (*cakkavāḷa-sīmā*).
Among these, the "precinct boundary" refers to the enclosure of an enclosed monastery, or for one that is unenclosed...

It is delimited by the area suitable for a boundary. Furthermore, the "proximate boundary" (upacārasīmā) should be understood as the space within two throws of a clod by a man of medium strength, measured from either the place where monks regularly assemble, or from the edge of the dining hall, or from the dwelling where they reside permanently.
Moreover, that boundary expands when the monastery expands and contracts when it contracts.
It diminishes; even a hundred yojanas becomes merely a precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*). Whatever gain is given there reaches all those who have entered within the boundary.

Furthermore, the entry of bhikkhunīs into the monastery, the inquiry regarding lodgings, the announcement of probation (*parivāsa*) and penance (*mānatta*), the interruption of the rains residence (*vassa-cheda*), the provision of support (*nissaya*), the taking of lodgings, and so forth—all these rules are to be understood as pertaining to this very boundary.
As for the "boundary of gain" (*lābha-sīmā*), it refers to that which [is established by] kings, royal ministers, and others...
Having had a monastery built, they delimit an area of one *gāvuta*, half a *yojana*, or one *yojana* all around, establishing it thus:
"This is the boundary for the acquisition of our monastery; whatever arises within this interval, we give all that to our monastery.
This is called the "boundary for acquisitions" (*lābhasīmā*). Furthermore, within kingdoms such as Kāsī and Kosala, there are many districts.
Therein, the delimitation of a district is a district boundary (*janapada-sīmā*); the delimitation of a kingdom such as Kāsī or Kosala is a kingdom boundary (*raṭṭha-sīmā*);

the area where the commands of a single king prevail is a royal domain boundary (*rajja-sīmā*); a great island or an intermediate island delimited by the edge of the ocean is an island boundary (*dīpa-sīmā*);
the interior enclosed by the mountain range of a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) is a world-system boundary (*cakkavāḷa-sīmā*); the remainder [is explained] in the Nidānakathā.
The method is exactly as previously stated. In that regard, what is given with the words, “We give it within the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*),” reaches only the area of the broken boundary;
it does not reach even the intermediate space (*sīmantarika*) outside of that boundary.

However, what is given with the words, “We give it within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*),” reaches even those standing within the internal divisions, in the broken boundaries, or in the intermediate spaces; this applies to what is given within a common communion boundary (*samānasaṃvāsasīmā*).

What is given at a place that does not reach the boundary of a broken border or the intermediate space between boundaries reaches only those included within the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) or the acquisition boundary (*lābha-sīmā*).
What is given within village boundaries and so forth also reaches the places where a formal boundary (*sīma*) has been bound inside those boundaries.
What is given within an inner boundary (*abbhantara-sīmā*) or a water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepa-sīmā*) reaches only those included therein.
Even what is given at the boundaries of a country and so forth reaches those places within the boundaries that have been fixed for them;

therefore, if something is given while standing in Jambudīpa with the thought, "We give this to the Saṅgha in Tambapaṇṇidīpa," even a single person going from Tambapaṇṇidīpa is permitted to take possession of it for all [the monks].
Even if, right there, a single monk who shares the same communion [receives it] for those who share the same communion...
If he takes a share, he should not be prevented. However, if someone enters the monastery and says "I give it to the boundary" without specifying "to such-and-such a boundary," he should be asked:
"There are many kinds of boundaries; which one do you have in mind?
If he replies, "I do not know this distinction; let the Saṅgha residing within the boundary take it," then it should be divided among those residing within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*).
Regarding the *katikā*: here, a *katikā* refers to an agreement for equal distribution of gains (*samānalābhakatikā*). It should be made in this way:

when the monks have assembled in a monastery, those who wish to take charge of a particular monastery and desire to establish equal distribution of gains should mention its name, state some reason such as, "The monastery named so-and-so is ancient and has little gain," and then...
"Does it please the Saṅgha to share the gains of this monastery together with that monastery?"—this should be announced three times.
To this extent, one who is seated in that monastery is as if seated here; and in that monastery, it should be done in exactly the same way.
To this extent, one who is seated here is as if seated there. When the gains are being distributed in one monastery, [it is the same] in the other.
It is permissible to take a portion from what remains.
Regarding the phrase "the designation of alms" (*bhikkhāpaññatti*): here, the "designation of alms" refers to the place where the donor’s act of relinquishment is designated.
Therefore, one may say, "I give it to wherever my regular offerings are made," or "Give it there."
When this has been said, wherever his turn for providing food occurs, or from where he regularly feeds the monks,
or wherever a dwelling place has been built by him— in all such cases, it is considered as already given. However,
if there are fewer monks at a particular fixed location, or if there is only a single robe, one should record it in the schedule (*mātikā*) and accept it according to what he says.

Regarding the phrase "he gives to the Saṅgha": here, what is given by entering a monastery and saying, "I give to the Saṅgha," reaches those within the functional boundary (*upacārasīmā*) as well as those outside it who are connected with them as a single unit. Therefore, if there are recipients for them, a share must be given even to those who have not arrived.
However, that which is given by seeing monks outside the functional boundary and saying, "To the Saṅgha," [is different].
It reaches those within a single contiguous assembly. However, it does not reach those who are more than twelve handspans away from the assembly.
Regarding the phrase "to both Saṅghas": here, half of what is given to both Saṅghas must be given to the monks and half to the nuns.
Even if there is only one monk or one nun, [it must be divided accordingly]. At the very least...
Even for one who is not fully ordained, only half [of the portion] should be given.

However, when it is said, "To both Saṅghas and to you," if there are ten monks and ten nuns, having made twenty-one portions, one should be given to the individual, ten to the community of monks, and ten to the community of nuns; thus, that which was obtained by the individual [belongs to him].
Thus, he is permitted to receive from the Saṅgha according to his own seniority; why? Because it is included by the mention of "both Saṅghas.
The same principle applies even when it is said, "of both Saṅghas and the Cetiya. However, in this case, there is no portion belonging to the Cetiya that reaches the Saṅgha;
rather, there is one portion equivalent to the share obtained by a single individual. [The text continues: "Of the Bhikkhu-Saṅgha..."
But when it is said, "And for the bhikkhunīs," one should not divide it in the middle; rather, having counted both the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs, it should be distributed.
When it is said, "For the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, for the bhikkhunīs, and for you," the individual does not receive separately;
he receives only one portion from the total share that falls to him. But when it is said, "And for the cetiya," [the distribution is made] for the cetiya.
A single portion for an individual is obtained. Even when it is said, "for the monks and the nuns," it should not be given by dividing them in the middle;
rather, it must be apportioned according to the number of individuals. Their inclusion together with the individual *cetiyas* is exactly like the immediately preceding method.
And just as the method was set forth beginning with the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*), so too [should it be applied] to the community of nuns (*bhikkhunisaṅgha*).

It may also be understood by taking the first case as the starting point. Even when it is said, “For the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and for you,” the individual does not receive [the gift] separately, but the cetiya does.
Even when it is said, “For the bhikkhus and for you,” the individual does not receive it separately, but the cetiya certainly does.

Regarding the phrase "to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence": if, having entered the monastery, one says, "I give this to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence," it reaches those who completed the previous rains residence there without interrupting it, even if they have gone outside the boundary, but not others.
However, if one standing outside the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā) says, "To the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence..."
If he says, "Wherever [they have stayed]," it reaches all those who have completed the rains residence and are present.
But if he says, "Of those who have completed the rains residence in such-and-such monastery," it reaches only those who completed the rains residence there, up until the suspension of the Kathina.
If he speaks thus starting from the first day of the hot season, it reaches all those present there, but not others.
"Designates and gives" means that having designated and delimited [the recipients], he gives. How so?
Having invited the bhikkhus for either today’s or tomorrow’s rice gruel, and having had them drink the gruel at his house, he says: "I give these robes to those who drank my gruel.
It accrues only to those who were invited and drank the gruel; the same applies to meals, snacks, and so forth.
The same principle applies even when one has been invited.

"He gives to an individual" means he gives either in the person's absence, saying, "I give this robe to so-and-so," or in their presence, having placed it at the feet [of the recipient], saying, "This is for you. This is the brief explanation; the detailed account is as follows.

However, this is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*. Thus, with reference to whatever is obtained by way of the characteristics of out-of-season robe-cloth (*akālacīvara*) through these eight matrix-terms (*mātikāpada*), it is said: "Out-of-season robe-cloth should arise.
"By one who desires" means by one who wishes. "It should be made up quickly" means it should be made up swiftly within ten days.

"No completion" means that if there were no completion, the robe intended for the formal act (adhiṭṭhānacīvara) would not reach the required measure when being made, but would instead be deficient; this is the meaning.
"With the expectation of [receiving] more" means: "On such-and-such a day, the Saṅgha will receive robes, and from those, a robe will arise for me. With this...

By means of a method [of seeking] from the Saṅgha, a group, relatives, or friends, or from any other place, with the thought, "I shall obtain a rag-robe," or "With this allowable article I shall acquire a robe"—thus, while there is still an expectation of obtaining a robe.
"Beyond that" means if he should keep it for longer than the limit of one month; the meaning is that it is an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*). However, if his original robe...
The expected robe-cloth is fine, while the expected robe-cloth is coarse; it is not possible to join them together.

Since there are still nights remaining and the month is not yet full, one must not have the robe made against one's will. Only after obtaining another expected robe-cloth may it be made within the time limit.
If one does not obtain another, even the expected robe-cloth itself should be determined as a requisite cloth (parikkhāra-coḷa).

Now, if the original robe-cloth (*mūlacīvara*) is coarse and the expected robe-cloth (*paccāsācīvara*) is fine, one may determine the original robe-cloth as an accessory cloth (*parikkhāracoḷa*) and set aside the expected robe-cloth itself as the original robe-cloth; that [expected cloth] then receives another month’s grace period.
By this means, as long as one has not obtained it, one is permitted to set aside another [piece of cloth] as the original robe-cloth.
The procedure for relinquishment should be understood according to this method: "Venerable sir, this non-seasonal robe-cloth of mine has exceeded one month and is to be relinquished.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of monks who, having accepted a non-seasonal robe-cloth, let one month pass;

it is a common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti), not a specific instruction (anāṇattika). Everything following this is exactly the same as what was stated regarding the first *kathina* [rule]. The only difference is that in that case there was an exceeding of ten days, whereas here there is an exceeding of one month. The rest is identical.
The commentary on the training rule concerning out-of-season robes is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning old robes:
In the fourth [rule], "to one who is not a relative" means one who is not a kinsman, neither by the mother's side nor by the father's side, up to the seventh generation.
The meaning is: "not connected in any way whatsoever.

"A bhikkhunī" refers to one who has received full ordination (upasampadā) in either the pure community of bhikkhus or in the dual community (ubhatosaṅgha), such as the Sākiyānīs. "An old robe" means one that has been dyed and made allowable (kappa), and has been worn or put on even once;
or, at the very least, one that has been carried on the shoulder or on the head by way of use along the road.
He has gone away, or he is lying down with his head [toward the robe]; this too is indeed an old robe. "Should have it washed" means:

if he says the word "wash," or makes a gesture of the body, or gives hand-to-hand, or places it at the base of the feet, or, standing within a space of twelve spans, throws it upward, or sends it into the hand of another.
If it has been washed by her, it is as if she herself had washed it; the same principle applies to having it dyed or pounded.

If she gives it into the hands of a trainee nun (sikkhamānā), a novice nun (sāmaṇerī), or a female lay follower (upāsikā) for the purpose of washing, and she washes it after having received full ordination (upasampadā), there is likewise an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If it is given into the hands of a male lay follower (upāsaka) or a novice monk (sāmaṇera), he...
If, after changing his gender, he receives full ordination and washes it;

or if it has been given to a junior bhikkhu, and he too, having changed his gender, washes it—it is likewise an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya). The same rule applies to having it dyed or beaten.
[He should say: "Venerable sir, this old robe-cloth of mine, which was washed by an unrelated bhikkhunī, is to be relinquished."
By this method, the procedure for relinquishment (nissajjana) should be understood here.
It was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the Elder Udāyī regarding the matter of having old robes washed;

it is a non-common rule (asādhāraṇapaññatti), pertaining to the triad of offenses involving a laywoman, due to the command beginning with “wash,” and when a nun has been so commanded regarding the setting up of a hearth and so forth.

In all such applications, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the bhikkhu. However, once [the cloth] has been washed, merely lifted up, merely dyed, or merely beaten, it becomes subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).

For one who causes two or even all three of these acts—washing and so forth—to be performed, there is relinquishment with respect to one article, while for the others there is an offense of wrong-doing.
But if, having been told "wash it," the person performs all of them, the offense arises solely on account of the washing.
But for one who says, "Do whatever needs to be done with this robe," there are two *dukkaṭa* offenses along with one *pācittiya* offense for a single utterance;
likewise for one who causes a nun— who is ordained on one side (*ekatoupasampannā*)— to wash it, or for one who uses it without having relinquished it,
or for one who causes someone else’s sitting mat or rug to be washed, or [for one who causes it to be washed] by a relative.

There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who perceives her as unrelated or is in doubt; likewise, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) for one who perceives her as related when she is unrelated, or is in doubt.
Hereafter, in such instances, we shall refer to this as a "triple-offense of confession" (*tika-pācittiya*).
Furthermore, if a female friend who is unrelated washes [the robe] without being told "wash it," or if another [robe] that has not yet been used...

If one washes the requisites oneself, or if trainee nuns (*sikkhamānā*) or novice nuns (*sāmaṇerī*) wash them, there is no offense; for those who are insane and so forth, there is likewise no offense.
The three factors here are: the fact that it is an old robe, the giving of instructions to an unrelated nun while standing within range, and her performing the washing and so forth.
This arises from acting as a matchmaker (*sañcaritta*); it is an action (*kiriya*), and it is not to be resolved through recognition (*no-saññā-vimokkha*).
It is without consciousness, an offense by way of formal rule, bodily action, verbal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning old robes is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning the acceptance of robes.
In the fifth [offense], the phrase "from one who is not a relative" is exactly as previously stated; therefore, we shall not examine it further hereafter.
"Robe-cloth" (*cīvara*) refers to any one of the six types that is fit for formal assignment (*vikappanupaga*); this same method applies to all training rules connected with robe-cloth.
However, where there is a specific distinction, we shall explain it there. Regarding the phrase "should accept," here [it means] either with the hand...
Whether he places it in the hand or sets it at the feet, if robes are thrown while he is giving a Dhamma talk,
even if he releases his attention from the vicinity, if they are thrown over him and he consents, it is indeed accepted. However,
it is permissible to take what has been placed in the hand of anyone who is not fully ordained, thinking, "He will accept it as a rag-robe (paṃsukūla)."
It is indeed permissible to take even a rag from a heap of refuse and so forth, provided one has made a formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) regarding it. "Except for an exchange" means that,
setting aside what one takes as an exchange— having formed the intention, "I will give at least a piece of a gourd," or "I will give"— any other item,
down to a cloth or a water-strainer that is subject to formal assignment (vikappaṇupaga), is permitted.

For one who takes it, there is an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). In this regard, the procedure for relinquishment should be understood according to this method: "Venerable Sir, this robe-cloth of mine, received from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī, except in exchange, is an article to be relinquished.
This was laid down at Rājagaha concerning the Elder Udāyī, in the matter of receiving robe-cloth, with the proviso: "except in exchange."
This is the supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*) here; it is a non-common rule (*asādhāraṇapaññatti*), not subject to formal instruction (*anāṇattika*).

For the act of stretching out the hand and so forth for the purpose of taking [the robe], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); upon obtaining it, it becomes subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*); it must be relinquished; it is an offense entailing confession after the third [admonition] (*tikapācittiya*).

There is an offense of wrong-doing for one who perceives a relative who is ordained on one side as a non-relative, or for one who is in doubt. [There is no offense] in the case of taking [an item] out of trust, in temporary use, or regarding a bowl-bag and so forth.

There is no offense regarding requisites that do not need to be formally resolved upon, in taking [items] from the hands of a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*) or a novice nun (*sāmaṇerī*), and for those who are insane and so forth.
Herein, there are three factors: the robe being of a type suitable for assignment (*vikappanupaga*), the absence of an exchange, and taking it from the hand of one who is not a relative.
It originates from acting as a matchmaker (*sañcaritta*); it is both an action and a non-action; the rest is exactly like the fourth [offense].
The commentary on the training rule concerning the acceptance of robes is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning requesting from one who is not related:
In the sixth [rule], "householder" (*gahapati*) refers to a person who has not gone forth among monks; "housewife" (*gahapatānī*) refers to a woman who has not gone forth among nuns.
This same method applies to all training rules concerning householders. "Should ask for" means she should either ask for it herself or cause another to ask for it.
"Except at the right time": except for one whose robes have been stolen or whose robes have been lost, for her that occasion is excluded;
in any other instance of asking for them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), and upon obtaining them, it becomes an offense involving relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). In this regard:

“Venerable sir, this robe-cloth, which I requested from an unrelated householder outside of the [proper] occasion, is to be relinquished”—the procedure for relinquishment is to be understood according to this method.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Upananda in the matter of requesting robe-cloth, [beginning with the words]: “Outside of the occasion.”
This is the subsequent rule (anupaññatti) here; it is a common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti), not subject to formal instruction (anāṇattika). It is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for three cases;
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who perceives a relative as a non-relative, or for one who is in doubt.

There is no offense for one who requests [food] at a proper time, or when a relative has invited [him], or for one who requests it for the sake of another relative who has invited him, or for one who takes it with his own wealth, or for those who are insane and so forth.
The four factors here are: the robe being subject to alteration, the absence of a [proper] occasion, requesting from one who is not related, and the acquisition [of the robe] through that [request].
The origin and other details are exactly like those of the fourth [offense].
The commentary on the training rule regarding requesting from one who is not related is finished.

7. Commentary on the Seventh Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) Regarding the seventh: "That" refers to that robe which has either been stolen or lost. "Abhihaṭṭhuṃ" is a compound where *abhi* is a prefix (*upasagga*) and *haṭṭhuṃ* means "to bring";
thus, the sense is "to take," meaning "to offer. "Pavāreyya" means "should invite," that is, one should cause [the other] to desire or generate a wish [for it].
The meaning is that one should invite them by saying, "Take as much as you wish. Or, just as in the phrase "having seen renunciation as security" (*nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato*),
the sense is "having shown," so too here in the expression "should invite by bringing forward" (*abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyyā*),
it means either by physically bringing it near and placing it before them, or [saying], "From our storehouse of cloth, take as much as you desire."
The meaning is that one should either say "Take it" or, having brought it forward, invite [the donor] by word.
"With the inner and outer robe as the limit" (*santaruttaraparamaṃ*) means that for this robe, the inner and outer robe are the maximum;
what is meant is that the upper robe together with the lower robe constitutes the highest permissible limit. "From that, the robe may be accepted" means from that robe which has been brought forward.
Only so much robe-cloth may be accepted, and no more than that.
Herein is the analysis: for one whose determined robes have all three been lost, two may be consented to;
having worn one as an undergarment and the other as an upper garment, another should be sought from a suitable place. For one whose two have been lost...
Therefore, one [robe] must be accepted. However, if he normally goes about wearing only an inner and upper robe, two must be accepted;
in this way, he will be equal to one who accepts only one. For one who has lost one of the three, nothing at all should be accepted.
But for one who has lost one of the two, one must be accepted. For one who has only one, and that too is lost—
Two [robes] may be accepted. However, for a bhikkhunī, when five [robes] are lost, two may be accepted;
when four are lost, one may be accepted; when three are lost, nothing may be accepted—let alone when two or one are lost.
For by whatever means, she must remain with no more than an inner and outer robe; beyond that, in the act of requesting [more], there is an offense.
It is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), and by the acquisition [of the robe], it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya).

In this regard, the procedure for relinquishment should be understood according to this method: "Venerable sir, this robe-cloth, which was requested from an unrelated householder to the extent of being excessive, is to be relinquished.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks, on account of the matter of requesting many robes.

This is a common designation, not a formal injunction, and carries a triple offense of *pācittiya*. There is an offense of *dukkaṭa* for one who perceives a relative as a non-relative, or for one who is in doubt.

It does not apply to one who takes [the robe] after making two robes and saying, "I will bring the remainder," nor to one to whom it was said, "Let the remainder be yours alone," nor to one who takes what was given because of [the robe] being cut or lost, according to the stated method.
There is no offense for one who requests from those who have been invited by kinsmen, for one who takes with his own wealth, or for those who are insane and so forth.

Herein, the four factors are: being of lower status than oneself, the reason being such as having been stolen and so forth, requesting from one who is not a relative, and the acquisition through that [request].
The origin and other characteristics are exactly the same as in the fourth [offense].
The commentary on the preceding training rule is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning What is Set Aside (*Upakkhaṭa-sikkhāpada*):
Regarding the eighth [rule], "having designated a monk" means having pointed him out by saying, "I shall give this to such-and-such a monk."
"Materials for robes" means the price for robes, such as gold and so forth. "Is prepared" means it has been set aside; it has been gathered and placed [there].
"Having had it exchanged" means having bartered it, or having had it made, or having purchased it—this is the meaning. "I will clothe him with a robe" is a conventional expression;
however, the actual meaning here is: "I will give it to the monk named so-and-so. In that case...

The syntactical connection here is as follows: "He" refers to that monk who, having approached where that householder or housewife is, should—without being previously invited—enter upon a deliberation regarding the robe.
"Should enter upon a deliberation" means he should enter upon a specific mode or an excessive arrangement.
To show how he enters upon that, the text says, "It would be good indeed," and so forth.
In this context, *sādhu* is a particle used for making a request. *Vata* denotes reflection. *Mam* refers to oneself.
*Āyasmā* addresses another. *Evarūpaṃ vā evarūpaṃ vā* refers to any one among the [four] courses of action and so forth.
*Kalyāṇakamyataṃ upādāya* means having taken hold of a desire for what is beautiful or a desire for excellence with the mind; it is connected with the phrase “if he were to commit such an offense.”

But if, upon his making such a request, someone first increases the price beyond what was intended and exchanges it for something more beautiful, then for that transaction, the monk incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense; with the acquisition [of the cloth], it becomes a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*.
In this regard: "Venerable sir, this robe-cloth of mine, not previously invited to accept, having approached an unrelated householder..."
The procedure for relinquishment is to be understood by this method: “having fallen into [the state of] having made a formal determination, it is to be relinquished.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Upananda, regarding the matter of making a formal determination about a robe;

it is a general rule, not a specific instruction, and constitutes an offense of *pācittiya* under three conditions. If one perceives a relative as a non-relative, or is in doubt, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*. [This applies to] a costly [robe].
There is no offense for one who wishes to have [a robe] made up by exchange for something of little value, or for one who says, "Give me another such as this for that same price";
likewise for one who makes a request through a relative or one who has been invited, or for one who takes it with his own wealth;

and there is no offense for those who are insane and so forth. In this context, there are three factors: the desire for more regarding the robe, the request from one who is not a relative, and the acquisition thereof by means of that request.
The factors, such as the origin and so forth, are exactly the same as in the fourth [offense].
The commentary on the training rule concerning what has been set aside is finished.
9. Commentary on the second training rule concerning what has been set aside.
In the ninth [case], the meaning should be understood by this same method. For this is similar to the subsequent rule (anupaññatti) of the preceding one;
the only difference here is that while in the former case harm was done to one person, here it is done to two.

All else is exactly the same as before. And just as with two people, so too the offense should be understood for one who takes after having harmed many. Regarding the procedure for relinquishment (nissajjana-vidhāna):

And by this method, the variation in phrasing should be understood: “Venerable sir, this robe-cloth of mine, which was not previously invited for, having approached unrelated householders, has been subjected to a specific determination; it is to be relinquished.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning what is prepared ends.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Kings (*Rājasikkhāpada*).
In the tenth [rule], *rājabhogga* means: one to whom there belongs (*bhogga*) that which is to be enjoyed (*bhujitabba*) from a king; thus, he is *rājabhogga*.
There is also the reading *rājabhoga*, meaning one to whom there is enjoyment (*bhoga*) from a king. *Cīvaracetāpanna* refers to what is unallowable, such as gold and so forth.
*Pahiṇeyya* means "he should send. The passage beginning with *iminā* (by this) is stated to demonstrate the purity of the source from which it was brought.

For if one were to send [the gift] saying, "Give this to the monk named so-and-so," then because the source of its arrival would be impure, the monk would not even be permitted to designate a *kappiyakāraka* (a person who makes things allowable) regarding that unallowable object.
*Ābhataṃ* means "brought. The passage beginning with *na kho mayaṃ* (but we did not... is as follows:

Even if the price for a robe has been brought in accordance with what is allowable (*kappiya*), it becomes unallowable through such a message from a messenger; therefore, it is stated [in the text] that this must be refused.
For these four—gold, silver, a *kahāpaṇa* coin, and a *māsaka* coin—are objects involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-vatthu*);
as are pearl, gem, beryl, conch shell, rock-crystal, coral, ruby, and *masāragalla*.

The seven types of grain, female and male slaves, fields, lands, flower gardens, fruit orchards, and so forth—these are improper objects (*dukkaṭavatthu*) and are not permitted to be accepted for one's own sake, nor for the sake of a *cetiya*, the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual;
therefore, it was said, "Indeed, we do not... and so on, in order to show that it is not permissible to consent to such things.
Regarding the phrase "We accept the robe-cloth": this is permissible to say because it has been brought specifically for oneself;
therefore, it was stated. "At the proper time" means at the appropriate and fitting time; the meaning is: "When we have need of it, then we accept the allowable robe-cloth.
"A service-provider" means a *kappiyakāraka* (one who makes things allowable). "He should be pointed out" refers to [the question]: "But does the venerable one..."
Because it was stated using the appropriate formula, "Is there anyone who can act as a steward?", it is permitted. However, if the messenger asks, "Who will take this?
or "To whom shall we give it?", one must not point [a person out]. The mention of "an attendant" or "a lay follower" is said because they are suitable;
nevertheless, anyone other than the five types of fellow practitioners who is capable of acting as a steward is permissible.
“‘This one, friends,’ is said for the purpose of showing what constitutes a permissible statement for a bhikkhu; for it must be spoken in this way.
One should not say, ‘Give this to him,’ and so forth. ‘He has been requested by me’ means he has been instructed by me:
the sense is that he has been told, ‘If you have need of a robe, give a robe [to him]. For it is only when it has been announced in this manner by a messenger...”
It is proper to urge him [for payment], not merely because he has gone after having been handed the money into his hand. However,
if he was designated in the presence [of the donor] as "this is the agent for the service," and the messenger, having given the purchase-money into his hand right there in person, departs saying,
"Buy a robe for the Elder and give it to him," then even if one has not said, "He has been commissioned by me," it is proper to urge him.
If, however, the messenger goes while saying to the bhikkhu, “I will give this into his hand;
you may take the robe,” or if he sends someone else to announce it, then in such a case it is indeed permissible to urge the other [bhikkhu] as well.
This phrase “by messenger” is merely for the sake of illustration. This applies even when one acts in this manner after having brought the robe oneself.
In that case as well, this is the defining characteristic. "I have need of a robe, friend"—this is an indication of the characteristic of formal urging (*codanā*).
For if one urges by means of speech, this is the statement; it may be expressed in any language whatsoever.
However, it is not permitted to speak in such a manner as "Give me" or "Bring me," and so forth. "Should he cause it to be produced"—thus...
Having made a verbal declaration, he should press the matter three times; if he succeeds by means of obtaining [the robe], that is "wholesome" (kusala), meaning it is excellent.
"Up to six times" (*chakkhattuparama*) is a neuter noun used adverbially. For up to six times, he must stand silently for the sake of that robe;
he must not sit, nor accept food, nor preach the Dhamma.
When it is asked, "For what reason have you come?", one should say only this much: "Know, friend.
If he sits down or performs other such actions, he violates the proper occasion and destroys the purpose for which he came;

this is stated for the purpose of showing the characteristics of admonishing by means of bodily action. And here, according to the highest limit, three forms of admonition and six occasions are permitted.
A double ground is permitted for accusing; therefore, if one only accuses and does not stand [in the formal act], six grounds are obtained.
If one only stands and does not accuse, twelve grounds are obtained.
If one does both, two grounds must be subtracted from one accusation. In that regard, if one [accuses] repeatedly on a single day...
If he goes six times and urges [the donor], or if having gone only once he says six times, "Friend, I have need of a robe"; or likewise,
if on a single day he goes again and again and stands twelve times,
or if having gone only once he stands in various places— he too destroys all the urgings and all the locations.
What need is there to mention one who does this on various days? This is the decision in this matter.
However, in cases where the donor goes and sits down by the attendant himself, it is permissible to remind him even a hundred times.
But as for an attendant who is not designated by either party—an attendant who stands at the mouth [of the bowl] while facing away, or an attendant who is out of sight—he is not [to be reminded].
It should be said: thus, ten makers of what is allowable (*kappiyakāraka*) are shown here.
"Beyond that" means beyond the measure of the place where the aforementioned objection was stated. "Forfeiture" (*nissaggiya*):

for one who makes further effort beyond that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in all applications; upon acquisition, it becomes subject to forfeiture. And in this context: "Venerable sir, this [is mine]..."

The procedure for relinquishment is to be understood according to this method: "If a robe has been procured after urging more than three times or standing [waiting] more than six times, it is an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
Regarding the phrase "from whom the means of purchasing a robe was brought for him":
it refers to whichever king or royal official from whom the means for purchasing a robe was brought for that bhikkhu; or alternatively, "from where [it was brought]" (*yatvassa*).
The reading is as follows; this is the meaning. "Therein" means in the presence of that king or royal official;

for this locative expression is used in the sense of proximity. "It does not accomplish any purpose for that bhikkhu" means that the act of purchasing does not bring about even the slightest result for that bhikkhu.
"Venerable sirs, apply yourselves to your own [welfare]"—venerable sirs...
"May they obtain their own wealth; may what belongs to you not be lost"—this means that what belongs to you should not perish.

"This is the proper conduct therein" means this is the conformity to the Dhamma (*anudhammatā*) following the supramundane Dhamma; the meaning is that it is the nature of the formal observance (*vattadhammatā*).
Therefore, one who does not act in this way incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to the breach of the formal observance.
At Sāvatthī, concerning Upananda, it was prescribed on account of this matter when he did not wait even though he was told, "Venerable sir, please wait until tomorrow.

This is a general rule, not a specific injunction; it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for three cases. There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who perceives a meal as being in excess when it is actually deficient, or for one who is in doubt.
[There is no offense] if the meal was obtained without being asked for, or if it was given after the owners had been urged to do so.
There is no offense for those who are insane and so forth. The four factors here are: the fact that the monk acting as the steward has been designated;
the fact that it was sent by messenger; the effort made beyond that; and the acquisition through that effort. The origins and other characteristics are exactly the same as in the fourth [offense].
The commentary on the training rule concerning kings is finished.
The first section, on robes, is concluded.
2. The section on wool.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Silk (Kosiyasikkhāpada).

In the first [rule] of the Section on Wool (Eḷakalomavagga), "mixed with silk" means mixed even with a single silk thread, even if it has been blown there by the force of the wind at the place where it was made.
"Rug" (santhatam) refers to silk threads laid one upon another on a level patch of ground.
The characteristic of what is to be done is that after spreading it out and sprinkling it with sour gruel and so forth, one should have it made;

[if one does so], it is an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*). Regarding the acts of making and having it made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); upon acquisition, it becomes an offense of expiation.

And here, the procedure for relinquishment should be understood according to this method: "Venerable sir, this rug of mine, mixed with silk, which was had made, is an offense of expiation. Of this very [offense]...
Following the sequence of the words, everything beyond this should be understood. Since it can be known by this much alone, we shall not present what follows.
This was laid down at Āḷavī concerning the group of six monks, in the matter of having a rug made mixed with silk.

This is an uncommon designation (*asādhāraṇapaññatti*). There is an offense of threefold instruction (*sāṇattika*) for having it made for one's own sake; there is an offense of fourfold *pācittiya* by way of completing what was left unfinished by oneself;
and there is an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*) for obtaining and using what has been made by another when it was made or caused to be made for the sake of someone else.
There is no offense in making canopies and the like, nor for those who are insane and so forth. [The factors of the offense are: the state of being mixed with silk, and for oneself...
The three factors here are: the making or having made of what has been spread for a purpose, and the acquisition.
The origins and so forth are according to the method stated under the training rule on having washed.
The commentary on the training rule concerning silk is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Pure Black Wool.

Regarding the second rule, "pure black" means pure black wool that has not been mixed with other fibers. This was prescribed at Vesālī concerning the group of six monks (*chabbaggiya*) in the matter of making a rug (*santhata*) of such a kind. The remainder is exactly like the first rule.
The commentary on the training rule concerning pure black wool is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Two Parts In the third [rule], "two parts" means two portions. "To be taken" means to be accepted. "Of the cow-herders" refers to those of Kapilavanna.
Here, however, is the detailed analysis: having weighed them among as many [cow-herders] as one wishes to deal with, [one should take] two portions.
Black wool may be taken [for three parts], one part of white wool, and one part of brown wool.
If there is even a single black hair in excess, it becomes an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*); if it is less, it is permissible.
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks, regarding the act of making such a rug; it is an offense that is both intentional and unintentional.
The remainder is exactly like the first [rule]. However, these three, even if obtained after having been relinquished, are not permitted to be used.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the two parts is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Six Years.
In the fourth [offense], "within six years" means on the near side of six years; the meaning is "within.

"Except by the consent of the Saṅgha" means that, setting aside the case where the Saṅgha grants a blanket-permission for a sick monk, it is an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya) for one who, not having obtained such permission, makes another blanket within the interval of six years.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhus regarding the practice of having a rug made every year;
"except by the agreement of the bhikkhus" is the subsequent rule (anupaññatti) here.
For one who has obtained such permission, it may be made every year in whatever place he goes, for as long as his illness has not been cured, or even if cured, it recurs.
It is permissible to have it made for the sake of another, and having received what has been made, it is also permissible to use it;
the remainder is exactly like the first [rule].
The commentary on the training rule concerning the six years is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule on Sitting Mats (*nisīdana*).
In the fifth [rule], "old sitting mat" (*purāṇasaṇṭhata*) refers to that upon which one has sat or lain down even once.
"On all sides" means that after cutting away from one side—whether circular or square—the portion taken up remains the measure of a span (*vidatthi*).
It should be accepted in this manner. However, when spreading it, one should spread it either in one place or by interweaving the strands to make them mixed;
in this way, it becomes more durable. Regarding "if there is none": if there is an old rug, it must not be taken [without permission].

But if there is none, it is permissible even without taking permission; it is also permissible to have one made for another's sake, and once it has been made, it is permissible to use it after receiving it.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhus on the occasion of the matter of the relinquishing of a rug; the rest is exactly like the third [offense].
The commentary on the training rule on sitting mats is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule on wool.
In the sixth [case], "one who has set out on a journey" means one who has set out upon a long road designated as a journey; all of this is merely to illustrate the basis of the rule.
However, there is no fault for one who receives [food] by means of what is rightfully obtained from any place whatsoever.

"At most three leagues" (tiyojanaparamaṃ) refers to a region measuring three leagues from the place where it was received. "With one's own hand" (sahatthā) means with one's own hand, that is, by oneself.

The meaning is "they must be taken away. "When there is no one to take them" means when there is indeed no other person to take them. However, if there is someone, it is permissible to have them carried.

But if one carries them oneself—even for the purpose of treating a wind ailment—after merely tying them with a string and inserting them into the ear-cavity, a *dukkaṭa* offense is incurred upon exceeding three *yojanas* by one foot; upon exceeding a second foot, [the same offense follows].
An offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
It was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning a certain monk on the occasion of traveling more than three *yojanas*;

it is a unique prescription (*asādhāraṇa-paññatti*), not a formal injunction (*anāṇattika*), and constitutes a triple *pācittiya*. For one who perceives the distance as exceeding three *yojanas* when it is actually less, or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
There is no offense in taking back what was taken within three *yojanas*; in taking it beyond that distance after having gone there with the intention of staying;
in taking what was stolen or abandoned and then recovered; in causing another to take it; and even in taking goods tied together by a string.

There is also no offense for those who are insane and so forth. [The factors of the offense are: the wool of sheep being unworked into a finished article, the first acquisition [of the article], and oneself...

Taking [the wool] and placing it in the vehicle of another who is unaware, or traveling more than three *yojanas*, returning it, and the intention not to dwell [there]—these are the five factors here.
It originates from sheep’s wool; it is an action (*kiriya*); it is not released through perception (*nosaññāvimokkha*); it is without mental concomitants (*acittaka*);
it is an offense by formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*); it is bodily action (*kāyakamma*); it possesses three types of consciousness (*ticitta*); and it possesses three types of feeling (*tivedana*).
The commentary on the training rule regarding sheep’s wool is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Having Sheep’s Wool Washed:

This was laid down in the seventh [offense] concerning the group of six monks among the Sakyans, with reference to the matter of having sheep’s wool washed. In this regard, the entire analysis should be understood according to the same method as that stated for the washing of old robes.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the washing of sheep’s wool is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule concerning gold and silver:
“Gold and silver” refers to both gold and coinage; furthermore, it includes the *kahāpaṇa*, as well as copper coins, wooden coins, resin coins, and so forth.
All those who engage in worldly transaction are here referred to simply as "silver.
"Should take up" means that he himself might take it up, whether it is being given to him for his own sake, or he sees it lying somewhere unclaimed.
"Or should cause to be taken up" means that he might have another take it up for him. "Or should consent to what is deposited" means [when someone says], "Let this be yours, sir."

Thus, whether in the presence of another or in their absence—by means of speech alone, by a hand gesture, or by saying "this is yours"—if one has relinquished gold or bullion with the thought, "In such-and-such a place there is my gold and bullion;
let that be yours," and if the other person, without rejecting it through body or speech, accepts it mentally, this is called "consenting" (*sādiyeyya*). If...

However, if one consents with the mind and desires to take it, yet rejects it by body or speech, saying, "This is not allowable," or if, without rejecting it by body or speech, one remains pure in mind and does not consent, thinking, "This is not allowable for us," it is permissible.
Regarding "an offense involving forfeiture" (*nissaggiya*): for one who performs any of the acts such as taking up [the object] among those things that are not bound to a price...
Regarding the objects [involved], it is an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya-pācittiya) according to the number of objects.
When relinquishing it, one must do so right in the midst of the Saṅgha, saying: "Venerable sirs, I accepted money; this, venerable sirs, is my relinquishment;
I relinquish this to the Saṅgha. If any householder should come there, [one should say]: "This..."

He should be told, "Know [this]. But when he asks, "What should be brought by this? one should not say, "This or that," but rather explain what is allowable, saying, "Ghee and such things are allowable for the monks.
If he brings it, then—excluding the receiver of the money—it should be divided and consumed by everyone. However, as for the receiver of the money, whatever [accrues] on account of that...
Once it has arisen, even if someone else obtains it and offers it back, it is not permitted to use it—even the shade of a tree growing from that very spot.
However, if he does not wish to bring anything back, he should be told, "Cover this.
If he places it anywhere or takes it away, he should not be stopped. If he does not cover it, [he must be one] endowed with the five factors.
A monk may be appointed as a money-remover. He must remove the money without making a sign, just as one would sweep away excrement.
If he makes a sign, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
This was laid down at Rājagaha concerning Upananda in the matter of accepting money; it is a general rule.

This is a formal act of censure (*sāṇattika*), a triad of offenses of expiation (*pācittiya*). There is an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who perceives what is not money as money, or is in doubt about it;
for one who takes [it] for the sake of the Saṅgha, a shrine, and so forth; and for the acceptance of pearls, gems, and the like.

There is no offense for one who deposits [it] according to the method of the Jewel Precept (*ratanasikkhāpada*), nor for those who are insane and so forth. [The factors of the offense consist of: the nature of gold and silver, the fact that it is intended for oneself, and the acts of taking and so forth.
"Being of another nature"—these are the three factors here. Regarding the origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth: it may be an action because one incurs an offense through the act of taking;
it may be a non-action because of the non-performance of a prohibition. The rest is exactly as explained in the section on matchmaking (sañcaritta).
The commentary on the training rule concerning gold and silver (jātarūpa-sikkhāpada) is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Trade in Money (*Rūpiyasaṃvohāra-sikkhāpada*).

In the ninth [rule], "in various ways" (*nānappakāraka*) means manifold, by way of having been made and so forth. "Trade in money" (*rūpiyasaṃvohāra*) means the exchange of gold and silver (*jātarūparajata*).

For while the acceptance of the articles subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya-vatthu*) and the articles subject to an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa-vatthu*) was prohibited by the preceding training rule, by this [present rule]...

Exchanging. Therefore, for one who exchanges an article that is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for articles that are either articles of wrong-doing or articles that are allowable (kappiya), there is an offense of wrong-doing. However, for one who exchanges an article subject to forfeiture (nissaggiya) for an article subject to forfeiture, or for an article of wrong-doing, or for an allowable article;
or for one who exchanges articles of wrong-doing and allowable articles for an article subject to forfeiture—there is an offense of wrong-doing.

For one who exchanges it, there is an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*); that must be forfeited in the midst of the Saṅgha according to the same procedure as before, and regarding the article once forfeited, one must proceed according to the method stated therein.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks, in the matter of trading in money; it is a common rule.
It is not subject to an *aññatti* (formal act of instruction). There are two factors here: the fact that what one exchanges with one's own wealth is indeed silver, and the act of exchange itself.
As for the action, the rest is exactly as explained in the preceding training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning trade in silver is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Buying and Selling (*Kayavikkaya-sikkhāpada*).

Regarding the tenth [rule], "in various ways" (*nānappakāraka*) means manifold, by way of allowable goods such as robes and so forth. "Buying and selling" (*kayavikkaya*) means both buying and selling.
By means of this [phrase]: "Give this for that; bring that; exchange it; have it bartered for."
For according to this principle, one who takes another’s allowable article incurs buying, while one who gives away one’s own allowable article incurs selling.

Therefore, with the exception of the five [types of] fellow-practitioners, whatever allowable article one receives—even if it belongs to one’s mother—after having given one’s own allowable article, that is an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). This is by virtue of the characteristics already stated.
It must be relinquished to the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual—whichever is appropriate—with the instruction: “Having eaten this, or having taken this, bring such-and-such or do such-and-such.

Having thus caused dye and so forth to be brought, or having caused the requisites such as water-pots to be made, or having caused building work such as clearing the ground to be done, the object must be relinquished while it still exists; if it no longer exists, one must simply confess the *pācittiya* offense.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Upananda regarding the matter of buying and selling:
for one who asks the price, saying, "What is this worth?", and having appointed another person— even his own son or brother—
as a *kappiyakāraka* (one who makes things allowable), with the intention of taking the goods from that person's hand, [saying], "Take this and give me such-and-such."
There is no offense for one who explains, saying, "This is ours, and we have need of this and that," and then takes what was obtained with his own wealth;
nor for one who engages in buying and selling with fellow practitioners of the Dhamma;
nor for those who are insane and so forth. There is no offense regarding that which he exchanges with his own wealth, or that by means of which he exchanges.
The three factors here are: being an allowable object, being contrary to the Dhamma, and the occurrence of buying and selling.
The remainder is exactly as explained in the section on trading in money.
The commentary on the training rule concerning buying and selling is finished.
The second chapter: The Section on Goat’s Hair. 3.
The Section on Alms Bowls.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Alms Bowls.
In the first chapter of the *Patta-vagga*, "an extra bowl" (*atireka-patta*) refers to one that has neither been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) nor assigned to another (*avikappita*).

Furthermore, it must be of a standard size—either large, medium, or small. Its measurement is stated in the Canon by way of the passage beginning, "It takes up half an *āḷhaka* of cooked rice," and so forth (*Pārājika*, 602).
Regarding this, the following is the detailed analysis: [it refers to] unbroken, old *sāli* rice grains that have been well-husked and purified.
Having taken two Magadhan *nāḷis* of those rice grains, he cooked them into a well-prepared, non-sticky, non-clumped, and very clear boiled rice—
resembling a heap of jasmine buds— which was thoroughly drained; having placed it all without remainder into the bowl,
[he prepared] a portion equal to one-fourth of that rice, neither too thick nor too thin, which could be lifted with the hand and consisted of all its constituent ingredients.
Bean soup should be added; then, a condiment such as fish or meat should be added in an amount corresponding to the mouthfuls, sufficient for as many mouthfuls as will be eaten.
However, ghee, oil, buttermilk, and rice-gruel do not count toward the number [of mouthfuls]. For these belong to the same category as the boiled rice;
they can neither be subtracted from nor added to the count. Thus, all of this may be added.
If it stands level with the lower rim of the bowl’s mouth, or if, when cutting with thread or a razor, the thread or the razor touches its lower edge, this is called an "excellent" (ukkaṭṭha) bowl.
If it stands protruding beyond that rim, this is called an "excellent-with-protrusion" (ukkaṭṭhomaka) bowl. If it does not reach that rim, [it is a deficient bowl].

It is entirely contained within; this is called the "superlative superlative" bowl. One measuring half the size of the superlative is the "middling. One measuring half the size of the middling bowl is the "inferior.
The classification of these should also be understood according to the method already stated.
Thus, among these nine, two—the superlative superlative and the inferior inferior—are not bowls; the remaining seven are bowls of appropriate measure.
This is the brief summary here; the detailed account, however, is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.
Therefore, having obtained an iron bowl or a clay bowl that is of the proper measure and fit for a recluse, one should formally resolve upon it within ten days after relinquishing the old bowl.
If, however, even a mere *kākaṇika* coin’s worth remains to be paid from its original cost...
It does not become one that has entered into a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*); it must be assigned by one who does not relinquish it.

In this regard, the characteristics of relinquishment (*paccuddharaṇa*) and determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) should be understood according to the method already stated in the *Cīvara-vagga*; we shall explain the characteristic of assignment (*vikappana*) further below.
However, if some monk who does not possess a bowl obtains ten bowls and wishes to use them all for himself alone, [he should assign] one...
Having determined upon one bowl, on the following day it must be relinquished and another determined upon;
