by this method, it is possible to maintain [the practice] even for a hundred years. However, if a bowl has a hole anywhere from two finger-breadths below the rim down to a size sufficient for a grain of rice or a husk to pass through, it is not fit for determination.

It does not exist. Once again, when holes have been made and it has become ordinary, it must be formally resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhātabba*). The rest regarding the relinquishment of the formal resolution is exactly according to the method stated for the three robes (*ticīvara*).

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks (*chabbaggiya*) on the occasion of the matter of possessing an extra bowl; it is a non-common rule (*asādhāraṇapaññatti*). The sequence of the commentary on the remainder should be understood by the same method as stated for the first training rule in the Chapter on Robes (*cīvaravagga*).
The commentary on the training rule on bowls is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Fewer than Five Straps (Ūnapañcabandhana-sikkhāpada).
Regarding the second [rule]: "Having fewer than five straps" means that its five straps do not reach completion;
thus, the meaning is that it has fewer than five straps. The instrumental case is used here to indicate a characteristic of such a state. In this context, since...
Even for one whose bowl has no binding, the five bindings do not fulfill the requirement because they are entirely absent;
therefore, it is said in the word-commentary: "A bowl with fewer than five bindings means a bowl that is either unbound or has a single binding," and so forth.

And because it is stated as "with one having fewer than five bindings," for one who possesses a bowl with five bindings or a bowl with the space for five bindings, that [bowl] is not a valid bowl for him.

Therefore, it is permissible to request another bowl. However, if there is even a single line measuring two finger-breadths below the rim of the bowl, one should pierce that bowl at its lower edge with a needle, solder it, and then cook it;
or else, having bound it with a cord made of thread, a rope, bark-fiber, or tin-wire, one should place that binding upon the food.
To prevent it from sticking, it should be covered with a triple-layered patch or with some kind of resin-like substance such as *silesa*.
That bowl must then be formally resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhahitvā*) before being used. Alternatively, a small hole may be made and [the patch] bound on;
or it is also permissible to bind it after burning molasses and applying stone powder. However, for one whose [streaks] are two lines or even just one, measuring four finger-breadths—
Two binding straps should be given for that [alms-bowl]. For one whose [circumference] is three or even one *chaḷaṅgula*, three [straps] should be given.
For one whose [circumference] is four or even one *aṭṭhaṅgula*, four [straps] should be given.

One whose [circumference] is five or even one *dasaṅgula* has not yet reached the limit, whether it be bound or unbound; another must be requested. This, then, is the determination regarding the clay bowl.

However, in the case of an iron bowl, even if there are five or more holes, if those holes have been plugged with iron filings, lac, or a metal ring and are smooth, it may be used; another one need not be requested.
But if even a single hole is large, even if it has been plugged with a metal ring, it is not smooth.
It does not exist; food sticks to the bowl; this bowl is unallowable, and another must be requested.

However, if one requests another while there already exists a bowl that has reached the state of being a mere fragment, or an iron bowl, or a clay bowl with fewer than five repairs, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of requesting;
upon acquisition, it becomes subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*), and it must be relinquished. When relinquishing, [it should be done] in the midst of the Saṅgha.
It must be relinquished in this manner; therefore it is said, "It should be relinquished before an assembly of monks. And as for that assembly of monks:
here, those monks should first gather together, each having taken his own bowl which he has normally determined for himself.
Then, the appointed bowl-distributor, having described the existing qualities of the bowl, should say, "Venerable sirs, please take this."
The senior monk (thera) should be addressed. If the bowl does not please the senior monk, or if he does not take it because of his fewness of desires, it is permissible.
However, if he does not take it out of compassion for him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

But if he does take it, having had the senior monk’s bowl given to a second senior monk, by that same method it should be passed down until it reaches the most junior member of the Saṅgha; that bowl is then relinquished by him.
However, that which has the edge of the bowl as its limit must be given to that bhikkhu.
He, too, must use it with care, exactly as he received the bowl after making his request.
But if, feeling loathing for it, he sets it down in an improper place, uses it without proper care, or discards it, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Regarding the group of six among the Sakyans, many rules were laid down concerning the soliciting of bowls;

these are common regulations (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), not subject to specific instructions (*anāṇattika*). Whether it be one without a band, one with one band, two bands, three bands, four bands, or a place for no band, or a place for one, two, three, or four bands—if one causes [bowls] to be made in this manner, for each individual bowl there are ten ways [of transgression].
There are ten kinds of bowls. However, by way of having it made for oneself, there is one hundred offenses of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).

There is no offense in the case of one whose bowl is lost, one whose bowl is broken, one who has been invited by a relative of one's own, one who has been invited by a relative of another, one who asks for it on behalf of that very person, one who takes it with one's own wealth, and in the case of those who are insane and so forth. [This applies] to a bowl that has reached the stage of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhānupaga*).
Having fewer than five new bindings, making it one's own, not having made a formal request, and obtaining it by means of that—these are the four factors here.
The origins and so forth are exactly as stated in the training rule on having clothes washed.
The commentary on the training rule concerning fewer than five new bindings is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Medicines (Bhesajja-sikkhāpada).
Regarding the third [rule], "to be swallowed" (*paṭisāyanīyāni*) means they are to be swallowed; that is, they are to be consumed.

By this, he shows that there is no offense even when seven days have passed for those things which were taken up by oneself and then set aside; for it is not permitted to swallow them [after that period].
"Medicines" refers to those things so designated whether or not they perform the function of medicine.
"Ghee" means the ghee of cows and other animals whose meat is permitted; the same applies to butter.
"Oil" means that produced from sesame, mustard, madhūka, castor, vasā, and so forth. "Honey" means specifically bee-honey. "Treacle" means starting from the juice of sugarcane...
All products of the sugarcane, whether uncooked or cooked without a base, are to be understood as "molasses" (*phāṇita*).

"Having received those" means having received those medicinal substances themselves, not their bases. By this [rule], with the exception of ghee and oil, if one receives the bases for those things here that are "to-be-eaten-at-the-proper-time" (*yāvakālika*) and then makes [medicines] such as ghee from them, even if they exceed seven days, [they are permissible].

He shows that there is no offense. However, castor oil that has been received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time is permitted to be used for the purpose of using oil;

therefore, with the exception of human fat, any other kind of fat may be received before midday, cooked by oneself, and even if it results in oil, it may be used for seven days without consuming meat.
It is permissible. However, that which has been cooked by one who is not fully ordained and given on the same day before the meal is permissible even if it contains meat;
yet, it is not permissible at all to cook the raw material for other things that are to be consumed only during the day (yāvakālika).

It is permissible to cook clarified butter (*sappi*) or fresh butter (*navanīta*) that has already been produced, but it is not permissible to consume that as containing meat, even if it is on the same day before the meal.

However, ghee and other items made by an unordained person cooking milk and so forth that were received before the morning meal—even if they contain solid food—are permitted for that very day before the meal;
from after the meal onwards, they are not to be consumed, though there is no offense even if seven days have passed.
"They may be used after being stored" means having been kept in storage before the meal.
Those [medicines] received before the morning meal on that same day are permitted even for use with solid food;
however, from after the meal onwards, both those [received then] and those received after the meal must be used for seven days without being mixed with solid food—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, because of the expression "must be used," one may, within the seven-day period, resolve upon them for purposes such as anointing the body.
There is no offense regarding those items set aside: mustard seeds, madhūka seeds, castor seeds, and bones that are for the purpose of making oil for life-long use;
having received them, the oil made on that very day is "seven-day" (sattāhakālika). Oil made on the second day may be used for six days;
made on the third day, for five days; made on the fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day, it may be used on that very day. If...
If it remains until the rising of the dawn, it becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
That which was prepared on the eighth day is not fit for consumption; however, because it is not subject to forfeiture, it is permissible for external use.

Even if one does not prepare it oneself, if seven days elapse for mustard seeds and so forth accepted for the sake of oil, or for ghee and so forth not mentioned in the text, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Honey-syrup made from *madhūka* flowers with cold water—
However, it is of the same nature as molasses; mango-syrup and the like are "to be used during the day" (*yāvakālika*).

As for that which here is "to be used for seven days" (*sattāhakālika*), even if one receives it after relinquishing it, it is not permitted to smear it on a wound or the like, nor is it permitted to swallow it.
It should be applied to a lamp or to something black in color; it is permitted as physical use for another monk. That which...
However, if one gives it away without expectation and later receives it again, it is permissible even to swallow it.
In the case of ghee and so forth that have been set aside separately, or those not mixed together in a single vessel, there are offenses according to the number of items.

This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhus regarding the matter of exceeding seven days; the rest should be understood in the same manner as stated in the first training rule of the Cīvara-vagga.
The commentary on the training rule concerning medicines is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭika*):
"When one month of the hot season remains" means that of the four months of the hot season, one—the final month—remains. "It should be sought" means...
From the first day of the last month of summer until the final day of the month of Kattika, one may either arouse mindfulness by means of such thoughts as,
“It is the time for a rainy-season robe,” or one may make a formal request at a place where the Saṅgha has been invited,
or at a place where one’s own relatives have been invited, saying, “Please give me a rainy-season robe. And so forth.
It should be sought out. For one who arouses mindfulness in a place where one is not known or has not been invited, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the breach of the proper conduct;

or, for one who makes a request by saying "Give me" and so forth, regardless of the manner, there is a formal offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya-pācittiya) under the training rule concerning requesting from those not related. Having made it, it should be worn; [this refers to] from the first day of the latter half of the summer month...

From [the beginning] until the final day of the month of Kattika, it should be worn after having been finished by a needle-worker, dyed even once with a simple dye that changes the color slightly, and marked with the *kappa-bindu*.
Up to this point, the last month of the hot season is the field for seeking [the robe];
the last fortnight is also the field for making and wearing it; and during the four months of the rainy season, all of that [is permitted].
The meaning "it is allowable" has thus been shown. Furthermore, regarding the last month of the summer season that is permitted:

even if a rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*) has been sought out during this period, it is not allowable to resolve upon it [as one's own]. If, after that month has passed, the rains are postponed, one receives the allowance for another month;
however, having washed and put it away, on the day of the entry into the rains retreat (*vassūpanāyikā*),...

It must be formally resolved (*adhiṭṭhātabba*). If, through forgetfulness or incapacity, it has not been performed, one receives a grace period of six months—consisting of two months of the dry season and four months of the rainy season.
However, if the *kaṭhina* robe is spread in the month of Kattika, one receives another four months; thus, there are ten months in total. Beyond that, [one must maintain] mindfulness.

For one who sets aside that original robe-cloth with the expectation [of receiving more], there is a period of one month; thus, he receives the privilege for eleven months, but beyond this, he does not receive it even for a single day.
"If less than a month remains of the summer" means during the first part of the last month of the summer, up until the winter.

"The first day" means, for that duration. "Should seek" means: for one who seeks from a place where he is not known or not invited among these seven months of the "back-season," there is a *nissaggiya pācittiya* offense due to the act of causing a thought to arise;
for one who requests it, there is a *nissaggiya pācittiya* offense under the training rule regarding requesting from one who is not known;
however, for one who requests it from someone who is known or has been invited, there is no offense under that same training rule.

For one who causes the thought [of acquisition] to arise, there is an offense under this training rule. "When less than half a month of the summer remains" means during the first half-month preceding the last half-month of the summer.
"Having made it, he should wear it": for one who wears it after having made it—even if it was acquired through lawful means—within that interval, it is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks regarding the matter of seeking a rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭika*);
it is a rule not shared [with other classes of persons], it is without formal instruction, and it is an offense of *pācittiya* for three cases.

There is an offense of *dukkaṭa* for one who perceives it as more than [the limit] when it is less than a month and a half, or for one who is in doubt; likewise for one who, while possessing such a rain-cloak, lets his naked body be rained upon.

However, there is no offense for one bathing in lotus ponds and the like; nor for one whose robe has been stolen or lost and who puts on a garment due to such an emergency, thinking, "Thieves will carry off me if I am not clothed"; nor for those who are insane and so forth.
In this context, the factors for the offense of seeking [the robe] are: the robe being intended for oneself, seeking it at an improper time, and obtaining it by means of that seeking.

There are three factors. Having one’s own robe, the absence of an emergency, the fact that it is one’s own rain-cloak, and wearing it at an improper time—these are the four factors for the offense of wearing [a rain-cloak].
The origins and other details are exactly as stated in the training rule on having [a robe] washed.
The commentary on the training rule on the rain-cloak is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Taking Away a Robe.
In the fifth [rule], "having given a robe oneself" means having given it personally while expecting services and the like in return.

"Should take it away" means that for one who, seeing another not performing services and so forth, takes it away with the perception that it is his own, there are offenses according to the number of times the act is committed.

Regarding the phrase "should cause to take away": here, for the command "take away," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); for each of the commands given to those who actually take it away, there are offenses according to their number.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Upananda in the matter of taking away a robe; it is a common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti).

This is a formal act involving an instruction; it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for three cases. If one perceives a person not fully ordained as fully ordained, or is in doubt, or perceives them as not fully ordained;

or if one takes away any requisite other than the last robe that has been assigned to a fully ordained person—excluding the robe itself—or takes anything whatsoever from one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
However, if [the item] was given by that person when they were either satisfied or angry, there is no offense.
There is no offense for one who takes it with the consent [of the owner], or for those who are insane, and so forth. The five factors here are:

the robe being the last one that has reached the stage of being formally assigned (*vikappanupaga*); having been given by oneself; the perception that it belongs to oneself; the person being fully ordained (*upasampanna*); and either the taking away or causing it to be taken away out of anger.
The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other characteristics are the same as those for taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), except for the feeling (*vedanā*).
But here, "feeling" refers specifically to painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the snatching away of robes is finished. 6.
Commentary on the training rule concerning the hinting by means of a thread.

"Six kinds of thread" (chaṭṭhaṃ suttaṃ) refers either to the six types of thread such as linen (*khoma*) and so forth, or to what is suitable for them. "Having requested" (*viññāpetvā*) means having asked for the purpose of obtaining a robe.
"Should have it woven" (*vāyāpeyya*) means that one should have it woven by means of an improper request, saying: "Friends, please weave a robe for me.

"Forfeiture" (*nissaggiyaṃ*) refers to the weaver who, for the purpose of weaving a robe, performs the work of spinning the distaff, setting up the loom, and so forth, for one who causes it to be woven in this manner.
If one undertakes the work, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for all such efforts; upon acquisition, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
This was laid down at Rājagaha concerning the group of six monks regarding the matter of having cloth woven, as a general rule, not by specific instruction;
it applies to one who has requested the thread and then has it woven by a weaver who was also requested [for the purpose], even if it is only a span (*vidatthi*) in length.

If it exceeds [the size] by even a hand’s breadth in width, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). Thus, as the robe increases in size, the offenses increase accordingly according to this measure.

However, for one who has the cloth woven from yarn obtained without prior request, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense here, just as there was a *nissaggiya* offense previously. For that very reason, for one who has the cloth woven from both requested and unrequested yarn...

If the robe is the stated measurement, like a field-bound plot, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for the border made of unallowable thread, and likewise an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the other [border]. If the borders are smaller than that, there are offenses of wrong-doing for all the borders.
Then, having made it allowable in length by means of an intervening thread, or having made it unallowable across the width—
It is finished; according to the previously stated measure and calculation, there are *dukkaṭa* offenses.

By this same method, the classification of offenses regarding what is allowable (*kappiya*) or unallowable (*akappiya*) should be understood for thread woven by an allowable weaver with unallowable thread, as well as for thread woven by both allowable and unallowable weavers—whether the cloth itself is allowable, unallowable, or both.
There is a triad of *pācittiya* offenses: for one who perceives it as woven when it has not been woven, or for one who is in doubt [regarding whether it has been woven].

It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). There is no offense for one who requests thread for the purpose of sewing robes, making a waistband, a shoulder-strap, a bowl-bag, or a water-strainer; or for one who has a suitable thread woven by relatives or those who have invited him; or for one who requests it for another’s purpose;
or for one who uses his own wealth; or for those who are insane and so forth. [There is also no offense] regarding thread requested for the sake of a robe, provided it is intended for oneself.
Causing an unallowable weaver to weave by means of an unallowable request—these are the three factors here.
The origins and other details are exactly as stated in the training rule on having cloth washed.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the request for thread is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Great Weavers Regarding the seventh rule:
"If, in that case, a monk... means: where there are weavers, whether in a village or a town, there. "Without having been previously invited" means:
having not been invited by the owners of the robes. "Should make a choice" means: he should make a selection of superior quality or an excessive arrangement.
[He] would incur [an offense]. Now, in order to show the manner in which it has become differentiated, this passage beginning with "Indeed, friends...
was spoken. Therein, *āyataṃ* means long; *vitthataṃ* means broad; *appitaṃ* means dense.
*Suvītaṃ* means well-woven; it is woven evenly in all places. *Suppavāyitaṃ* means well-beaten; in all places...
Having made it even, the thread was stretched out. "Well-scratched" means well-scratched with a stylus.
"Well-shaved" means well-shaved with a comb; the meaning is that it was well-washed. "Even by way of a mere alms-food gift":
here, it does not become an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) for a monk merely because of the giving of alms-food; however, if those [laypeople], by his word...

If, having taken thread from the hands of the owners of the robe-cloth, they make it even slightly longer, wider, or woven, then for that act there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the monk;
upon acquisition, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Upananda, regarding the matter of making a formal determination (*vikappa*) with respect to robe-cloth; it is a general rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*).

This is not subject to a formal injunction (*anāṇattika*); it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) in three cases. If one perceives a relative as a non-relative, or is in doubt about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

There is no offense for those who have been invited by relatives, or for weaving on behalf of another, or for weaving with one’s own wealth, or for one who desires to have something expensive woven but has it woven cheaply, or for those who are insane and so forth. [The offense applies to] approaching weavers who are neither relatives nor have been invited.
The four factors here are: making a formal determination (*vikappa*), the robe being intended for oneself, the increase of the yarn according to his word, and the acquisition of the robe.
The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth are exactly as stated in the training rule on having [the robe] washed.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the great weaver is finished.

8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Early Obtaining of Robes (*Accekacīvarasikkhāpada*) In the eighth [rule], "not more than ten days away" (*dasāhānāgata*): "ten days" (*dasāha*) means a period of ten days. "Not arrived after those ten days" (*dasāhānāgatā*) means not having reached ten days;
this is the meaning. That which is "not more than ten days away" (*taṃ dasāhānāgataṃ*): the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative by virtue of absolute connection (*accantasamyoga*).
"Kattika-temāsa-puṇṇamā" means the full moon day of the first Kattika month;
here too, because the first word is not used in the objective sense (*anupayoga*), the accusative case is employed in the locative sense according to the previous method.
This is what is meant: from the time that the first invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is said to be "ten days away," if during those days there is indeed an urgent robe-cloth for a monk...
"Whatever [robe-material] might arise, it should be accepted by a monk who knows,
'This is urgent,'" thus the time for storing robe-material that has arisen from the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pavāraṇā is shown.
Granted, this is already established by the rule, "An extra robe may be kept for ten days at most," but it is stated here by way of a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
However, having shown a meaning as if it were something never before taught, the training rule was established.

"Urgent robe-cloth" refers to that which has been given after one of these individuals—a traveler, a sick person, a pregnant woman, or one whose faith has newly arisen—has announced, "I shall give you the rains-residence robe.
If that [robe] is distributed before the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he by whom it was received must not break the rains-residence; if he does so, then...
The robe belongs to the Saṅgha. "Until the robe season" means: when the kaṭhina has not been spread, until the last month of the rainy season;
when the kaṭhina has been spread, until five months.

This was laid down concerning a number of bhikkhus in Sāvatthī regarding the matter of exceeding the robe season for an urgent robe. The rest here should be understood in the same manner as stated in the first training rule of the Robe Chapter.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the early robe is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning danger:
Regarding the phrase "Now, while it was raining" (*upavassaṃ kho pana*), here *upavassa* means "while it was raining"; that is, having rained, it is said.
In this context, the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*) should be understood as in the case of *upasampajja* and similar forms; the meaning is "having entered the rains residence and having dwelt [there].
This phrase is connected with the words "a bhikkhu dwelling in such lodgings," which implies the following:
having entered the rains residence and having dwelt there, thereafter, until the conclusion of the full moon of the month of Kattika.
"Furthermore, those forest lodgings... [as above] ...one should deposit them within an inhabited area.

In this context, "forest lodgings" refers to dwellings constructed in an area measuring five hundred bow-lengths starting from the village boundary post (*indakhīla*), using the teacher’s standard bow as the measure for the furthest point.
However, if the village is unenclosed, it starts from the place where an enclosure would be required.

It should be measured. If there is a boundary for the monastery, or in the case of an unenclosed area, it should be measured by the natural path as far as the very first resting place from the village, or the shrine, or the Bodhi tree, or the place of regular assembly;
it is not permitted to make another path or to measure by a non-path. These are considered "places of danger."
By observing places where thieves and others have established themselves, these [locations] are considered "dangerous" (*sāsaṅka*); the meaning is that they are so recognized.

They are "frightening" (*sappaṭibhaya*) because they are accompanied by fear; the meaning is that they possess a present and powerful threat, due to seeing people being killed, plundered, or maimed by thieves.
"He should deposit it within a village" means he should deposit it in whatever alms-village he prefers, located in any direction around a forest dwelling.
Furthermore, this must be done with the fulfillment of certain conditions; herein are those conditions:
having entered the first rains-residence, one has been invited at the Great Invitation ceremony—this is the first condition. It must be the month of Kattika itself.
This is the second factor. The lodging must be of the minimum size of five hundred bow-lengths;
this is the third factor. It is not permitted [to live] in a place that is either smaller than that measure or larger than four *gāvuta*;

for what is intended here is precisely that place where, having gone for alms and finished eating, one is able to return to the monastery again on the very same day. It must indeed be a place that is risky and fearful.
This is the fourth factor. "Some condition whatsoever" means some cause or reason whatsoever.
"By that robe" means by that robe which was left behind in the village. "For the sake of separation" means for the sake of living apart from it.

"If he should stay separated for longer than that" means if he should cause the seventh dawn to rise while staying in that same lodging beyond six nights; this is the meaning. [This applies] to one who is unable to do otherwise.
However, having entered the village boundary and stayed either in the assembly hall or anywhere else,

it is permissible to depart once one has ascertained the status of the robe-cloth. "Except by the consent of the Saṅgha" means that, setting aside the case where the Saṅgha grants permission for a sick bhikkhu to be separated from his robe-cloth,
for one who has not obtained such consent and stays apart for more than four nights, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya).

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhus regarding the matter of being separated from one’s robe; the rest here should be understood in the same manner as stated in the second training rule of the Cīvara-vagga.
The commentary on the training rule concerning danger is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning What is Dedicated.

"In the tenth [case], 'belonging to the Saṅgha' means that which is the property of the Saṅgha. For because it has been dedicated to the Saṅgha, even though it has not yet come into their hands, it is in one sense the property of the Saṅgha.

'Gain' refers to the object to be obtained, such as robes and so forth. 'Dedicated' means that it has been directed toward the Saṅgha through a verbal expression such as "we shall give" or "we shall make," or by means of a hand gesture."
"To divert it to oneself" means that by saying things such as "Give this to me," one makes it one's own.
However, if it has already been given to the Saṅgha, it is not permissible to take it; it must be returned to the Saṅgha itself.
But for one who diverts to oneself what has been diverted [to others], whether to fellow practitioners of the Dhamma or to laypeople—even down to what belongs to one's mother—[it is an offense].
There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the act of application; by the acquisition [of the object], it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks (*chabbaggiyā bhikkhū*) regarding the matter of diverting [offerings). It is a general rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), not a specific injunction (*anāṇattika*).

[It applies] to one who is in doubt about whether [the offering] has been diverted, and to one who perceives as diverted what has not been diverted, as well as to one who is in doubt about that which has not been diverted.
It is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who diverts to another Saṅgha or other recipients anything that has already been dedicated to the Saṅgha, a shrine, or a specific individual.
It is also an offense for one who, while perceiving it as not yet dedicated, is asked, "Where shall we give it? and replies, "Give it wherever your mind feels confidence;
let your gift of merit receive its enjoyment," and so forth; as well as for those who are insane and so on.

There is no offense. The three factors here are: the state of having been dedicated to the Sangha, knowing that [it has been so dedicated], and one’s own redirection [of it]. The origin and other characteristics are the same as those for taking what is not given.
The commentary on the training rule concerning what has been dedicated is finished.
The third chapter, the Chapter on Robes,
is finished. Thus ends the commentary on the offenses involving forfeiture and confession (Nissaggiya-Pācittiya) within the Commentary on the Pātimokkha for the Resolution of Doubts.
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa) 1.
The Chapter on False Speech (Musāvādavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Training Rule on False Speech (Musāvādasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā)
Regarding the first offense in the section on false speech among the *pācittiya* rules:
"speaking a deliberate lie" (*sampajānamusāvāda*) refers to speaking a falsehood when one has previously known [the truth] and knows it at the very moment of speaking.

Here, "speaking" (*bhaṇana*) means the act of making oneself understood through body or speech by representing what is non-existent as existent, or what is existent as non-existent; and the locative case here is used in the sense of "on account of" or "by means of."
Therefore, for one who speaks a deliberate lie, on account of that, by reason of that, and with that as the condition, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
In this context, and in other similar cases, the meaning should be understood in this way.
This rule was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Hatthaka the Sakyan, regarding the matter of denying what one has recognized and so forth.

This is a common designation and is not a formal injunction (*anāṇattika*). For one who speaks falsely for the purpose of proclaiming a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*), it is a *pārājika* offense;
for the purpose of charging someone with a groundless *pārājika*, it is a *saṅghādisesa*; for the purpose of charging someone with a *saṅghādisesa*, it is a *pācittiya*;
for the purpose of charging someone with a failure of conduct (*ācāravipatti*), it is a *dukkaṭa*. [The offense applies] in cases such as saying, "Whoever dwelt in your monastery," and so forth.

For one who speaks falsely with the intention of proclaiming a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*) by means of a figurative expression, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) if the listener understands;
there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) if the listener does not understand; and for one who speaks merely falsely [without such intent], there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) here.
There is no offense for one who speaks impulsively without having reflected, for one who says something else thinking, "I will say something else," or for those who are insane and so forth.
The two factors here are: having deception as one's primary motive, and the act of making oneself understood by the person to whom one intends to speak that particular matter with a deceptive mind.
The origin and other characteristics are the same as those for taking what is not given.
The commentary on the training rule concerning false speech is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule on Reviling Speech (*omasavāda-sikkhāpada*). Regarding the second [offense], "reviling speech" (*ovijjhanavacana*):

by means of any [speech]—whether true or false—concerning birth, name, clan, occupation, craft, illness, gender, defilement, or offenses; [addressed] to any bhikkhu, whether he has committed a *pārājika* offense or not.
The meaning is: "In whatever speech, hand gesture, or by means of any other designation, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for words of abuse.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks (*chabbaggiya bhikkhus*) on the occasion of the matter of reviling;

it is a common rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), without a specific formal instruction (*anāṇattika*), and applies to those same ten grounds of abuse in the manner beginning with, "There are here some outcasts (*caṇḍāla*)," and so forth.
For one who reviles by using indirect speech; for one who reviles with phrases outside the canonical texts (pāḷimuttaka), such as “You are a thief, you are a cutpurse,” and so forth;

and for one who reviles any person not fully ordained (anupasampanna) in whatever manner—there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Herein, even a nun is included in the category of those not fully ordained.
For one who speaks merely out of a desire for sport, without the intention to revile, there is an offense in all such cases.
This is a wrong speech (*dubbhāsita*). There is no offense for those who prioritize the meaning and the teaching of the Dhamma, nor for those who are insane and so forth.
Regarding this [offense], there are four factors: the fact that the one being reviled is fully ordained; the reviling by means of birth and so forth, without using another pretext;
the awareness, "He is reviling me"; and the absence of prioritizing the purpose and so forth. The origin and other characteristics are the same as those for taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*).
But feeling here is suffering.
The commentary on the training rule concerning abusive speech is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning slander.
Regarding the third [offense], "slander among monks" (*bhikkhupesunñā*):

when a monk hears words from one who is slandering other monks by means of grounds for abuse such as birth and so forth—whether out of a desire for favor or with the intention of causing a schism—and then, being free from anger, conveys those words of slander to another monk either by body or by speech, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). This is the meaning.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks (*chabbaggiya*) regarding the matter of instigating slander.

It is a common rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), not a specific injunction (*anāṇattika*). According to the stated method, for one who reviles under another pretext, or for instigating speech, or for instigating verbal abuse outside the canonical text (*pāḷimuttaka*), or for instigating toward one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Here too—

A bhikkhunī standing in a place where she has not been ordained. There is no offense for one who speaks merely out of a desire to censure evil, neither out of a desire for affection nor with the intention to cause schism;

nor is there an offense for those who are insane, and so forth. Having heard a bhikkhu reviling another by way of birth and other such categories—without using any other pretext—and then repeating those words to that bhikkhu, [there is an offense] if there is either a desire for affection or an intention to cause schism.
"His knowing"—these are the three factors here. The origins and so forth are exactly like those for the offense of taking what is not given.
The commentary on the training rule concerning malicious talebearing is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning reciting the Dharma word-for-word.

"In the fourth [case], one should recite the Dhamma word by word" means that one should recite word by word both the Dhamma not included in the Three Councils—such as the *Rājovāda*, *Tikkhindriya*, *Catuparivattana*, *Nanda-Upananda-kulumpasutta*, *Maggakathā*, and so forth—and the Dhamma of the Tipiṭaka which was included in the Three Councils.

The meaning is that each individual division among the words, phrases, syllables, and phonemes constitutes a single unit. Regarding the term "offense of expiation" (*pācittiya*): with the exception of monks and nuns, among these [categories] beginning with words...
For one who recites any portion [of the Dhamma] together with other persons, there is an offense of *pācittiya* according to the counting of words and so forth.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks (*chabbaggiyā bhikkhū*) on the occasion of the matter of reciting the Dhamma word by word (*padaso*).

It is a common rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), it is not a formal instruction (*anāṇattika*), and it is a *pācittiya* of the threefold type (*tikapācittiya*). [The offense applies when] one perceives someone as not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) while they are actually fully ordained (*upasampanna*).
Or there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who is in doubt. There is no offense in reciting the formal instruction (uddesa) together with one who is not fully ordained;
in performing the recitation (sajjhāya); in receiving the formal instruction in his presence; in speaking a text that is mostly mastered;
in telling someone who is reciting to correct a mistake by saying, "Speak thus"; in speaking together [with him]; and for those who are insane and so forth.
The three factors here are: not being fully ordained (*anupasampannatā*), reciting the Dhamma with its stated characteristics word by word, and concluding together.

It originates from the recitation of words (*padasodhammasamuṭṭhāna*), is an action (*kiriyā*), is without liberation through perception (*nosaññāvimokkha*), is without consciousness (*acittaka*), is an offense by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), is verbal action (*vacīkamma*), possesses three types of consciousness (*ticitta*), and possesses three types of feeling (*tivedanā*).
The commentary on the training rule regarding reciting the Dhamma word-for-word is finished.
5. Commentary on the First Training Rule Regarding Sharing a Bed:
In the fifth [rule], "with one who is not fully ordained" means anyone except a bhikkhu, including even a lower animal that constitutes a ground for a *pārājika* offense.
"More than two or three nights" means beyond two or three nights.
"Lying down together" means lying down in one place—whether in a lodging that is entirely covered and enclosed, or mostly covered and enclosed—either successively or simultaneously.
"Should arrange" means should prepare or provide. In that context, without touching the covering, [the bed] is one and a half cubits in height.
Even that which is enclosed by a wall or similar structure should be understood as "completely enclosed. Therefore, if a dwelling endowed with this characteristic—
even if it is a seven-storied palace or a four-sided hall with a hundred rooms— is a single precinct,

then for three nights one may stay there together with another person who has not received full ordination, whether that person is staying in that same place or elsewhere, or whether they are that specific individual or someone else.
Having lain down on the fourth day, when the sun has set, if one lies down after either closing or not closing the door to the womb-chamber,
or if one who was already lying down does not rise when the other lies down,
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for each instance of rising and lying down by both parties, and according to the number of those who are not fully ordained.
This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, has been stated in all its aspects in the *Samantapāsādikā*.
This rule was laid down at Āḷavī concerning a number of bhikkhus regarding the matter of lying down with one who is not fully ordained: "more than two or three nights.
This is an additional rule (*anupaññatti*) here; it is a common rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), and it is without an instruction (*anāṇattika*).

There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for three [cases]; for one who perceives a person as not fully ordained when they are actually fully ordained, or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding those who are half-covered or half-enclosed, and so forth.
For one staying for less than two or three nights; for one who leaves before dawn on the third night and stays again;
for one staying in dwellings that are entirely covered or entirely unenclosed, and so forth; and for one who lies down while the other is sitting.
There is no offense for one who lies down while the other is sitting, nor for those who are insane and so forth.

The factors here are three: a lodging that constitutes the basis for an offense of expiation (pācittiya), lying down there together with one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna), and the setting of the sun on the fourth day.
As for the origin and other characteristics, they are the same as those of the rule concerning wool (eḷakaloma).
The commentary on the first training rule concerning sleeping in the same bed is finished.
6. Commentary on the second training rule concerning sleeping in the same bed:

In the sixth [rule], "with a woman" (*mātugāmena*) means with any human female, even one born on that very day. However, *yakkhinīs* and *petīs* whose forms are visible, as well as *paṇḍakas* and female animals who have become objects for sexual intercourse, constitute the basis for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) here.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the Venerable Elder Anuruddha regarding the matter of sleeping together with a woman;
the rest should be understood according to the method stated in the immediately preceding training rule, except for the delimitation of the night,
for there [in that case] there is an offense on the fourth day, whereas here there is an offense even on the first day.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning sleeping in the same bed is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Teaching the Dhamma:
Regarding the seventh rule, "more than five or six sentences," one verse-line is considered one sentence; thus, the measure of a sentence is to be understood in this way throughout.

It should be understood as follows: "He should teach the Dhamma" means he should speak either the Dhamma characterized by the training rules (sikkhāpada) regarding the mastery of words, or the Dhamma of the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā).
"Except in the presence of a person capable of understanding" means except when a man capable of understanding is present.
However, even if she is standing with a yakkha, a peta, or an animal that has assumed human form, [she may teach] the Dhamma.

It is not permissible to teach [the Dhamma]. Regarding the *pācittiya*: according to the definition stated in the second *niyama*, for one who teaches the Dhamma by means of verses and so forth to a woman who understands—excluding a human male—the offense is a *pācittiya* calculated by the number of verses and so forth;
and for one teaching many [women], it is a *pācittiya* calculated by the number of women.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the Elder Udāyī regarding the occasion of teaching the Dhamma to a woman.

"Except with a wise person" is the subsequent rule (anupaññatti) here; it is a common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti), not a specific instruction (anāṇattika), and carries a triad of offenses of expiation (pācittiya).
[The offense applies] when one perceives a woman as a woman, or is in doubt, in the case of non-women such as yakkhinīs, petīs, paṇḍakas, human beings in female form, or female animals.
And for one confessing [the offense], there is an *dukkaṭa*. For one confessing with six words or fewer than that; or when the person possesses the stated characteristics;
or when one has risen oneself and sat down again; or when a woman has risen and he sits down again;
or when one is confessing to another woman—[if he asks]: "Venerable sir, what is the purpose of the *Dīghanikāya*? and so forth.
There is no offense for one who teaches the entire *Dīghanikāya* when questioned; for one who speaks for another purpose while a woman is listening;
or for those who are insane and so forth. [The factors constituting an offense are: teaching a discourse with the aforementioned characteristics beyond six sentences;

the listener being a woman as defined by the stated characteristics; the absence of a change in posture; the absence of a "maker of what is allowable" (*kappiyakāraka*); and the absence of a question-and-answer session.
These are the five factors here. The sections on origin and so forth are exactly like those in the *Padasodhamma*; the only difference is that here there is both doing and not doing.
The commentary on the training rule regarding teaching the Dhamma is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding the Proclamation of Supernatural Powers (*Bhūtārocanasikkhāpada*).
In the eighth [offense], "a state beyond human condition" (*uttarimanussadhamma*) refers to the quality belonging to those humans who are meditators and to the Noble Ones (*ariya*),

as defined by the characteristics stated in the fourth *pārājika*. "An offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) when it is true" means that when such a state of meditation or other qualities exists within oneself,
an offense of expiation is incurred for one who reports it to anyone other than the monk or the nun themselves.
This was laid down at Vesālī concerning the Vaggumudā-tīrīya bhikkhus, in the case of their reporting what had actually occurred;

it is a general rule (sādhāraṇa-paññatti), not a specific instruction (anāṇattika). It applies to one who reports, in a non-figurative sense, meditative states (jhāna) and other such qualities existing within himself;
provided that the person to whom he reports immediately recognizes him as "one who has attained jhāna" or "an Ariyan" by whatever means.
If one knows that matter by way of its characteristic form, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). If one does not know it, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

However, whether one knows or not that it was announced by means of a circuitous way, it is simply an offense of wrong-doing. There is no offense for one who announces this to one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*) when such a reason exists, nor for a beginner (*ādikammika*).
Furthermore, since noble ones (*ariya*) do not possess states such as insanity, and [this applies] to those who have attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*),...
However, when that [superhuman state] exists, the meditative absorptions (jhānas) fall away; therefore, they are not included here.

The four factors in this case are: the actual occurrence of a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), the announcement of it to one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna), the understanding of it at that very moment, and the statement "other than this.

It originates from the announcement of what has occurred, is an action (kiriya), is without liberation through perception (no-saññā-vimokkha), is without consciousness (acittaka), and is an offense by rule (paṇṇatti-vajja).
There is bodily action and verbal action; with wholesome and indeterminate consciousnesses, there are two types of consciousness; with pleasant and neutral feelings, there are two types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the disclosure of what has occurred is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning the disclosure of what is grave.

"In the ninth [offense], 'of a bhikkhu' means one who has not committed a *pārājika*. 'Gross offense' (*duṭṭhulla*): although this is a designation for two categories of offenses, here it refers specifically to the *saṅghādisesa* offenses.

'Except by the authorization of the Saṅgha' means that which the Saṅgha grants to a bhikkhu who repeatedly commits offenses, for the sake of future restraint, regarding both the offenses and the families."
Whether having made or not having made [the agreement], if one makes an agreement after looking back three times, then setting that aside,

for one who reports the offense together with the basis according to the method beginning, "This person, having emitted semen, has committed a *saṅghādisesa*," when it does not accord with the agreement,
there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
It was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks (*chabbaggiyā bhikkhū*) on the occasion of the matter of reporting a grave offense (*duṭṭhullāpatti*);
it is a common rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), not a specific instruction (*anāṇattika*), and constitutes an offense of expiation for the third time (*tikapācittiya*).

There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who perceives what is not grave as grave, or for one who is in doubt; it includes the remaining six classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*), and the transgression of the first five training rules (*sikkhāpada*) regarding those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).

Whether one reports a grave offense (*duṭṭhulla*) or another that is not grave (*aduṭṭhulla*), there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). There is no offense for one who reports merely the subject matter or merely the offense;
for one who reports without exceeding the limits established by the consent of the Saṅgha; and for those who are insane and so forth.

For a monk possessing the characteristics already stated, it is a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*) with its specific basis; however, for one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), it is not.
The three factors here are: the making known [of the offense] and the absence of formal authorization by the Saṅgha. The origin and other details are similar to those for taking what is not given;
however, the feeling in this case is exclusively painful.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the making known of a grave offense is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Digging the Earth.
Regarding the tenth [rule], "earth" refers to two kinds of earth: earth that has been formed (*jāta-pathavī*) and earth that has not been formed (*ajāta-pathavī*).
Therein, earth that has been formed is threefold, according to whether it is pure or a mixture of heaps; therein, "pure earth" means natural, pure soil.
Or pure clay. "Mixed earth" means that where one-third consists of either dust, clay, stone, gravel, potsherds, pebbles, or sand.
"Heaped earth" is defined as "a heap of dust or a heap of clay that has been piled up for more than four months";
however, by the stated definition, a mixed heap as well as fine dust resting on a flat rock is included.
And when it rains upon the earth, whatever has been moistened once becomes dry after the lapse of four months; that moisture then goes entirely into the mass of the earth itself.
This threefold earth—whether by way of being heated on a stove, cooked in a pan, or otherwise—is called "unburnt earth" (*ajāta-pathavī*) as long as it is not burnt;
however, when it is burnt, or when it is mixed with stones and the like exceeding the aforementioned proportions, it is called "unborn earth" (*ajāta-pathavī*).
This is the name [of the offense]; what need is there to mention [earth] broken by pure stones and the like?

In this context, that which is called "earth that has been dug up" is unallowable earth (*akappiyapathavī*). If a monk himself digs such earth, or disturbs it by means of digging, breaking, scratching, cooking, and so forth, he incurs a *pācittiya* offense for each instance of that action.
Furthermore, if he causes it to be dug, or causes it to be disturbed in the manner already described, [he likewise incurs an offense].
For one who, having delimited it as "this spot" or "this earth," commands by way of saying "dig! or "break!

and so forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the command; once commanded, even if they dig for an entire day, there is only a single offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for the commander.
If the other person commands again and again, there is an offense of expiation for every single utterance.
This was laid down at Āḷavī concerning the monks of Āḷavī in the matter of digging the earth; it is a general rule, accompanied by an injunction.
For one who is doubtful about whether it is earth or not, and for one who perceives it as earth when it is not earth, or who is doubtful about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
[The following are prohibited: "Dig a lotus pond," "dig a pit," "dig a bulbous root," and so forth, without having first determined the location.

While speaking, [he might encounter] dried-up mud that has cracked open due to the heat, or *gokaṇṭaka* grass, or a riverbank that has collapsed and become detached from the earth below, or even a large clod of earth broken by a plow—indeed, for one who disturbs all such unformed earth, [the Buddha said]:
"Know the pit for this pillar; give me the clay; give me the clay."
There is no offense for one who says, "Bring it; I have need of earth;

prepare some clay for me," while unintentionally breaking [the ground] by overturning a tree or the like, or scratching with a toe or similar means through lack of mindfulness, or for one who does not know that the earth has become manifest or thinks, "I am digging," or for those who are insane and so forth.
[The factors constituting the offense are: earth that has become manifest, the perception that it is earth, and the act of digging or causing it to be dug.

"Another person": these are the three factors here. The origin and so forth are similar to those of taking what is not given; however, this is a formal offense (paṇṇattivajja), involving three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule regarding digging the earth is finished.
The First Chapter on False Speech.
2. The Chapter on Vegetation.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Vegetation.

Regarding the first [offense] in the *Bhūtagāma-vagga*: "In the case of 'destroying plants' (*bhūtagāmapātabyatā*)," here "plants" (*bhūtā*) means they "come into being" (*bhavanti*) or "have been" (*ahesuṃ*);
the meaning is that they are born (*jāyanti*), grow (*vaḍḍhanti*), and have been born and grown (*jātā vaḍḍhitā*). "Plant" (*gāma*) means a mass (*rāsi*);
a "plant-mass" (*bhūtagāma*) is either a mass of plants or the plants themselves as a mass. This is a designation for established green grass, trees, and so forth. Of what is to be destroyed...

"Bhāva" means the state of being something to be consumed; the meaning is that it is to be enjoyed according to one's desire through cutting, breaking, and so forth. "In that state of consuming the vegetable kingdom" (*bhūtagāma-pātabyatāya*):

this locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*). The meaning is: "On account of the consumption of the vegetable kingdom"—that is, due to the causes such as cutting the vegetable kingdom—there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Therefore, whichever monk [cuts] anything whatsoever grown among earth, water, walls, and so forth...

If one disturbs—even down to a very fine blade of grass, a mustard seed, or a grain of husk—by uprooting, cutting, piercing, or the like, or causes it to be disturbed by digging the earth according to the method described above, one incurs a *pācittiya* offense.
This was laid down at Āḷavī concerning the monks of Āḷavī in the matter of cutting down trees; it is a common rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*).

This is a formal act involving an injunction (*sāṇattika*). It concerns any one of the following—root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, seed-seeds, or propagated seeds—which has been separated from its original site (*bhūtagāma*), whether it is contained in a vessel, heaped up, or even planted in the ground;
provided that either only the root has emerged, or only the sprout has emerged, or even if a leaf-sheath only a span in length has come forth, whether the root has emerged or not.

As long as the sprout has not yet become green from the root, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who damages it; likewise for one who is doubtful regarding a grove of living beings or a grove of seeds.
There is no offense for one who perceives what is not a grove of living beings or seeds as such, or for one who is doubtful about both.

Furthermore, there is no offense for one who does not perceive it as such, nor for those who are insane and so forth. Nor is there an offense for one who damages it unintentionally, through lack of mindfulness, or unknowingly.
There is no offense for one who speaks such things as "cut the tree" or "cut the creeper" without specifying "this tree," or for one who says,
"know this flower or fruit," "give this," "bring this," "I have need of this," or "make this allowable.
However, that which has been separated from the group of living beings by such an allowable statement—

Furthermore, seed-grown produce must be made *kappiya* (rendered allowable) by having someone do so before it may be consumed. In this way, the protection of the seed-planting grounds is also accomplished.
When making it *kappiya*, it must be done with fire, a fingernail, or a knife.
When using fire, one must touch it in some part with any kind of fire and, having said "it is *kappiya*," perform the act. With a knife...
When performing [this act] with any sharp instrument whatsoever— even such things as a needle or a nail-cutter—
one must act in such a way that it merely pierces or cuts with its point or its edge. When performing it with a claw, one may use any claw other than those of oxen,
buffaloes, and so forth, provided it is not putrid, whether belonging to humans or to animals.
Even if it is brought after having been cut with a fingernail, it must be prepared in the same manner as described for a knife.
In that regard, even if there is a heap of seeds as large as a mountain, or a thousand trees cut and tied together, or a great bundle of sugarcane set aside,
once a single seed, or a branch of a tree, or a stalk of sugarcane has been made allowable (*kappiya*), [the whole becomes allowable].
Everything has been done. If one pierces a wooden peg that was tied together with them [the sugarcane] with the intention, "I shall make it allowable," it is indeed permissible.
However, if one pierces the creeper by which the load was tied, it is not permissible.
When rice is brought mixed with black pepper, pākka, and so forth, even if one pierces a grain of rice when told, "Make it allowable," [it is permissible].
It is indeed permissible; the same principle applies to sesame and rice as well. However, when these are placed in gruel, they do not remain as a single mass;
therefore, one must pierce each individual grain before using it. In the case of wood-apples (*kapiṭṭha*) and the like, the inner pulp moves about, leaving the shell behind;
one must have it broken apart and then have it made allowable (*kappiya*). If it remains a single mass, even within the shell—

It is permissible to do so. However, regarding fruit that is immature and seedless, or that which has produced seeds but from which the seeds have been removed before consumption—therein there is no necessity for the formal act of making it *kappiya* (lawful).

In this case, the three factors are: a collection of living beings (*bhūtagāma*), the perception thereof as such, and the destruction or causing of destruction. The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other characteristics are exactly the same as those for digging the earth.
The commentary on the training rule concerning plants is finished.
2. Commentary on the second training rule concerning speaking otherwise:
One who speaks otherwise is so called because he says something other than the matter which the expert in the Vinaya asks about in the midst of the Saṅgha.
“Evasive speech” is the name for this. “A harasser” means one who causes disturbance;
this is the name for silence [in this context], referring to that harasser who speaks evasively. “Pācittiya” refers to two Pācittiya offenses stated in relation to two distinct matters.
Therefore, when a monk who has committed an offense with a remainder is being questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha and, not wishing to speak of it, uses other words—
If one covers over another's offense by distracting them in such and such a way, or if one harasses another through silence,

then for those who act in that manner again after the Saṅgha has already performed the *aññavādaka-kamma* (act of making speak otherwise) and the *vihesaka-kamma* (act of harassment) as authorized by the Blessed One,
there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was laid down at Kosambī concerning the Elder Channa in the matter of evading one question with another; it is a rule of common application, not a specific injunction.

In the case of a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*), there is a *pācittiya* offense for each of the three [stages]; in the case of an illegitimate legal act (*adhammakamma*), there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for each of the three.

However, if one acts in such a manner toward someone who has not been formally charged with evasion or harassment, there is only a *dukkaṭa*. This applies also to one who does not know that the other person has committed an offense.
There is no offense for one who asks, "What are you saying? when [the other] is ill;

or for one who does not speak with the intention that "there will be quarrels and so forth in the Saṅgha," or "they will perform a legal act (kamma) contrary to the Dhamma, by an incomplete assembly, or against one who does not deserve such a legal act";
and also for those who are insane and so forth. [Likewise, there is no offense] regarding the fact that a legal act has been performed according to the Dhamma, or regarding the basis of an offense.
Or being questioned, one either evades one thing with another out of a desire to conceal it, or remains silent;

these are the three factors here. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to those of taking what is not given. However, this may be an action, or it may be a non-action, and it is associated with painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning speaking otherwise is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning complaining.
Regarding the third [rule]: by whatever speech they complain, saying such things as, "Out of favoritism, so-and-so does this," and so forth.
When monks, desiring to bring disrepute upon one who has been fully ordained and appointed by the Saṅgha—
such as an assigner of lodgings and so forth— cause him to be disregarded by other monks, cause him to be looked upon with contempt, or consider him to be inferior,
that speech is *ujjhāpanaka*. And when, by speaking in such a manner, they revile him and proclaim his ill-repute everywhere, that is *khiyyanaka*.
Regarding that censure and disparagement: "an offense of expiation" (pācittiya) refers to two offenses of expiation stated for two distinct bases.
Therefore, if one censures or disparages a monk who has been duly authorized and ordained out of a desire for his disrepute, there is an offense of expiation for him.
This was laid down at Rājagaha concerning the monks of Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, regarding the matter of censuring and slandering;

it is a general rule, not a specific injunction. For a formal act (*sammuti-kamma*) performed upon one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), if it is a legitimate act (*dhamma-kamma*), there is an offense of *pācittiya* for each of the three [stages];
if it is an illegitimate act (*adhamma-kamma*), there is an offense of *dukkaṭa* for each of the three. However, in the presence of one who is not fully ordained...
Likewise, for one who speaks disparagement of anyone while they are speaking, or in the presence of anyone, if that person is not authorized, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
However, if one speaks disparagement of a person who is not ordained—whether authorized or unauthorized—in the presence of anyone at all, it is also a *dukkaṭa*.
Furthermore, it is a *dukkaṭa* for one who reviles or censures another who acts out of natural inclination, such as through favoritism (*chanda*) and so forth.
There is no offense for those who are insane and so forth. The six factors here are: being authorized by a formal act of the Saṅgha (dhammakamma);
being fully ordained; not having gone astray; desiring to speak dispraise of him; the person in whose presence one speaks being fully ordained; and either censuring or reviling.
The origin and other characteristics are the same as for taking what is not given; however, this [offense] results only in painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning causing annoyance is finished.
4. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Lodgings:
Regarding the fourth [rule], "belonging to the Saṅgha" means that which is the property of the Saṅgha. Among beds and so forth, anything whatsoever made by way of the term "bed" is included.
The same principle applies to the bed (mañca) and the chair (pīṭha) as well.

A seat made by covering a frame with any kind of cloth or allowable leather, excluding human hair and palm leaves, and filling it with any kind of fur, leaves, grass, bark, or rags, is called a mattress (bhisī).
It is permissible to sit on it or lie down upon it; there is also a prescribed measurement for it.
And there is nothing improper here. However, a *koccha* (a bolster or cushion) is made from one of such materials as bark, reeds, *muñja* grass, or *pabbaja* grass;
it is bound together after being rolled up inside, wide at both the bottom and the top, shaped like a drum (*paṇava*), and wrapped in the skin of a lion or similar animal in the middle.
There is nothing unallowable regarding the skins used here. For even a seat made of gold is permitted. [The text continues with: "In the open air... (*ajjhokāse*).
In this context, setting aside those eight months which are designated as "the months of the rains" by the convention of the rainy season (*avassika-saṅketa*),
even if it does not rain during the other four months, it is nevertheless not permitted to spread out [the bedding] in an open natural area or in a pavilion that leaks.
However, in a place where it rains during the winter, for the other four months as well...
It is not permissible. However, in the summer, when the sky is entirely free of clouds and clear, it is therefore permissible if one goes at that time for some business.
But it is never permissible at the foot of a tree where crows and other birds have a fixed dwelling.
Thus, wherever and whenever it is not permissible to spread out [the robe], all such cases should be understood here as being included within the category of "open air" (*ajjhokāsa*).
"Having spread out" means having spread it out in such a place for one's own sake or for the sake of another.
For even if it has been spread for the sake of someone else, as long as that person has not sat down there, or has not said, "Go," the responsibility for the rug remains with the one who spread it.
"Having had it spread" means having had it spread by one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). For this alone constitutes an impediment for him.
Once one is fully ordained, the responsibility for the rug spread belongs to the spreader alone;
however, this remains so only as long as the one who gave the order has not sat down there or said, "You may go.

For when a fully ordained person sits on a rug that he himself had spread or on an ordinary rug, the entire responsibility for it rests upon the one who sat down. Therefore, it is indeed the responsibility of the one who had it spread.

It becomes a *saṅkha* (a formal agreement). "While departing, he neither removes it nor causes it to be removed" means that either he himself does not remove it and place it in a suitable location, or he does not cause another to do so.
"Or he departs without asking permission" refers to a bhikkhu, a sāmaṇera, or an ārāmika who is conscientious and regards [the object] as his own personal impediment.

If, having failed to inform [the resident] in such a manner and having not handed over that lodging to him, one departs without concern, and should pass beyond the range of a stone’s throw of a man of medium strength:
for the first step passing beyond the range of the stone’s throw, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); for the second step passing beyond it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
However, if standing in the dining hall, one has [already] assigned [the lodging] to a certain place for the midday rest...
Having sent [the message], "Go!", and then departing from there to go elsewhere, one is to be dealt with according to the lifting of the *pādukā* (shoes).
This was laid down concerning a number of bhikkhus in Sāvatthī regarding the matter of departing without having removed the spread (*santhata*) and without asking permission;

it is a general rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), not a specific instruction (*anāṇattika*), an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for the triad, and an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*) for the triad in the case of what belongs to an individual.
If one places a mattress, an upper covering, a floor-covering, a wooden board, a piece of hide, a foot-wiping cloth, a wooden bench,
or any other kind of wooden or earthenware object— even down to a bowl-stand—
in an open space characterized by the aforementioned features and then departs, it is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, for a forest-dweller, if [such objects] are not available...
In the case of one who lives under a roof, it is permissible to go after having fastened everything to a tree or having made arrangements so that termites do not eat it.
However, for one who lives in the open air (*abbhokāsika*), even if he has built a small shed for his robes, he must protect them.

When going away with items belonging to himself, or those belonging to a person in whom he has confidence, having performed repairs and such, or while drying [the robes], [he may leave] thinking, "I will come back and remove them."
When one is departing, if seniors rise [to leave], or if a non-human being sits there, or someone powerful seizes it,
or lions and other beasts come and stay in that place— in such ways the lodging becomes an impediment; likewise, when the lodging is thus impeded,
or when facing calamities that create obstacles to life or the holy life, or for those who are insane and so forth.
There is no offense. Herein, there are six factors: the bedding and so forth belonging to the Saṅgha; spreading or having it spread in a place possessing the characteristics already mentioned;
not being obstructed; the absence of an emergency; lack of concern; and exceeding the distance of a stone’s throw.
The origin and other details are exactly the same as for the first *kaṭhina* rule; however, this one is both an action and a non-action.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning lodgings is finished.
5. Commentary on the second training rule concerning lodgings:
"In a monastery" means in a cell, or in any other entirely enclosed lodging as previously described. "A bed" means...

"Bed" (*seyyā*) is said to be: a mattress (*bhisī*), a felt rug (*cimilikā*), an upper coverlet (*uttarattaraṇaṃ*), a floor-covering (*bhūmattharaṇaṃ*), a wooden board (*taṭṭikā*), a piece of hide (*cammakkhaṇḍo*), a sitting mat (*nisīdanaṃ*), a counterpane (*paccattharaṇaṃ*), a grass mat (*tiṇasanthāro*), and a leaf mat (*paṇṇasanthāro*).

Among these, a "felt rug" (*cimilikā*) is that which is made for the purpose of preserving the color of a prepared floor. An "upper coverlet" (*uttarattaraṇaṃ*) is that which is suitable to be spread over beds, chairs, and so forth.
A bedspread (*paccattharaṇa*). A floor-covering (*bhūmattharaṇa*) is a mat made of reeds or the like, which, when there is a rug (*cimilika*), is spread over it;
when there is none, it is to be spread on the bare ground. A mat (*taṭṭikā*) is a mat made from palm leaves and so forth.
A piece of hide (*cammakkhaṇḍa*) is any kind of skin; for while the use of lion skins and the like is restricted to personal wearing, their use in the enjoyment of lodgings is permitted.
However, there is no such thing as "unallowable skin. A "bedspread" (*paccattharaṇa*) consists only of a woolen rug (*pāvāra*) and a fur blanket (*kojava*);

the rest is self-evident. Thus, having taken even one of these ten types of beds according to his own *vassa*-allotment, whatever monk is traveling abroad should, in a monastery possessing the aforementioned characteristics, either spread it out himself or have it spread out. As for...
If it has been placed [there] by ants, it is not being eaten; likewise, by way of placing it there, he neither removes it nor causes it to be removed.

If, according to the method stated in the preceding training rule, he goes away without asking permission, then for one who crosses the enclosure of that enclosed monastery, or the vicinity of an unenclosed one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) with the first step, and with the second step...

This is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). However, where there is no suspicion of termites, it is permissible to go even without asking for permission; nevertheless, asking for permission remains a duty (*vatta*).

This rule was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of seventeen monks, regarding the case of departing without asking for permission after having spread out bedding in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha and failing to remove it;
it is a general rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), not a specific instruction (*anāṇattika*), and constitutes a triple offense of expiation (*tikapācittiya*).
For an individual, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each of the three cases.

However, having spread out [the bedding] or having had it spread out either in the vicinity of a monastery possessing the aforementioned characteristics—whether outside and near it, in an assembly hall, in an unroofed pavilion, in a roofed one, or at the foot of a tree where many gather—or having spread out beds and chairs within the monastery or in the vicinity of such a monastery as described; [therein lies the offense].
Or, having had it spread out, for one who departs without performing the removal and other necessary duties, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
