However, regarding what belongs to oneself or to a person in whom one has confidence, if one departs after performing the removal and other duties, and having abandoned the obstruction according to the previous method;
or if one goes across a river or to another village while still having concern [for the bedding], thinking, "I will return this very day and take care of it."
Having gone to the place where the intention to go arose, he remains right there and either sends someone [to inform the Sangha] or asks for leave;
or he is obstructed by some obstacle such as a river in flood, a king, or thieves, and is unable to return;

or it concerns one who is in distress or one who is insane and so forth—in these cases, there is no offense. [The following applies to] a bed with the stated characteristics, its belonging to the Sangha, and [a bed] with the stated characteristics.

In this context, there are seven factors: spreading out [a mat] in a monastery, having it spread out, being unobstructed, the absence of danger, departing in a particular direction without looking back, and crossing the boundary of the precincts.
The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are exactly as described in the immediately preceding training rule.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning lodgings is finished.

6. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Sitting Down (Anupakhajja-sikkhāpada) Regarding the sixth [rule], "knowing" means knowing, "This person is not to be made to move. For this very reason, it is stated in its word-commentary (padabhājana):
"He knows, 'He is senior'; he knows, 'He is ill'; he knows, 'He has been assigned by the Saṅgha. Indeed, one who is senior [is so] by virtue of himself...
One who is elderly is not to be displaced because of his age; one who is ill is not to be displaced because of his illness.

Furthermore, the Saṅgha—having observed the great service and distinguished qualities of a storekeeper, or of Dhamma-preachers, Vinaya-holders, group-reciters, or teachers—and having designated a monastery for permanent residence, may assign it to them;
therefore, he to whom it has been given by the Saṅgha is also not to be displaced. "Previously arrived" means...
"Previously arrived": having entered the vicinity of the bed and chair, or of that bhikkhu as he enters or exits.
In this regard, for the bed and chair, the vicinity in a large dwelling is one and a half cubits all around;
in a small one, it is one and a half cubits from wherever space allows. Of that...
The precinct extends from the stone for washing the feet upon entering, as far as the bed and chair;
and from the bed and chair upon departing, as far as the place for urination.

"Should he spread out a bed" means that, because of his desire to cause him distress, if he spreads out even one of the ten types of beds within that precinct, or causes it to be spread out, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
In this regard, for one who sits or lies down [there], it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*); for one who does both, there are two offenses of expiation;
for one who does so repeatedly, there is an offense of expiation for each instance according to the number of acts.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks, in connection with the matter of occupying a bed by encroaching upon another.

This is a common designation (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), not a formal injunction (*anāṇattika*). It is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for the triad [of actions], and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the triad regarding what belongs to an individual (*puggalika*).

Whether outside the designated precincts, or in a waiting hall (*upaṭṭhānasālā*) and so forth, or within the precincts of the monastery (*vihāra*), there is likewise only an offense of wrong-doing for both spreading out [the bedding] oneself or having it spread out, as well as for sitting or lying down upon it.
However, for one who spreads it out in a monastery belonging to oneself or to a trusted person, and for whoever...
There is no offense for one who enters [the dwelling] because he is ill, or oppressed by cold or heat, or in cases of emergency, or for those such as the insane.

The four factors here are: it being a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, knowing that it is not to be vacated, the desire to cause crowding, and sitting or lying down within the precincts. The origin and other characteristics are exactly the same as for the first *pārājika*.
This, however, is only painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning encroaching is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning throwing out.
"In the seventh [offense], 'angered' means being provoked to anger. 'Displeased' means having a dissatisfied mind.

'Should expel or cause to be expelled, it is a pācittiya': here, in the case of palaces with many stories or quadrangles with many rooms—when one seizes someone in such dwellings, stops them in the middle, and makes them pass through by a single effort, there is one pācittiya."
For one who repeatedly causes [the person] to pass out by various means, there are *pācittiya* offenses for each door crossed.
The same principle applies even when one does not touch with the hand but says “Come out! and drives them out by speech.
However, for one who causes another to drive him out, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense at the mere moment of commanding “Drive him out!”, provided that once commanded, he passes through many doors.

When he has gone out, there is one *pācittiya* offense for the other. However, if he is instructed with such specific limitations as, "Throw him out through so many doors," or "Throw him out as far as the main gate," there are *pācittiya* offenses according to the number of doors.
This was concerning the group of six monks at Sāvatthī, regarding the matter of throwing a monk out from a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha.
The formulated rule: a common formulation, a threefold instruction, a triad of *pācittiya* offenses, and a triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses for an individual.
[It concerns] the removal from a dwelling or its precincts of that person or their requisites;
or, in the case of one who is not fully ordained, the removal from a dwelling or its precincts of one who is not fully ordained or their requisites.

In the case of throwing out [a monk] oneself or causing him to be thrown out, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Furthermore, this should be understood according to the number of requisites when the requisites are unconnected [to the Sangha].

In the case of throwing out oneself or one who is trusted, or in the case of throwing out a quarrelsome person from his own dwelling or from the entire monastery grounds, or in the case of throwing out his requisites or causing them to be thrown out—

Or, there is no offense for one who ejects from his own residence a person lacking a sense of shame, a madman, or those disciples or co-residents who are not conducting themselves properly, nor for the ejection of their requisites;
likewise, there is no offense for oneself when one is mad and so forth. [The factors are: a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha;
the state of being free from quarreling and other such behaviors on the part of the ordained person; and the actual ejection or causing another to eject out of anger.
Thus, there are these three factors here. The origins and so forth are similar to those of the offense of taking what is not given; however, this [offense] is of painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning expulsion is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Upper Story of a House.
In the eighth [case], "in an upper chamber" (*uparivehāsakuṭiyā*) means in a two-storied or three-storied hut whose upper floor is not covered.
However, in order to show the specific type of hut intended here, the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) states: "not striking the head of a man of medium height.
"With a fixed base" (*āhaccapādaka*) means a base that has been inserted after piercing the wall-panels. "Should sit down upon" (*abhinisīdeyya*) means having overcome [the space].
"He should sit having covered [it]," or this accusative case ending refers to the sense of the ground; the meaning is that he should sit or lie down on a bed or a bench.
However, the word *abhi* here is merely a prefix (*upasagga*) for the sake of the verse's meter.
Therefore, it refers to a monk who, in a "Vehāsakuṭī" (an upper-story cell) defined by the aforementioned characteristics, even to the very minimum extent, as far as the middle size...
If a man sits or lies down on a bed or chair with detachable legs placed upon scales that are so high that his head does not touch the lowest part of the scales at all,
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for each instance of contact, according to the method explained in the training rule concerning "sitting down by pushing" (anupakhajja-sikkhāpada).

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhu, on account of his suddenly sitting down or lying down on a bed or bench with detachable legs in an upper chamber; it is a general rule, not a specific injunction,

an offense of *pācittiya* for the triad [of factors], a *dukkaṭa* for the triad in the case of what belongs to an individual, and it applies to a dwelling belonging either to oneself or to one who trusts one.
In a lofted hut that strikes the head, or one that is unusable because materials such as straw have been placed beneath it,
or where the upper surface is covered with paving stones or finished with plaster and the like—

if one sits on a chair with legs fixed to that [surface], or if someone standing on a chair with legs fixed to that same lofted space picks up something or becomes entangled; [in these cases, there is no offense].
Or, for one who has a support-beam provided—meaning a beam inserted above the head and feet—for one sitting there, and for those such as the insane, there is no offense.
A dwelling belonging to the Sangha, a loft-hut where the head does not strike [the ceiling], with its lower part being usable;
or sitting or lying down on a seat with legs that strike [the floor] when no support-beam has been provided—these are the four factors here.
The origins and other details are similar to those of the *eḷakaloma* [wool] rule.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the upper-story hut (*vehāsakuṭi*) is concluded.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning large dwellings (*mahallakavihāra*).
"In the ninth [case], 'large' means having an owner. 'Vihāra' means plastered inside and out.
'As far as the door-frame'—here, by way of the maximum limit, the 'door-frame' refers to an area of two and a half cubits surrounding the wooden door-panel.
'For the purpose of fixing the bolt' means for the sake of making the door-fastening with its panels stable. For the door-panel must be easy to turn."
At the time of opening it, one strikes the wall; at the time of closing it, one strikes the door-bolt. By that striking, the wall shakes;
then the clay moves, and having moved, it either becomes loose or falls away. Therefore the Blessed One said: "As far as the door-recess for the insertion of the bolt.

In this regard, although there is nothing stated in either the summary table (mātikā) or the word-commentary (padabhājana) to the effect that "this specific thing must be done," [the meaning is established by implication].
It has been stated; however, in the *Aṭṭhuppatti*, because of the context—"he had it plastered again and again, he had it smeared again and again"—the meaning should be understood as follows:
from the door-frames up to the door-bolts, it must be repeatedly smeared or have it smeared for the purpose of installing the bolts.
Regarding the phrase "for the preparation of the light-slits" (*ālokasandhiparikammāya*), here "light-slits" (*ālokasandhi*) refers to the window shutters.
At the time of opening them, they strike the wall surface by a measure of one span (vidatthi) or even more;

however, the surrounding area (upacāra) is obtainable here in all directions. Therefore, the intention here is that an area equal in width to the door should be plastered or caused to be plastered in all directions for the purpose of preparing the light-entrances (ālokasandhi).

Having thus shown what must be done regarding plastering work (*lepa-kamma*), he now says "of two or three layers of roofing" (*dvatti-chadanassa*) and so forth, in order to show what must be done regarding roofing (*chadana*).
Therein, "the turn of two or three layers of roofing" means two or three turns of roofing; "turn" (*pariyāya*) is said to mean a circuit (*parikkhepa*);
the meaning is that two circuits or three circuits must be determined. In a place free from vegetation (*appaharite*).

"Standing" means standing where there is no green growth. Here, "green growth" (*harita*) refers to the primary crops, such as the seven kinds of grain, and the secondary crops, such as the varieties of beans, peas, sesame, horse gram, bottle gourds, and cucumbers.
Even that which has been sown in a field and has not yet come to fruition, but will do so once the rain falls, is included within the category of "green growth.
Therefore, one who makes a formal determination while standing upon such [growth]—
He incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). This is also the delimitation for one who resolves while standing on ground that is not yet overgrown with grass:
a man sitting at the side of a ridgepole or the pinnacle of a gabled house, looking down through the opening of the roof-covering, sees the monk standing on a certain patch of ground;
and likewise, standing where he is, looking up at the one seated above, [he sees him].
One sees that one must stand upon it; even though the interior is not yet overgrown with grass, one is not permitted to stand there.
"Beyond that" means: when covering by way of a path, it refers to three paths; when covering by way of successive turns, it refers to three turns;
when covering with bricks, stone slabs, or plaster, it is calculated by the number of bricks, stone slabs, and lumps of plaster; and when covering with grass and leaves.
There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for each count of roofing tiles and for each count of handfuls of grass.
This was laid down at Kosambī concerning the Elder Channa, regarding the repeated act of having [the hut] roofed and plastered;

it is a general rule, not a specific instruction, and constitutes an offense of expiation under three conditions. It applies when one perceives the work as exceeding twenty-three layers, even if it is less.

Or there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who is in doubt. There is no offense in the case of making white color and so forth; or when [the work] is less than two or three stages; or in the case of a cave, a grotto, a grass hut, and so on;

or when having it built for another purpose; or when one has it built with one's own wealth; or for one who resolves upon [the construction of] the remaining [buildings] while excluding the dwelling-house (*vāsāgāra*);
or for those who are insane and so forth. [The factors of the offense are: the state of being a large monastery (*mahallaka-vihāra*), and the state of being one's own dwelling-house.
"Further determination" (uttari adhiṭṭhāna): these are the three factors here. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are exactly as stated in the case of matchmaking (sañcaritta).
The commentary on the training rule regarding large dwellings is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule regarding water containing living beings (sappāṇaka-sikkhāpada).
In the tenth [offense], "knowing it contains living beings" means knowing by any means whatsoever—either having seen or heard—that "this contains living beings.
"Sprinkles or causes to be sprinkled" means that he either sprinkles with that water himself or causes another to sprinkle it by command.
In this regard, for one who sprinkles without interrupting the stream, there is a single offense for each jar; for one who interrupts the stream, [there is an offense for each interruption].

There are offenses according to the number of actions (*payoga*). If one makes the *mātikā* (the head of the list) the primary object, even if it remains submerged for a whole day, it is only a single offense.
For one who ties [objects] here and there and carries them elsewhere, there are offenses according to the number of actions.

Even for one who throws many grasses, leaves, branches, and so forth into water with a single action, it is only a single offense; however, for one who throws them in individually, there are offenses according to the number of actions.
Regarding the offenses: this refers to that which, when poured in such a manner, reaches exhaustion or becomes turbid, causing small creatures to die;
it is said with reference to such [water], not to a great body of water. For the one who causes it to be poured, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) by the single command;
even if many [vessels] are poured by a single command, for the one who gives the command, there is only one offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was laid down at Āḷavī concerning the monks of Āḷavī regarding the matter of pouring water; it is a general rule, consisting of three injunctions.
For one who pours water that is waterless while perceiving it as containing living beings, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for both parties if they are in doubt.

There is no offense for one who perceives it as waterless, or for one who pours it unintentionally, through forgetfulness, or unknowingly, nor for those who are insane and so forth. [The rule concerns] water.
The presence of living beings; the knowledge that "by pouring [this], the living beings will die";

and the water being of such a nature that it is poured on grass and so forth for some purpose other than the intention to kill—these are the four factors here. The origin and other characteristics are similar to those of taking what is not given;
however, this is a formal offense (paṇṇattivajja), involving three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning water containing living beings is finished.
The second chapter, the Section on Plants and Seeds, is concluded.
3. The Section on Exhortation.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Exhortation (Ovādasikkhāpada).

Regarding the first rule of the Exhortation Chapter (*Ovādavagga*): "Unappointed" (*asammatō*) means one who has not been authorized by the Blessed One through a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthena kammena*) for the office of exhorter of bhikkhunīs, despite being endowed with the eight qualities required of a bhikkhu.
"Should exhort" (*ovadeyyā*) means [he should exhort] the community of bhikkhunīs.

Or, whether there be many [monks] or just one, he should exhort her by reciting the eight *garudhammas* beginning with: "A nun who has been ordained for a hundred years must perform salutation, rising from her seat, joining of palms, and respectful service toward a monk ordained on that very day.
At the conclusion of the exhortation, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks (*chabbaggiya*) regarding the matter of exhorting [nuns]. It is a non-common prescription (*asādhāraṇapaññatti*), not subject to formal authorization (*anāṇattika*).
For one who exhorts nuns who have only recently been fully ordained (*upasampanna*) by means of some other rule, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Even if he is authorized, if that act of authorization is an illegitimate legal act (*adhammakamma*), then for that illegitimate legal act, for one who perceives it as an illegitimate legal act...

For one who exhorts a faction of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, there is a *pācittiya* for each of the three cases; likewise, for one who is doubtful but perceives it as a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*), there are nine *pācittiya*s.
Including the case where it is done by a complete Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, there are eighteen *pācittiya*s based on illegitimate legal acts (*adhammakamma*).
However, if that is a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*), then for one who perceives a legitimate legal act as such and [exhorts] a complete Bhikkhunī Saṅgha...
Having set aside this final phrase, "he exhorts while perceiving them as being in concord," there are seventeen *dukkaṭa* offenses by that same method:
for one who, when it is said, "We are in concord, Venerable Sir," speaks another teaching; for one who, when it is said, "We are in discord, Venerable Sir," speaks the eight *garudhammas*;
and for one who, without having concluded the exhortation, speaks another teaching—there is likewise a *dukkaṭa*. However, he who...

If one, perceiving it as a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*), while it is indeed a legitimate legal act, and perceiving the united community of nuns (*bhikkhunīsaṅgha*) to be united, instructs them;

if one recites the text of the heavy rules (*garudhamma-pāḷi*); if one provides an exposition; if, being told "Venerable sir, please restore [her]," one restores her; if, when asked a question, one speaks;
if one speaks for another purpose while the nuns are listening; or if [one does so] to a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*) or a novice nun (*sāmaṇerī*).
Or if he says [this], there is no offense for him, nor for those who are insane and so forth.

The three factors here are: the state of not being authorized, the fact that the nun is fully ordained, and the speaking of the eight *garudhammas* by way of exhortation. The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other such details are exactly like those for the training rule on reciting the *Pātimokkha*.
The commentary on the training rule on exhortation is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sunset:

Regarding the second rule, "should advise," it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one who advises—whether formally authorized or not—by means of the eight weighty rules (garudhamma) or by any other teaching.
This was established concerning the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka at Sāvatthī, based on the incident of advising after the sun had set.

This is a formal rule (*paññatta*), a unique formal rule (*asādhāraṇapaññatti*), not a mere instruction (*anāṇattika*), and carries a *pācittiya* offense for three cases: when the sun has set and one perceives it as having set, or when one is in doubt;
and there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who exhorts a person who is fully ordained on only one side.

As in the preceding training rule, there is no offense according to the method of recitation and so forth. Here, the factors are: the state of the sun having set, the state of being fully ordained, and the act of exhorting.
There are three factors. The sections beginning with "origination" (samuṭṭhāna) are exactly like those in the *Padasodhamma*.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the disappearance [of the sun] is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Nuns' Quarters.
"In the third [offense], 'a nunnery' means even a place where a nun has stayed for one night.
'Should exhort'—here, the *pācittiya* applies only to one who exhorts by means of the *garudhammas*. However, if he is not authorized, there are two *pācittiyas*.
Furthermore, if he exhorts even after the sun has set, there are three. But for one who is authorized, even if he exhorts during the night..."

There are only two [cases]. For there is no offense of expiation (pācittiya) for a monk based on giving instruction regarding the heavy rules (garudhamma) simply because he has been formally authorized.
"Ill" means she is unable to go for the purpose of receiving instruction or for communal living.
This refers to the case concerning the group-of-six monks among the Sakyans, regarding the matter of approaching the nuns' quarters to give instruction.

The rule laid down as “except at the proper time” is here a subsequent addition (*anupaññatti*), a non-common addition (*asādhāraṇapaññatti*), not a formal injunction (*anāṇattika*), and entails an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for three cases:
for one who instructs a person not fully ordained while perceiving them to be fully ordained, or while being in doubt;

for one who instructs someone fully ordained in only one respect by means of any [method]; and for one who instructs another by means of some other teaching, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). At the proper time, for one not fully ordained...
There is no offense according to the method of recitation and so forth, as in the previous training rule.

Herein, there are four factors: entering the residence, being fully ordained, the absence of the [proper] occasion, and exhorting [the nuns] regarding the heavy rules (garudhamma). The origin and other characteristics are similar to those of the first Kathina rule;
however, this is an action (kiriya).
The commentary on the training rule regarding the nuns' quarters is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Worldly Gain (Āmisa-sikkhāpada):

"On account of worldly gain" means for the sake of any one of the requisites, such as robes and so forth. "Monks" refers here to those monks who have been duly ordained. "An offense of expiation" (pācittiya) means that an offense of expiation is incurred by one who speaks in this manner out of a desire to disparage such monks.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks (*chabbaggiyā bhikkhū*) on the basis of the offense of saying, "They exhort for the sake of material gain.

It is a non-common rule (*asādhāraṇapaññatti*), not subject to formal authorization (*anāṇattika*). In the case of a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*), it is a triad of *pācittiya* offenses; in the case of an illegitimate legal act (*adhammakamma*), it is a triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses.
This applies to one who is unordained (*anupasampanna*), whether authorized or unauthorized, and to one who is ordained (*upasampanna*), whether authorized or unauthorized.

For one who speaks thus, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). In this regard, a monk who has received formal consent at the proper time and remains on the level of a novice is called "one who is consented to" (*sammata*) though not fully ordained.
However, for one who speaks thus while exhorting [others] out of natural inclination for the sake of robes and so forth, and for those who are insane and so on, there is no offense.
[The factors for the offense are: being fully ordained, and having received consent in accordance with the Dhamma.

The absence of worldly motives and the speaking thus out of a desire for disrepute—these are the four factors here. The origin and other characteristics are the same as those for taking what is not given;
however, this [offense] is exclusively of painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning worldly motives is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Giving of Robes (Cīvaradāna-sikkhāpada).
This fifth rule was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a certain monk, based on the occasion of the giving of robes.

The rest of the explanatory method here should be understood in the same manner as stated under the training rule concerning the acceptance of robes. For in that [latter rule], the monk is the recipient.
In this case, it is a nun; this is the distinction, while the rest is exactly the same.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the giving of robes is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule regarding the sewing of robes.
"In the sixth [offense], 'a robe' means one suitable for wearing as an undergarment or an upper garment. Regarding the phrase 'should sew or have it sewn':
for one who sews it oneself, each time the needle is inserted and withdrawn, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Even if one pierces it a hundred times and withdraws the needle once, there is only a single offense of expiation. However, if one is told 'sew it,' even if one performs all the needlework..."

If he has it completed, there is one *pācittiya* offense for the sender. But if, having been told, "Whatever must be done with this robe-cloth, all that is your responsibility," he has it completed, there is a *pācittiya* offense for him at every stage of the journey. For the sender, even if there are many [tasks], there is only one [offense] for a single instruction;
however, in the case of repeated instructions, no further offense need be mentioned.

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the Elder Udāyī regarding the matter of sewing robes; it is a non-common rule (*asādhāraṇapaññatti*), consisting of three rules and a triad of offenses of expiation (*pācittiya*).

There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who sews for a relative when perceiving her as a non-relative, or when in doubt, or for one who sews for one who is ordained on only one side (a male lay follower).
There is also an offense of wrong-doing for one who sews other requisites such as bags (*thavikā*), and for one who sews for a female trainee (*sikkhamānā*) or a novice nun (*sāmaṇerī*).
There is no offense for one who is sewing a robe, nor for those who are insane and so forth. The three factors here are: that it belongs to an unrelated nun;
that it is suitable to be used as an undergarment or an upper garment; and that there is either the act of sewing or causing to be sewn according to the stated characteristics.
The origin and other details are exactly the same as those for the offense of matchmaking (sañcaritta).
The commentary on the training rule concerning the sewing of robes is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning making an appointment:

Regarding the seventh [rule], "having made an appointment" (*saṃvidhāya*) means having arranged it; the meaning is, having made a signal for the time of departure. "A single road" (*ekaddhānamaggaṃ*)...
"One road" means a path reckoned as a journey, or a journeying road from one side. "Traveling with a caravan" means it is to be traveled together with a caravan;

the rest of the words have their meanings obvious. Here, however, is the analysis: for one who makes an appointment on an improper ground, there is first an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) due to the act of making the appointment.
In that regard, setting aside the nuns' quarters, the interior of a monastery, and a sitting hall—
The phrase "the lodging of a non-Buddhist ascetic" refers to any remaining improper ground; the meaning is that it applies to one who makes an appointment while standing there.

However, having made an appointment, if one does not cancel the fixed time—whether for today or tomorrow—but instead makes an appointment regarding the gate or the path, and travels with a nun as far as another village nearby, then [the offense applies]. This is the sense.
"Regarding its vicinity (*upacāra*): there is no offense so long as one does not enter the vicinity established by people.

However, for one who enters it, there is an act of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) on the first foot and an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*) on the second foot; thus, there are offenses of expiation according to the number of times one enters the village-vicinity.
But when there is no village, if one exceeds half a *yojana*, there is an offense of expiation according to the number of half-*yojanas*."
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six bhikkhus regarding the matter of setting out on a journey together:

“Except at the proper time. This is here an additional rule (anupaññatti), a non-common rule (asādhāraṇapaññatti), not subject to an instruction (anāṇattika), and entails a pācittiya offense for three cases:
for one who, when no arrangement has been made, perceives that it has been made, or is in doubt; and for one who [sets out] with a bhikkhunī who has not made an arrangement.
If one goes by oneself alone without having made an appointment, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

There is no offense for one who goes after having made an appointment at the proper time, for one who does not make an appointment oneself, for one who goes without a prior agreement, for one who goes during times of distress, or for those who are insane and so forth. [The factors for an offense are:
two people traveling together on a path after making an appointment, the absence of a prior agreement, the absence of the proper time, the absence of times of distress, and entering another village.

"Or crossing over half a *yojana*": these are the five factors here. However, in connection with the training rule for women, there is an offense when together with those who are ordained on one side and so forth;

it originates from travel, is an action, is not to be resolved through mindfulness, is without [evil] intention, is an offense by formal precept (*paṇṇattivajja*), is bodily action and verbal action, consists of three types of consciousness, and consists of three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning making arrangements is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule concerning boarding a boat:
Regarding the eighth rule, “having made arrangements,” this means having made preparations with the intention of sporting, or having made an appointment for the time of boarding.
The meaning is as follows: "Going upstream" means going against the current of a river for the sake of sport. "Going downstream" means likewise going with the current.
However, there is no offense in cases where they carry her either upstream or downstream for the purpose of reaching a landing place (*tittha*).
"Except for crossing transversely" is an ablative expression used in the sense of the accusative.

"Except for crossing horizontally" means excluding that [specific case]. Regarding the *pācittiya* offense: when traveling along the bank of a river containing villages, it is a *pācittiya* according to the count of intervening villages;
or when traveling along the bank of a river not containing villages, or through the middle of a river measuring one *yojana* in width, it is a *pācittiya* according to the count of half-*yojanas*.
However, in the case of the ocean, it is permissible to travel as one pleases.

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six bhikkhus in connection with the matter of boarding a boat: “Except for crossing transversely. This is the subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*) here; the rest should be understood in the same manner as stated in the immediately preceding training rule.
The commentary on the training rule concerning boarding a boat is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Boiling.
"Prepared by a bhikkhunī" (navame bhikkhuniparipācitaṃ) means prepared by a bhikkhunī;

it refers to what is obtained as something that has been made ready by manifesting the virtues of a bhikkhu in the presence of householders who have not been invited by him or by his own relatives, saying, "Give to the noble one! Prepare for the noble one!
The phrase "previously undertaken by householders" (pubbe gihisamārambhā): here, "undertaking" (samārambho) means that which has been commenced.
This is the name for what has been prepared. "Gihisamārambha" means the undertaking by householders.

The meaning is that, with the exception of food prepared for monks prior to the nun's own preparation—whether it be food for which householders have already made preparations for the sake of the monks, or the property of those who have given leave due to kinship—one incurs a *pācittiya* offense if one knowingly eats something else. And that indeed...
Regarding the counting of swallowings, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the act of receiving.
This was laid down at Rājagaha concerning Devadatta, in the case of eating alms-food prepared by bhikkhunīs;
"except when previously undertaken by a householder" is the subsequent rule (anupaññatti) here. It is a non-common rule (asādhāraṇapaññatti), and it is not subject to an instruction (anāṇattika).

For one who eats food prepared by a nun who has been ordained on only one side (ekatoupasampannā), there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who perceives it as prepared when it is unprepared, and for one who is in doubt regarding both.

There is no offense for one who perceives it as unprepared in both cases, or in the case of what has been undertaken by a layperson, or when it has been prepared by a trainee nun (sikkhamānā), a novice (sāmaṇera), and so forth, or regarding anything other than the five kinds of cooked food, or for those who are insane and so forth. [The same applies] for a bhikkhunī.

The five factors here are: the state of being cooked, the knowledge that it has been cooked, the absence of any undertaking by a householder, its being one of the [four] such as boiled rice, and the swallowing of it. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as for the first *pārājika*;
however, this is an offense of formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), involving three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the ripening [of beings] is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sitting in Secret:

In the tenth [training rule], the entire method of exposition is to be understood according to the same procedure as that stated for the second *aniyata* (undetermined) offense. For this training rule—

This [training rule] shares the same delimitation as the second *aniyata* offense and the fourth training rule concerning Upananda; however, it was formulated separately by way of a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
The commentary on the training rule regarding sitting in private is concluded.
The Third Chapter: On Exhortation.
4. The Chapter on Food.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Lodgings.
In the first section of the *Bhojanavagga*, "by one who is not ill" means by one capable of traveling even half a *yojana*.

"A single [meal]" means for one day. "An alms-meal at a guest-house" (*āvasathapiṇḍa*) refers to food prepared by those desiring merit in places such as rest-houses, without specifying "for these many" or "for so many heretics," or simply "just this much. It should be eaten.
Whether by a single family or by various families, having come together, it is to be eaten on one day only at one place, or at various places,
whether designated as an indefinite location such as "today at one place, tomorrow at another," or at a specific place;
beyond that— that is, starting from the second day, whether at that same place or at another place— of those...
In the case of accepting what belongs to another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks, based on the incident of eating alms-food received from a lodging-house (*āvasathapiṇḍa*) after having stayed overnight.

“By one who is not ill”—this is the subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*) here; it is a common rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), it is not a formal instruction (*anāṇattika*), and it is an offense of expiation of the threefold type (*tikapācittiya*).
For one who perceives a sick person as not sick, or who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For one who perceives a sick person as sick, if he eats once while traveling on the way, once at the destination, once on the way back, and once at the place of arrival;
and if, having thought "I shall go," he eats and sets out—
If he turns back due to some obstacle and, having ascertained that it is safe, goes on again and eats one day;
or if his own masters invite him and give him food; or if it is prepared specifically for monks and not prepared for as much as they require;
or if, setting aside the five kinds of cooked food, he eats something else; and for him [there is no offense], as well as for those who are insane and so forth.
There is no offense. The three factors here are: being alms-food from a lodging, not being ill, and eating after having stayed overnight.
The origin and other details are similar to the training rule on wool (*eḷakaloma*).
The commentary on the training rule on lodgings (*āvasatha*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Group Meals (Gaṇabhojana-sikkhāpada).
Regarding "a group meal" in the second [rule]: it refers to a meal for a group. Here, "group" means four or more bhikkhus;
it refers to eating any one of the five kinds of staple foods, such as boiled rice and so forth, obtained through an invitation or a request from them.

The meaning. Herein, this is the analysis: if someone approaches four bhikkhus and, using any synonym or any other language, mentions the names of the five kinds of cooked food, inviting them in such a manner as "I invite you with rice;
please accept my rice," and so forth—if they are thus invited either collectively or individually—
Whether they go together or separately and then take [the food] together, or later eat it together or separately, it constitutes *gaṇabhojana* (eating in a group).

Here, the act of receiving is the sole criterion. If, having requested rice and so forth by name, whether together or separately, and having gone [to receive it], they take it together, this too is indeed *gaṇabhojana*. Of that twofold [type],...
Thus, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in receiving [the food], and for every swallow, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
The time of illness and so forth: when even walking on one’s feet is impossible because they are cracked, this is the time of illness.

For those who have performed the *kaṭhina* ceremony, the five months [following] are the time for the distribution of robes; for others, it is the month of Kattika—this is the time for the giving of robes. When, while a robe is being made...
When one performs even a slight task that must be done regarding a robe, this is the "robe-making season.
When one desires to go, or actually goes, or has already gone for half a *yojana*, this is the "journeying-season.

The same principle applies to the season of embarking on a boat. When four monks, having wandered for alms in the village where they seek food, are unable to sustain themselves, this is the "great assembly season" (*mahāsamaya*).
When any renunciant invites one for a meal, this is the occasion of a meal for a recluse; it is permissible to eat on these occasions.
This was laid down in connection with Devadatta at Rājagaha regarding the matter of eating after having requested [food].

“Except on the proper occasions”—this is the sevenfold supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*) here; it is a common rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), it is not a formal instruction (*anāṇattika*), and it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) in three cases.

If one eats with a group while perceiving it as such, or while being in doubt about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, there is no offense for one who does not perceive it as eating with a group;
nor is there an offense in the following cases: when two or three people take food together; when many people, having wandered for alms, eat together;
among those who receive regular meals and the like; in all instances except for the five kinds of cooked food; and for those who are insane and so forth.
The three factors here are: eating in a group, the absence of an occasion, and swallowing. The origin and other characteristics are the same as those for the rule on wool.
The commentary on the training rule concerning eating in a group is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Eating in Succession:
Regarding "eating in succession" (paramparabhojana) in the third [training rule], it refers to one who has been invited by five [persons] to eat, as explained in the method for eating in a group;
that is, from whichever meal one was first invited, to eat out of order from those meals, or without making a formal assignment (avikappetvā).
Regarding the food of another person: therefore, if a bhikkhu—
without having assigned his first invitation to any one of the five classes of fellow practitioners by saying in their presence,
"I give my expected meal to you," or "I assign it to you," or by saying in their absence, "I give it to so-and-so," or "I assign it to so-and-so"— later [accepts a meal].

If one swallows even a single grain of rice from alms-food obtained at a family where one has been invited, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). The exceptions (samaya) are exactly as previously stated.
This rule was laid down at Vesālī concerning a number of monks on the occasion of eating food other than that for which they had been invited;
"except at the proper times" constitutes here a threefold supplementary regulation (anupaññatti), though in the Parivāra, the act of assigning the meal to another (vikappana) is also included.
Regarding the statement, “four subsequent rules,” these are: a non-common rule, a non-instruction, and an offense of expiation for three [cases].
For one who eats in succession and perceives it as eating in succession, or is doubtful about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

However, for one who does not perceive it as eating in succession—such as when it is at the proper time, or when having made an assignment, or when two or three invitations from those closely associated have been combined into one—[there is no offense].

There is no offense for one who eats after having made [a prior arrangement], or eats according to the sequence of invitations; or for one invited by an entire village or a group who eats at any one of those places;
or for one who, while being invited, says, "I shall take almsfood"; or for one among those who receive a regular meal and so forth;
or for anyone except when it concerns the five kinds of cooked food; and there is no offense for those who are insane and so forth.
Taking food in succession, the absence of an occasion, and swallowing—these are the three factors here.
The origin and other characteristics are exactly the same as those for the first *kaṭhina* [offense], but this is a "non-action" offense (*akiriya*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning taking food in succession is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Kāṇamātā.
Regarding the fourth [rule]: "With cakes" (*pūvehi*) means with any kind of edible food prepared for the purpose of a gift, such as *atirasaka*, *modaka*, *sakkhalika*, and so forth.
"With flour-mixtures" (*manthehi*) means with any kind of ingredients such as sesame, oil, rice, and so forth, prepared for the purpose of provisions for a journey.
"Two or three bowlfuls" means two or three bowlfuls that do not exceed the lower rim of the mouth of the bowl.

"If more than that" means that even if one takes a third bowlful stacked on top, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the count of cakes remaining above the lower rim of the mouth of the bowl.
Regarding the phrase "having accepted two or three bowlfuls," here, by whom [the two]...
If [the food] has been taken, then upon seeing a monk outside, one should say: "Two bowlfuls have been taken by me here; you may take one.
If that [monk] also sees another, he should say: "Two bowlfuls were taken by the first comer;
I have taken one; you must not take [any]. This applies even to the successive notification by one who first took a single [bowlful].
The same method applies here. However, for one who has himself accepted three [meals], upon seeing another, he should say, "Do not accept anything here.
If he does not speak thus, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); and even for one who accepts after hearing those words, there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.
Thereafter, having brought it out, it should be shared with the monks; from the place where it was obtained, it should be taken to the nearest assembly hall or monastery.
Or, wherever he turns back after being assigned, having gone there, he should set aside one bowlful for himself and give the remainder to the community of monks.

However, it is not permitted to give according to personal friendship. If one person has already taken [his share], nothing may be given to him against his will; it should be done according to his preference.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhus, regarding the matter of receiving without knowing moderation;

it is a general rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti), not a specific instruction (anāṇattika), and carries an offense of pācittiya under three conditions. For one who perceives what is less than two bowlfuls as being more, or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.
However, for one who perceives it as less—provided it is not for the sake of a gift to be sent away nor for the sake of provisions for a journey—[there is no offense].

There is no offense for one who takes what has been prepared, or what remains from what was prepared for that purpose, or when the journey has been abandoned, or when those who are kinsmen or have given permission are giving it, or when one takes it with one's own wealth; as well as for those who are insane and so forth.

Herein, the characteristics mentioned are: the state of being cakes or dough, the state of not being "leftover," the state of the journey not having been abandoned, the state of not being kinsmen and so forth, and the taking of an excess.
The five factors, beginning with the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*), are exactly the same as those for the offense of acting as a go-between.
The commentary on the training rule concerning Kāṇamātā is finished.
5. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
"In the fifth [case], 'having eaten' (*bhuttāvī*) means having finished eating; whoever has swallowed even as much as a mustard seed of the five kinds of staple foods, he is called such.

'Having been invited' (*pavārito*) means one for whom an invitation has been performed according to the five factors stated in the Canon: "food is seen, a meal is seen, [the donor] stands within arm's reach and offers it, and a refusal is seen."* *The text here refers to the specific criteria for a formal invitation.*

The meaning is "one who has rejected [the invitation]. In this context, because one who has left off eating is called "invited" (*pavārita*) by the phrase "food is being presented," and because one who has left off eating has both eaten something and not eaten something—referring to that which was eaten—one is also reckoned as "one who has finished eating" (*bhuttāvī*). Therefore, by the expression "one who has finished eating":
We do not see any separate accomplishment of purpose here;

rather, it should be understood that this was stated for the sake of the euphony of the syllables, acting as a supplement to the word *pavārita*, just as the expression "two nights or three nights" (*dirattatiratta*) is used in such contexts.
Furthermore, among the requisites for the invitation (*pavāraṇa*), eating is made manifest; thus, unfinished food is seen, and he is one who is eating that.
The meaning is that there is a person present. "Food is seen" means that food sufficient for an invitation (*pavāraṇa*) is visible;
the meaning is that one of the foods, such as boiled rice and so forth, is food that ought to be refused.
"Standing within arm's reach" means that the donor, having taken the food sufficient for an invitation, stands in a space measuring two and a half cubits. "He offers" means...
"If the donor physically brings that food to him" means that he offers it. "A refusal is manifested" means that a refusal is seen;
the meaning is that if the bhikkhu refuses what has been brought to him either by body or by speech.
In this way, one is considered to have finished the invitation (*pavārita*) by way of these five factors.

In this regard, the analysis is as follows: first, concerning the terms “solid food” (*āsana*) and so forth, that which one eats, or that food which is brought within arm’s reach and then refused, should be understood as being one or another of these:
boiled rice (*odana*), sour gruel (*kummāsa*), flour (*sattu*), fish (*maccha*), or meat (*maṃsa*).
Among these, “boiled rice” (*odana*) refers to rice from the following [grains]: *sāli*, *vīhi*, barley (*yava*), wheat (*godhuma*), millet (*kaṅgu*), panic seed (*varaka*), and *kudrūsaka*.
Having taken the grain of the seven kinds of crops, they may cook it for any purpose— thinking, "Let us cook rice," or "Let us cook gruel"—
and if, when they eat it either warm or cold, a solid mass (*odhi*) is perceived at each place where it has been taken during the meal,
it is *odana* (boiled rice) and it generates an invitation (*pavāraṇa*). However, as for the milk-rice (*pāyāsa*) or sour gruel (*ambilayāgu*) [taken] from the hearth...
As soon as it has been poured out, while still very hot, one is able to stir it and drink;
even in the place where it is held by the hand, no sediment (*odhi*) is apparent, and it does not produce fermentation (*pavāraṇa*).
However, if, once the heat has subsided, it becomes thick and shows sediment, it again produces fermentation; its previous thin state is no longer preserved. Even if there are many...
If even a mere handful of rice grains has been placed into leaf-plates or bamboo shoots, and at the time of eating a solid portion (*odhi*) is discernible, it generates an *pavāraṇā*.

At an invitation where there is no rice gruel (*ayāguka*), if they say, "We shall give rice gruel," and pour water, sour gruel, milk, and so forth over the cooked food, saying, "Take the rice gruel," then even though it is thin, it still generates an *pavāraṇā*. If...
However, if they place it into boiling water or other liquids, cook it, and then give it, it is included within the category of *yāgu* (rice gruel).
If even a piece of fish or meat the size of a mustard seed, or a tendon, has been placed in the *yāgu*, it generates an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
With the exception of the grains mentioned as being permissible, if one uses rice other than those—such as bamboo-grain rice (*veḷutaṇḍula*) and so forth—or with tubers, roots, or fruits...
Or by whatever [food] a meal has been prepared, it does not generate the *pavāraṇā*. "Kummāsa" (gruel) means that which is made from barley;
however, gruel made from others such as mung beans (*mugga*) and so forth does not generate the *pavāraṇā*. "Sattu" (flour) means that which is made by roasting the seven types of grain.
Even the powder or the groats made by grinding the husked grains of rice—even those roasted in a rough fire—[does not generate the *pavāraṇā*].

It goes only to the gathering of enemies. However, they do not offer the husks of rice that have been split by equal cooking and dried in the sun, nor any grains of rice, nor parched rice, nor rice-gruel and flour preparations made with parched rice.
Regarding fish and meat, if there are only two pieces of fish or two pieces of meat, the size of a grain of rice, for one who is drinking rice-gruel—
Whether they give from a single vessel or from various vessels, if one does not eat those [items] but rejects some other food sufficient for an invitation (*pavāraṇa*), one has not invited.
Then, if one [item] has been eaten and another remains in the hand or in the bowl, if one rejects something else, one has invited.
Even if two have been eaten, provided that not even as much as a mustard seed remains in the mouth...

There is none; even if one rejects other [foods], one does not perform the *pavāraṇā*. However, if one who eats unallowable meat—produced through corrupting a family, medical practice, claiming superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*), or acquired by means of money and so forth—as well as unallowable food or any other food, whether allowable or unallowable, and rejects it, one does not perform the *pavāraṇā*.
Thus, regarding whatever one eats, and regarding the food brought within arm’s reach that one rejects, the *pavāraṇā*...
Having understood that [the offense] is produced, this exposition should now be understood for the purpose of knowing how one incurs it:
regarding the phrase "food is eating," first, if someone has swallowed even a single grain of rice, and while still having an expectation for food— whether in the bowl, the mouth, or the hand—
he rejects another food that possesses the aforementioned characteristics, [he incurs an offense].

he invites [the other to stop]. However, if he is indifferent—if he has no desire to swallow what remains in his bowl or elsewhere, or if he wishes to give it to another, or if he wishes to go elsewhere to eat—then even though he rejects the food, he does not invite [the other to stop].
Regarding the phrase "standing within arm's reach," if the monk is sitting, then from the rear edge of his buttocks...
Starting from the edge of the cloth when standing; starting from the edge of the heels when sitting;

or starting from the far edge of the side on which one lies when reclining—excluding the hand that has been extended—the nearest limb of the donor, whether seated, standing, or reclining, is delimited by its near edge, measuring two and a half cubits.
It should be understood as "the reach of the hand. For one who refuses what has been brought while standing within that [reach], the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) remains valid;
it does not cease beyond that point. "Brings" means that, standing within the reach of the hand, one extends [the object] for the purpose of taking it.

However, if even a monk sitting immediately next to him does not bring the bowl—which is already held in his hand or resting on a stand—without having first brought it [forward], [the invitation remains valid].
If one says, “Take some food,” there is no *pavāraṇā* for one who refuses it.
The same rule applies even when a food tray has been brought and placed on the ground before one, and this is said.
However, if one lifts it slightly or moves it aside and says, “Take [some],” there is *pavāraṇā* for one who refuses it. This also applies when [the donor] is serving while holding the food tray.
Another person merely takes hold of it, thinking, "I shall carry this," but it is the server alone who actually carries it;

therefore, that food is considered as if brought by the server himself. Consequently, for one who refuses a person wishing to give out of a desire to bestow, there is an act of *pavāraṇā* (invitation).
However, if it has been merely touched by the server and the other person carries it, then [the same applies] regarding the desire to give.
For one who refuses while another is taking [the food], there is no *pavāraṇā*. However, when [food] has been lifted with a ladle, there is [an offer].

Even when two portions are equal, one who refuses [his own] still performs the *pavāraṇā*. When food is being given to the person immediately next [to him], if the other covers his bowl, that which is brought to another is indeed considered refused;
therefore, there is no *pavāraṇā*. Regarding the term "refusal" (*paṭikkhepo*) here:

A refusal does not take effect when something is offered by speech alone; however, there is an invitation (pavāraṇā) for one who refuses what has been brought by the body—either through a bodily gesture such as moving a finger or the like, or through a vocal gesture such as saying "Enough, do not give it.
For example, if one person brings meat broth and says, "Please accept the broth," and another hears this and refuses it, [the invitation is established].
There is no invitation (*pavāraṇā*). However, if one says, "Meat broth," and the other refuses it, there is an invitation. Even if one says, "Take this," there is indeed an invitation.
If meat has been set aside and one says, "Meat broth," even if there is a piece the size of a mustard seed, there is an invitation for one who refuses it.
If there is none, it is permissible. [If it is] mixed with *kaḷīra*, jackfruit, and so forth—
They cook fish and meat; having taken it, he says, "Take some bamboo-shoot soup," or "Take some jackfruit curry"—even in this case, he does not invite [the monks to eat).
Why? Because he has spoken using the name of something that is not permitted to be invited.
However, if he says, "Fish and meat are the curry," or "Take this," then he does invite them. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation is as follows.
However, this is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*. Furthermore, regarding walking and the other modes of conduct, one must eat without disturbing whichever posture one has invited [the donor] to use.
"Not leftover" (*anatiritta*) means not excessive; that is, not more than what is required.

Moreover, it is either something for which the seven types of formal acts of the Vinaya—such as the "making permissible" (*kappiyakata*)—have not been performed, or it is not in excess for one who is ill. Therefore, in the word-commentary, it says "not made permissible," and so forth.

It has been stated: therein, whatever fruit, root-tuber, or the like has not been made permissible by the five ascetic-permissible [means], and whatever is unpermissible meat or unpermissible food—this is called "unpermissible.
That which is unpermissible, having been made "leftover" by saying, "This is enough for all," should be understood as "made unpermissible. Regarding "made unaccepted": by a monk...
It is "not yet accepted" when it has been made leftover in the manner previously described.
It is "not moved" when the monk who has come to have it made allowable has not lifted it up even slightly or shifted it away.

It is "made outside the hand's reach" when it is made by one standing outside the hand's reach of the person who has come to have it made allowable. It is "made by one who has not eaten" by whoever...
He makes it "leftover" (atiritta) by doing so while he has not yet finished eating food sufficient for the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇa).
That which is made by one who has already eaten, who has been invited to stop, and who has risen from his seat, is self-evident.

"It is enough of all this"—this constitutes what is not said by making a verbal utterance; thus it is "not said. Thus, by these seven modes of formal monastic act (vinayakamma), that which is leftover is permissible (kappiya).
That which is not made [into *atiritta*] and that which is not left over from one who is ill—both of these are *anatiritta*.
However, *atiritta* should be understood by way of its opposite.
Furthermore, in this context, "it has been made by one who has finished eating" means even a single grain of rice from the bowl of someone sitting immediately next to him.
Or, having eaten meat or sinew, even if it was prepared after he had finished eating, if one who has already finished his meal and been invited sits down right at daybreak,
then even when the time is near [the end of the day], he is permitted to have the alms-food brought to him by a monk made allowable (*kappiya*).
However, if while he is eating once that has been made allowable, they pour other food over him, [it becomes impermissible].
He is not permitted to do that again. For it is said that what has not been done must be done, and it must be done by the same person who did not do it;
therefore, when it is being made in that same vessel, it becomes as if already done along with the first attempt, and thus it is not allowed to be made.
However, it is permissible to make it in another vessel, either by that same person or by someone else. Thus...

It is permissible to eat it even if mixed with what has not been made; moreover, it is permissible for others who have already finished their meal (*pavārita*) to eat it, provided that they set aside what was made specifically for them.
However, one must eat it after ensuring that neither the mouth nor the hands are soiled, so as not to mix it with what has not been made.
But as for what is left over by one who is ill (*gilānātiritta*), it is not...

It refers exclusively to what remains after a sick person has eaten; however, anything brought for the sake of a sick person with the thought, "He shall eat it today, or tomorrow, or whenever he wishes," all that should be understood as "leftover from a sick person" (*gilānātiritta*).

Whether it be solid food (*khādanīya*) or soft food (*bhojanīya*), whatever is suitable for the proper time (*yāvakālika*). If one should chew or eat it, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

In this context, for one who has been invited according to the method stated, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of receiving any non-leftover food (*anatiritta-āmisa*) for the purpose of consumption;
for every act of consuming it, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of monks, on the occasion of eating otherwise than as prescribed, regarding that which is "not leftover" (*anatiritta*).

This is the subsequent rule (anupaññatti) here; it is a non-common rule (asādhāraṇapaññatti), not a formal injunction (anāṇattika), and constitutes an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for three cases.

There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who takes *yāmakālika* and other medicines for the purpose of food, and likewise for one who swallows them when they are not medicinal. It is also an offense of wrong-doing for one who perceives what is not leftover as leftover, or for one who is in doubt.
However, there is no offense for one who perceives it as leftover and takes it with the thought, "I shall eat it after having it made leftover."

There is no offense for one who takes it for the sake of another; for one who consumes *yāmakālika* (medicines to be taken until the watch of the night) and so forth by way of their permitted use as non-material food (*nirāmisa*); and for those who are insane and so forth.

The three factors here are: the state of having been invited (*pavārita*), the fact that the material food is not leftover (*anatiritta*), and the swallowing at the proper time (*kālena*). The origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other characteristics are exactly the same as in the first *kathina* rule.
This, however, is a "functional-non-functional" (kiriya-akiriya).
The commentary on the first invitation training rule is finished.
6. Commentary on the second invitation training rule.
"In the sixth [offense], 'one should invite by bringing over' means: having brought it over, one should invite him thus, 'Come, monk, eat or consume.
'Knowing' means: knowing his state of having been invited, either by hearing or by seeing. 'Aiming at disparagement' means:
looking toward disparagement, censure, or making him feel ashamed. 'In the case of having eaten, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)'—here, regarding the bringing over..."
In that case, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If he takes it, there is again a *dukkaṭa* for the one who offered it.
While he is eating, however, for every mouthful swallowed by him, there is a *dukkaṭa* for the offerer; at the conclusion of the meal, it is a *pācittiya*.
This was established in Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhu, regarding the basis for the invitation to offer food that is not left over (*anatiritta*).

This is a formal rule (paññatti), an exclusive formal rule (asādhāraṇapaññatti), and not a general instruction (anāṇattika). If one has been invited and perceives oneself as having been invited, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

For one who is in doubt, for one who brings things such as those allowable at night (yāmakālika) for the purpose of food, and for the acceptance and consumption of those [foods], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who, when not invited, perceives themselves as having been invited, or for one who is in doubt. However, for one who perceives themselves as not having been invited...

There is no offense for one who gives after having had food made over (atiritta), or gives saying, “Eat what has been made over,” or gives saying, “Go, taking it for the sake of another,” or gives night-stored foods (*yāmakālika*) and so forth saying, “Use them when there is a proper reason. There is also no offense for those who are insane and so forth.

[The factors for an offense are: being invited (*pavāritatā*), the perception of being invited (*pavāritasaññitā*), the expectation of reproach (*āsādanāpekkhatā*), and [giving] that which is not made over (*anatirittena*).

"Bringing [food] to her," "inviting her," and "the conclusion of the meal"—these are the five factors here. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to those of the offense of taking what is not given;
however, this [offense] is of painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).
The commentary on the second training rule concerning inviting is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Eating at the Improper Time (Vikālabhojana-sikkhāpada).
Regarding the seventh [rule], "at the improper time" (*vikāle*) means when the time has passed; the intended meaning is from the passing of midday until the rising of the dawn.
Therefore, whatever root or fruit—whether raw or cooked—a bhikkhu takes during this interval, [it is an offense].
If one accepts solid food or soft food that has become mere "flesh" (i.e., ordinary food) for the purpose of swallowing it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of accepting it;
for every swallow, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was laid down at Rājagaha concerning the group of seventeen monks regarding the matter of eating at the improper time; it is a common rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*).

This is not subject to an *anāṇatti* (instruction); it is a triad of *pācittiya* offenses regarding the acceptance and consumption of food for the purpose of nutriment—such as *yāmakālika* (medicines to be taken within a watch of the night) and so forth—when one perceives it as evening when it is actually time, or when one is in doubt, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.

There is no offense for one who, when it is time, perceives it as time and consumes *yāmakālika* medicines and so forth provided there is a valid reason, nor for those who are insane and so forth. "I allow you, monks, for one who has had his teeth cleaned..."
"Monks, it is not to be taken out through the mouth-opening and swallowed," according to this authorized method, there is no offense even for chewing tooth-sticks (*romaṭṭha*).
Here, the three factors are: being at the wrong time (*vikālatā*), being within the proper time (*yāvakālikatā*), and swallowing (*ajjhoharaṇa*).
The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other characteristics are similar to those of the rule concerning wool (*eḷakaloma*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning eating at the improper time is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Storing Up:
Regarding the term *sannidhikāraka*, "kāra" means making, doing, or action; these are one in meaning. Thus, it refers to one for whom there is the act of storing up (*sannidhi-kāra*).
"Sannidhikāra" means that which is stored; it is the name for having accepted [food] and spent one night with it.

Therefore, for one who accepts anything—whether "for-the-time-being" (yāvakālika) or "for-a-watch" (yāmakālika)—that has been so stored, thinking "I shall swallow it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) at the moment of acceptance, and for every act of swallowing, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). This holds even if the bowl has not been properly washed.
There is oil that, when rubbed with a finger, leaves a mark;
or oil that has entered between the rings of a strainer; or that which drips when being warmed over a heat;

or that which is visible when warm rice-gruel is taken—when eating from such a bowl on the following day, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). However, if a monk, without regard for it, gives it to the novices...
If one has renounced [the food] and then eats it after receiving what was deposited by those [donors], that is permissible.

However, for one who receives it oneself and eats the allowable food on the second day while it has not yet been renounced, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Regarding non-permissible items, however, in the case of human flesh, there is an offense of expiation together with a grave offense (thullaccaya);
in the remaining cases, there is an offense of expiation together with an act of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). As for the "time-limited until midnight" (yāmakālika) [medicines], if...
For one who swallows it as a *paccaya* (requisite), there is a *pācittiya*; for one who swallows it for the purpose of food (*āhāra*), there is a *dukkaṭa* along with that [other offense].
However, for one who, having been invited (*pavārita*), swallows what has not been made into *atiritta* (leftover), an additional *pācittiya* increases in all its variations.
If one swallows it at an improper time (*vikāla*), there is no offense in any variation on account of it not being *atiritta*, provided...

There is no offense regarding the "wrong-time" condition (*vikāla-paccaya*) in the case of "within the watch of the night" (*yāma-kālika*) and so forth. In all remaining cases, the *pācittiya* offense for the wrong-time condition indeed increases.
However, a monk’s stored food (*sannidhi*) is permissible for a nun, and a nun’s stored food is permissible for a monk;
this is permissible because it was authorized in the *Bhikkhunī-kkhandhaka*.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the Venerable Belaṭṭhasīsa on the occasion of the matter of eating stored-up food;
it is a general rule, not a specific injunction, and constitutes an offense of expiation for three factors.

However, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in accepting and consuming for the purpose of food those items that are permitted for seven days or for life respectively. Just as these [other items] are not allowable for the purpose of food, so too [is this].
In the same way, there are also those mixed with "only-for-the-time" (yāvakālika) substances; for it has been said:
"Monks, that which is 'for-a-watch' (yāmakālika), if received on that very day, is allowable at the proper time, but not allowable at the improper time," and so forth.
Therefore, even if one obtains such and such [substances] mixed with this or that, provided they are of unmixed flavor or have been well washed, as follows:
No admixture with the other [medicines] is perceived; it is permissible to consume them according to their own respective times.
However, if they have become mixed in flavor or are not properly washed, it is not permissible.

For when the three [medicines], such as those for a watch of the night (*yāmakālika*) and so forth, are mixed in flavor with the "time-allowed" (*yāvakālika*) medicine, they take on its own nature; likewise, two [medicines for a watch of the night] [take on the nature of the time-allowed].
Things such as those for a seven-day period bring their own specific nature along with them; that which is for a seven-day period brings its own specific nature—that of being for life—along with it.

Therefore, when combined with something received on that same day, a life-long medicine (yāvajīvika) that was either received on that same day or received previously remains permissible for seven days;
one received two days prior remains permissible for six days; one received three days prior remains permissible for five days... and so forth.
It should be understood that what has been received for seven days is allowable on that very day.
For this very reason, it was not said, "Monks, a lifetime medicine received on the same day as a seven-day medicine," but rather, "What is received is allowable for seven days.
And here, in the cases of exceeding the time limit, the watch of the night, or the seven days, [the rules] concerning eating at the wrong time and the storage of medicines apply.

The offenses should be understood according to these [rules]. Among these four types of "time-bound" (kālika) items, however, only this pair—namely, that which is for as long as life lasts (*yāvajīvika*) and that which is for seven days (*sattāhakālika*)—may be stored in an improper storehouse (*akappiyakuṭī*), and they do not generate the offense of storage (*sannidhi*).
Nevertheless, by means of that which has been brought inside an improper storehouse...
Together with the other two [types of storage], even that which was received on that very day is not permitted; for it is called "mouth-storage" (*mukhasannidhi*).
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated that it is "stored inside" (*antovuṭṭha*). In this regard, the only difference is merely in name; as for the offense, it is indeed a *dukkaṭa*.
Therein, "unfit hut" (*akappiyakuṭi*) refers to the property of either the Saṅgha or an individual who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), intended for the purpose of dwelling.

What is "cooked inside"? That which has been cooked within a house—meaning in a place sufficient for sleeping together—and belongs to the Saṅgha or to an individual who is fully ordained, provided it is cooked during the daytime or during the watch of the night, is called "cooked inside. What is "cooked within what is cooked inside" (antopakka)?
That which has been cooked there [inside]. What is "cooked by oneself" (sāmaṃ pakkaṃ)? Whatever has been cooked by oneself anywhere. All of that is unfit for consumption.
Even if one is in association with such a person, one goes the same way as they do; for one who swallows everything [thus obtained], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Therefore, for the purpose of releasing the effort once it has entered within, the Blessed One authorized four kinds of "proper grounds" (*kappiyabhūmi*);
the detailed exposition of these is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*. However, where these are not available, [one may use] what belongs to one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
It is permissible to consume [food] after having prepared it. It is also permissible to cook for oneself or to re-cook;
however, for one who perceives what is not stored (*asannidhikāraka*) as being stored (*sannidhikāraka*), or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

For one who perceives it as not stored, having set aside the three types of food—such as that which is to be consumed at the proper time (*yāvakālika*) and so forth—and consuming them without exceeding their respective times, or for one who consumes life-long medicine (*yāvajīvika*) whenever the requisite conditions exist, and for those who are insane and so forth, [there is no offense].
There is no offense. In this case, there are three factors: the food, the state of storage, and its consumption.
The origin and other characteristics are exactly like those of the rule concerning wool. The commentary on the training rule regarding the maker of stored food is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Luxurious Foods.
Regarding the ninth rule, "luxurious foods" (*paṇītabhojana*) refers to foods produced from the seven types of grain that are mixed with luxuries.
Just as a chariot yoked to thoroughbred horses is called a "thoroughbred chariot," so too here, foods mixed with luxuries [are termed luxurious foods].
"Exquisite foods": those which are mixed with what is exquisite are called "exquisite foods. To show their classification, he said, "such as ghee, fresh butter," and so forth;
