therein, ghee and the others are to be understood by the very definition stated in the *Bhesajja-sikkhāpada* (the Training Rule on Medicines). As for fish and the rest, all of them are "aquatic."
A fish possessing the characteristics already stated is simply a "fish. However, what is intended here are the meat, milk, and curd of those [animals] whose meat is permitted.
"Such refined foods" refers to those which, because they are mixed with ghee and the other aforementioned items, are called "refined foods";
such are the refined foods. "Not being ill" means one who does not require them even without [those refined foods].

It is comfortable. Regarding the phrase "having requested for one's own sake": here, one who is not ill and requests pure ghee and so forth for the purpose of medicine is to be dealt with according to the Mahānāma training rule;
one requesting the four [kinds of food] beginning with fish is to be dealt with according to the training rule on requesting curry and boiled rice;
one requesting foods mixed with ghee and so forth is to be dealt with according to this [present] rule.

In this regard, the analysis is as follows: for one who requests, saying, “Give me rice with ghee,” “Give me rice after pouring ghee over it,” “Give me rice mixed with ghee,” “Give me rice together with ghee,” or “Give me both ghee and rice”—for such a request, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for the acceptance, there is an offense of wrong-doing; and for each swallow, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). [Regarding] “ghee-rice”...

However, when it is said, "Give [me] food," since there is no such thing as "ghee-food" distinct from "rice-food"— just as there is no such thing as "ghee-food" apart from rice— there is only a *dukkaṭa* offense for requesting soup and rice. But if, when it is said, "Give me rice with ghee," one gives the rice and then says,
"Eat this having made ghee," and provides butter, milk, or other allowable articles (*kappiya-bhaṇḍa*), thinking, "Take ghee with this..."
“Eat,” [is permissible] exactly according to the original substance. However, when it is said, “Give the meal with cow-ghee,” one may give cow-ghee;

if that is unavailable, one may give fresh butter and so forth in the manner previously described, or one may even give the cow itself, saying, “Eat from this with ghee,” exactly according to the original substance.
But if, having been asked, “Give with cow-ghee,” one gives goat-ghee and so forth, it is a transgression of the convention (*visaṅketa*).
For if this were the case, it would mean that one thing was given when another was requested; therefore, there is no offense.
This same principle applies to cases such as "Give me goat-ghee. If, when told "Give me pure ghee," one gives impure ghee, there is indeed a breach of agreement (*visaṅketa*).
But if, when told "Give me impure ghee," one gives precisely impure ghee, there is no offense either in the act of receiving or in its consumption.
It is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). By this method, the legal determination is to be understood for all instances.

However, if one has requested [medicine] from all [of these], such as ghee and so forth, whether at one place or at various places, and having received it, makes it into a single mixture of blended flavors and then swallows even a single drop with the tip of a blade of kusa grass, there are nine offenses of expiation (pācittiya).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks regarding the matter of requesting exquisite food.

Herein, "one who is not ill" is a subsequent rule (anupaññatti), a non-common rule (asādhāraṇapaññatti), and one without an instruction (anāṇattika). It is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for three cases;

there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who is ill but perceives himself as not ill, or for one who is in doubt. For one who perceives himself as ill, or having requested it while actually ill...

There is no offense for one who eats when not ill, for one who eats from the remains of what was offered to the ill, from a place where one is invited by relatives, when requested for the sake of another, when taken with one’s own wealth, and for those who are insane and so forth.

The four factors here are: the quality of being fine food, the state of not being ill, the acquisition through a formal request, and the act of swallowing. This offense is originated by a journey; it is an action.
It is without perception, a liberation, without consciousness, an offense by way of designation, bodily action, verbal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning exquisite food is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning tooth-sticks.

In the tenth [offense], "what is not given" means that for one who takes by means of the body or what is connected to the body, standing within arm's reach, it has not been given by any means—whether by body or by what is connected to the body—and this is the name for what has not been formally accepted.
For indeed, even if it belongs to oneself, it is not permitted for a bhikkhu to swallow what has not been formally accepted.
However, what has been formally accepted—even if it is the property of a trusted person—is permitted.
Its characteristic is to be understood by reversing what was stated [in the preceding rule]. For if anyone who is not ordained— even down to an animal—
stands within arm’s reach of a monk or a nun and gives [something] by means of any one of the body parts and so forth,
and if that [gift] is received by the monk with any part of his own body, or with something connected to it, or with something portable...

Even if it is on a bed, or even if it is on a leaf from a tree not grown for that purpose, provided it is capable of being held—even if only touched by a needle—it is indeed accepted once it has been received.

There is nothing here called "connected-to-the-connected"; even when something is being given for nasal treatment and is taken into the nose, or when one who is ill receives it through the mouth, it is still considered accepted.
Everything is permissible; here, the mere intention (*ābhoga*) alone is the criterion.
Furthermore, if there was a prior intention and one subsequently falls asleep while the alms are being placed in the bowl, it is considered accepted provided one remains within arm’s reach.

Even that which falls into the hand of one who is already seated with the thought, "I shall receive it in my bowl," is likewise permissible. Dust that has fallen from a vessel brought by another is also permissible.
In this regard, the range of reach (*hatthapāsa*) for those standing, sitting, or lying down should be understood according to the method explained in the training rule on *pavāraṇā*.
However, if among the donor and the recipient one is in the air and the other is on the ground, then for the one on the ground, it is the nearest limb— excluding the head—
that reaches up to the outstretched hand of the one in the air, whether for the purpose of giving or receiving.
The distance from his near side must be delimited by the measure of an arm’s reach (*hatthapāsa*).

Even if one is at the well, another on the edge of the well, another at a tree, and another on the ground, the distance must still be delimited by the measure of an arm’s reach according to the method already stated.
Standing there, even if two or three novices [are present], provided they are such that an average man would be able to lift them up—
When those carrying such a burden place their hand upon the ground for a bhikkhu to grasp, or lift it up and place it even partially in the bhikkhu’s outstretched hand, it is considered accepted.
However, whatever dust falls into the bowl of one wandering for alms is not accepted; therefore, [one should eat] only after having accepted it.
Alms should be accepted. For one who accepts alms without having formally received them, there is an offense of wrong conduct (*vinayadukkaṭa*);
however, there is no offense for one who subsequently accepts and eats that same food after it has been formally received.

If, when told, "Please give [the food] after you have formally received it," the giver continues to offer the alms because they did not hear or did not heed those words, one is released from the *vinayadukkaṭa*; one must then formally receive other alms.

If a great wind blows dust here and there such that it is impossible to collect alms-food, it is permissible to take food with a pure mind, having made the mental resolve: "I will give this to one who is not fully ordained.

After giving it to one who is not fully ordained, it is permissible to eat it again, either if it is given back by him or if it is received through his trust. Regarding tears, saliva, mucus, and so forth:
Whatever falls from its place into the hand or onto the bowl should be accepted; even the tip of a finger [that falls] is considered accepted.
However, if it falls and is severed midway, it must not be taken; it is called "already grasped" (*uggahitaka*), and even if it is accepted later, it is not permitted.
But as for medicine or roots and fruits that were taken for the sake of one's mother or others, and [then used] for the sake of shade—
Or, having shaken up a branch bearing fruit and departed, it is permissible for him to take back whatever he desires from there and consume it.
However, if someone takes hold of a branch with fruit that has grown there, or a creeper, and shakes it, the fruit obtained by him from that [branch] is not permissible;
he incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa* for improper conduct (*durupaciṇṇa*), whereas for another person it is permissible.
However, it is permissible to lean against or grasp a fruit-bearing tree; whatever sprouts or other growths arise on what has been accepted and set aside are themselves considered accepted.

For as long as one does not become indifferent toward what has left the hand, or as long as it does not leave the hand due to such indifference, so long does the state of acceptance not cease. This, in brief, is the summary here.
The detailed explanation, however, is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.

"The mouth-door" refers to the throat-pipe. For whether something has entered by way of the mouth or by way of the nose, because it is to be swallowed through the throat, all of that is indeed what has been introduced through the mouth-door.
"Food" refers to anything whatsoever, whether it belongs to the period of the day (*yāvakālika*) or the period of the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*).
Whether it be for seven days or for as long as life lasts— all this is called "nutriment" because it is something to be swallowed.
In this context, everything that is either grain or what conforms to grain— including the nine kinds of great fruits and secondary foods known as the palm,

coconut, plantain, breadfruit, bottle-gourd, pumpkin, *pussaphala*, *tipusaphala*, and *eḷāluka*— as well as whatever else, such as forest roots, leaves, flowers, and fruits, serves the purpose of food.
It pervades; because all of that must be consumed until the time of midday, it is called "timely" (yāvakālika).

These eight drinks—mango drink, rose-apple drink, breadfruit drink, plantain drink, madhuka drink, grape drink, lotus-root drink, and phārusaka drink—and whatever minor fruit drinks conforming to them, such as those made from vetta, tintiṇika, citron, kapittha, kosamba, karamanda, and so forth, [are also timely].

All these [medicinal substances] are called "yāmakālika" (suitable for use until the end of the watch of the night) because they may be prepared by those who are not fully ordained using cold water, or ripened in the sun, and may be stored until the last watch of the night before being consumed. The same principle applies to the remaining permitted fruits, leaves, flowers, and their remnants.
The five medicinal tonics, such as ghee and the rest, are called "sattāhakālika" (suitable for use for seven days) because they may be stored for seven days before being consumed.

This, however—excluding the three [kinds of food] that are for a limited time (*yāvakālika*), those that are independent of time (*kālavimutta*), and water—is called "for as long as life lasts" (*yāvajīvika*).

This refers to everything else, such as roots, fruits, and so forth, which serves neither the purpose of solid food (*khādanīya*) nor soft food (*bhojanīya*); because it may be stored for life and consumed when there is a need, it is termed *yāvajīvika*.
"Should take in" means should introduce [into the mouth]. "Except for water and tooth-cleansing sticks" (*aññatra udakadantaponā*).

This was stated for the purpose of dispelling the remorse of those who feel remorse regarding water—even though it is not food—due to the perception that it is food, and regarding tooth-sticks due to the perception that "this has been brought to the mouth.
For it is permissible to drink water as one pleases, and to use tooth-sticks by way of their function as tooth-cleansers.
However, with the exception of these two, everything else is for the purpose of swallowing.

For one who takes it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the moment of grasping; for each swallow, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). Even if the juice from a tooth-stick enters the mouth of one who is unaware, there is likewise an offense of expiation.
This was prescribed at Vesālī concerning a certain monk, regarding the matter of consuming food that has not been given.

“Except for water and tooth-sticks”—this is the subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*) here; it is a common rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), not a formal injunction (*anāṇattika*), and constitutes an offense of expiation involving three factors (*tikapācittiya*).
For one who perceives what has been accepted as not accepted, or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

For one who perceives it as accepted—regarding water and tooth-sticks, or the four kinds of gross impurities—if there is a reason [to take them] but no attendant to prepare them, and one takes them oneself...
There is no offense for one who is consuming [the food], nor for those who are insane and so forth.
In this context, even if a messenger is difficult to speak with or incapable, the *kappiyakāraka* (one who makes things allowable) must remain within the group of non-present persons;

however, if there is no charcoal, he may burn dry wood, and if that is also lacking, he may even cut fresh wood from a tree to do so; it is also permissible to dig up earth for the sake of clay. This, moreover—
Any of the four kinds of *mahāvikaṭa* (raw meat) known as *kālodissa* may be taken by oneself at the very moment one is bitten by a snake;

on other occasions, it must be consumed after having been formally accepted (*paṭiggāhetvā*). In this case, there are four factors: the fact that it has not been formally accepted, the fact that it has not been authorized [for consumption], the absence of any means of clearing away the smoke and so forth, and the act of swallowing.
As for the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other characteristics, they are similar to those of the *eḷakaloma* (wool) offense.
The commentary on the training rule concerning tooth-sticks is finished.
The fourth chapter, the Chapter on Food, is concluded.
5. The Chapter on Naked Ascetics (Acelaka-vagga).
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Naked Ascetics (Acelaka-sikkhāpada).

Regarding the first [rule] of the Chapter on the Naked Ascetics (Acelakavagga): for one who gives any kind of material gift to these heterodox practitioners, such as the naked ascetics, in a single act, there is one *pācittiya* offense; for one who gives by repeatedly cutting off portions, there is a *pācittiya* offense for each individual act.
This was laid down at Vesālī concerning the Venerable Ānanda, in the case of a female wanderer giving two cakes.
This is a unique designation (*asādhāraṇapaññatti*), not a formal injunction (*anāṇattika*), and carries a *pācittiya* offense for three cases.

There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who gives water or a tooth-stick to a non-Tīrthika while perceiving them to be a Tīrthika, or when one is in doubt; likewise for one who causes a non-ordained person to give [the items] to a non-Tīrthika while perceiving them to be a non-Tīrthika;
and for one who, having placed a vessel near them, says, "Take this," to those [non-Tīrthikas]. Their...
There is no offense for one giving from a vessel that has been set down, for one giving an external coating, or for those who are insane and so forth. Here, the three factors are:

being a member of another sect, the act being unauthorized, and giving with one’s own hand food fit for consumption into a mouth for the purpose of consumption when it has not been placed in a vessel.
The origins and other characteristics are similar to those of the *eḷakaloma* (sheep’s wool) rule.
The commentary on the training rule concerning naked ascetics is finished.
2. Commentary on the second training rule concerning inciting [a nun].
Regarding the phrase "having caused to give or not having caused to give": this means having caused some kind of material gift to be given, or not having caused it to be given. "Should incite" means:
Desiring to engage in laughing, playing, or sitting together with a woman, he should dismiss her by saying, “Go,” and so forth.
“This very thing” means making this very improper conduct the cause, and not some other appropriate reason. It is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
first, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the mere act of dismissing her, but when she [leaves] from either the range of sight or the range of hearing...
If he discards it with one foot, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); if he discards it with the second foot, there is an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*).
In this context, the range of sight (*dassanūpacāra*) in the open air extends twelve cubits, and likewise for the range of hearing (*savanūpacāra*).
However, if there are walls, doors, fences, or the like in between, the crossing of the range occurs precisely when the object is obstructed by them.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Upananda in the matter of sending away [a nun]. It is a common rule;

it is a penalty for an instruction involving sending away, based on an instruction. It is a *pācittiya* offense for three [cases], a *dukkaṭa* offense for three [cases] regarding one who is not fully ordained, and likewise a *dukkaṭa* offense for both when attributing blame to each other.
This applies to one who sends her away using such plausible reasons as, "We two shall not live together," and so forth.
There is no offense for those who are insane and so forth. The three factors here are: the desire to engage in improper conduct; the instigation of one who is fully ordained for that very purpose;
and the transgression of the vicinity by one thus instigated. The origins and other characteristics are the same as those for taking what is not given.
The commentary on the training rule concerning instigation is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Eating Together (*Sabhojana-sikkhāpada*).
In the third [rule], *sabhojana* means "together with both persons"; thus, it refers to that which is "with eating together. Alternatively, *sabhojana* means "possessing enjoyment" (*sabhoga*).
For a man who is obsessed by lust, a woman is his "enjoyment," and for a woman, a man is her enjoyment; therefore, this is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) of this [rule].
“It is both a woman and a man,” and so forth, is what was said. “He should sit intruding” means he should sit having entered;

that is, in a bedroom belonging to that family which is large—such as one built within a great four-sided hall—and where he sits close to the bed, leaving a hand’s-breadth from the door-panel (*piṭṭhasaṅghāṭa*), or in the case of a small [bedroom].
The meaning is: "having passed beyond the middle, he should sit down"; for one who sits thus, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Upananda in the case of sitting down intruding upon another; it is a general rule of training, not a specific instruction.

It is an offense of expiation according to the threefold classification: there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who is in a dwelling and perceives it as a dwelling, or for one who is in doubt.

There is no offense for one who is conscious of the sleeping chamber, who does not sit beyond the area defined by the stated characteristics, when there is a second monk present, or when both have departed, or when sitting with those free from lust; nor is there an offense for those who are insane and so forth.
However, there is an offense for a wife and husband who are not free from lust, due to their presence together in the sleeping chamber and the fact that there is no second monk.
"Absence [of a third person]" and "sitting down without encroaching"—these are the four factors here. The origin and other details are similar to those of the first *pārājika*.
The commentary on the training rule concerning eating with [a person of the opposite sex] is finished.
4–5. Commentary on the training rules concerning sitting in a secluded, concealed place and sitting in private.
The fourth and fifth [offenses] were prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning Upananda, regarding the matters of sitting on a concealed seat and sitting in private;
they are common prescriptions, and their origins and other characteristics are exactly the same as those of the first *pārājika*.
The rest of the method of exposition should be understood according to the same method as that stated for the two *aniyata* rules.
The commentary on the training rule concerning being concealed by a private place and sitting in private is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning wandering for alms:
Regarding the sixth [rule], "invited" means invited to any one of the five kinds of cooked food. "Having finished his meal" means...
"Being already engaged in a meal together through that very invitation-meal":
having seen a monk within the vicinity of the boundary (upacārasīmā) in the range of sight— meaning,
without having asked permission in such words as "I am going to the house of so-and-so" or "I am going on an alms-round," using the kind of ordinary speech with which it is possible to ask for leave.
"Before the meal or after the meal" means whether that meal for which he was invited has been eaten or not yet eaten.
"He should enter among families" means he should enter other families than the one for which he was invited.
"Except at the proper time, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)" means if that monk, setting aside both types of proper time as they have been described...
If he enters another family after midday has passed, then there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) upon stepping onto the threshold of the house;
for him who crosses the door-sill with the first foot, there is another offense of wrong-doing; if he crosses with the second foot, it is an offense entailing confession (*pācittiya*).
This was laid down concerning Upananda at Rājagaha, regarding the matter of engaging in improper conduct toward a monk who was present. “A monk who is present... [and so forth].
"Without having asked permission, whether before the meal or after the meal, except on an appropriate occasion"—this is the fourfold supplementary rule (anupaññatti) here.
It is a common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti), it is not a formal instruction (anāṇattika), and it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for three cases.

For one who has not been invited but perceives themselves as invited, or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). In that case, for one who has not been invited but perceives themselves as such, [the rule applies] provided that a monk is present and has been asked for permission; if none is present...
There is no offense for one who enters without having asked permission from a bhikkhu; for one who goes by a path that passes through another’s house or the vicinity of a house;
for one who goes to an intermediate monastery, a bhikkhunī’s residence, a lodging for ascetics of other sects, a place of rest, or a house where food is being prepared;
in cases of emergency; and for those who are insane, etc. [There is also no offense] in accepting an invitation to any of the five kinds of cooked food.
The five factors here are: not asking permission from a peaceful bhikkhu; entering another house from a house where one is invited to eat; failing to pass beyond the midday mealtime;
and the absence of either a proper occasion or an emergency. The origin and other characteristics are exactly the same as for the first *kathina* rule;
however, this is a "non-action" offense (*akiriya*).
The commentary on the training rule for conduct is finished.
7. Commentary on the Mahānāma Training Rule:
Regarding the seventh [rule], "the invitation for requisites for four months," this refers to the invitation for sick-requisites for four months; all of this—
This was stated by way of illustration. Herein, this is the meaning: whether it be an invitation for four months, a repeated invitation, or a permanent invitation, all of them may be accepted;

one should not refuse them thinking, "I have no illness now," but rather one should consent to them thinking, "But when there is illness, I shall request [food]. Regarding the phrase, "if he should accept more than that": here—

If there has been a limit set therein by nights or by medicines, such as "only this many nights" or "only this many medicines may be requested," then beyond that limit of nights or limit of medicines,
whether it be medicine for the sake of a medicinal purpose or another medicine for the sake of another medicinal purpose, [it is not permitted].
For one who requests [medicine], there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was laid down concerning the group of six monks among the Sakyans regarding the matter of requesting medicine;

it is a general rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), not subject to a specific instruction (*anāṇattika*), and constitutes an offense of expiation for the triad [of factors]. There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who perceives more than that as being more than that, or for one who is in doubt.
For one who perceives that there is nothing superior to what has been invited, when there is need for medicines other than those invited, or for those that are more excellent,
or even after the nights during which he was invited have passed, if there is need and he informs [the donor] by declaring the situation as it truly is and makes a request;
and in the case of relatives, or regarding personal invitations, or regarding invitations that are not limited in time.
If they request [medicine] when another has already invited them, or for the sake of someone else, or with their own wealth, there is no offense for them, nor for those who are insane and so forth.

Herein, the four factors are: the state of being invited by the Sangha, the requesting of medicine from that [invitation], not being ill, and exceeding the limit. The origins and other characteristics are similar to those of the "go-between" offense.
The commentary on the Mahānāma training rule is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule concerning an army on march:
"On march" (*uyyutta*) means one who has undertaken military service; the meaning is that he has departed from the village. "Army" (*senā*) refers to the fourfold host.
"Except when there is such a cause": if one goes merely for the purpose of seeing the army when no such cause exists, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense at every step;
if one stands within the range of sight and looks, there is a *pācittiya* offense. The "range of sight" is defined as the place where one standing can see;
if, having left that place, one looks again and again, there is a *pācittiya* offense for each individual act of looking.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks regarding the matter of going to see an army; "except for such a reason" is the subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*) here.
It is a common rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), it is not a formal instruction (*anāṇattika*), and it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for three types of cases.

For going to see each individual [animal] among elephants and so forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) according to the same method already stated; likewise for one who perceives [the troops] as mobilized when they are actually not mobilized.

And for one who is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, there is no offense for one who perceives it as a military array, or who, while standing in a monastery, sees [the army] coming toward the place where he himself stands or coming from the opposite direction, provided there is such a reason or in cases of emergency; nor is there an offense for those who are insane, and so forth.
[The following are offenses: going for the purpose of seeing a military array; seeing it other than in a permitted place; and [seeing it] when there is no such reason.
"Or the absence of danger"—these are the four factors here. The origin and so forth are similar to those of the sheep's wool [rule].
However, this is a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), an unwholesome mind, and possesses three types of feeling (*vedanā*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning troops deployed for battle is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Staying with an Army. Regarding the ninth rule:

"If more than that" means beyond three nights; on the fourth day, when the sun has set, whether the army is standing, sitting, or lying down, even if one adopts any posture in the air by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks, based on the instance of staying with an army for more than three nights.

This is a common designation; it is not a formal injunction (*anāṇattika*). It is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for three cases: for one who perceives it as more than three nights when it is less than three nights, or for one who is in doubt.

For one who perceives it as less, or for one who, having departed before dawn on the third night, returns and stays again; or for one staying because of illness or on account of what must be done for the sick;
or for one whose army is besieged by an opposing force, or for one hindered by some obstacle, or in cases of emergency—there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

There is no offense for those who are insane and so forth. The three factors here are: staying for more than three nights, the setting of the sun while with an army, and the absence of illness and other such conditions. The origins and other characteristics are the same as those for the Eḷakaloma [offense].
The commentary on the training rule regarding dwelling with an army is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Martial Displays (*Uyyodhika-sikkhāpada*).
In the tenth [rule], "martial display" (*uyyodhika*) refers to a place where they fight by leaping up again and again; it is a name for a site of combat.
"The head of the army" (*balagga*) means that they know the excellence of the force there; the meaning is "a place for counting the forces. "The array of the army" (*senāviyūha*)...
“Senābyūha” is a name for the arraying of an army. “Anīkadassana” means the viewing of a division (*anīka*).

Regarding the definition of a division: “A chariot consists of four men; a horse, three men; an elephant, twelve men. By this characteristic, three elephants constitute a rear elephant-division (*hatthānīka*);
the same principle applies to the horse-division (*assānīka*) and the chariot-division (*rathānīka*). Furthermore, there are four [types of divisions] with weapons in hand.
Men are the last contingent. For anyone among them who goes to see [the army], there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for every step;

for one who stands within the range of sight and looks, there is a *pācittiya* offense; but for one who has left the range of sight and looks again and again, there is a *pācittiya* offense for each individual act.
The rest should be understood according to the method stated in the training rule on the army on campaign (*uyyuttasena-sikkhāpada*); this is the classification of the offenses.
And here, there is none at all.
The commentary on the training rule concerning military displays is finished.
The fifth section, the Chapter on the Naked Ascetics, is concluded.
6. Surāpāna-vagga 1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Drinking Surā:

Regarding the first rule of the Surāpāna-vagga, "drinking surā and meraya," *surā* here refers to intoxicating liquor made from flour and such ingredients, while [meraya] refers to that made from flowers and such.

Fermented liquor (*āsava*) and spirits (*meraya*): for one who drinks either of these, even from the seed stage down to a mere blade of *kusa* grass, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for every act.

This was laid down at Kosambī concerning the Elder Sāgata regarding the matter of drinking intoxicants; it is a general rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), not a specific injunction (*anāṇattika*). It is a triple offense of expiation.
For one who perceives what is not an intoxicant as an intoxicant, or who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). For one who does not perceive it as an intoxicant...
There is no offense for one drinking non-intoxicant *majja* that has the color, smell, and taste of intoxicant, such as salted sour gruel (*loṇasovīraka*) or fermented rice water (*sutta*);
nor for one drinking soups and the like in which a small amount of intoxicant has been added for the purpose of making them fragrant;

nor for one drinking *ariṭṭha* made from non-intoxicant substances like *āmalaka* juice that resembles intoxicant; nor for those who are insane and so forth. [The factor of] the nature of intoxicant (*majjabhāva*).
In this case, there are two factors: "his" and "drink. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to those for the wool-clipping offense.
However, this is a worldly offense (lokavajja), it is associated with unwholesome consciousness (akusalacitta), and it has three feelings (tivedana).
The commentary on the training rule regarding the drinking of fermented liquor is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Prodding with the Fingers.

Regarding the second rule, "prodding with the fingers" (*aṅgulipatodaka*) refers to touching [another] under the armpits or elsewhere with the fingers; furthermore, for one who, with the intention of joking, touches a person who has received full ordination (*upasampanna*) by means of any part of the body, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks, in the matter of joking by prodding with the fingers; it is a common formulation (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*).

This is not subject to an *aññatti* (formal injunction); it is a *pācittiya* offense for the triad [of intentional contact], and a *dukkaṭa* offense for the triad regarding one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).

Furthermore, in this case, even if it is a nun [touching] a monk, or a monk [touching] a nun who is not fully ordained, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense in all instances involving bodily contact and so forth.

There is no offense for one whose intention is not to laugh, for one who touches when there is a necessary purpose, or for those who are insane and so on. [The offense occurs] through the intention to laugh.
"For one who is fully ordained, bodily contact with the body"—these are the two factors here. The origin and other details are exactly the same as for the first *pārājika*.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the poking with a finger is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning joking.
In the third [offense], "in water that is subject to laughter" refers to water-sports.

Therefore, for a monk who, while walking in water above the ankle, dives or surfaces with the intention of laughing—for one entering for the purpose of such diving and so forth, there is a *dukkaṭa* for each hand-span and each foot-step;
for each instance of diving and surfacing, there is a *pācittiya*; having dived...
For one who goes by swimming hand over hand or foot over foot, or for one who crosses by means of whichever limb they cross, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for each such action.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of seventeen monks regarding the matter of playing in water; it is a general rule.

This is not subject to a formal injunction (*anāṇattika*); it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for three cases: if one plays in water while perceiving it as a place for playing, or if one is in doubt;

likewise, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who plays by striking the water with a hand, a foot, a stick, or a pebble while on a boat, or for one who plays by throwing water from a vessel, sour gruel, or mud as a game of tossing.
It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, it is permissible to cut away syllables that merely indicate the meaning. There is no offense for one who does not intend to laugh;
for one who descends and performs acts such as submerging while having a purpose; for one crossing to the other side; for those in times of distress;
and for the insane and so forth. Here, the two factors are: being above the ankles and playing with the intention to laugh. As for the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth:
"Similar to the first *pārājika* offense.
The commentary on the training rule concerning laughing is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning disrespect (*anādariya*).

In the fourth [offense], "disrespect" (*anādariya*) refers to showing disrespect toward either a person or the Dhamma. Therefore, if a monk, when being addressed by one who is fully ordained and regarding what has been prescribed,
shows disrespect out of a desire not to carry out those words or a desire not to train in that Dhamma,
he incurs a *pācittiya* offense for that disrespect.
This was laid down at Kosambī concerning the Elder Channa regarding the matter of showing disrespect; it is a common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti), not a formal injunction (anāṇattika),

involving a pācittiya offense for the triad [of persons], a dukkaṭa offense for the triad regarding one who is not fully ordained, and also for showing disrespect when one is told— by either one who is fully ordained or one who is not fully ordained—
in the manner of "This does not lead to effacement," etc., regarding what has not been laid down.

It is indeed a *dukkaṭa*. However, there is no offense for one who has received a traditional recitation (*uggaha*) handed down through the lineage and says, "Such was the recitation and the inquiry of our teachers," nor for those who are insane and so forth.
Here, the two factors are: speaking to one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*) regarding what has been prescribed, and showing disrespect.
The origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other characteristics are similar to those of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), but this [offense] is of painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning disrespect is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Terrifying Others:

In the fifth [rule], "should terrify," this means one should bring forward forms and so forth for the purpose of terrifying, or one should tell a frightening story. Whether the other person is actually afraid or not, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the one who did the terrifying.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks regarding the matter of frightening [others].

It is a common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti), not requiring a formal injunction (anāṇattika), and carries an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the threefold set. There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the threefold set regarding one who is not fully ordained.

There is no offense for one who acts in such a way without the desire to frighten, nor for those who are insane and so forth. [The offense occurs] when the person is fully ordained and there is the desire to frighten them within the range of their sight or hearing.
They declare that these two factors are present here. As for the origin and other details, they are exactly the same as in the preceding training rule.
The commentary on the training rule concerning frightening [others] is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Fire.
"In the sixth [offense], 'desiring to kindle' means wishing to warm oneself. 'Should kindle' means should set on fire;
'except for such a requisite' means except for lighting a lamp or making a fire for cooking rice-pots and so forth—without such a requisite as these. Herein, this is the analysis:
for one kindling the fire himself, from the time of setting up the fire-drills until the flames arise,"

In all such applications, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); when it has actually caught fire, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). For one who causes [fire] to be kindled by command, there is an offense of wrong-doing;
even if much is kindled by a single command, there is only one offense of expiation.
This was prescribed concerning many monks in the Bhagga country, regarding the incident of kindling a fire to warm themselves.
“‘Not being ill, except on such an occasion’—these are the two supplementary rules (anupaññatti) here: the common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti) and the triad of offenses (sāṇattika).

There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for each of the three cases; there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who is ill but perceives themselves as not ill, or for one who is in doubt;

likewise for one who shakes out [the bedding] when it has been folded back, and for one who, having shaken it out when it was not yet folded, places it back in its original position. [The same applies to] that which has been folded.”

However, for one who kindles it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) alone. There is no offense for one who is ill, for one who perceives another as ill, for one who warms himself with embers already extinguished by another, for one who has such conditions as a lamp, a torch, or a sauna, for one in cases of emergency, and for those who are insane and so forth.
Herein, the factors [of the offense] are: being not ill, the absence of an authorized reason, the desire to warm oneself, and the act of kindling.
There are four factors. The origin and so forth are to be understood in the same manner as explained for the Sañcaritta [offense].
The commentary on the Joti-sikkhāpada is finished.
7. Commentary on the Nahāna-sikkhāpada.

"Seventh: 'One should bathe'—if a bhikkhu, in the Middle Country, from the day of bathing onwards until half a month has not yet passed, prepares bath-powder or clay with the thought, 'I will bathe,' except on the [permitted] occasions, then for him there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for all preparatory acts from that point forward;
at the conclusion of the bath, it is a *pācittiya*. On the [permitted] occasions, even the mere sweeping of the courtyard [is allowed]."
The time for action (*kamma-samaya*) refers to the time of traveling a league (*addhayojana*), whether one is about to go, is going, or has already gone.
Or, when one is covered by a dusty wind, or when two or three drops of water fall upon the body, it should be understood as the time of wind and rain (*vāta-vuṭṭhi-samaya*).
The rest is self-evident.
Concerning a number of bhikkhus in Rājagaha, this was laid down regarding the matter of bathing without knowing moderation:

"Except at the proper time. Herein, there are these six subsequent rules (anupaññatti): it is a common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti), it is not a formal instruction (anāṇattika), it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for three cases, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who perceives it as more than a fortnight when it is less, or for one who is in doubt; and there is [no offense] for one who perceives it as more.
There is no offense for one bathing at the proper time; or for one who, while crossing to the other side of a river, bathes in a place where a bank has been constructed by throwing up sand;
or for all those in border regions; or in times of distress;

or for those who are insane and so forth. [The rules apply to] the Middle Country, bathing less than half a month [apart], or during the proper times, or when crossing to the other side of a river, or in times of distress.
"Non-existence"—these are the three factors here. The origin and other details are exactly like those for the sheep’s wool [rule].
The commentary on the training rule regarding bathing is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Making [Raiment] Discolored.
In the eighth [case], *alabhi* means "obtained" (*labha*); "gain" (*lābha*) is simply gain itself. What was obtained? A robe (*cīvara*). Of what kind? New.

Thus, where it should have been said "by the obtaining of a new robe" (*navacīvaralābhena*), the nasal vowel has not been elided, and it is stated as "by the obtaining of a new robe" (*navañcīvaralābhena*);
the meaning is "by the new robe that was acquired. Furthermore, the two words standing in the middle are merely particles (*nipātamatta*). "By a bhikkhunī" (*bhikkhuniyā*).
The example of one who has received [the robe] is as follows; the rest is clear from the meaning of the words. Here, however, is the detailed analysis:

having obtained a robe suitable for wearing as an undergarment or an upper garment, once it has been finished and dyed, in whatever place, with bronze-blue, or bottle-green, or mud-colored, or with any kind of black dye—such as the eye-circle of a peacock, or the back of a finger— [...]* *Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated.*
Having taken a *kappa-bindu* (a mark of ownership) of a certain size, that robe may be used; for one who uses it without having taken [the mark], there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of monks, based on the occasion of not recognizing their own robes;

it is a general rule (*sādhāraṇa-paññatti*), without a formal injunction (*anāṇattika*), and constitutes an offense of expiation according to the threefold classification. For one who perceives it as taken when it has been taken, or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). For one who perceives it as taken [when it has indeed been taken], [there is an offense of expiation].

There is no offense for one who uses a robe that has lost its *kappa* (marking), when the space for the *kappa*-marking has worn out, when what was marked as *kappa* has been sewn together with what was not marked as *kappa*, or when the door-panels, the inner lining, and the border have been added later; nor is there an offense for those who are insane, and so forth.

Here, the phrase "a robe of the type described" refers to the fact that the *kappa*-marking has not been performed, not to the loss of the robe and such, and it refers to either the lower garment (*nivāsana*) or the upper robe (*pārupana*).
There are three factors. The factors of origination and so forth are similar to those of the sheep’s wool [offense], but this is a "kiriya-akiriya" (action-non-action).
The commentary on the training rule concerning making unattractive is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Reassignment.
"Having assigned in the ninth [case]"—here there are two kinds of assignment: assignment in the presence (*sammukhā-vikappanā*) and assignment in the absence (*parammukhā-vikappanā*).

How does assignment in the presence occur? Having ascertained whether the robes are one or many, and whether they are present or absent, one says: "This robe," or "These robes," or "That robe," or "Those robes."
Or, having spoken thus, one should say, "I dedicate this to you. This is one kind of dedication in the presence [of the recipient].
Up to this point, it is permissible to set it aside; however, it is not permissible to use it, to dispose of it, or to resolve upon its use.
But when it is said, "This is my property; use my property or dispose of it as you see fit," then—
There is what is called "renunciation" (paccuddhāra); from that point on, even using [the robes] and so forth is permitted. Another method:

having likewise understood whether the robes are one or many, and whether they are stored or not stored, [one says] in the presence of that very bhikkhu, “this robe” or “these robes,” or “that robe” or “those robes.”
Or, having spoken thus, one should take the name of whichever among the five co-religionists is personally preferred and say:
“I assign this to the monk Tissa,” or “I assign this to the nun Tissa, the trainee, the novice monk Tissa, or the novice nun Tissa.
This is another form of face-to-face assignment (*sammukhā-vikappanā*). Up to this point...
It is permissible to store it, but it is not permissible for even one of the uses such as consumption.
However, when that bhikkhu says, "Use the property belonging to the bhikkhu Tissa... [or] the property belonging to the novice nun Tissā;
dispose of it or do with it as you see fit," this is called a formal relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*). From that point on, even uses such as consumption are permissible.

How is there an assignment in the absence of the person? Having understood the singular or plural nature of the robes as well as their state of being present or absent, one should say, "This robe" or "These robes," or "That robe" or "Those robes," and then say, "I give this for the purpose of assigning it to you.
That person should then be asked, "Who is your friend? or...
"Or [the object] is visible. Then the other person should say, in the same manner as before, "To the three bhikkhus," or... pe... "To the novice nun Tissā.
Then that bhikkhu must say, "I give [it] to the bhikkhu Tissa," or...
pe... "I give [it] to the novice nun Tissā"; this is the assignment in the absence of the recipient. Up to this point, it is permissible to set aside [the object].

None of these, such as using [the bowl], are permitted. However, when that monk says before a second person according to the method already described, "Use this belonging to so-and-so, or dispose of it, or do with it as you see fit," it is called a formal relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*);
from that point on, even using it and other such acts are permitted. This also applies to the formal relinquishment of a bowl (*pattavikappanā*).

The same method applies here. Thus, regarding these two ways of assigning, if one has assigned a robe to any one of the five types of fellow practitioners by any of these two methods of assignment, and then—

without having performed the formal relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*) in the manner described, or without taking it on trust from one for whom a formal disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) has been performed—
one uses it, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Upananda, regarding the matter of consuming [food] that has not been relinquished;

it is a general rule, without a specific instruction, and constitutes a *pācittiya* offense for the three [cases]. However, there is an act of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who resolves upon it or disposes of it;
likewise for one who, while relinquishing it, perceives it as not relinquished or is in doubt about it. For one who perceives it as relinquished, [there is no offense].
However, there is no offense for one who uses it out of trust, nor for those such as the insane.

In this case, there are three factors: the robe having been formally assigned by oneself, the robe being of a kind suitable for assignment, and the act of using it. The origin and other characteristics are exactly the same as in the first *kathina* rule;
however, this is classified as "action-and-non-action" (*kiriya-akiriya*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning assigning (vikappaṇa) is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning hiding (apanidhāna).
"Bowl" means one that is fit for formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna). "Robe" means one that is fit for assignment (vikappaṇa). "Sitting mat" means one with a border.
It is said: "A needle-case" means one with a needle or one without a needle. "A waist-band" means a strip of cloth or a pig-tail braid.
"Should set aside" means having removed, he should place it down. "Seeking laughter" means having the intention of making others laugh.
Regarding the *pācittiya*: for one who sets it aside himself, there is a *pācittiya*; for one who commands another to do so, there is a *dukkaṭa* for the command; when it has been set aside by him...
For the other, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks regarding the matter of hiding [the bowl];

it is a common rule, a formal injunction, an offense of expiation for three cases, and an offense of wrong-doing for three cases involving one who is not fully ordained. Furthermore, the types of bowls and so forth mentioned are as follows:
Excepting other requisites, for one who hides the property belonging to either one who is fully ordained or one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) alone.
There is no offense for one who retrieves what was poorly placed, for one who retrieves it thinking, "I will give it back after giving a Dhamma talk," or for those who are insane and so forth.
Hiding the bowls and other items belonging to one who is fully ordained [constitutes the offense], provided there is an intention to harass.
"Or with the intention of laughing"—these are the two factors here. The origin and other details are the same as those for taking what is not given.
The commentary on the training rule concerning hiding is finished.
This is the sixth chapter, the Section on Drinking Liquor.
7. The Chapter on Living Beings (Sappāṇakavagga).
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Intentional Killing.

In the first [rule] of the Chapter on Living Beings, "a living being" (pāṇa) refers to an animal. For one who kills it, whether small or large, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya); however, in the case of a large [animal], the unwholesome [kamma] is greater due to the greatness of the effort employed.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the Elder Udāyī regarding the matter of depriving a living being of life; it is a common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti), a formal injunction (sāṇattika).

For one who is in doubt about whether it is a living being, or for one who perceives what is not a living being as a living being, or for one who is in doubt [about it being a living being], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

There is no offense for one who does not perceive it as a living being, who acts unintentionally, who does not know, who lacks the intention for death, or for those who are insane and so forth. The rest is exactly as stated in the section on the human form.
The commentary on the training rule concerning intentional action is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning water containing living beings:

Regarding the second [rule], "containing living beings" means that which contains those living beings who die through its consumption. For one who knowingly consumes such [water], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for every single act of using it.

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks (*chabbaggiya*) on the occasion of knowingly using water containing living beings. The rest here should be understood in the same manner as stated under the training rule on sprinkling (*siñcana-sikkhāpada*).
The commentary on the training rule on water with living beings is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Reopening (Ukkoṭana-sikkhāpada)
In the third [formula], "according to the Dhamma" means by that very Dhamma which was taught for the settling of whichever legal issue it may be.
"The legal issue has been settled" means the legal issue has been laid down; the meaning is that it has been resolved by the very Dhamma spoken by the Teacher in the *Samathakkhandhaka*.
We shall, however, demonstrate the method of its resolution among the methods for settling legal issues (*adhikaraṇasamatha*). For the sake of a further formal act...

"Should reopen" means that by going to the presence of each respective monk and saying things such as "the legal act was not properly performed," one should cause it to be reopened for the purpose of performing it again;
one should not allow it to remain established in its current state. For one who acts in this way, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
However, whatever legal matter has been settled in accordance with the Dhamma is indeed well-settled. If, however, [it is] interrupted...
If one protests against a formal act (*kamma*), it should be performed after having informed that person. Otherwise, both the formal act is invalidated and the performers incur an offense.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks regarding the matter of reopening a settled case; it is a general rule, not a specific instruction.
It applies to one who is doubtful when the act is legitimate (*dhammakamma*), and to one who perceives an illegitimate act as legitimate, or who is doubtful about it.
...or a *dukkaṭa*. For one who perceives both [the act and the assembly] as illegal (*adhamma*), that is, for one who knows:
"An illegal act has been performed by an incomplete assembly, or an act has been performed on one who does not deserve it," there is no offense, as well as for those who are insane and so forth.

Herein, the three factors are: the state of being suppressed according to the Dhamma, the knowledge [of that], and the reopening [of the case]. The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth are similar to those of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*). This...
...but painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning reopening [a settled case] is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning grave matters.

In the fourth [offense], "grave offense" (duṭṭhulla) refers to a *saṅghādisesa*. For one who, having learned of such an offense by any means whatsoever, conceals it, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Even if one thinks, "Now I will not tell anyone," and having thus laid down the burden, later reports it, there is still an offense of expiation;
for he will report it only after having committed the offense. However, if, having thus laid down the burden...
If, for the very purpose of concealment, one informs another, and that person in turn informs yet another, by this means even a hundred ascetics may incur the offense before the limit is broken.

But how is the limit broken? For if one who has incurred the offense informs one person, and that person informs another, and the latter turns back and informs the very person to whom the first had informed him—thus, by the third person...
When it has been announced to a second person by the individual, the limit is reached.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhu, in the matter of concealing a grave offense;
it is a non-common rule, not a formal injunction. For a grave offense, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the first word, and for the others...

In two cases there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); in the case of a non-gross offense, there is a triad of offenses of wrong-doing; and in the case of a transgression—whether gross or non-gross—committed by one who is not fully ordained, there is likewise only an offense of wrong-doing.

This applies to one who does not report [the matter] thinking, "There will be quarrels and so forth for the Saṅgha," or "This person is harsh and cruel, and he will cause an obstacle to life or an obstacle to the holy life."

There is no offense for one who does not see a suitable monk, for one who does not wish to conceal [the offense], for one who does not report it thinking, "He will be known by his own deed," and for those who are insane and so forth.

Herein, the two factors are: knowing a grave offense (duṭṭhulla-āpatti) of one who is fully ordained (upasampanna), and the abandonment of responsibility with the thought, "I will not report it because I wish to conceal it.
The origin (samuṭṭhāna) and other characteristics are the same as those for the formal admonition (samanubhāsana-saṃsa).
The commentary on the training rule concerning grave offenses is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Those Under Twenty Years of Age:
Regarding the fifth [rule], "under twenty years of age" means one who has not completed twenty years from the moment of conception. "Should ordain" means...

Having become a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), one should grant full ordination (*upasampadā*). Whether that person knows or does not know that the candidate is unordained (*anupasampanna*), once ordained, he remains indeed unordained.

However, if after ten years have passed he grants another full ordination, and if the quorum of the community (*gaṇa*) is fulfilled by excluding him [the first candidate], then the second is properly ordained.
For as long as he [the first candidate] does not realize it, there is no obstacle to his heavenly rebirth (*sagga*).
There is no obstacle to his liberation; however, having recognized this, he must undergo ordination again.

"And those monks are to be censured" means that, setting aside the preceptor, the rest are to be censured, and all incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). This is the *pācittiya* offense in that case:
it should be understood that this *pācittiya* applies specifically to the person who, having been a preceptor, performs the ordination.
Therefore, whoever seeks out a group, a teacher, a bowl, or a robe with the thought,
"I shall ordain in this manner," or who demarcates a boundary, or delimits the range for the throwing of water—

having committed offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding all these tasks during the motion (ñatti) and the two subsequent proclamations (kammavācā), he incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya) at the conclusion of the final proclamation.
This was laid down at Rājagaha concerning a number of bhikkhus regarding the matter of ordaining one less than twenty years of age;

it is a non-common rule, not a formal injunction. There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who is unsure whether the candidate is less than twenty years of age, for one who perceives a candidate who is full twenty years of age as being less, and for one who is unsure.
There is no offense for one who perceives both cases as being full twenty years of age, nor for those who are insane and so forth.
There is no offense. The three factors here are: being under twenty years of age, perceiving them as being under twenty, and conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*).

The origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other characteristics are the same as those for taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*); however, this is an offense of formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), involving three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning those under twenty years of age is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Caravan of Thieves:

Regarding the sixth [rule], those who, having deceived a king or wishing to evade customs duties, are thieves traveling along a road—whether their crimes have already been committed or not—and regarding whom one here has the perception of them being a "caravan of thieves," having recognized their status as such a caravan...

For one who travels after making an appointment with such a person, the determination of the offense regarding both the appointment and the journey should be understood according to the method explained in the Ovāda-vagga.
[This was spoken] concerning a certain bhikkhu at Sāvatthī, who had made an appointment to travel along a common road with a caravan of thieves.
It is prescribed regarding the matter of the mode of proceeding; it is a common rule of training (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), not a formal injunction (*anāṇattika*).

There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who travels having made his own arrangements while others have not made arrangements; for one who is in doubt about whether it is a caravan of thieves; and for one who perceives a caravan that is not of thieves to be a caravan of thieves, as well as for one who is in doubt. [There is no offense] for one who perceives it to be a caravan that is not of thieves, or for one who has not made arrangements, or by reason of a difference in the time of departure.
Or in times of distress, or for one who is traveling, or for those who are insane and so forth, there is no offense.
The four factors here are: being a caravan of thieves, knowing [it is such], making an arrangement, and traveling without a prior agreement.

It originates from a caravan of thieves; it is an action; it is liberated by perception; it involves volition; it is an offense of formal rule (paṇṇattivajja); it is bodily action and verbal action; it consists of three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning traveling with thieves is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning making an appointment:
Regarding the seventh [training rule], it was promulgated at Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhu who traveled along a road together with a woman.
It is prescribed regarding the matter of the practice; the rest here should be understood in the same manner as stated in the training rule concerning making arrangements with a nun.
The commentary on the training rule concerning making arrangements is finished.
8. Commentary on the Ariṭṭha Training Rule:
In the eighth [rule], they are called "obstructive" (*antarāyika*) because they create an obstacle to heaven and liberation.

These are fivefold, by way of: (1) kamma, (2) defilements (*kilesa*), (3) karmic result (*vipāka*), (4) slander (*upavāda*), and (5) transgression of the formal rule (*paññatti*). Among these, just as contact with soft rugs and such is permissible, so too is contact with women permissible.
Not seeing the fault in the transgression of sexual intercourse, but referring to the obstacles that consist in the transgression of the formal rule, it was said:
"Those things called 'obstructive states' by the Blessed One are not, for one who indulges in them, capable of being obstacles.
"In many ways" means by numerous reasons such as "sensual pleasures are like a skeleton," and so forth. "That bhikkhu by the bhikkhus" refers to those who see him.
Or if they hear it, they must speak to him three times thus: "Venerable sir, do not speak thus... [as before] ...it is sufficient for your indulgence in this to be an obstacle.
If he does not relinquish it when this has been said, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); and there is also an offense of wrong-doing for those who heard it but did not speak out.
He should again be dragged into the midst of the Saṅgha and addressed in the same manner; and if he still does not relinquish it there, [there is likewise an offense].

And for the others not speaking [to correct him], there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Even if he still does not relinquish [his view] in this way, he must again be formally admonished up to three times by means of a legal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (ñatticatuttha-kamma).
If he still does not relinquish it, then for each proclamation after the initial motion—there being two such proclamations—there is an offense of wrong-doing;
at the conclusion of the final proclamation, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Ariṭṭha, regarding the matter of not relinquishing an evil view.

It is a common rule, without a specific instruction, and constitutes a *pācittiya* offense for the three [cases]; there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for the three cases of an illegitimate legal act (*adhammakamma*).

There is no offense for one who has not been formally admonished, for one who relinquishes [the view], or for those who are insane and so forth. [The factors of the offense are: the legitimacy of the legal act, the formal admonition, and the failure to relinquish.
These are the three factors here. The origins and so forth are exactly the same as in the case of *samanubhāsana*.
The commentary on the training rule concerning Ariṭṭha is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning social intercourse with one who has been suspended (*ukkhepanīyakamma*).

In the ninth [offense], "one who speaks thus" refers to one who says, "I have been taught the Dhamma by the Blessed One," and so forth. "One who has not performed the subsequent duty" (akatānudhamma):

"subsequent duty" (anudhamma) refers to the reinstatement (osāraṇā) granted after observing the concordant conduct for one who has been suspended according to the Dhamma and Vinaya—whether for failure to recognize an offense, for failure to make amends for it, or for failure to relinquish an evil view. That reinstatement is what is called the "subsequent duty."
One for whom [the formal act] has not been performed is called "one who has not acted in accordance with the Dhamma" (*akatānudhamma*); the meaning is "together with such a person.

"Should associate" (*sambhuñjeyya*) means he should engage in either material association (*āmisa-sambhoga*) or Dhamma association (*dhamma-sambhoga*). "Should live together" (*saṃvaseyya*) means he should perform Sangha business, such as the Uposatha ceremony.
"Or should lie down together" (*saha vā seyyaṃ kappeyya*) means he should lie down under one roof, even if they are in separate quarters. Regarding that, in the case of material enjoyment:
For one who gives or receives many [items] with a single effort, there is one *pācittiya*; if there is an interruption, there is a *pācittiya* for each individual effort.
Regarding the sharing of the Dhamma: for one who recites or causes another to recite by the foot and so forth, it is according to the method stated for the *padasodhamma*;
regarding living together, it is by way of the conclusion of the formal act (*kamma*); regarding sleeping together, it is when one has lain down while the other is still present.
The delimitation of the offense should be understood by way of the application of lying down.
It was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks, in the matter of eating together with the monk Ariṭṭha;

it is a common rule, not a specific instruction, [applying] to one who is doubtful about whether a person has been suspended, or to one who perceives a person as suspended when they have not been suspended.

And there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who is in doubt. For both [cases], there is no offense for one who perceives that he has not been suspended, or for one who knows that "he has been reinstated" or "he has relinquished that view," or for those who are insane and so forth.

Here, the three factors are: the state of not having performed the *anuddhamma* act, the knowledge [of the facts], and the performance of communal living (*sambhoga*) and so forth. The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other characteristics are similar to those of the offense of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*). This...
However, it is a transgression by formal rule (paṇṇattivajja), involving three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning communal living with one who has been suspended (ukkhitto) is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Thorns (kaṇṭaka).
"In the tenth [case], 'a novice' (samaṇuddesa) means a *sāmaṇera*. 'Wander' (*cara*) means go. 'Away' (*pira*) means away from one's own group.
'Perish' (*vinassa*) means depart; the meaning is: "go to a place where we do not see you. Regarding "one who has been thus expelled" (*tathānāsita*):

here there are three kinds of expulsion—expulsion by way of living together, expulsion by way of wearing the marks, and expulsion by way of disciplinary action. Among these, expulsion due to non-recognition of an offense and so forth is [the first]."
“Expulsion by co-residence” means: “The corrupter is to be expelled; expel the bhikkhunī Mettiyā”—this is called “expulsion by change of gender.
“From this day forward, friend novice, you shall no longer point to that Blessed One as your teacher”—this is called “expulsion by disciplinary action”;
it is this [latter] which is intended here. Therefore it is said, “thus expelled. “Should she curry favor” means:
"He might support [him] thinking, 'I will give him an alms bowl, or a robe, or a recitation, or an inquiry.

"He might serve him" means that by accepting things such as powdered scent or clay, he would cause himself to be served by him. "Sharing enjoyments and sharing a bed" is exactly according to the method stated in the immediately preceding training rule;
therefore, the determination of the offense here should be understood by the same method stated there.

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks (*chabbaggiya*) on the occasion of the matter involving the instigation of the novice Kaṇṭaka; the rest is exactly as stated in the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) regarding Ariṭṭha.
The commentary on the Kaṇṭaka training rule is finished.
The seventh chapter, the Section on Living Beings (*Sappāṇakavagga*), is concluded.
8. Sahadhammika-vagga. 1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Those Who Follow the Dharma (Sahadhammika-sikkhāpada).

Regarding the first [rule] of the Sahadhammika-vagga, "when one is being addressed by those who follow the Dharma," the meaning of this is as explained under the training rule concerning the difficult-to-correct (dubbaca).
"Stated. Regarding "in this training rule," the meaning is: "I will not train in that which has been stated in this training rule for the time being.

Regarding "an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)," it should be understood that for one who speaks thus out of a pretext born of fear of disrespect, there is an offense of expiation for every single utterance.
"By one who is training" means by one who, having received the exhortation with the head bowed, desires to train.
"Having sacrificed. "To be known" means it must be understood. "To be questioned thoroughly" means one must inquire, "What is the meaning of this?
"To be investigated" means it must be reflected upon and weighed.
This was prescribed regarding the Elder Channa at Kosambī in the context of such speech; it is a common prescription.

There is no formal instruction (anāṇattika); it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for three cases, and an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for three cases regarding one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna).
Even when speaking in this manner to someone by both parties using an unenjoined formula such as, "This is not for the sake of effacement," there is likewise only an offense of wrongdoing.

There is no offense for one who says, "I shall know, I shall train," nor for those who are insane and so forth. Speaking according to what has been enjoined to one who is fully ordained, out of a desire not to train—
"Speaking thus" constitutes two factors here. The origin and other details are similar to those for taking what is not given; however, this [offense] is of painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning one who lives according to the Dhamma is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Slandering.
"Being recited for a second time" means when they are being spoken by a teacher to a pupil, or when they are being turned over through the practice of recitation.
"By the minor and lesser rules" means by those that are minor and those that are lesser. "Only as far as" is a statement defining the limit of their application.
This is what is meant: for these [rules] are indeed for those who recite them, cause them to be recited, or practice their recitation.

They lead [to these states] as long as anxiety, remorse, vexation, doubt, and mental scruple arise, such that one thinks: "Is this allowable? Is it not allowable? Alternatively, the phrase "yāvadeva" (only so far) is a definitive delimitation.
Its connection is with the word "lead" (*saṃvattanti*); it means they lead excessively indeed to anxiety, vexation, and scruple.
This has been stated. Regarding "one who disparages the training rules": the meaning is that there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one who thus disparages or censures the training rules.

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks (*chabbaggiya*) in the matter of the disparagement of the Vinaya; it is a common rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), without a specific instruction (*anāṇattika*), and constitutes an offense of expiation under three conditions.
For disparaging one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) under three conditions; [the same applies] for both.

In disparaging another teaching, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). There is no offense for one who does not intend to disparage, but says, "Come now, first master the Suttantas, the Gāthās, or the Abhidhamma;
afterwards you will master the Vinaya," nor for those who are insane and so forth.
Furthermore, there is no offense here for the desire to censure, nor for disparaging a training rule in the presence of one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*). These are the points in this matter.
There are two factors. The factors such as the origin and so forth are similar to those for taking what is not given; however, this [result] is painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning frivolous talk is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning concealing.
"In the third [case], 'every half-month' means in regular succession every half-month. 'When it is being pointed out' means when it is being pointed out by way of the Uposatha.

'And whatever offense he has fallen into therein' means whatever offense he has fallen into for that improper conduct, which he speaks of thus because, having committed that misconduct, he wishes to make known his state of having fallen into it through ignorance. 'And that shall be dealt with according to the Dhamma' means..."
Because it was committed through ignorance, there is no release; rather, one must deal with that offense according to how the Dhamma and the Vinaya are established.
The meaning is that one who is subject to confession should be made to confess, and one who is subject to rehabilitation should be rehabilitated.

Furthermore, "additional delusion should be imposed upon him" means that, beyond the formal legal procedure (*yathādhammakaraṇa*), [the offense] should be addressed by means of such words as "Friend, for you... and so forth.
Having censured that person, delusion (moha) must be imposed upon him by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*).
