"This is the offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for one who causes delusion" means that this offense of expiation is to be understood as applying to that person who causes delusion after delusion has already been imposed;
it does not apply to one who causes delusion when it has not been imposed.

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks regarding the matter of deluding; it is a common rule, not a specific injunction, and constitutes a *pācittiya* offense for three instances.
For an illegal act, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for three instances; and for one who has not been accused of deluding, there is only a *dukkaṭa*.

This applies to those by whom [the proclamation] was not heard in detail, or those by whom it was heard in detail fewer than two or three times, as well as to those who did not intend to delude, and to those who are insane, and so forth.
There is no offense. The four factors here are: causing delusion, the desire to cause delusion, the fact that it has been heard according to the stated method, and the act of deluding.
The origin and other characteristics are similar to those of the taking of what is not given; however, this [offense] is of painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning deluding is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Striking.
Regarding the phrase "should give a blow" in the fourth rule: if a blow is given with the intention of striking, even if the person dies as a result, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) alone.
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks, based on the incident of giving a blow; it is a common prescription.

There is no formal instruction (anāṇattika); it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for three cases, and an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for three cases regarding one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna).
However, even in the case of one who is fully ordained, if there is an intention to deform them by cutting off the ears or other parts, it is likewise only an offense of wrongdoing.

But there is no offense for one whose intention is to escape while being harassed by someone, nor for those who are insane and so forth. [The factors of the offense are: being angry, lacking the intention to escape, and dealing a blow to one who is fully ordained.
These are the three factors here. The origins and so forth are similar to those of the first *pārājika*; however, this [offense] is of painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
The commentary on the training rule regarding striking is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule regarding the hand-thrown weapon (*tala-sattika*).
"He should discharge a set of seven slaps on the fifth [day]" means that, demonstrating the manner of giving a blow, he should strike either the body or what is connected to the body.

In this case, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) due to the act of discharging. However, if, having discharged it, he gives a blow by mistake, because it was not given with the intention to strike, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). By that blow, whatever [is struck] on the hands or other parts—
If it breaks, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) alone. All else here should be understood according to the method already stated in the preceding training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning the "handful of palm-leaves" (*tala-sattika*) is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Groundless Accusations (*amūlaka-sikkhāpada*).

In the sixth [offense], "groundless" means devoid of a basis such as what was seen and so forth. "Should revile" means either to accuse or to cause another to accuse. "Pācittiya": if the one accused understands at that very moment, "He is accusing me," it is a pācittiya for the accuser.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks, in the case of groundlessly reviling with a *saṅghādisesa* offense;
it is a common rule, a formal injunction, a pācittiya in three cases, and pertains to failure in conduct or failure in view.

There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who does not disparage; there is a triad of offenses of wrong-doing for one who is not fully ordained. There is no offense for one who perceives it as such, nor for those who are insane and so forth. The four factors here are:
the state of being fully ordained, the groundlessness of the *saṅghādisesa* charge, the act of disparaging, and the realization [of the offense] at that very moment.
The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other characteristics are the same as those for taking what is not given; however, this [offense] is of painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
The commentary on the rule concerning groundless accusations is finished.
7. Commentary on the rule concerning intentional speech:

"He would cause remorse" means that by saying things such as, "I think you are less than twenty years old," he would arouse it. Thus, when no other condition for causing remorse exists, for one who intentionally causes it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for every single utterance.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks regarding the matter of causing remorse;

it is a general rule, not a specific injunction, and constitutes a *pācittiya* offense for the triad [of factors]. There is a *dukkaṭa* offense for the triad when [the person addressed] is not fully ordained.

There is no offense for one who does not intend to cause remorse but speaks thus out of pure desire for their welfare, nor for those who are insane and so forth. [The factors are: the state of being fully ordained, and the desire that they be uncomfortable.
"Causing remorse": these are the three factors here. The origin and other characteristics are exactly the same as in the preceding [precept].
The commentary on the training rule regarding intentional action is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Eavesdropping.
In the eighth [offense], "of those who have fallen into dispute" means those who have entered into a legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) increased by quarrels and strife.
"Eavesdropping" (*upassuti*) means the vicinity of hearing; the meaning is that one should stand where it is possible to hear their words.
For one who goes with the desire to provoke them, thinking, "I will listen there," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at every step, even if one is walking in haste.
The same principle applies even when one is moving away. However, where one stands and hears [the conversation], there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for one standing there.
Even if those people come to one’s own standing place while conversing, one must make oneself known by clearing one’s throat or saying, “I am here.
If one does not do so, there is still an offense of expiation for hearing it.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks regarding the matter of eavesdropping;

it is a general rule, not a specific instruction, and constitutes an offense of *pācittiya* for three cases, an offense of *dukkaṭa* for three cases involving those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*),

and there is no offense for one who goes thinking, "Having heard this, I shall desist, I shall abstain, I shall pacify [the dispute], I shall liberate myself," nor for those who are insane and so forth.

The state of being fully ordained, the intention to accuse, and the hearing—these are the three factors here. This offense, originating from traveling with a caravan of thieves, may be an act (*kiriya*) or a non-act (*akiriya*);

it is liberated by awareness (*saññāvimokkha*), involves consciousness (*sacittaka*), is a worldly transgression (*lokavajja*), is bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and verbal action (*vacīkamma*), is unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and is associated with painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning eavesdropping is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning obstructing formal acts:

Regarding the phrase "of formal acts that are legitimate" in the ninth [rule], this refers to formal acts performed in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction—namely, a formal act consisting of a motion (*apalokanakamma*).

Regarding these four formal acts—the act consisting of a motion (*ñattikamma*), the act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), and the act consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatutthakamma*)—herein is a brief exposition of their legal determination:

therein, an act of information (*apalokanakamma*) is a formal act to be performed by announcing a particular matter three times with the approval of a united Saṅgha, saying, "Does it please the Saṅgha? and then proclaiming, "It is pleasing to the Saṅgha."
It is said [thus]. Furthermore, an act that is to be performed with the consent of a harmonious Saṅgha by means of a single motion (*ñatti*) is called a *ñattikamma*.
An act that is to be performed by means of both a single motion and a proclamation (*anussāvana*) is called a *ñattidutiyakamma*.
An act that is to be performed by means of a single motion and three proclamations is called a *ñatticatutthakamma*.

Among those, the formal act of seeking permission (apalokanakamma) applies to five instances: reinstatement (osāraṇā), banishment (nissāraṇā), shaving (bhaṇḍukamma), the supreme penalty (brahmadaṇḍa), and the characteristic of a formal act (kammalakkhaṇa).
Therein, banishment should be understood as the expulsion of a novice monk who is like a thorn;

reinstatement is to be understood as the readmission of one who is behaving properly after seeing him in such a state. Shaving is the request for the cutting of the hair of one who desires to go forth.
[This is] the name. When monks are being provoked by the ill-spoken words of a talkative monk, [others should say]:
"The monk named so-and-so is talkative; he dwells provoking the monks with ill-spoken words. That monk may say whatever he wishes;
the monks should neither speak to the monk named so-and-so, nor should they give him exhortation or instruction."
"He must not be exhorted. [The formal act is to be performed as follows: "Venerable sirs, I ask the Saṅgha:
'Does the granting of the *brahmadaṇḍa* to the monk named so-and-so meet with the approval of the Saṅgha? A second time I ask... A third time I ask:
'Venerable sirs, does the granting of the *brahmadaṇḍa* to the monk named so-and-so meet with the approval of the Saṅgha? Thus is the formal act to be performed.

It is called the "Brahmin’s Staff" (brahmadaṇḍa). Furthermore, regarding the grounds such as exposing one's thighs for the purpose of being seen, the Blessed One authorized the "act of non-prostration" (*avandiya-kamma*) for bhikkhunīs, saying:
"Monks, that bhikkhu must be made unworthy of salutation by the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs. When the bhikkhunīs [inform the Saṅgha]:
"Venerable ladies, a certain venerable bhikkhu named so-and-so displays conduct that inspires lack of confidence in the bhikkhunīs,"...
"The Bhikkhunī Saṅgha approves of this act of non-prostration toward that noble one"—this is what must be performed by the bhikkhunīs while they are still seated in their own quarters.

Since such an act is characterized by the formal procedure (*kamma*) itself, and not by acts such as reinstatement (*osāraṇā*), it is therefore called "characterized by the procedure" (*kammalakkhaṇa*). Furthermore, this which is called "characterized by the procedure" was prescribed based on the bhikkhunīs.
Furthermore, it is also permitted for monks; therefore, when monks give robes and other requisites to those whose robes have been stolen and so forth,
or when they use items that ought to be removed, or remove such items, or when they make a formal agreement (*katika*) of such a lawful nature,
they must perform an act of notification (*apalokanakamma*) after having announced it three times.
All this enters into the characteristic of formal acts (*kammalakkhaṇa*). Thus, a formal act by way of announcement (*apalokanakamma*) proceeds in five instances.

A formal act by way of motion (*ñattikamma*), however, proceeds in nine instances: reinstatement (*osāraṇa*), expulsion (*nissāraṇa*), the Uposatha ceremony, the Pavāraṇā ceremony, authorization (*sammuti*), giving, receiving, postponement, and the characteristic of formal acts itself. Therein: "Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me..."
“Such-and-such a person is seeking full ordination from the Venerable such-and-such; he has been instructed by me.
If it is the proper time for the Saṅgha, let such-and-such come; he should be told, ‘Come. This is the formal admission (*osāraṇā*) of one seeking ordination;
this is what is called “admission. “Let the Venerable Ones listen to me: this monk, such-and-such, is a preacher of the Dhamma...”
"Neither the Sutta nor the Suttavibhaṅga applies to this case; he, failing to discern the meaning, misinterprets the meaning based on the mere shadow of the phrasing.

Venerable sirs, if it seems appropriate to you, let us have the monk named so-and-so expelled and settle this legal dispute ourselves"—thus [is the speech] of the Dhamma-preacher in a formal decision of censure.
The removal of a bhikkhu is called "removal" (*nissāraṇā*). "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs: today is the Uposatha...
[as above] ...let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha"—a motion (*ñatti*) established by way of the Uposatha ceremony is called "Uposatha. "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs:
today is the fifteenth day of the Invitation (*pavāraṇā*); if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha invite [one another]."
Thus, a motion established by means of the *pavāraṇā* ritual is called a *pavāraṇā-ñatti*. [The formulas are: “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me:
such-and-such a person desires ordination from such-and-such a person; if it is timely for the Saṅgha, may I instruct such-and-such a person”;
and, “If it is timely for the Saṅgha, may such-and-such a person instruct such-and-such a person.”
Thus, a motion (*ñatti*) established for the purpose of appointing oneself or another is called an appointment (*sammuti*). [For example: "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs:
this robe-cloth, which is subject to forfeiture by the monk so-and-so, has been surrendered to the Saṅgha;
if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this robe-cloth to the monk so-and-so. In this way...
The giving away of robes, bowls, and so forth that have been relinquished is called "giving. [One should say: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me:
this monk named so-and-so remembers an offense, discloses it, makes it plain, and confesses it.
If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, I shall accept the confession of the offense of the monk named so-and-so. He [the recipient] should then say, "Do you see it?"
‘Yes, I see it,’ and ‘You should exercise restraint in the future’—this is called the acceptance of an offense as an acceptance.

“Let the venerable residents listen to me: if it is timely for the venerable ones, let us now perform the Uposatha, let us recite the Pātimokkha, and at a later time we shall perform the Pavāraṇā”—this is the postponement of an already performed Pavāraṇā, which is called postponement.
The name [of this category] is as follows: in the settling of a *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass), there is a motion that encompasses all;

and for each individual side, there is one motion—thus, these three motions constitute what is called the characteristic of the formal act (*kammalakkhaṇa*). Thus, a formal act consisting of a motion (*ñattikamma*) proceeds through nine grounds.

A formal act consisting of a motion followed by a second resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*) proceeds through seven grounds: reinstatement (*osāraṇa*), expulsion (*nissāraṇa*), authorization (*sammuti*), giving (*dāna*), and rescinding (*uddhāra*).

"Instruction is the characteristic of the formal act. In this context, "expulsion" (*nissāraṇā*) refers to the removal by means of overturning the bowl (*pattanikkujjana*) of a lay follower who possesses eight factors, such as striving for the non-acquisition of requisites for the monks, so that the Saṅgha may not associate with him.
It should also be understood that "readmission" (*osāraṇā*) occurs for that same person when he conducts himself properly, by means of righting the bowl (*pattukkujjana*).

That [procedure] was explained in the *Khuddakakkhandhaka*, in the section concerning the story of Vaḍḍha Licchavi. "Formal authorization" (*sammuti*) should be understood by way of these authorizations:

the authorization for the boundary, the authorization for not being separated from the three robes, the authorization for the rug, the authorization for the designator of meals, the distributor of lodgings, the storekeeper, the receiver of robes, the distributor of rice-gruel, the distributor of fruits, the distributor of solid food, the distributor of minor items, the distributor of bathing cloths, the distributor of bowls, the supervisor of monastery attendants, and the supervisor of novices.
"Giving" is to be understood by way of the giving of the *kaṭhina* robe and the giving of robes for the deceased.
It should be understood. The lifting [of the kathina] should be understood by way of the lifting of the kathina.
The teaching should be understood by way of the designation of the site for a hut and the site for a monastery.

Furthermore, regarding those two formal proclamations consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiyakammavācā) that were spoken—namely, one on each side in the settlement by "covering over as with grass" (tiṇavatthāraka)—and those formal proclamations spoken in cases such as the imposition of delusion (mohāropana), [these should be understood].
By way of this, the characteristic of an act (*kammalakkhaṇa*) is to be understood; thus, an act consisting of a motion followed by a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) goes to seven points:
rehabilitation (*osāraṇa*), expulsion (*nissāraṇa*), authorization (*sammuti*), granting (*dāna*), censure (*niggaha*), formal admonition (*samanubhāsana*), and the characteristic of the act itself.
Therein, regarding the seven acts beginning with the act of condemnation (*tajjanīyakamma*):
Expulsion (*nissāraṇā*) should be understood by way of [the offense], and reinstatement (*osāraṇā*) by way of the subsiding of those very same actions;

authorization as a teacher of bhikkhunīs (*bhikkhunovādakasammuti*) is by way of formal authorization (*sammuti*); the granting of probation (*parivāsa*) and the granting of the trial period (*mānatta*) is by way of giving (*dāna*); sending back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassana*) is by way of restraint (*niggaha*);
and the one who follows a suspended monk (*ukkhittānuvattikā*), the eight cases involving a third time (*aṭṭha yāvatatiyakā*), Ariṭṭha, and Caṇḍakāḷī—these are the matters that involve a third time.

By way of these eleven formal admonitions (*samanubhāsanā*), they are "formal admonitions"; by way of the legal acts of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*) and rehabilitation (*abbhāna-kamma*), they should be understood as having the characteristic of a legal act (*kamma-lakkhaṇa*).
Thus, the legal act consisting of a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*) proceeds through seven stages.

Furthermore, among these four types of legal acts, the legal act of mere notification (*apalokana-kamma*) must be performed only after having notified [the Saṅgha], whereas the others proceed by way of a motion and so forth.

It should not be done. Even a *ñattikamma* (a formal act consisting of a motion) should be performed by establishing only one motion; it should not be performed by way of a *apalokanakamma* (a formal act consisting of a mere announcement) and so forth.

However, regarding a *ñattidutiyakamma* (a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation), there are both those that may be performed and those that may not; among these, [the following] may be performed:

the authorization of a boundary (*sīmā-sammuti*), the abolition of a boundary (*sīmā-samūhanana*), the distribution of the *kathina* robe-cloth, the suspension of the *kathina*, the designation of a site for a hut (*kuṭi-vatthu-desanā*), and the designation of a site for a monastery (*vihāra-vatthu-desanā*).

These six formal acts (*kamma*) are heavy; they must not be performed by merely seeking permission (*apaloketvā*), but must be carried out after proclaiming the motion and the second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakammavāca*).
The remaining thirteen permissions—the permissions for assigning lodgings, for appointing a distributor of robes, and for appointing a distributor of food—are light formal acts;
it is permissible to perform them even by merely seeking permission, but they must certainly not be performed by way of a formal act consisting of a motion and so forth.
Even a formal act consisting of a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (ñatticatutthakamma) must be performed with its own specific characteristics, and not by way of other formal acts.

Thus, when these formal acts are performed with the attainment of the subject matter, the motion, the proclamation, the boundary, and the assembly—each according to its own respective characteristic—they are called "legitimate" (dhammika) because they have been carried out in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction; that is, because the Dhamma exists within them.

Thus, for one who, having given their consent for these legitimate legal acts, subsequently falls into the state of criticizing them, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for every single word.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks regarding the matter of falling into the state of criticizing; it is a common rule of training.

There is no offense for one who is ignorant; there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who is doubtful regarding a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*), and for one who perceives an illegitimate legal act (*adhammakamma*) as being legitimate.

There is no offense for one who perceives it as an illegitimate legal act, knowing: "They are performing a legal act that is either illegitimate, or performed by an incomplete assembly, or upon one who is not subject to such a legal act," nor for those who are insane and so forth.
[The factors for an offense are: the status of it being a legitimate legal act, and the perception of it as a legitimate legal act.

Having given their consent, they then criticize; these are the three factors here. The origins and so forth are the same as for the offense of taking what is not given, but this [offense] is of painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the obstruction of work is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Going After Having Given One’s Consent.

Regarding the tenth [training rule], "the discussion of the legal determination" (*vinicchaya-kathā*) refers to the period when the discussion of the legal determination is still ongoing—that is, as long as the matter reported has not yet been legally determined, or as long as the formal motion (*ñatti*) has been established but the proclamation of the act (*kammavācā*) has not yet been concluded. Any bhikkhu who, in this regard...
If, out of a desire to disrupt the proceedings, one leaves the reach of the assembly's hand, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the act of leaving,
and an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) once one has left.
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning a certain monk, regarding the matter of departing without having given one's consent.

This is a common designation (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), not a formal injunction (*anāṇattika*). There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who is in doubt regarding a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*), and for one who perceives an illegitimate legal act (*adhammakamma*) as being a legitimate legal act, or who is in doubt about it.

However, there is no offense for one who perceives it as an illegitimate legal act, or for one who, having known that "there will be quarrels and so forth in the Saṅgha, or they will perform a legal act through illegality, by an incomplete assembly, or upon one who is not subject to a legal act," [refrains from participating].

If one has become ill, or is attending to the needs of the ill, or is afflicted by excrement and so forth, and goes away with the thought, "I will return again," not wishing to invalidate the legal act (*kamma*), there is no offense for him, nor for those who are insane and so forth. [The factors for a valid act are:

the proceeding of a formal discussion (*vinicchayakathā*), the nature of a legal act according to the Dhamma (*dhammakammatā*), the perception that it is a legal act according to the Dhamma (*dhammakammasaññitā*), being situated within the same boundary (*samānasīmā*), and belonging to the same community of affiliation (*samānasaṃvāsaka*).
The desire to cause anger and the departing from the vicinity of the hands—these are the six factors here. It originates from formal admonition;

it is both an action and a non-action; it is liberated by perception; it involves the mind; it is a worldly offense; it is bodily action and verbal action; it is unwholesome consciousness; and it is painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule regarding departing without having given one's consent is finished.

11. Commentary on the Rule Concerning the Weak (Dubbalasikkhāpada) In the eleventh [rule], "by a united Saṅgha" means having given the robe together with a Saṅgha that is of common affiliation and standing within the same boundary.
"According to intimacy" (*yathāsanthutaṃ*) means according to whoever is intimate by way of friendship, being seen together, or being a companion.

"Of him" is the meaning. "Pācittiya": for a monk who has been appointed by the Saṅgha himself through the assignment of lodgings and so forth, if he later criticizes [the appointment], there is a pācittiya offense for every word spoken.
This was laid down at Rājagaha concerning the group of six monks, regarding the matter of criticizing after having given a robe; it is a general rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti).
There is no formal instruction (*anāṇattika*). Regarding a legal act (*dhammakamma*), there is an offense of expiation involving three factors (*tikapācittiya*).
With the exception of a robe, if one gives another requisite that is subject to distribution or dispersal and subsequently objects to it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"Subject to distribution or dispersal" means everything except the five heavy articles (*garubhaṇḍa*). For they are spoken of as five heavy articles by way of category; therein, the monastery...
First, a park site; second, a monastery and a monastery site; third, a bed, a bench, a mattress, and a pillow;
fourth, an iron cauldron, an iron vessel, an iron bucket, an iron pan, a hatchet, a small axe, a large axe, a spade, and a chisel;
[and] creepers, bamboo, muñja grass, pabbaja grass, grass, clay, wooden articles, and earthenware.
The fifth. For these five items belonging to the Saṅgha may not be disposed of or divided by the Saṅgha, nor by a group or an individual;

even if they have been disposed of or divided, they remain the property of the Saṅgha alone. However, one may exchange durable goods for durable goods, or other [goods]—whether they be unsuitable or suitable and of high value—for the purpose of providing benefit to the Saṅgha.

It is permissible to exchange [an item] by means of a formal exchange (kappiyaparivattana). It is also permissible to dispose of inferior items for the purpose of preserving excellent lodgings and so forth, and having disposed of them, to use [the proceeds].
Furthermore, among the three preceding groups [of items], there is nothing that constitutes "heavy goods" (agarubhaṇḍa);
in the fourth group, however, there are iron pots, vessels shaped like water-jars (arañjara), iron censers, and iron cauldrons.
These three are heavy goods (garubhaṇḍa), even if they consist of only as much water as can be held in a handful.
Furthermore, a metal vessel made of any kind of iron—whether black iron, copper, brass, or bell-metal—that holds a *pāda* in the island of Sri Lanka, is to be divided;
and a *pāda*, by the Magadhan *nāḷi* measure, amounts to five *nāḷis*. Anything exceeding that is a heavy good.
These, first of all, are the metal vessels mentioned in the Canon (pāḷi).

However, even those not mentioned in the Canon—such as the water-pot (bhiṅgāra), the alms-bowl (paṭiggaha), the small bowl (uḷuṅka), the ladle (dabbikaṭacchu), the plate (pāti), the tray (taṭṭaka), the saucer (sarakasa), the box (samugga), the charcoal pan (aṅgārakapalla), the incense burner (dhūmakaṭacchu), and so forth—even these small items are indeed "heavy goods" (garubhaṇḍa).
Furthermore, the iron bowl (ayapatta), the iron basin (ayathālaka), and the copper-iron pot (tambalohathālaka)—these, however, [are also heavy goods].
Regarding vessels: various types of vessels made of bronze, iron, or copper are permitted for use by the Saṅgha or as gifts from householders;
however, they are not permitted for personal use.

Apart from those vessel types, other articles made of allowable metal—such as a collyrium box, a collyrium stick, a nose-pick, an ear-cleaner, a needle, or a small pair of tweezers—are also permitted.
Small items such as an iron thorn, a key, a gong, a walking stick, a piercing tool, a small sling, solid cast iron, wrought iron,
and all kinds of vessels are to be shared. Furthermore, smoke-pipes, iron lamps, tree-lamps, hanging lamps, suspended lamps, images of women, men, or animals,
or whatever else may be hung upon walls, ceilings, doors, and so forth— even down to an iron peg— are likewise to be shared.
All metal vessels are indeed heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*); even if one has received them for oneself, they must not be used for private consumption.
They are permitted only for communal use by the Saṅgha or as items provided by householders.
The same principle applies to bronze vessels as well. Trays, bowls, and the like made of milk-stone are also indeed heavy goods.

However, a small oil-jar (*ghaṭaka*) is indeed a heavy article (*garubhaṇḍa*) if it exceeds the size of one that can be held by the hands; likewise, vessels made of gold, silver, brass, or crystal are not permitted even if they belong to a layperson.
Regarding the use of lodgings (*senāsana*), however, everything is permitted, whether it has been formally dedicated (*āmāsa*) or not.
As for tools such as axes and the like, any axe with which one performs work other than merely cutting tooth-sticks or scraping the ears is [considered a heavy article].
It is not possible to [use it] for that purpose; this is "to be shared" (*bhājanīya*). Any other [tool] made in whatever manner is "heavy property" (*garubhaṇḍa*);
furthermore, even a surgeon’s lancet is indeed heavy property, as is an axe. However, that which is made under the category of weaponry is "not to be touched" (*anāmāsa*);
there is no such thing as a heavy property for a spade, a handle, or a pickaxe. As for the handle of a broom or a hoe—
However, that which is without a handle and consists merely of the fruit—such as can be placed in a small box and carried about—is to be shared out (*bhājanīya*).
The tip [of the handle] is also included by the very act of carving it.
If those people who provided the axes and other tools for the monastery find their own houses burnt or plundered, they might say: "Venerable sir, give us the implements; we shall provide them again."
If they say, “We shall bring it,” it should be given. If they do bring it, they are not to be stopped; nor are those who do not bring it to be reproached.

All iron implements belonging to smiths, turners, carpenters, reed-workers, jewelers, and bowl-binders—such as hammers, tongs, scales, and so forth—become heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*) from the moment they are given to the Saṅgha.
This also applies to the tools of tin-smelters, goldsmiths, and leather-workers.
The same method applies here. However, this is the distinction: among the tools of a tipu-caster, the small knife for cutting tipu;
among the tools of a goldsmith, the small knife for cutting gold; and among the tools of a leather-worker, the small knife for cutting prepared leather—these are to be shared.
Among the tools of a barber and a tailor as well, with the exception of the large knife and the large forceps.
All *mahāpipphalika* is permitted; the others are heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*).

Among creepers and the like, any creeper such as the *vettavalli* that measures half an arm-span—if it has been given to the Saṅgha, or grows there naturally, or has been protected and guarded—is a heavy good.
If, when work for the Saṅgha or work for the Cetiya has been performed, it remains in excess...

It is allowable to include even personal property; however, ropes or cords made of thread, bark-fiber, coconut husk, or hide—whether single-stranded or double-stranded—that have been made by twisting together thread, bark-fiber, coconut husk, or hide, and which belong to the Saṅgha, are heavy goods (garubhaṇḍa).
But thread that has not been twisted, as well as bark-fiber, cotton, coconut husk, and hides, are common property (bhājanīya).
Furthermore, those ropes and such items that have been given [to the Saṅgha] must not be withheld from anyone who takes them for their own business.

Any bamboo—even if it is only as thick as an eight-finger-width needle-handle—that has been given to the Saṅgha, or grows there [on Saṅgha property], and is protected and guarded, is "heavy property" (garubhaṇḍa).
Even that may be given for personal use once it has been used for the affairs of the Saṅgha or for work on a Cetiya, provided there is a surplus.

It is permissible. However, as for oil-tubes used for massaging the feet, walking sticks, sandals with handles, umbrella-sticks, and umbrella-ribs—these items here are considered common property (*bhājanīya-bhaṇḍa*);
people who have come from a burnt house may take them and go, and they should not be stopped.

As for *muñja* grass, *pabbaja* grass, and other thatching grasses—even if only the size of a handful—if they are included among the items designated for thatching, [they are likewise common property].
Whatever has been given to the Saṅgha, even a single leaf from among palm leaves and so forth,
or what grows there [in the monastery], or what grows on a grassy plot belonging to the Saṅgha outside the monastery— if it is protected and guarded as valuable property—

even that may be used for the business of the Saṅgha or the business of a shrine (cetiya), provided it is in excess of what is needed for personal business. Those whose houses have been burnt may take [such items].
Those who are departing should not be stopped; even a scrap of cloth measuring eight finger-breadths, if empty, is indeed a heavy object.

Whether it be ordinary clay, five-colored clay, lime, or any substance such as Sajjurasa, kaṅgu-stone, or resin—whatever is difficult to obtain, whether brought from afar or found locally, if it has been given and is protected and guarded, even if only the size of a palm fruit.
It is heavy ware; even that, when used for the business of the Saṅgha or for work on a cetiya, may be given as an extra item for personal use.
However, asafoetida, vermilion, yellow orpiment, red arsenic, collyrium, and so forth, are items to be shared out.
As for wooden ware, any kind of wooden vessel made from bamboo that conforms to the stated measurements, whether it has been given to the Saṅgha or produced there, [is permissible].
Or, whatever is a valuable object that is guarded and protected; furthermore, all things fashioned from wood, bamboo, leather, stone, and so forth, are included under "wooden articles.
Among these, those not included among beds and chairs—starting from stools and the like, down to seats made of cloth, straw, or leaves—all such seats are included.
A curved board, a long board, a board for washing robes, a rubbing board,
a mallet for the rubbing board, a knot for cutting tooth-sticks, a staff-mallet, a boat, a water-pool, a dye-tub, a water-dipper,
a box made of wood, ivory, or bamboo— with or without legs— a casket, and a chest with a handle for the feet.
A large basket, a water trough, a water basin, a ladle, a wooden water-cup, a water-saucer, and a water-conch—whatever among these has been given to the Saṅgha is heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*).
However, a conch-shell bowl is distributable (*bhājanīya*), as is a wooden water-pot.
A foot-rest, whether it be made of wood or made of cloth, leaves, and so forth, is entirely heavy property. A stand (*ādhāraka*).
The bowl-cover, the palm-leaf fan, the fan, the broom, the basket, the wooden stick-broom, and the hand-broom— among these, anything whatsoever,
whether small or large, made from wood, bamboo, leaves, leather, or other materials, is indeed "heavy property" (garubhaṇḍa). Furthermore,
anything whatsoever made of wood or stone that belongs to the structural components of a house, such as pillars, beams, staircases, or floor-boards, [is also heavy property].
Any kind of mattress frame, any kind of floor-covering, or any kind of unallowable skin—all these belong to the Saṅgha and are heavy goods;
it is permissible to use them as floor-coverings. However, sheepskin falls under the category of bedspreads, and that too is indeed a heavy good.
Allowable skins are to be distributed [among the monks]. But according to the Kurundi, everything measuring the size of a bed—
It is stated that leather is a heavy article.
A mortar, a pestle, a winnowing fan, a grindstone, a small grindstone, a stone trough, a stone basin, and all farming implements are heavy articles;
likewise, every vehicle equipped with wheels is a heavy article. Furthermore, the legs and the crossbars of beds and chairs [are heavy articles].
And among these—axes, hatchets, and so forth, as well as staves—whatever is unfinished is *bhājanīya* (to be shared);

however, that which has been planed and polished is heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*). Permitted [items] are: a staff, an umbrella, a fist-sized leaf-fan, a walking stick, sandals, a pair of fire-sticks, a water-strainer, and a bowl for holding the feet;
a jar of *āmalaka* fruit that is not excessive, and a pitcher of *āmalaka*.
A gourd-bowl, a gourd-pitcher, and a horn-bowl—all these are "vessels" (*bhājanīya*); beyond that, they are "heavy articles" (*garubhaṇḍa*).

Whether it be an elephant tusk or any kind of horn, if it is uncarved, it is a vessel exactly as it was found; the determination regarding beds, chairs, and so forth made from them is the same as before.
Even if carved and finished, a casket for asafoetida, a casket for ointment, or a toggle-ring [is a heavy article].
The mirror, the collyrium box, the collyrium stick, and the water-wiper—all these are indeed "vessels" (*bhājanīya*).
Among earthenware items, everything used for human enjoyment and utility—such as jars, pots, and other clay vessels;
as well as bowls, basins, charcoal pans, incense burners, lamp-stands, lamp-shades, roof-tiles, and ceiling-tiles.

"Stūpika" refers to all heavy goods. Among these aforementioned heavy goods, when taking anything such as bamboo for one's own use, it should be taken after performing an exchange (*phātikamma*) that is either equal to or greater than its value.

However, a water-jar, a bowl, a platter, a golden vessel, or a water-pot that do not exceed the size of a "foot-measure" (*pādaggaṇhanaka*) from what is not left over—these are here to be distributed.
And just as with earthenware vessels, so too with metal vessels, a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*) belongs to the category of items that may be used.

Thus, regarding an item that is both usable and dispensable—meaning another requisite belonging to the class known as "dispensable" or "to be dismantled"—if one uses it until it is worn out after having given [another], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
however, it is not permitted to give away the other kind. If one gives it away through a sense of ownership, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
If one takes it with the intent to steal, one must be dealt with after having the value of the goods assessed.

And just as there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for one who wears out another’s requisites after having given them, so too there is precisely a *dukkaṭa* offense for one who wears out a robe or other requisites belonging to the Saṅgha after having given them, provided he has not been authorized by the Saṅgha.
In all cases involving one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), there is a triple *dukkaṭa*. However, in the case of ordinary [requisites]...

There is no offense for one who, seeing another making [a robe] by way of desire and so forth, becomes despondent, thinking, "What is the use of giving it to him? Even if he receives it, he will squander it;
he will not apply it properly," as well as for those such as the insane. [The factors constituting an offense are:

being fully ordained (upasampanna), having received formal authorization (sammuti) in accordance with the Dhamma, the giving of a robe that has reached the stage of being assigned to the Saṅgha, and subsequently desiring to disparage [the recipient].
"Causing to fall away": these are the four factors here. The origins and so forth are similar to those for taking what is not given; however, this [result] is a painful feeling.
The commentary on the weak training rule is finished.
12. Commentary on the Training Rule on Diverting [Alms-food].
In the twelfth [offense], everything is exactly according to the method explained in the *Pariṇāmana-sikkhāpada* of the Thirtieth Chapter. This indeed is the distinction:
there, because it was dedicated by oneself, it is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*; here, because it was dedicated to another person, it is a simple *pācittiya*.
The commentary on the training rule concerning diverting [merit] is finished.
The eighth section, on those of the same Dhamma, is concluded.
9. The section on gems.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Inner Apartments (Antepurasikkhāpada). Regarding the first [rule] of the Ratana Chapter: "Of a khattiya" means one of khattiya birth;

"anointed on the head" means one who has been anointed on the head with the khattiya-consecration. "The king has not yet departed from here" means one in whose presence the king has not departed; in such a case where the king has not departed.
The meaning is "in the bedchamber. A "jewel" refers to the chief queen. "Niggataṃ" means gone out; "aniggataratanakaṃ" means one from whom the jewel has not yet departed.
The meaning is "in that bedchamber where the jewel has not yet departed. Regarding the phrase "he should cross the threshold":
here, without having made known his arrival, he [should cross] first the door-sill of the bedchamber.
For one who steps across [the threshold], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); for the second step, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the Venerable Ānanda regarding the matter of entering the king’s inner palace;

it is a unique rule (asādhāraṇapaññatti), not subject to formal authorization (anāṇattika), and constitutes a triple offense of expiation (tikapācittiya) for one who, having been informed, perceives that he has not been informed.

And there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who is in doubt. There is no offense for one who perceives [the other] as not having been informed; nor for one who is not a khattiya, nor for one who has not been consecrated by khattiya-consecration;
nor for one entering a bedchamber when both have departed, or when either of the two has departed;

nor for one who enters what is not a bedchamber; nor for those who are insane and so forth. [The factors for the offense are: being a khattiya, being consecrated, and [entering] from the bedchamber of both.
Non-departure, lack of formal announcement, and crossing the threshold—these are the five factors here. The origins and so forth are similar to those of the first *kathina* rule;
however, this is a "non-action" (*akiriya*).
The commentary on the rule concerning the royal palace is finished.

2. Commentary on the Jewel Training Rule (Ratanasikkhāpada) In the second [rule], "jewel" (*ratana*) refers to the ten kinds beginning with pearl. "That which is considered a jewel" (*ratanasammatam*) refers to whatever is used for the enjoyment or utility of human beings.
"Within a monastery" (*ajjhārāme*) means: within the enclosure of a walled monastery, or, in the case of an unwalled one, within two *leḍḍupāta* throws.
"Inside. Regarding "dwell within": for an enclosed area, it refers to the interior; for an unenclosed area, it is within the range of a falling pestle.
Herein, this is the analysis: for one who acquires gold or silver for one’s own sake, or causes it to be acquired, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
For the sake of the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, or for the construction of a shrine, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
In the case of the remaining treasures, such as pearls and so forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for anyone who does so for the sake of all [the Sangha].

For one who has items—whether they be allowable things (*kappiyavatthu*) or unallowable things (*akappiyavatthu*)—stored away under the pretext that they belong to the storekeeper, even if they are the property of one’s own mother, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
However, it is permissible to store away such things after making them one’s own property. But when told, “Store this away,” if one says, “No...”
"It is not permissible," he should be refused. If those who are angry throw [the items] down and depart, there is what is called an "obstruction" (*palibodha*);

they must be settled. If carpenters and others, or royal favorites, while working on the monastery, say, "Settle whatever implements or bedding you have and give them to us," whether out of desire or fear—
It must certainly not be done; however, it is permissible to show a place that is well-guarded.

Even within the monastery grounds or the vicinity of the residence, one should take up [the requisites] or have them taken up, and after making a mark, deposit them in exactly such a place where the suspicion arises, "This will be taken by monks or by novices."
It should be announced: “Let whoever has lost property come forward. Then, when someone comes, he should be asked, “What kind of property did you lose?
If he can identify it by its distinguishing marks, it should be returned. If not, he should be told, “Search for it.
When departing from that residence, [the property] should be placed in the hands of suitable monks; if there are none such, [it should be placed in the hands of] those who are suitable...
Having placed [the goods] in the hands of householders, one may depart.
But if one neither departs nor sees the owner, one should have a permanent resting place, a shrine, or a lotus pond constructed.
If after the lapse of a long time the owner arrives, one should show it to him and say, "Please give your consent. If he does not give his consent, [one may use it].
If one urges, "Give me wealth," it should be given after having been exhorted [to do so].
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhu regarding the matter of taking up precious objects;
"except within a monastery or within a dwelling"—this is the twofold subsequent rule (anupaññatti) here, which is a common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti).

This concludes the section on formal authorization (*sāṇattika*). For one who takes [an object] with disrespect from a place where it is permitted and does not put it back, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
There is no offense for one who takes [an object] from a permitted place and puts it back; for one who takes it on trust or temporarily;
for one who takes it with the perception that it is refuse-rag cloth (*paṃsukūla*); and for those who are insane and so forth. This concludes the section on what is not permitted.
The four factors here are: that it belongs to another, the absence of the perception that it is a rag-patch robe taken in trust, and either taking it oneself or causing it to be taken.
The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to those of the Sañcaritta rule.
The commentary on the Jewel-offense training rule (Ratana-sikkhāpada) is finished.

3. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Entering a Village at an Improper Time Regarding the third rule, "without having asked a monk who is present," this follows the same method as what was stated for traveling.

"At an improper time" (*vikāla*) means from the moment the midday meal has passed until before dawn; within this interval, one may say, "I ask permission to enter the village at an improper time," or "village..."
If one enters without having asked for permission— unless there is such an urgent matter to be done—

then for one crossing the boundary of an enclosed village or entering the vicinity of an unenclosed village, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the first foot and an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for the second foot.
Even if many people enter the village together for some business, they must all ask one another [for permission].
One must take leave. However, for those going to another village because that task was not accomplished in the first village, there is no further requirement to take leave.

But if, having desisted from their effort and returning to the monastery, they wish to enter another village along the way, they must certainly take leave. This applies whether at a family home or in a rest-house.
Or, having finished his meal, if he wishes to go for alms of oil or alms of ghee, he should ask permission if there is a monk nearby;
if there is none, he may proceed, saying, "There is no one. However, once he has descended onto the street, even if he sees a monk, there is no requirement to ask permission.
Furthermore, if the path goes through the middle of the village, if he is traveling by that way...
If the thought arises, “I will go for the sake of such things as oil,” then upon seeing a monk, one must ask permission.

However, for one who goes without stepping off the path, there is no requirement to ask permission; but for one who does step off the path, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the method already stated.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks, regarding the matter of entering a village at an improper time: “While [a monk] is present...”
"Bhikkhu," "without having asked permission," and "except for such an urgent business"—these are the three subsequent rules (anupaññatti) here.

It is a non-common rule (asādhāraṇapaññatti), it is without formal instruction (anāṇattika), and it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the triad [of cases]. There is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for one who perceives it as the wrong time when it is the right time, or for one who is in doubt.
However, there is no offense for one who perceives it as the right time, or for one who has urgent business, or for one who is present [and asks].

There is no offense if one enters after having asked for permission, or if one enters without asking when no one is present; or if one goes toward any one of the following: the interior of a monastery, a nuns’ residence, or a lodging for female wanderers;
or if the path to the village passes through [the monastery] and one goes by that way;

or in cases of emergency; or for those who are insane and so forth. The factors for the offense are: the presence of a monk, the failure to ask for permission, the absence of any of the permitted reasons, and entering the village at an improper time.

These are the three factors here. The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth are exactly the same as for the *kaṭhina* rule; however, this [present rule] is both an action and a non-action (*kiriya-akiriya*).
The commentary on the training rule regarding entering a village at an improper time is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding the Needle Case.

In the fourth [case], "splitting" itself is the "splitter"; that which possesses this is "one who splits. Therefore, for having made or caused such a needle-case to be made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); but upon acquisition, having split it, one must confess an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was laid down with reference to many monks among the Sakyans, concerning the instance of requesting many needle-cases;

it is a common rule (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), it is accompanied by an injunction (*sāṇattika*), and it applies whether one has had it made oneself, or had it made by others, or whether others have had it made themselves, or had it made by oneself.
For one who obtains [the robe] after having it finished by others, there is an offense of *pācittiya* for each of the four parts.
In the cases of making or causing another to make [an item] for the sake of someone else, or in using [something] after obtaining it when it was made by another, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.

For one who makes any of these—namely, a toggle, a fire-drill, a spindle, a cosmetic box, a cosmetic stick, a perfume box, or a water-sponge—from bone or other such materials, and for those who are insane and so forth, [there is no offense].
There is no offense. The three factors here are: it being a needle-case, it being made of bone or similar materials, and its acquisition through having it made or had made for one's own sake.
The origin and other details are the same as for the Sañcaritta (go-between) rule.
The commentary on the Sūcighara (needle-case) training rule is finished.

5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Beds and Stools (Mañcapīṭhasikkhāpada) In the fifth [rule], "bed" (mañca) refers to any one among [furniture] such as the *masāraka* and so forth. A "stool" (pīṭha) is of the same kind; however, unlike a bed, it is not excessively long, nor is it square like a chair (*āsandika*). "Cutting" (*chedanaka*) is similar to "breaking" (*bhedanaka*).
This rule was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Upananda, regarding the practice of lying on a high bed; it applies to one who makes [a bed] according to the prescribed measure.

There is no offense for one who, having obtained something exceeding the prescribed measure, buries it so that only the portion within the measure is visible, or makes it flat, or constructs a frame, and then uses it; nor is there an offense for those who are insane and so forth.

Furthermore, there is no offense in the case of a bed or chair exceeding the measure, whether it is obtained by making it oneself or having it made by another for one's own use. These are the points here.
There are two factors. The remainder is exactly like the training rule on needle-cases.
The commentary on the training rule on beds and chairs is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule on stuffed with cotton.

In the sixth [offense], "tūlonaddha" means "covered with cotton"; that is to say, having spread out a *cimilika* (a coarse cloth) and inserted cotton, it is covered over again with a *cimilika*. "Uddālanaka" is exactly like "bhedanaka.
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks regarding the matter of having a bed covered with cotton made;
[it applies to] a waistband, a girdle, a shoulder-strap, a bowl-bag, a water-strainer, and a bolster—having obtained a cotton-covered item made by another.
There is no offense for one who uses [the bedding] after tearing it apart, nor for those who are insane and so forth. Herein, a pillow-cover is permitted only of the size of the head;

"of the size of the head" means that from the width at two of its three corners, the distance between them is one span and four finger-breadths, while in the middle it is one fist-span, and in length it is one and a half spans or two spans.
[The offense of] using a bed or chair upholstered with cotton down—
"Obtaining it either by making it oneself or by having it made for one's own sake"—these are the two factors here. The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the training rule concerning stuffed with cotton is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Sitting Mat.

“Seventh: ‘Sitting mat’ (*nisīdana*)—this is the name for an accessory made by spreading out a cloth similar to a rug, cutting it into two places at one end to a measure of a Sugata-span, and joining it with three fringes (*dasa*).
Regarding the Chabbaggiyas at Sāvatthī, this was laid down in the section on the possession of sitting mats that were of no fixed measure.
‘Three fringes and a span’—this is the subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*) here; it is a non-common rule (*asādhāraṇa-paññatti*), [applying] to that which is measured or less than the measure.”
There is no offense for one who makes it himself, or for one who, having obtained something made by another that exceeds the proper measure, cuts it down and uses it;
nor is there an offense for one making anything such as a canopy and so forth, or for those who are insane and the like.

In this case, there are two constituent factors: that the sitting mat exceeds the proper measure, and that it is made or caused to be made for one’s own sake or obtained [in such a state]. The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the training rule concerning sitting cloths is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule concerning the itch-covering cloth:

In the eighth [rule], "itch-covering cloth" (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi*) refers to a robe permitted for the purpose of covering the afflictions of itch, boils, discharge, and severe scabies in the area below the navel and above the kneecaps.

At Sāvatthī, concerning the group of six monks, this was laid down regarding the matter of wearing an unmeasured itch-covering cloth; it is a common rule. The rest should be understood in the same manner as stated for the sitting mat.
The commentary on the training rule on the itch-covering cloth is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Rainy-Season Robe.

In the ninth [chapter], at Sāvatthī, concerning the group of six monks, this was laid down regarding the practice of wearing unmeasured rain-cloaks (*vassikasāṭikā*); whatever else needs to be said here is exactly according to the method already stated for the sitting mat (*nisīdana*).
The commentary on the training rule on the rain-cloak is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Nanda.

In the tenth [chapter], regarding the Venerable Nanda at Sāvatthī, the rule concerning the wearing of a robe of the Sugata’s measurement was laid down; it is a general rule, and the rest is exactly as stated in the section on the sitting mat.
The commentary on the training rule of Nanda is finished.
The ninth chapter, the Ratana-vagga, is concluded.
The explanation of the pure *pācittiya* offenses in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* commentary on the *Pātimokkha* is finished.
The section on the *pāṭidesanīya* offenses.
1. Commentary on the First Rule of Confession (Pāṭidesanīya Sikkhāpada).

Regarding the first of the rules of confession, because of the statement "having entered among the houses," even if she is standing within a monastery or similar place while giving, if one receives it from her hand while standing oneself in the street, a crossroads, a junction, or in a house—any of these—[it constitutes an offense].

There is no fault in [the recipient] taking it. However, for one who stands on a carriage road or similar place while the donor is giving, or who—whether standing on a carriage road or elsewhere, or even inside a monastery or similar place—takes any kind of food for the purpose of swallowing it, there is an *dukkaṭa* offense in the act of receiving;

for every swallow, there is a *pāṭidesanīya* offense. The manner in which this must be confessed has already been shown in the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) by way of the formula beginning with "It is censurable, friend," and so forth.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhu, regarding the matter of accepting food from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī who had entered an inhabited area;
it is a non-common rule (asādhāraṇa-paññatti), not subject to formal authorization (anāṇattika).

As this is, so too are the remaining [rules]; they constitute the threefold *pāṭidesanīya*, and apply both to the acceptance and the consumption of items such as those that are for a watch of the night (*yāmakālika*) and so forth.
It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). The same applies even for a temporary meal given by one who is ordained on only one side.

The same principle holds for those who perceive a relative as a non-relative, or who are in doubt about it. However, for one who perceives her as a relative, or when she causes a relative to give it, or when she gives it after having set it aside;
and for one who, standing within the monastery, the bhikkhunī’s residence, or the lodging of a female ascetic, goes outside the village and [brings it back], [there is no offense].

There is no offense for one who gives [food] such as that to be consumed at the proper time (yāmakālika) with the thought, “Use it if there is a reason,” or for one who consumes it after taking it from the hands of a trainee nun (sikkhamānā) or a novice nun (sāmaṇerī), or for those who are insane and so forth. The factors [constituting the offense] are:

being fully ordained; the person being unrelated by blood; receiving it directly with one’s own hand from the hands of one standing inside a house; the food being of the type to be consumed during the day (yāvakālika); and the act of swallowing.
These are the five factors here. The origins and so forth are similar to those of the sheep’s wool [rule].
The commentary on the first *pāṭidesanīya* training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the second *pāṭidesanīya* training rule.

In the second [offense], the phrase beginning with “here they serve soup” shows the manner of offering. The phrase beginning with “Step back first, sister” shows the manner in which one should be dissuaded.
Regarding this, the following is the detailed analysis: if even a single monk has not been dissuaded, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for those who accept food for the purpose of eating;
for every act of swallowing, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
At Rājagaha, concerning the group of six [monks], this was prescribed regarding the matter of not preventing a nun who is giving directions:
it is an offense of confession (pāṭidesanīya) of the threefold kind for one who does not prevent a woman ordained on one side from giving directions;

likewise, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who does not prevent a person not fully ordained, whether perceiving her as fully ordained or being in doubt. However, for one who perceives her as not fully ordained...
If she causes her own meal to be given, or causes the meal of others to be given, or causes that which was not given to be given,
or causes it to be given where it was not intended to be given, or causes it to be given equally to all,
or if she accepts and eats what has been directed by a trainee nun (sikkhamānā) or a novice nun (sāmaṇerī), then— excluding the five kinds of cooked food— [she commits an offense].
In all cases, there is no offense for those who are insane and so forth.

The five factors here are: being fully ordained; it being one of the five kinds of food; leaving a meal in a village in a manner other than the permitted ways; not being restrained [by others]; and swallowing.
The origin and other characteristics are similar to those of the Kathina rules.
The commentary on the second *pāṭidesanīya* training rule is finished.
3. Commentary on the third *pāṭidesanīya* training rule:

Regarding the third [rule], "those authorized for trainees" (*sekkhasammatāni*) means those who have received authorization as trainees. "Previously uninvited" (*pubbe animantito*) means before stepping across the threshold of the house.
"Without having previously been invited and without even entering the vicinity [of a house]," refers to one who is not ill—meaning one who is able to go for alms.
Regarding the *pāṭidesanīya*: for one who enters the vicinity of a house and takes food, there is first an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the very moment of receiving it;
then, for one who eats it anywhere after having received it, there is a *pāṭidesanīya* offense with every mouthful swallowed.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhus, regarding the matter of receiving food without knowing moderation:
“Not previously invited, not being ill. Herein, there are these two subsequent rules (anupaññatti):

the threefold offense of confession (pāṭidesanīya). There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) both for receiving and for consuming [food] that is for a watch of the night and so forth; likewise for one who perceives as one authorized by the Asekhas someone authorized by the Sekhas.

And for one who is in doubt. Furthermore, for one who—perceiving it as the alms-food of those recognized as *asekkha* (those beyond training)—takes the alms-food prepared in the house of another, whether he was previously invited, or is ill, or [the food belongs to] them;

and for one to whose house [the food] has been brought out, or who gives it having first brought it out to places such as the assembly hall without seeing the bhikkhu, or who places it at the threshold of the door—it is [an offense] for him regarding that.
There is no offense for one who is eating from a regular meal, a ticket-meal, a fortnightly meal, a Uposatha meal, or a meal on the first day of the lunar half-month;

for one who eats "time-of-watch" food and so forth given with the thought, "Enjoy this provided there is a requisite reason"; and for those who are insane and so forth. [The factors for an offense are:
being designated as a trainee (*sekkha*), not having been previously invited, not being ill, entering the vicinity of a house, and [eating] anything other than the regular meals and so forth.
"Taking and eating food" constitutes the five factors here. The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth are similar to those of the *eḷakaloma* [offense].
The commentary on the third *pāṭidesanīya* training rule is finished.
4. Commentary on the fourth *pāṭidesanīya* training rule.

In the fourth [offense], the passage beginning with "those forest-dwelling [lodgings]" and so forth should be understood according to the method already explained in the training rule regarding being separated from one's robes. Regarding the phrase "previously unannounced":
here, having entered either a monastery or the vicinity of a monastery with a woman, a man, a householder, or a person gone forth, [one says] "for such-and-such a family, venerable sir..."
When it has been announced, "Hard food or soft food will be brought," let that which was announced be brought exactly as announced;
or, having surrounded that with another, even if it is much, if one hears,
"Having informed the family named so-and-so, he goes taking hard food or soft food along with it."
Or if other families bring [food] along with them, all that is called "announced.
However, what is not thus announced and not brought is called "unannounced. One who is "not ill" is one who is able to go for alms.
"Confession-offense" (pāṭidesanīya) refers even to such food as might be given by travelers passing through the middle of the monastery.

For one who accepts [food] in a monastery or in the vicinity of a monastery and then consumes it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the act of accepting, and for every act of consuming,
there is an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*).
This was laid down concerning many monks among the Sakyans, regarding the matter of not reporting that thieves were staying in the monastery.
“Not being ill”: this is one supplementary rule (anupaññatti) here. Regarding the three offenses of acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya):

even in the case of receiving for the purpose of food among those things such as "time-limited" (yāmakālika) and so forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) both upon acceptance and upon consumption.

The same applies to one who has made a formal announcement (paṭisaṃvidita) while perceiving that it was not announced, or to one who is in doubt about it. However, for one who perceives that it was announced, for one who is ill, and for one who has made a formal announcement—[there is no offense].

There is no offense for one who consumes what has been brought [to him], or what remains from a meal given to the sick, or what was received outside the monastery, or roots, fruits, and so forth grown right there, or anything among the "time-limited for a watch" (yāmakālika) foods and the like, when it is obtained with the thought, "I shall consume this provided there is a suitable occasion";

nor is there an offense for those who are insane and so forth. Furthermore, there is no offense for one who uses a forest dwelling as previously described, or who consumes a time-limited food that was not produced on the spot.
The seven factors here are: being not ill, the remainder of not being ill, not having made known [the intention], receiving within the monastery, and swallowing.
The origin and other characteristics are exactly like those of the *kathina* rule; however, this is both an action and a non-action.
The commentary on the fourth *pāṭidesanīya* training rule is finished.
The explanation of the offenses entailing acknowledgment (*pāṭidesanīya*) in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* commentary on the *Pātimokkha* is finished.
The Section on the Training Rules (*sekhiyakaṇḍa*).
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Circular Fold (*Parimaṇḍala-sikkhāpada*).
Regarding the first of the *Sekhiya* rules, "circularly" (*parimaṇḍala*) means a circle all around.

"The training is to be observed" (*sikkhā karaṇīyā*) means that the training must be practiced everywhere—in the monastery as well as in inhabited dwellings—with the thought, "I shall robe myself thus. Furthermore, in this context, because the duties prescribed in the *Vatta-khandhaka* are also included...

Because they are to be trained in, they are indeed *sekhiya* (rules of training); therefore, no specific limit [of offense] was established for them as is done in the case of the *pārājika* and other categories.

Furthermore, for the purpose of demonstrating the discipline of conduct (*cāritta-vinaya*), the text is formulated in all training rules not by naming the offense—as in "whatever monk should wear his lower robe hanging down, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*)—but rather by stating "the training is to be observed. However, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), it says "there is an offense of wrong-doing."
Because it has been so stated, it should be understood that in all cases there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for showing disrespect.

Now, regarding the term "all around" (*parimaṇḍala*): here, it means that when one wears the lower robe after covering the navel-circle and letting the robe hang down eight finger-breadths from the bone of the shank below the knee-circle, it is said to be "worn all around."
If one wears it in such a manner—without wearing it properly, out of disrespect, letting it hang either in front or behind—there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
This applies not only to him alone, but also to others; for at that time, the group of six monks wore laypeople’s clothing:
they wore elephant-trunk garments, fish-tail garments, four-cornered garments, palm-leaf garments, and hundred-fold braid garments.

The faults regarding the lower robe (*nivāsana*) are stated in the *Khandhaka*: "Wearing it in a manner like a *saṃvalliya*. For one who wears it in such a way, there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

In this context, "elephant-trunk style" (*hatthisoṇḍaka*) refers to wearing it so that from the base of the navel it hangs down in the shape of an elephant's trunk, like the lower garment of women wearing a *coḷika*.
"Fish-tail style" (*macchavālaka*) refers to hanging it with one end tucked in and the other end trailing.
"Wrapped around" (*nivatthaṃ*). "Four-cornered" (*catukkaṇṇakaṃ*) means wrapped around after displaying four corners—two above and two below.
"Palm-leaf-shaped" (*tālavaṇṭakaṃ*) means wrapped around after hanging down a cloth in the shape of a palm leaf.
"Hundred-fold" (*satavalikaṃ*) means wrapped around by folding a long cloth many times and forming a pleated skirt (*ovaṭṭikaṃ*), [arranged] on the left and right sides.
Or it refers to that which is worn after displaying continuous folds. However, if one or two folds are discernible starting from the knee, it is permissible.
"Folding together" (*saṃvalliya*) means wearing it after binding the waist like a laborer or a weaver.
It is not permissible for one who is ill, nor for one traveling on a road, to wear it in such a manner. As for the road...

While walking, if one or two ears are lifted up and caught on top of the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*), or if one wears a saffron robe (*kāṣāya*) inside in that manner while wearing another robe outside, all of this is not permitted.
However, one who is ill is allowed to show the waistband (*ovaṭṭika*) of the inner saffron robe and wear another robe over it; this is not permitted for one who is not ill.

When putting on the two [robes], they should be worn with the inner robe tucked in. Thus, avoiding everything forbidden in this Khandhaka—namely, the hanging down and so forth—one should wear the lower robe (nivāsana) perfectly circular, free from any distortion, and endowed with the characteristics as described.
For one who does not wear it thus but makes any such distortion, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Furthermore, regarding the detailed analysis beginning with "The cause, the person, and the subject matter," that which was made resonant [with sound] was laid down at Kosambī;
the pair concerning using a hand soiled with food to hold a water-pot, a cup, or to wash a bowl containing rice was laid down among the Bhaggas concerning a number of monks;
and all the remaining rules were laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks by hanging [the bowl] down.

These rules were laid down concerning the matter of the inner robe (*nivāsana*) and so forth. Regarding the solicitation for soup and boiled rice, as well as in the teaching of the Dhamma and other such instances, there is one supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*) made on account of illness;
all of these are common rules (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*), not based on specific instructions (*anāṇattika*).

In all cases, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); there is no other classification of offenses (*āpatti-bheda*). The examination of failure (*vipatti-vicāraṇā*) has already been stated. At the end of all [these rules], the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth are [to be understood].
We shall demonstrate this. However, the non-offense and the factors [of the offense] must be stated in all cases; this is now being explained.

First, regarding this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), there is no offense for one who acts unintentionally, through lack of mindfulness, without knowing, when ill, in times of distress, or for those who are insane and so forth.
In that context, "unintentionally" means not intentionally thinking, "I will wear it unevenly," but rather [thinking], "I will wear it evenly."
There is no offense for one who, having become distracted, puts on the lower robe unevenly.
There is no offense for one who puts it on in that manner due to lack of mindfulness, even if he was otherwise preoccupied. There is no offense for one who does not know how to put it on evenly;
however, the proper procedure for wearing the lower robe must be learned. Furthermore, there is no offense for one whose shanks are withered or who has large masses of flesh.
Or, for the sake of its suitability, it is permissible to wear it even after lowering it by more than eight finger-breadths.
"For one who is ill" means that if there is a wound on the calf or the foot, it is permissible for him to wear it either raised up or lowered down.
"In cases of emergency" means when wild beasts or thieves are pursuing one; in such emergencies, there is no offense. [The same applies to] those who are insane and so forth.
The method is exactly as previously stated. In this case, there are three factors: lack of respect, the absence of a reason for non-offense, and wearing the lower robe unevenly.
And just as here, so too everywhere else, there are only three factors: the two preceding ones and the doing of the opposite of what was stated in each respective instance.
Therefore, from now on, I shall not mention those [factors] again, but will speak only of the non-offenses themselves.
2. Commentary on the Second Training Rule on the Circular Garment (Parimaṇḍala-sikkhāpada):

Regarding the second rule, which prohibits, "Monks, one should not wear the lay-style robe," wearing it without so doing—having made both corners even—is called the "circular wearing" (parimaṇḍala-pārupana). In that regard, whatever...
That which is worn in a manner other than the characteristic of being perfectly circular—
such as the white-clothed, the wanderer’s, the single-robe, the liquor-drinker’s, the harem-dweller’s, the Mahājeṭṭha,
the hut-enterer’s, the brahmin’s, or the *pāḷikāraka*— all this is called the "layperson’s wearing. Therefore, just as with the white cloth...
The Aḍḍhapālaka Nigaṇṭhas wrap themselves [in this manner], as do some wanderers who, having bared their chests, place the cloak upon both shoulders;

as do people wearing a single garment who, having covered their backs with one end of the wrapped cloth, place both corners on both shoulders; and as do those intoxicated by liquor and the like with their cloth.
Having wrapped it around the neck, they let both ends hang down over the chest or throw them over the back;
or as the women of the inner apartments, having shown only the pupils of their eyes, cover themselves with a veil;
or as Mahājeṭṭhā, having put on a long robe, covers her entire body with one end of it; or as farmers [cover] a field-hut.
When entering, they wrap the cloth around it, tuck it under both armpits, and cover the body with one end of it;
just as Brahmins insert the cloth between both armpits and tuck it into the tops of their shoulders,
and just as a monk who wears the *pāḷikā* robe uncovers the left arm that was covered by the single-shoulder draping.
He places the robe on the shoulder; having thus put it on, one should avoid all these faults of wearing the robe and other similar defects, and wear it without agitation and in a circular manner.

If one puts it on in such a way and, whether in the monastery or in a village, acts with negligence or makes any improper gesture, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense in cases similar to those mentioned previously, just as before.
