And here, it is thus in all cases. However, where there will be a distinction, I shall explain that.
3–4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Being Well-Covered. Regarding the third rule:
"well-covered" (*suppaṭicchanna*) means thoroughly covered; having fastened the toggle, [the robe] is worn with the neck [covered] against the wind.
The meaning is: "having covered both ears, having made them even, having tucked [the robe] up so as to cover it as far as the wrist, I shall go among the houses.
However, for one who goes without doing so, but rather with the knee or the chest exposed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
In the fourth [case], starting from the throat, the head; starting from the wrist, the hands; and starting from the flesh of the calves...
Having uncovered the feet and covered the rest, one who sits down is said to be "well-covered.
However, there is no offense for one who has entered upon the rains residence in such a manner. 5–6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Being Well-Restrained.
In the fifth [training rule], "well-restrained" means being well-disciplined without playing with one's hands or feet. The same method applies to the sixth as well.
7–8. Commentary on the Training Rule on Lowered Eyes:
In the seventh, "with lowered eyes" means having one’s eyes cast downward, looking only a yoke’s length ahead upon the ground.
While looking [ahead], it is appropriate to stand in one place and observe whether there is any danger from elephants, horses, or other such threats.
The same principle applies to the eighth [precept] as well.
9–10. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Suspended [Bowl].

Regarding the ninth [offense], "with the robe lifted": the instrumental case (*ukkhittakāya*) expresses the manner in which one has been so characterized. The meaning is: having had the robe lifted either on one side or on both sides; one must not go in such a manner starting from within the threshold of the gatepost (*indakhīla*).
Regarding the tenth, even when taking out a spittoon while seated, the robe must be taken out without being lifted up; however, there is no offense for one who has entered his dwelling. 11–12.
Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Laughing Loudly (*ujjagghika-sikkhāpada*).
In the eleventh [offense], "ujjagghikāya" means laughing with a loud laugh. Here too, the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic mark of a state (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa).
The same principle applies to the twelfth as well. In both cases, there is no offense for one who merely smiles when the matter is simply laughable.
13–14. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Loud Sounds.
In the thirteenth [precept], "not making noise" means not being loud or making a great clamor. The same principle applies to the fourteenth as well.

Here, however, the definition of "not making noise" is as follows: if, in a house twelve cubits long, the senior of the Saṅgha sits at the beginning, the second senior in the middle, and the third senior at the end, and the senior of the Saṅgha converses with the second senior—
The second elder hears his voice and discerns the manner [of speaking]. The third elder, however, hears only the sound and does not discern the manner;
at this point, it is called "little noise. But if the third elder also discerns the manner, it is called "great noise."
15…Pe…20. Commentary on the Training Rules concerning Shaking the Body, etc.
Regarding the six rules that follow from here, “shaking the body” (*kāyappacālaka*) means shaking the body again and again; this same method applies everywhere.
Therefore, one must walk and sit having held the body and other limbs steady and set them straight. Regarding those [rules] connected with sitting:
There is no offense for one who has entered the three rainy-season retreats.
21–22. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Leaning on the Hips:
Regarding the twenty-first and twenty-second rules, "leaning on the hips" means placing the hand on the hip and leaning against it.
23–24. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Being Veiled:
In the twenty-third and twenty-fourth [rules], "veiled" (*oguṇṭhita*) means having covered one's head.
25. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Squatting:

In the twenty-fifth [training rule], "on tiptoe" (*ukkuṭikā*) refers to walking while lifting the heels and touching the ground only with the tips of the feet, or lifting the tips of the feet and touching the ground only with the heels; here, the term expressing the action (*karaṇavacana*) has the very characteristic already described.
26. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding the *Pallatthika* (Crossed Legs):
In the twenty-sixth, "not with crossed legs" (*na pallatthikāya*), one must not sit with either the hands crossed or the robe (*dussa*) crossed.

For one who sits down disrespectfully, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, for one who has entered for the night, there is no offense here as well as in the preceding twenty-two and twenty-four rules.
The commentary on the twenty-sixth training rule concerning what is appropriate is finished.
27. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Receiving with Care.
Regarding the first [training rule] among those connected with food: "carefully" means having established mindfulness. 28.
Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Receiving with Mindfulness of the Bowl:

In the second [rule], "mindfulness of the bowl" (*pattasaññā*) is the awareness regarding the bowl; one who possesses that is "mindful of the bowl" (*pattasaññī*). The meaning is: being one whose mindfulness is fixed upon his own vessel.
29. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Receiving an Equal Amount of Curry.

Regarding the third [rule]: "An equal amount of curry" (*samasūpaka*) refers to a hand-held curry made with mung beans, peas, or lentils, etc., which constitutes one-fourth of the measure of the rice;
for one who takes more than that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Excluding...
However, the soup itself and all other varieties of soups and condiments are called "the essence of flavor" (*rasarasa*).
Regarding that essence of flavor, there is no offense here if it is for the sake of one's relatives, or for those who have been invited, or for the sake of another, or using one's own wealth.
30... [etc. ...32. Commentary on the Training Rule on Leveling the Bowl (*samatittika-sikkhāpada*).
In the fourth [rule], "level to the brim" means filled level to the top, arranged so as not to exceed the rim of the bowl's mouth when it has been determined (adhiṭṭhānupaga).
Regarding "alms-food," anything that is to be consumed within the proper time (yāvakālika) is permitted.

However, in the case of what is not determined (anadhiṭṭhānupaga), things to be consumed within the proper time, as well as those to be consumed during the watch of the night (yāmakālika) and so forth, are allowed even if they are heaped up anywhere; but as for that which is taken from two bowls...
Having filled one [bowl], he carries it to the monastery; or whatever—such as cakes, sugar-candy, fruits, and so forth—is placed inside and falls out below;
or things such as *takkola* and *vaṭaṃsaka* flowers that are given after being set upon [the bowl];
and whatever is placed in a leaf or a dish and set on top of the bowl—all that is not called "heaped up" (*thūpīkata*). Therefore, all of that...
It is permissible. However, in this case, there is no exemption even for one who is ill; therefore, he too must take exactly the same amount.
In all instances, it is not permissible to accept [the medicine] at all; but once accepted, it is permissible to consume it provided it has been properly accepted.
The fifth and sixth cases are exactly as described by the method already stated.
33–34. Commentary on the Training Rule on Going from House to House (*Sapadāna-sikkhāpada*).
Regarding the term "from house to house" (*sapadāna*) in the seventh [rule]: it means going in regular succession without leaving out any part here or there.

However, for one who gives to others, or pours into another vessel, or skips from this to that, as well as for one who takes the subsequent portion (*uttaribhaṅga*) out of order, [there is an offense].
There is no offense here even for one who takes [the food]. The eighth [training rule] is exactly as previously stated.
35. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Piled-up Food:

Regarding the ninth [rule], "piled up" (*thūpakata*) means from the top down to the middle. However, there is no offense for one who eats after gathering what remains in small quantities together and pressing them down.
36. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Covering of Rice (*odanappaṭicchādanasikkhāpada*):

In the tenth [training rule], there is no offense for one whose meal-provider gives curry after having covered the rice during times such as the festival of Māgha, provided that person does not cover it out of a desire for more; however, because the sick person is not included, there is indeed an offense for them.
37. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Requesting of Soup and Rice (*sūpodanaviññattisikkhāpada*):

In the eleventh [offense], the phrase "for the sake of relatives or those who have invited one, or for the sake of another, using one’s own wealth" is an addition not found in the case of non-offense.
38. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Perception of Censure (*Ujjhānasaññīsikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā*):

In the twelfth [offense], "perception of censure" (*ujjhānasaññā*) means the perception of censure; one who possesses that is "one who perceives censure" (*ujjhānasaññī*). Here too, one who is ill is not exempt. However, there is no offense for one who looks [at the gift] with the thought, "I will give it," or "I will have it given," provided he does not perceive censure.
39. Commentary on the Training Rule on Mouthfuls (Kabaḷasikkhāpada):

Regarding the thirteenth rule, "not too large," the peacock's egg is too large and the hen's egg is too small; the measure is that which is between these two. However, there is no offense regarding any kind of solid food, such as the various types of root-vegetables, or fruits.
40. Commentary on the Training Rule on Lumps of Food (Ālopasikkhāpada)
In the fourteenth [precept], "parimaṇḍala" means not long. Here, however, there is no offense even with regard to "uttaribhaṅga" (additional food) when it consists of solid foods or fruits.
41–42. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Not Bringing [Food]:
In the fifteenth, "anāhaṭe" means not brought; the meaning is that it has not reached the gateway of the mouth. In the sixteenth, "sabbahatthaṃ" means the entire hand.
43. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Having a Mouthful of Food (Sakabaḷasikkhāpada):
Regarding the seventeenth rule, "with a mouthful of food" (*sakabaḷena*), an offense is incurred for one who speaks to the extent that the speech remains incomplete.
However, if one who is preaching the Dhamma places haritaka or other such items in the mouth while speaking, to whatever extent [the speech is interrupted]...
The speech is not incomplete; it is sufficient as long as the mouth remains at that size.
44. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Throwing Lumps of Food:
Regarding the eighteenth rule, "throwing lumps of food" (*piṇḍukkhepaka*), this means throwing lump after lump [of food]. Here too, there is no offense regarding edible foods and fruits.
45. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Breaking off Mouthfuls (*kabaḷāvacchedaka-sikkhāpada*):

Regarding the nineteenth rule, "breaking off mouthfuls" means breaking off mouthful by mouthful. Herein, there is no offense even with regard to solid foods and fruits when they are used as a subsequent meal (*uttaribhaṅga*).
46. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Cheek-Filling (*avagaṇḍakāraka-sikkhāpada*):
Regarding the twentieth [offense], "one who makes goiters": like a monkey, having repeatedly formed goiters;
here, there is no offense for merely picking fruits. 47. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Shaking the Hand:

Regarding the twenty-first, "shaking the hand," it means shaking the hand again and again; however, in the context of what constitutes no offense, the phrase "shaking the hand while discarding refuse" is added as an exception.
48. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Scattering Rice Grains (*Sitthāvakāraka-sikkhāpada*):

Regarding the twenty-second rule, "scattering rice grains" (*sitthāvakāraka*), it means scattering rice grains repeatedly. Here too, the phrase "while throwing away refuse, one throws away a rice grain" is the additional factor that constitutes an offense;
otherwise, there is no offense. 49. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Protruding the Tongue (*Jivhānicchāraka-sikkhāpada*)...
In the twenty-third [training rule], "protruding the tongue," it means protruding the tongue again and again.
50–51. Commentary on the training rule concerning making a *capu-capu* sound:
In the twenty-fourth, "*capu-capu*," it means making the sound *capu, capu* repeatedly. In the twenty-fifth, the same method applies.
52… Pe… 54. Commentary on the Training Rules concerning Licking the Hand, etc.
Regarding the twenty-sixth rule, *hatthanillehakaṃ*: "licking the hand" means licking the hand repeatedly. For one who is eating, it is not permitted to lick even as much as a finger's breadth.
However, in the case of thick gruel, molasses, porridge, and so forth, having taken [the food] with the fingers, the fingers [may be licked].
It is permissible to eat after having placed [the food] in the mouth; the same principle applies to the twenty-seventh and twenty-eighth [rules].
Therefore, the bowl must not be licked even with a single finger, nor should even a single lip be licked with the tongue;
however, it is permissible to take [the food] with the flesh of the lips themselves and place it inside [the mouth].
55. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning What is Mixed with Worldly Pleasures (Sāmisasikkhāpada):
In the twenty-ninth [rule], "not with what is mixed with worldly pleasures" (na sāmisenāti), this is prohibited by way of its repulsiveness;
therefore, whether it belongs to the Saṅgha, to an individual, to a householder, or to oneself, and whether it is in a conch-shell bowl, a small bowl, or a platter, it is not [to be used].

It must indeed be taken; for one who takes it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, if a certain part of the hand is not smeared with food, it is permissible to take hold of it by that part;
in this context, the phrase "he accepts it thinking, 'I will wash it' or 'I will have it washed'" is an additional factor regarding the absence of an offense.
56. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Rice Grains:

In the thirtieth [training rule], the phrase “having lifted out, or having broken off, or having poured into a receptacle, or having taken out, he discards it” is additional to the cases where there is no offense.
Therein, “having lifted out” means having lifted rice grains out from the water, into one [receptacle].
Having made a heap in a suitable place, he discards the water. "Or having broken it up" means having broken up the rice grains and made them fit for flowing away with the water, he discards them.
"In a receptacle" means he discards them in a receptacle belonging to those who receive by means of a bowl.
"Having carried out" means having carried it outside, he discards it; for one who discards it in this manner, there is no offense.
The commentary on the training rule concerning eating with thirty people is finished.
57. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning One Holding an Umbrella:
Among those connected with the teaching of the Dhamma, "one who has anything at all in his hand that is an umbrella" is called *chattapāṇi*. He...
Having placed that umbrella on any part of the body, as long as one does not let it go with the hand, it is not permissible to teach the Dhamma to that person.

However, if someone else holds the umbrella for him, or if it is standing by his side, then as soon as it has left his hand, he is no longer considered "one with an umbrella in hand" (chattapāṇi), and it is permissible to teach him the Dhamma. This is the section on the Dhamma.
And here, this should be understood according to the method already stated in the *Padasodhamma*.
58–59. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning One Holding a Staff (*Daṇḍapāṇi-sikkhāpada*):
In the second [rule], "a staff" (*daṇḍa*) means one measuring four cubits (*catuhattha*) for a man of medium height; as for the state of "one holding a staff" (*daṇḍapāṇibhāva*), it is...
It should be understood in the same manner as stated for the *Chattapāṇi* (Umbrella-bearer) rule. The same method applies to the third [rule] as well.
For even one who stands having girded a sword does not come under the designation of a *Satthapāṇi* (Sword-bearer).
60. Commentary on the *Āvudhapāṇi* (Weapon-bearer) Training Rule.
In the fourth case, all varieties of bows together with the varieties of arrows should be understood as "weapons.

Therefore, it is not permissible to teach the Dhamma to one who is standing or sitting while holding a bow together with an arrow, or holding a bare bow, or a bare arrow, or a strung bow, or an unstrung bow. However, if his bow...
It is also tied to the shoulder; it is permissible as long as one does not yet take hold of it.
61–62. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Sandals:
Regarding the fifth rule, "for one who has put on sandals," this refers to one who merely steps [on them] without inserting the fingers into the gaps between the handles of the sunshade.
Or, having inserted it, it is "unfastened" by virtue of its position; this same principle applies to the sixth [offense] as well.
However, in this case, it is also not permissible for that which is called "unfastened" because the heel-strap has been removed and it remains in its place.
63. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Vehicles.

In the seventh case, even if he is carried by two people using their joined hands, or is carried on a bamboo pole after being placed in a cloth, or is seated even on the axle of an unsuitable vehicle such as a cart that has been dismantled and set down, he is still reckoned as one who has gone by vehicle.
However, it is permissible if both [the monk and the driver] are seated in the same vehicle. It is also permissible if they are seated separately.
It is permissible for one seated in a high vehicle to teach someone seated in a low one; it is also permissible when both are of equal status.
Likewise, it is permissible for one seated in front to teach someone seated behind. However, it is not permissible for one seated in a higher position behind to teach someone seated in front.
64. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Lying Down.

Regarding the eighth [offense], "to one who has gone to bed": it is not permitted for one standing or sitting on a high couch, a chair, or even on the ground to teach someone who is lying down—even if only on a straw mat or on natural ground.
However, it is permitted for one who has gone to bed to teach another who has gone to bed while lying down on a higher level or on an equal level. By one who is lying down...

However, it is permissible for one who is standing, sitting, or lying down [to teach] to another who is standing, sitting, or lying down; and for one sitting to teach another who is standing or sitting;
and for one standing to teach another who is likewise standing.
65. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Crossed Ankles.
In the ninth [precept], it is not permitted to teach one who is sitting in any posture such as the "hand-rest" position (hatthapallatthika).
66. Commentary on the Tenth Training Rule:

Regarding "one whose head is wrapped," this refers to one whose head is wrapped with a cloth or with a topknot (*moḷi*) and so forth, such that the hairline is not visible; for this very reason, it is stated in the exemption from offense: "having caused the hairline to be uncovered, he teaches."
67. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding the Veiled Head:
In the eleventh rule, "with the head veiled" means with the head covered; however, regarding the non-offense herein, the phrase "having uncovered the head, he confesses" is additional.
68. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding the Bare Ground:
In the twelfth [training rule], "having sat on the ground" means having sat upon the earth. "On a seat" includes even one who has sat down after spreading out a cloth or blades of grass.
69. Commentary on the Thirteenth Training Rule concerning a Low Seat:
"On a high seat" refers to one sitting even on a slightly elevated portion of the ground.
70. Commentary on the Training Rule on Standing:
Regarding the fourteenth rule, "one who is not standing [should not answer] one who is sitting":

if a great elder, while sitting on his seat, asks a question of a junior monk who has gone to attend upon the elder and is standing, he should not speak. However, out of respect for the elder, [the junior monk] should rise...
It is not possible to say, "Ask [me]," therefore it is permissible to say, "I shall speak to the bhikkhu standing behind me.
71. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Walking Behind:
In the fifteenth [training rule], if one walking in front asks a question, if one does not answer him but [speaks] to the one behind—

"I shall speak to the bhikkhu"—thus it should be spoken. However, it is permissible to recite the Dhamma that has been learned together [with him], or to speak it to one who is traveling with an equal burden.
72. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Traveling by a Wrong Path.

Regarding the sixteenth [training rule], "not by a side path": here, if both carts travel with equal loads on the cart road, whether by the track of a single wheel or by a side path, it is permissible.
73. Commentary on the Seventeenth Training Rule concerning Defecating While Standing:

Regarding the phrase "unintentionally" (*asañcicca*) in the context of non-offense—if, while one is going toward a concealed place, feces or urine are discharged suddenly, it is called "done unintentionally."
74. Explanation of the Training Rule on Excrement on Green Growth:
In the eighteenth [rule], even if the root of a living tree is visible in the earth or a branch is touching the ground, all of it is indeed reckoned as green growth (*harita*).
However, having sat upon the trunk, if one voids excrement in a place that is not green growth...

It is permissible to throw it down. If, while he is looking toward a non-grassy area, [the animal] suddenly exits, and he is standing in a place that is sickly (or afflicted), thinking, "What was done on non-grass is now overflowing onto grass"—this is an additional point regarding non-offense here.
In that case, even if he cannot find a non-grassy spot, having set aside a bundle of grass or a bundle of straw...
If one spreads green grass over it afterwards, it is indeed permissible. Here, "saliva" includes mucus as well.
75. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Defecating in Water:
In the nineteenth rule, the phrase "not in water" is stated with reference specifically to water used for consumption; it does not apply to water in latrines, the ocean, and so forth.
However, there is no offense regarding things that are not for use. When it rains and floods arise on all sides, if one cannot find a place free of water, it is permissible to do so in the water;
here too, the phrase "if made on dry land, it is submerged by water" is the additional factor regarding the absence of offense.
The rest is clear in all the training rules.
Furthermore, to illustrate the origin and other characteristics here, this supplementary explanation is given: these ten training rules—the four connected with loud laughter and high-pitched voices;

the one consisting of speaking with food in the mouth; and the five connected with sitting on the ground, sitting on a low seat, standing, walking behind, and walking along the path—have admonition as their origin.
In each case, there is a single act of volition (*kiriyā*), and they are exempt from the requirement of specific perception (*saññā-vimokkha*).

[These are] with consciousness, offenses against the world, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and painful feeling. The training rule on requesting soup or rice originates from theft and a caravan;

it is an act, released through perception, with consciousness, an offense against the world, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and painful feeling. [The following categories are: one with a sunshade in hand, one with a staff in hand, one with a weapon in hand, one with a sword in hand, one with shoes, one with sandals, one in a vehicle, one on a bed, one lying on his side, one wrapped up, and one with a covered head.

There are eleven origins of the teaching on the rules (dhammadesanāsamuṭṭhāna): those that are both action and non-action (kiriyākiriyā), those involving liberation through perception (saññāvimokkha), those associated with consciousness (sacittaka), those blameworthy by nature in the world (lokavajja), those consisting of verbal action (vacīkamma), those connected with unwholesome consciousness (akusalacitta), and those connected with painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).
The remaining thirty-five are classified according to their origins, such as the first *pārājika* offense, and so forth.
The commentary on the training rules (sikkhāpada) associated with the nineteen teachings on the rules is hereby concluded.
The commentary on the Sekhiya rules in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Pātimokkhavaṇṇanā* is finished.
Now follows the commentary on the *Adhikaraṇasamatha* (Methods for Settling Legal Issues).

"Seven among the methods for settling legal issues (*adhikaraṇasamatha*)" refers to their numerical limit. They are called "methods for settling legal issues" because they settle—that is, bring to an end—legal issues.

"They come up for recitation" means that they come up for recitation in order to inquire as to whether one is pure regarding offenses categorized as legal issues arising from transgressions (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), as well as regarding the remaining three types of legal issues which serve as their causes. "Of those that have arisen repeatedly" means...

"Of those that have arisen"—that is, of those that have arisen repeatedly. "Legal issues" (*adhikaraṇa*) refers to these four: the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), the legal issue of accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*), the legal issue of offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), and the legal issue of business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).
"For the settling and pacification" means for the purpose of settling and for the purpose of pacifying;

thus, these seven methods of settling (*samatha*)—beginning with resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*) and ending with covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*)—should be applied. Herein, this is the analysis.

Regarding legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*): first, the dispute among monks who quarrel over eighteen grounds as to whether it is "Dhamma" or "non-Dhamma" is called a *vivādādhikaraṇa* (a legal issue arising from a dispute).

Or, the censure, reproach, and formal accusation of those who accuse others of failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*), or of failure in conduct, view, or livelihood, is called an *anuvādādhikaraṇa* (a legal issue arising from an accusation).
The seven classes of offenses—namely, the five found in the *Mātikā* and the two in the *Vibhaṅga*—are called the "legal issue of offense" (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
The performance of the four types of formal acts (*kamma*) for the Saṅgha, such as the act of seeking permission (*apalokana*), is called the "legal issue of business" (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).

Among these, the "legal issue of dispute" (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) is settled by two means of settlement: by resolution in the presence of the parties (*sammukhāvinaya*) and by the majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*).
And, while being settled by *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of the accused), whether in the very monastery where it arose,
or on the way while those going elsewhere to settle it, or at the place where it was handed over to the Saṅgha after they had gone there—
if the Saṅgha is unable to settle it there, it is decided right then by persons appointed to a committee (*ubbāhikā*).

When there is such agreement, then that which consists of being face-to-face with the Saṅgha, being face-to-face with the Dhamma, being face-to-face with the Vinaya, and being face-to-face with the individual—this is called *sammukhāvinaya*. In this context, the presence of the performing Saṅgha by way of the concord of the Saṅgha is "being face-to-face with the Saṅgha";
the reality of the matter to be settled is "being face-to-face with the Dhamma," just as...

That [matter] must be brought together; likewise, its being before the Vinaya means the presence of the one who is to be reconciled. And "presence of persons" (puggala-sammukhatā) is the face-to-face presence of both parties—the one who disputes and the one with whom he disputes—both of whom are adversaries in the matter.
However, in the case of settlement by a committee (ubbāhikā), the "presence of the Saṅgha" (saṅgha-sammukhatā) is excluded here.
In this way, it is settled first and foremost through the resolution face-to-face (sammukhā-vinaya).

But if even this does not settle the matter, then the monks authorized by the committee hand him over to the Saṅgha itself, saying, "We are unable to settle it. Thereupon, the Saṅgha, having appointed a monk endowed with five qualities as the distributor of voting tickets (*salākaggāhāpaka*),
[proceeds] by means of those three methods of distributing voting tickets— namely, the secret ballot (*guḷhaka*), the open ballot (*vivaṭṭaka*), and the whispering into the ear (*sakaṇṇajappaka*).

Having distributed voting tickets by means of one [representative] from each group, when the assembled assembly consists mostly of those who speak according to the Dhamma, the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) is settled in accordance with what those speakers of the Dhamma say; thus it is settled both by resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*) and by majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*).
In this context, resolution face-to-face follows the method already explained; as for the formal act of majority decision (*yebhuyyasikakamma*):
This is called *yebhuyyasikā* (decision by majority). Thus, a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) is settled by two means of settlement.
A legal issue arising from an accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*) is settled by four means of settlement:

by presence (*sammukhāvinaya*), by recollection (*sativinaya*), by being of sound mind (*amūḷhavinaya*), and by further penalty (*tassapāpiyasikā*). When it is being settled by presence alone, there is both the one who accuses and the one who is accused.
Having heard their words, if there is no offense, both should be asked for forgiveness; if there is one, the matter is settled when it has been determined thus:
"This is the offense here. In that case, the characteristic of *saṃmukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of) is exactly as described by the aforementioned method.

However, when a monk whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) is accused of a failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*) on groundless charges, [the Buddha] prescribed *sativinaya* (settlement by recollection).

When the Saṅgha grants a verdict of past insanity (*sativinaya*) to one who requests it by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*), then the matter is settled both by the verdict of presence (*sammukhāvinaya*) and the verdict of past insanity.
Once the verdict of past insanity has been granted, no further accusation can be brought against that person.
This applies when a monk who was insane commits unmonastic transgressions due to his state of madness.
When he is being reproved by the monks, saying, “Venerable sir, you remember such an offense,” and although he says, “Friends, this was done by me while I was insane;

I do not remember it,” yet while being reproved by the monks, he again requests *amūḷhavinaya* (settlement for one who is no longer insane) so that there may be no further reproval, the Saṅgha grants him *amūḷhavinaya* by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a third proclamation (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*). At that time, [the case] is settled by *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of).

And when a dispute is settled by the verdict of past insanity (*amūḷhavinaya*), once that verdict of past insanity has been granted, no further accusation based on that same matter can succeed against that person. However,
when one who is being accused of an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*) or something bordering on an offense entailing defeat evades the issue by speaking of something else...
When the Saṅgha— perceiving that because of the prevalence of evil this person has become worse, thinking, "If he has not cut off the root [of his offense],
he will obtain reinstatement by conducting himself properly; but if he has cut off the root, his own destruction will follow"—

performs a *tassapāpiyasika* (further-punishment) legal act against him by a formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*), then it is by means of *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of).
And when it is settled by the procedure for the worse (*tassapāpiyasikā*), the legal issue arising from an accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*) is thus settled by four methods of settlement.

A legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is settled by three methods of settlement: by presence (*sammukhāvinaya*), by acting according to what has been admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*), and by covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*).
There is no settling of it by presence alone; however, when [it concerns] one person...
When a monk confesses a light offense in the midst of the Saṅgha or a group, according to the method explained in the commentary on the *nissaggiya* rules,

then the legal issue arising from that offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is settled by means of resolution in the presence of the parties (*sammukhāvinaya*) and by means of acting according to what has been admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*).

Regarding these, first, in the case of resolution in the presence of the parties, "presence of persons" (*puggalasammukhatā*) refers to the presence of both the one who confesses and the one to whom the confession is made.
The rest is exactly as previously stated. However, at the time of teaching for an individual or a group, the requirement of being in the presence of the Saṅgha is omitted.
As for the admission here—“Venerable sir, I have fallen into such-and-such an offense,” and the responses “Do you see [it]?

and “Yes, I see it”—the act of saying, “You should exercise restraint in the future,” based on that admission, is called *paṭiññātakaraṇa* (acting according to what has been admitted). Regarding the *saṅghādisesa* offenses:
The formal request for probation and so forth is called *paṭiññā* (admission); the granting of probation and so forth is called *paṭiññātakaraṇa* (acting according to admission).
However, when monks who have become partisans and are quarrelsome commit many unbecoming transgressions of the ascetic life, and later, when a sense of shame arises in them, they think:
"If we deal with one another regarding these offenses, this legal dispute might lead to harshness."
Seeing the fault in causing one another to commit an offense, thinking, "It would lead to harm," when they perform the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over with grass) legal act,

then the legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is settled both by resolution in the presence of the accused (*sammukhāvinaya*) and by the covering over with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*). For in that case,
as many as have come within arm’s reach do not manifest their view by saying, "This is not acceptable to me," and even while sleeping...
They become subject to the *okkanta* (falling away); with the exception of grave offenses (*thullavajja*) and those connected with householders, they emerge from all other offenses.
Thus, a legal issue concerning an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is settled by three means of settlement.
A legal issue concerning business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*) is settled by one means of settlement, namely, by face-to-face resolution (*sammukhāvinaya*). Thus are these four legal issues.
These seven methods of settling (samatha) settle [disputes] according to their respective suitability; therefore it is said:
"For the settling and pacification of disputes as they arise, the face-to-face settlement (sammukhāvinaya) should be granted... [and so on] ...up to the covering over with grass (tiṇavatthāraka).
This is the method of analysis here; the detailed exposition, however, is found in the Samathakkhandhaka itself, and its analysis is also stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.
Regarding this, I ask the venerable ones: "Are you pure in these seven ways of settling legal issues?
I ask whether you are pure in these seven methods of settling disputes, and whether there is nothing among you that needs to be settled by these means;
by this, the state of being pure from all offenses is inquired after.
"Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited," and so forth, is the concluding statement. In that context, "this much" refers to this many training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
"Contained in the Sutta" means it appears in the Sutta, namely the Pātimokkha. "Included within the Sutta" means it is comprised therein.
"It comes to be recited every half-month" means it comes to be recited every half-month by way of the Uposatha ceremony.
"United" means united by way of physical concord. "In harmony" means rejoicing well through a single inclination by way of mental concord.
"Without disputing" means not disputing even on account of any one of the eighteen grounds for dispute.
"Should train" means that the training in higher virtue should be accomplished by those who do not transgress this or that rule of training. From time to time...
However, as for that which was not stated, all of it has already been explained in the preceding training rules (sikkhāpada) and its meaning is self-evident.
The commentary on the settlement of legal issues (adhikaraṇasamatha) is concluded. [End of] the Commentary on the Pātimokkha from the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*.
The Commentary on the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha.
The Chapter on Defeat was proclaimed as the Pātimokkha for the benefit of the bhikkhunīs;
since the Protector has done this, the turn has now arrived for its commentary.
The Common Pārājikas 1–4:
Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sexual Intercourse.
Herein, the meaning of the phrases beginning with “Let him hear me” should be understood in the same manner as explained in the commentary on the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha.
For, venerable sir, there is only a difference in mere terminology and a difference in gender between that [text] and this one, beginning with the words "the noble lady" (*ayyā*) and so forth.

And because for a bhikkhunī there is no such thing as a formal renunciation of the training (*sikkhā-paccakkhāna*), therefore, instead of saying of the bhikkhunīs, "having entered upon the training and livelihood, having not renounced the training and not disclosed their weakness," it says: "But whichever bhikkhunī, out of her own will, engages in sexual intercourse..."
"It is said: 'One should practice the Dhamma. In this context, 'with desire' means with both the desire and the inclination associated with sexual passion.
However, if there is no desire, there is no offense even for one who has been forced by physical compulsion.
Therefore, for a fully ordained bhikkhunī, [it is an offense] toward any person—whether human, non-human, or of the animal realm—including males, hermaphrodites, or eunuchs."
If, with one's own sexual organ— whether it be alive or dead, covered or uncovered, intact or mostly intact—
one inserts even as much as a sesame seed into any of the three orifices (the anus,
the urinary tract, or the mouth), whether they are covered or uncovered, provided it is not touched by natural wind and is within the internal space; this constitutes an offense.
If she causes a part [of the organ] to enter intentionally, or if, while being caused to enter by another, she consents to any of the acts of entering, having entered, remaining, or withdrawing,
she incurs a *pārājika* offense. The rest here, as well as in the subsequent common training rules (*sādhāraṇasikkhāpada*),
should be understood according to the method already explained.
The Unshared Pārājika 5.
Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Those Who Raise Their Knees Above the Knees.
Regarding the four unshared pārājikas, first, in the phrase "one who is lustful" (*avassutā*), it refers to one who has passion for physical contact.
*Tintā* means "moistened. The same principle applies to the second word as well.
*Purisapuggalassa* refers to a person counted as a male, a human being of discerning mind, capable of engaging in physical contact.
*Adhakkhakaṃ* means below one's own collarbones. *Ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalaṃ* means above the kneecaps; and here, "above the knees" (*ubbhakapparaṃ*) is also included.
It is grasped with the thighs raised above the knees. "Touching" (āmasana) means stroking;
it is the rubbing right there without crossing over the area already touched. "Grasping" (parāmasana) means moving here and there. "Seizing" (gahaṇa) means merely taking hold.
"Contact" (chupana) means merely touching without rubbing. "Pressing" (paṭipīḷana) means squeezing after having seized a limb. "Should consent" (sādiyeyya): [means...]
If a bhikkhunī consents to a man’s touching her body, within the limits of her own body as previously defined, or if she herself, with her own body,
touches any part of the man’s body, this is called the offense of *ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā*,
a *pārājika*; such is the summary here.
Regarding the detailed analysis beginning with “The source, the person, the subject matter,” since all [of these] are unique designations (asādhāraṇa-paññatti),
from this point forward, after stating a supplementary rule (anupaññatti) as it exists, we shall not mention whether it is a common designation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti) or a unique designation;
rather, in the case of an injunction (āṇatti), where there is no injunction, we shall say nothing, but where one exists—
We shall explain that very point; the investigation of failure has already been stated.
However, the remainder must be stated for all cases, and this is now being said:
first, this training rule was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Sundarīnandā, on account of the incident of engaging in physical contact, when she was lustful toward one [of the monks].

If, with a body as defined [by the rule], she touches a man’s body; or if both are lustful, she touches what is connected to his body with her own body as defined, or with the remainder of her body connected to that defined part; for touching his body, there is a thullaccaya.
This applies to yakkhas, petas, paṇḍakas, animals, and those in human form who are lustful on both sides, using a body as defined.
Even for one who touches body with body, there is a *thullaccaya*; however, if the man lacks lust for physical contact, there is only a *thullaccaya* even within the sphere of a *pārājika* offense.
In all other cases—such as those involving body-to-body contact and its various permutations, as well as lust for sexual intercourse, laughter, or affection—there is a *dukkaṭa*.
[This applies] when it is unintentional, when done through lack of mindfulness, or when done unknowingly.

There is no offense for one who does not consent, nor for those who are insane and so forth. The factors, origins, and other details should be understood in the same manner as explained under the rule on physical contact in the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha.
The commentary on the training rule concerning touching above the knees is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Concealer of Faults (Vajjappaṭicchādikā-sikkhāpada).
In the second [rule], "of the community" means of other bhikkhunīs. "Standing" means standing within the [bhikkhunī] order. "Deceased" means one who has passed away.
"Expelled" means either lost by her own act through the removal of the [monastic] marks, or expelled by others. "Defected" means one who has gone over to another religious sect.

“I have known [it], noble lady”— this indicates the time at which she spoke those words. However, once it is known that she remains within the status of a bhikkhunī and has committed a *pārājika* offense,
the moment one thinks, “I will not tell anyone now,” and simply relinquishes the responsibility, this person becomes a *pārājika* offender for concealing a fault (*vajjappaṭicchādikā*).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, in the case of not reporting to the Saṅgha after having reproved oneself.
The rest here should be understood in the same manner as stated under the training rule on concealing a grave offense (*duṭṭhulla-āpatti*) in the *Sappāṇaka-vagga*.
For there it is a *pācittiya*, whereas here it is a *pārājika*; this alone is the distinction, while the remainder is exactly the same.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the concealer of a *vajja* is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning one who follows a suspended monk:
In the third [rule], "suspended" (*ukkhitto*) means suspended for not seeing an offense and so forth. "In accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammena*) means by means of the factual basis (*vatthu*).

"By means of the discipline (*vinaya*)" means having accused and reminded [the offender]. "By means of the Teacher’s instruction (*satthusāsana*)"—here too, the very act of accusing and reminding is what is called the Teacher’s instruction.

"Disrespectful" means lacking respect toward the Saṅgha that has performed the act of suspension (*ukkhepaniyakamma*), or toward that [Saṅgha] itself, or toward the group included therein, or toward the individual, or toward that formal act;
the meaning is one who does not practice proper conduct (*sammāvattanā*).
"Without atonement" (*appaṭikāraṃ*) means devoid of atonement; the meaning is "not restored. "One who has not made a companion" (*akatasahāyaṃ*):

in communal living such as performing formal acts together (*ekakamma*), those monks who share the same communion by way of acting together are called "companions. However, for one who does not have that communal living with them, he has not made them his companions;
thus, he is called "one who has not made a companion," and [the text refers to] him as "one who has not made a companion."
The meaning is: "not having entered into the state of common residence.
"She should follow him" means that whatever view that suspended monk holds—remaining in the very state of being suspended—that nun should follow by way of adopting that same view.
That nun [is subject to an offense] according to the method stated in the Saṅghabhedasikkhāpada and other rules, within the midst of the Saṅgha.

And when she is being addressed [by the Saṅgha] and does not relinquish that matter, at the conclusion of the formal act of admonition (samanubhāsanakamma), she becomes one who follows a suspended nun (ukkhitānuvattikā) and is thus guilty of a Pārājika offense.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā in the case of following a suspended nun; for the motion (ñatti), it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

With two formal proclamations (*kammavācā*), there are two *thullaccaya* offenses; with the third formal proclamation, which has reached the syllable "ya" in the phrase "She to whom it does not please, let her speak," there is a *pārājika* offense.

For an illegal procedure (*adhammakamma*), there is a triple *dukkaṭa*. The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated in the training rule on schism in the Saṅgha (*saṅghabhedasikkhāpada*) and other rules.
The commentary on the training rule concerning those who follow one who has been suspended is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Eight Points:
Regarding the fourth [point], "lustful" (*avassutā*) means being moistened by the passion for physical contact through intimacy with friends and worldly pleasures. This very...
For this meaning is stated in the *Sīhaḷa-mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, while its detailed analysis is provided in the *Samantapāsādikā*;

the same method applies to the second phrase as well. Furthermore, in expressions such as "taking the hand of a person," that which is taken by the hand by a person is called "the taking of the hand of a person"—this is the same method.
Also in the case of grasping the corner of the outer robe (*saṅghāṭikaṇṇaggahaṇa*). Regarding "grasping the hand" (*hatthaggahaṇa*):
here, the grasping of any limb whatsoever that does not constitute a field for an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*) is "grasping the hand";

the grasping of any part of what is wrapped or covered is "grasping the corner of the outer robe. In the phrases beginning with "should stand together," there is the unrighteousness (*asaddhamma*) known as bodily contact.
She stands within arm’s reach of a man for the purpose of enjoyment; or, standing there, she converses with him;
or, being told by the man, “Come to such-and-such a place,” she goes to that rendezvous;
or, she consents to the arrival of that man; or, she enters some concealed place with him. Of a man...
"Standing within arm's reach, she should apply her body"— this is how the meaning is to be understood. "This too is a *pārājika*" means that, just like the previous cases,

this nun also becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense called "the eight bases" (*aṭṭhavatthukā*) if, for the purpose of engaging in that which is not the true Dhamma— namely, physical contact— she fulfills these eight bases either in direct order or in reverse order.
At Sāvatthī, concerning the group of six bhikkhunīs, the eighth rule was laid down regarding the completion of the offense:
for going by appointment, there is an *dukkaṭa* for every step; upon merely entering the reach of a man’s hand, there is a *thullaccaya*;
and even when the man approaches her, there is a *dukkaṭa*. Upon entering the reach of his hand, there is a *thullaccaya*; as for the remaining cases...
For each [instance], there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) only; when the eighth is completed, it is a *pārājika* (defeat).

However, even if one has transgressed against each of these bases (*vatthu*) a hundred times, one is freed by confessing those offenses. Furthermore, in this context, it should be understood that the offense is determined by the count (*gaṇanūpikā*).
For an offense is counted as confessed only when one has made a formal renunciation of the burden, thinking, "I shall not commit this again"; thus, it is the number of confessions that matters.

It does not constitute an element of a *pārājika* offense. Therefore, one who has committed one [offense], having laid down the burden and confessed it, but then commits it again through the influence of defilements and confesses it once more—even if she thus fulfills the eighth [repetition]—is not *pārājika*.
However, for one who, after committing [an offense], confesses it while still intent on the thought, "I shall commit another basis [of offense] again," [it is different].
That offense is not subject to counting; even if confessed, it remains unconfessed and constitutes a factor for a *pārājika*.
There is no offense in the case of one who acts unintentionally, through lack of mindfulness, without knowing, or without consenting, nor in the case of those who are insane and so forth.

The three factors here are: lust for physical contact, the presence of intent, and the fulfillment of the eighth basis (*vatthu*). It originates from formal admonition (*samanubhāsana*); it is both an action and a non-action.

It is accompanied by perception, involves consciousness, is blameworthy according to the world, is bodily action, is verbal action, is an unwholesome state of mind, and is associated with two types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rules consisting of eight bases is finished.
"Venerable ladies, the eight *pārājika* rules have been recited": four of these were laid down for monks and are common to both [orders].
"These four" means that the eight *pārājika* rules have been recited by way of this recitation of the *Pātimokkha*;
such is the meaning to be understood here. The remainder is exactly according to the method stated in the commentary on the *Bhikkhu-pātimokkha*.
[End of] the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Pātimokkha-vaṇṇanā*.
The commentary on the Pārājika rules in the Bhikkhunīpātimokkha is finished.
The section on Saṅghādisesa offenses.

1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Litigation (Ussayavādikā-sikkhāpada) Regarding the first of the Saṅghādisesa offenses: "Litigating" (ussayavādikā) means disputing in the presence of judges for the purpose of a legal proceeding, out of a spirit of arrogance or a spirit of anger.
By the phrases "by a householder," etc., those who are fellow practitioners of the Dhamma (sahadhammika) are excluded.
The remaining [rules] include both householders and those who have gone forth. Regarding the phrase "this nun commits an offense entailing immediate expulsion" (*paṭhamāpattika*):
it is *paṭhamāpattika* because the first offense (*āpatti*) occurs at its very beginning; the meaning is that it must be incurred at the very moment of transgression.
One who has committed such an offense is called *āpanna*. "She causes the nun to be expelled from the Saṅgha" means she is one who effects expulsion (*nissāraṇīya*). That...
It is an offense entailing expulsion. "Saṅghādisesa" refers to that which bears this name.
It was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā in the case of a woman who brought a false accusation; it is a rule involving an injunction.
It concerns the act of searching for anyone—whether a companion, a witness, or an associate—by one who searches [for such a person] thinking, "I will bring a lawsuit."

It is an *dukkaṭa* offense. From the moment the thought arises while standing in a certain place, "I am going to go and settle a lawsuit," for every step she takes thereafter as she goes, there is a *dukkaṭa*.
Even if she merely reports her own case upon seeing a legal official who has come to the nuns' quarters, there is a *dukkaṭa*. When the other person has reported her case...
For the nun, it is a thullaccaya offense; the same rule applies even if she reports it first and the other person afterwards.
However, if the nun says, "Report the matter of both you and me yourself," he may report his own matter first or hers;
if he reports the first one, there is a dukkaṭa offense for the nun, and on the second [report], [the same applies].

[If she does not inform], it is a *thullaccaya*. The same rule applies when the nun informs [the judges] after being told this. Furthermore, if the nun causes another person to speak on her behalf, the same rule applies there as well.
For whether she informs in one way or another, at the first statement the nun incurs a *dukkaṭa*, and at the second, a *thullaccaya*. However, having heard the statements of both, by the judges...
When a formal decision has been made, it is called "the conclusion of the half-session. At that conclusion of the half-session, whether the nun wins or loses, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
However, as for one who is being dragged away by hostile persons, either by sending a messenger or by coming in person, saying, "Come, noble lady," [it is not so].

There is no offense for one who goes [to court], or for one who, while in her quarters, requests protection by pointing out misconduct committed by others without specifying [the perpetrator], or for one whom the judges, having heard from another source even though she was not told anything, themselves bring to a conclusion of the case; as well as for those who are insane and so forth.
The two factors here are: bringing a lawsuit without being dragged [into court] by others, and reaching a conclusion of the case.
The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other details are the same as those for the first *kathina* rule; however, this [present rule] is exclusively an act (*kiriyā*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning one who acts as a mediator (*ussayavādikā*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning one who causes a thief to leave the Order (*corivuṭṭhāpikā*).
In the second [offense], whatever belonging to another has been stolen starting from an amount worth five māsakas, this is called a "thief"; [the phrase] "that thief" refers to her.
"Known to be deserving of death" means that by virtue of that deed, she is known as "one who deserves execution.

"Without having obtained permission" means without having asked for leave. "A group" (gaṇa) refers to such groups as the Malla-gaṇa or the Bhaṭiputta-gaṇa. "A guild" (pūga) refers to a religious association (dhamma-gaṇa).
“Guild” (seṇi) refers to the guild of perfumers, the guild of cloth-dealers, and so forth.
For wherever kings hand over villages or market towns to groups and the like, saying, “You yourselves shall govern here,” there they alone become the masters;
it is with reference to them that this was said. And in this case, even after having obtained the permission of the king or of the groups and so forth, the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha...
She must indeed obtain permission. "Except when it is allowable" means: those who have previously gone forth among the heretics or among other bhikkhunīs are called "allowable";
setting them aside, for one who ordains another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding the search for the bowl and robes, the authorization of the boundary, and the motion (ñatti);
with two proclamations (kammavācā), there is a grave offense (thullaccaya); at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā regarding the case of ordaining a thief;
there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who is uncertain whether she is a thief, as well as for one who perceives a non-thief as a thief and is uncertain.

There is no offense for one who perceives her as not a thief, for one who does not know, for one who ordains after seeking permission, for one who ordains her when she is of the right age, or for those who are insane and so forth. [The offense applies to] one who is a thief.
Perceiving her to be a thief, and giving her the higher ordination except for an authorized reason—these are the three factors here.

This offense has its origin in the act of ordaining a thief; it is both an action and a non-action, is liberated by perception, is accompanied by consciousness, is an offense of transgression, is bodily action and verbal action, consists of three types of consciousness, and consists of three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning causing a nun to leave her robes is finished.
3. Commentary on the third training rule concerning going to another village.
Regarding the terms "to another village" and so forth in the third [rule]: first of all, there is no offense for one departing from her own village; however, having departed...
For one going to another village, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for every step;

when she has crossed over the boundary or the precinct of the other village with one foot, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*); as soon as she has crossed with the second foot, there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
The same rule applies even to one who, having departed from there, enters her own village again. However, if [the village] is enclosed by a broken wall or...

Alternatively, if it is possible to enter the area of the bhikkhunī monastery through a gap in the fence, then for one entering in this manner, she is considered to have entered a *kappiya-bhūmi* (an allowable area);

therefore, it is permissible. Standing outside the village, for one who enters on foot any non-permissible ground—whether her own village or another village—there is an offense; this is the summary here.
Regarding crossing a river: for one who crosses to the other shore alone, without a companion, across a river possessing the characteristics already described;
or for one who, having quarreled with her companion midway across the river, returns again to this shore; at the moment she lifts her first foot and places it on the bank, there is a *thullaccaya*;
upon lifting the second foot, there is a *saṅghādisesa*. This also applies when using psychic power, a bridge, a vehicle, or a boat.
However, it is permissible to cross to the other shore, and for one who has crossed for the purpose of bathing or similar reasons, it is also permissible to return to this shore on foot.

Regarding staying apart at night: if, without the mental resolve, "I will remain within arm's reach of my companion even before dawn," she stands beyond her companion’s arm's reach—even within the same room—and causes the dawn to rise, there is an offense.
As for the phrase "or alone with a group": here, even a single bhikkhunī constitutes a "group. "Should be left behind" means she is left out of sight; [the range of] sight...

The meaning is: "or she would abandon the range of hearing. Therefore, from the moment she has passed beyond the threshold of the gate, even if she is separated by trees, pillars, mats, walls, or other such things outside the village, once the second nun has abandoned the range of sight, if the range of hearing still exists, there is indeed an offense.
However, in the open air, the range of sight extends even to a great distance; in that case—

Just as with the sound of one lost on the road or the sound of an announcement for listening to the Dhamma, there is indeed an offense upon hearing the voice of one who calls out "Ayye" once that voice has passed beyond hearing.
However, if she is walking along the road and, having fallen behind, follows after with determination, thinking, "I shall catch up now," it is permissible.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhunī, in the case of traveling from one village boundary to another: "One..."
The three subsequent rules (anupaññatti) beginning with "or the further shore of a river" apply here;

however, for one who departs from her own village before dawn and reaches the further shore of a river included within another village at the time of sunrise, all four offenses occur simultaneously. This has also been stated:
“The training rules praised by the Best of Buddhas—
there may be four *saṅghādisesa* offenses;
one might incur them all with a single act.”
“This question has been considered by the wise.
By this method, the combination of three and two should be understood.

However, when the female companion has departed, or has left the order, or has died, or has gone over to another faction, or in times of misfortune, [the following applies]: going to another village, and so forth.

There is no offense for one who is insane, and so forth. The three factors here are: being in a state of solitude due to an obstacle; reaching any one of the conditions such as traveling between villages;
and the absence of an emergency. The origin and other characteristics are similar to those of the first *pārājika*;
however, this is an offense of formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), involving three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule regarding going to another village alone is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule regarding the reinstatement of one who has been suspended:
Regarding the fourth [rule], "suspended" means suspended for not seeing an offense and so forth. "Without knowing the consent of the Saṅgha."
"Without knowing the consent of that very assembly of officiants": she would perform the formal act of reinstatement (*osāraṇakamma*).

For her who acts in this way, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) regarding the search for a quorum, the authorization of the boundary (*sīmāsammuti*), and the motion (*ñatti*); with the two subsequent proclamations (*kammavācā*), there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*);
at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā regarding the matter of reinstatement (*osāraṇa*):

a *saṅghādisesa* offense for the triad [of factors], and a *dukkaṭa* offense for the triad of unrighteous formal acts (*adhammakamma*). There is no offense for one who reinstates [a nun] after having requested permission from the performing Saṅgha or having ascertained the consent (*chanda*) of the group, or for one who reinstates her while she is conducting herself according to the proper conduct (*vatta*), or when the performing Saṅgha is absent; nor is there an offense for those who are insane, and so forth. This applies to a righteous formal act (*dhammakamma*).
The two factors here are: being suspended, and reinstatement except for an authorized reason.
The origins and so forth are exactly as described in the training rule on schism in the Saṅgha; furthermore, this is a "non-action" offense.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the reinstatement of one who has been suspended is finished.
5. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning the Acceptance of Food In the fifth [rule], *avassutā* means "one who is lustful," being drenched with desire and passion (*chandarāga*).

*Avassutassa* refers to one who is likewise [lustful]. *Khādeyya vā bhuñjeyya vā* (should chew or eat): herein, there is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*) at the moment of acceptance; for every act of swallowing, there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
This was formulated at Sāvatthī concerning Sundarīnandā, regarding the matter of accepting food from the hand of one who is lustful by another who is lustful.
It is thus prescribed: in the case of receiving from one who is lustful on one side, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); for every swallow, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
This same principle applies even when it is from the hands of a *yakkha*, a *peta*, a *paṇḍaka*, an animal, or one with a human form, provided that both parties are lustful.
However, in that case, if only one party is lustful, there is an offense of wrong-doing. This applies everywhere, including the taking of water and tooth-wood.

Even the consumption [of such food] is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense for one who takes it when both parties are not related by blood, or if she takes it knowing them to be unrelated, or in the case of those who are insane and so forth.

Herein, the four factors are: something other than water or tooth-sticks that is fit to be swallowed; the fact that both parties are unrelated; taking it with one's own hand; and swallowing it. The origin and other characteristics are similar to the first Pārājika rule.
The commentary on the first training rule regarding the acceptance of food is finished.
6. Commentary on the second training rule regarding the acceptance of food:
In the sixth [rule], *yato tvam* means "since you. *Iṅgha* is a particle used in the sense of exhortation. *Ayampi* refers to one who exhorts in such a manner.
By means of that instigation, those words, and the acceptance by the other [nun], she incurs *dukkaṭas*;
by the number of mouthfuls swallowed, she incurs *thullaccayas*; and at the conclusion of the meal, she incurs a *saṅghādisesa*.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a certain nun, in this matter of instigation; it is an offense with a formal injunction (*sāṇattika*).
There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for encouraging a man or a *yakkha* and so forth to accept water for rinsing the teeth from their hands, and for their consumption of it;
this same principle applies to encouraging them to take other things from their hands, for their taking of them, and for their swallowing them.
However, at the conclusion of the meal, there is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*). [The phrase] "knowing [him] to be 'free from lust'" means either knowing him as such, or [knowing him as] "angry."
There is no offense for one who is insane and so forth, or for one who is inciting [another] by saying, "She does not accept," or "She does not accept out of compassion for the families.

There is an offense when there is a human male, except for an authorized reason, when she incites her by saying, "Take hard food or soft food and eat," and she takes it because of those words until the end of the other's meal. These are the points here.
There are three factors. The origins and so forth are similar to those for taking what is not given.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning the acceptance of food is finished.
7–8–9. Commentary on the training rules concerning matchmaking and so forth.
The exposition for the seventh, eighth, and ninth training rules should be understood in the same manner as that stated for the three rules concerning acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta*).
The commentary on the training rules beginning with acting as a go-between is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Renouncing the Training (*Sikkhaṃ-paccācikkhaṇa-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā*)
In the tenth [offense], what is meant by "Are these indeed nuns"? It means: "Are these alone the nuns? "Tāsāhaṃ" means "of them, I am.

The meaning of the words up to the third [repetition] is to be understood according to the method explained in the commentary on the *Bhikkhu-pātimokkha*, and the remaining analysis is likewise to be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on the *Saṅghabheda-sikkhāpada*.
This [offense], however, was concerning the nun Caṇḍakālī at Sāvatthī, regarding [the proclamation]: "The Buddha..."

This was laid down in connection with the statement beginning with “I renounce [the training],” and so forth. Herein, the specific distinction is that the very act of speaking constitutes the first of the four factors; the rest is exactly the same.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the renunciation of the training is finished.
11. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning those who are angry over a legal issue (*adhikaraṇakupita-sikkhāpada*).
Regarding the phrase "in some legal issue whatsoever" in the eleventh [rule], it refers to one of the four types of legal issues. "Defeated" (*paccākatā*) means overcome.
This [offense] was also established at Sāvatthī concerning Caṇḍakāḷī, based on the occasion for the statement beginning with, "The bhikkhunīs act out of favoritism."
The prescribed [procedure] is as stated; the remainder should be understood according to the method explained in the tenth [chapter].
The commentary on the training rule concerning being angry over a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇakupita*) is finished.
12. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Evil Conduct (*pāpasamācāra*).

In the twelfth [section], "associated" (*saṃsaṭṭhā*) means being mixed with householders through bodily and verbal actions that are not in conformity with those who have gone forth, such as pounding, cooking, and delivering messages.
They are called "of evil conduct" (*pāpācārā*) because their bodily and verbal behavior is evil. They are called "of evil reputation" (*pāpasaddā*) because their fame is evil.
They are called "of evil renown" (*pāpasilokā*) because their reputation, which consists of their mode of livelihood, is evil. [This refers to] the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs.
*Vihesikā*: one who causes vexation by protesting while another’s work is being performed.
*Vajjappaṭicchādikā*: one who conceals a fault, whether minor or trivial.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhunīs regarding the matter of living in association; the rest here is the same as before.

It should be understood in the same manner as stated in the tenth [chapter]. However, at the time of the formal act of admonition (*samanubhāsanakamma*), two or three [monks] may be admonished together.
The commentary on the first training rule regarding misconduct is finished.
13. Commentary on the second training rule regarding misconduct.
"In the thirteenth [offense], she should speak thus": she should speak thus to those nuns who have been formally admonished.

"Of such conduct" (*evācārā*): meaning "of such behavior"; the sense is that whatever kind of conduct you have, that is the kind of conduct [I am speaking of]. This method applies everywhere. "With contempt" (*uññāya*):
by treating them with disdain, knowing them as inferior. "With disregard" (*paribhavena*): by knowing them while disregarding them, thinking, "What can these women possibly do?"
"Through impatience" means through lack of forbearance; the sense is "through anger.
"Through boisterousness" means through the state of being powerful, that is, by proclaiming one's own strength and causing terror. "Through weakness" means through your state of frailty.
In all these cases, the sense should be understood as a conjunction, namely "and through contempt and disregard. "Separate yourselves" means become divided.
The meaning is: "Abandon unsuitable physical and verbal contact.

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, in the case involving the instigation: "Venerable ladies, you should live in close association; do not live apart from one another. The rest here should be understood in the same manner as stated for the tenth [offense].
The commentary on the second training rule regarding evil conduct is finished.
14. Commentary on the Training Rules Concerning Schism in the Sangha, etc.
The analysis regarding the four rules beginning with schism in the Sangha should be understood according to the method already stated.
For it is only a nun who does not cause a schism in the Sangha, yet she both exerts herself toward a schism and follows after it. "Venerable ladies, the seventeen [rules] have been recited."
Regarding the *saṅghādisesa* rules: there are seventeen such rules—seven common to both [monks and nuns] and ten not common to both—thus making seventeen in total.

"The *mānatta* penance must be observed for a fortnight before both Saṅghas" means that for a nun, even if she conceals an offense, there is no such thing as *parivāsa*, nor does she incur a *dukkaṭa* offense on account of concealment; therefore, whether she conceals it or does not conceal it...
One side must undergo the *mānatta* penance itself. Having cleared their own territory (*sīma*), that [penance] should be granted by the nuns within the monastery boundary (*vihārasīma*);
or, if they are unable to clear it, within a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*), having convened at least a quorum of four in the smallest possible extent.
If there is one offense, it is according to one person; if two or three, [they are granted] accordingly.

Whether they be numerous, or share the same basis, or have different bases—in accordance with each of these, one should take whichever one desires from among the bases, clans, names, and classifications of offenses mentioned in the commentary on the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha, and apply them accordingly.
Herein, this is a mere illustration by way of the first offense: when that bhikkhunī has committed it, she [must inform] the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs...

Having approached, arranged her upper robe over one shoulder, bowed at the feet of the senior bhikkhunīs, sat down on her haunches, and extended her hands in reverential salutation, she should speak thus:
“Venerable ladies, I have committed one offense of groundless accusation.
Venerable ladies, I ask the Saṅgha for a fortnight’s *mānatta* discipline for this one offense of groundless accusation. Thus [she should speak].
After having her request made three times, the Saṅgha should be informed by a competent and capable bhikkhunī:
“Venerable ladies, let the Saṅgha hear me. This bhikkhunī named so-and-so has committed one offense of groundless accusation.
She requests from the Saṅgha a fortnight’s penance (mānatta) for that one offense of groundless accusation. If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha...”
“May the Saṅgha grant a fortnight’s *mānatta* penance to the bhikkhunī named so-and-so for her one offense of insinuation.
This is the motion. ‘Let the noble Saṅgha hear me: this bhikkhunī named so-and-so... [as before] ...For the second time... For the third time I speak on this matter:
let the noble Saṅgha hear me... [as before] ...she should speak. The Saṅgha has granted a fortnight’s *mānatta* penance to the bhikkhunī named so-and-so.”
“For one charge involving a formal accusation, there is a probation (*mānatta*) lasting for a fortnight. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent. Thus do I hold it.
At the conclusion of this formal act (*kammavācā*), having undertaken [the observances] by saying, “I undertake the duties (*vatta*);

I undertake the probation,” and having informed the Saṅgha, while she still wishes to remain right there in the midst of the Saṅgha with her duties laid down—[this applies even if] other bhikkhunīs have departed from that place.
It should be laid down in the presence of either one bhikkhunī or a companion, saying: "I lay down the duty;
I lay down the *mānatta*. Alternatively, it may be laid down after announcing it in the presence of another visiting bhikkhunī.
From the moment it is laid down, she stands in the position of one who is of normal standing (*pakatatta*). Prior to dawn, that bhikkhunī [should be dealt with] by four bhikkhunīs...

Having taken [the robe], one should sit in a place concealed by thickets, bushes, and the like, having departed from the vicinity of the village and the vicinity of the monks' dwellings and having passed two *leḍḍupāta*s (the distance of a stone's throw). Four monks should also go there;
having gone, they should sit separately, not far from the nuns. Then, by that nun...
Having undertaken the duties in the manner already described, one should first announce it thus to the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs:
"Venerable ladies, I have fallen into one offense of false accusation;

I requested from the Saṅgha a half-month’s *mānatta* penance for that one offense of false accusation, and the Saṅgha granted me a half-month’s *mānatta* penance for that one offense of false accusation."
“I have given it; I am now undergoing the *mānatta* penance; I announce it, venerable ladies; may the Saṅgha remember me as one who announces.
Then, having gone into the presence of the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*), she should announce thus: “I, venerable sirs, have committed one offense...
[as before] ...I announce it, venerable sirs; may the Saṅgha remember me as one who announces. Having made this announcement, [she should go] to the community of nuns (*bhikkhunīsaṅgha*) itself.

She must sit nearby; from that point on, whether among the monks or among the nuns—excluding her companion—even if the nuns have departed, the *mānatta* penance is considered fulfilled within both Saṅghas.
Until dawn has risen, she must report [her state] to whichever monk or nun she first sees. Once dawn has risen...
