Having set aside her duties, she must go to the residence; in this way, fifteen sunrises are to be counted.
However, for one who has not set aside her duties, if there are no newcomers, she should announce it daily to four monks and four nuns;
but when there are newcomers, for one who announces it to all the newcomers, the fifteen days are accounted for according to the *Pārivāsikakkhandhaka*.
"One should conduct oneself properly in the manner already described"—this is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.

Regarding the phrase "for a bhikkhunī who has performed the *mānatta* penance": when a bhikkhunī has thus performed the *mānatta*, then the act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) must be performed for her in the same manner as described, provided there is a community (*saṅgha*) of twenty bhikkhunīs. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the Saṅghādisesa rules in the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha within the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* Pātimokkha Commentary is finished.
Commentary on the First Training Rule of the Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiya-kaṇḍa):

Regarding the first rule of the initial section among the offenses involving forfeiture, "should accumulate bowls" means that one should maintain a hoard of bowls; the meaning is that one should set aside a bowl fit for formal dedication without having formally dedicated it or assigned it to another within the course of a single day.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six bhikkhunīs regarding the matter of the accumulation of almsbowls.
The rest of the narrative path is to be understood in the same manner as stated in the commentary on the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha;

for there, an offense occurs upon the lapse of ten days, whereas here it occurs upon the lapse of one day—this alone is the difference between that [rule] and this one, while the remainder is exactly the same.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the accumulation of cloth is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning out-of-season robes:

Regarding the second [rule], "out-of-season robe" means, when the *kaṭhina* has been spread, during the months of the *kaṭhina*; when it has not been spread, during any time other than the month of the robe season.
It is that which has arisen at the proper time, or that which, even if given at the proper time, was specifically designated for [a particular group]. "Specifically designated" means:
having said, "Let those who have arrived share it," or having said, "This is for the community; this I give to you," or having placed it at the feet [of the recipients] out of a desire to give.
Thus, for one who, having determined this non-seasonal robe-cloth to be "seasonal robe-cloth," proceeds to distribute it, there is an offense in the act.

It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); whatever one has obtained for oneself becomes subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). Even after having relinquished it and received it back, it must be returned to the very person from whom it was taken;
this same principle applies to other training rules (*sikkhāpada*) of a similar nature.

At Sāvatthī, concerning Thullanandā, [the rule was laid down] regarding an out-of-season robe (*akālacīvara*) which she determined to be an "in-season robe" (*kālacīvara*) in the context of the case of a vessel.

It is prescribed: for one who is doubtful about an out-of-season robe, and for one who perceives an in-season robe as an out-of-season robe while being doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
There is no offense for both when perceiving it as an in-season robe, nor for those who are insane and so forth. Herein, the factors are:
the state of being an out-of-season robe, the perception thereof, the solicitation by means of a pretext after having determined it to be "an in-season robe," and the acquisition.
There are four factors. The [factors] beginning with the origin (samuṭṭhāna) are similar to those for taking what has not been given.
The commentary on the training rule regarding out-of-season robes is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule regarding the exchange of robes.
In the third [offense], "take" means: take it. "Should snatch away" means: for her who snatches it away herself, there is one offense even if many items have been placed there after being bound;

for others, there are offenses according to the number of objects. However, in the case of causing another to snatch it away, even if many items are snatched away by a single command, there is only one offense.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā regarding the case of exchanging a robe and then taking it back.

It is an offense of three *pācittiyas* with a formal injunction (*sāṇattika*); for other requisites, there are three *dukkaṭas*; and for a robe belonging to one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampannā*), there are likewise three *dukkaṭas*.
However, for her who gives it, or for her from whom she takes it on trust, and for those who are insane and so forth, [there is no offense].
There is no offense. The three factors here are: the state of being fully ordained; the robe that has been exchanged having reached the stage of being formally assigned;

and taking it back or causing it to be taken back while perceiving it as one's own. The origins and other characteristics are the same as those for taking what is not given, but this [offense] is of painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the exchange of robes is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning requesting something else:
In the fourth [rule], "having requested" means having made known, or having asked, "Please bring such-and-such. "She should request something else" means...
If, after having rejected what was requested by one who had previously been told, "What is troubling you, noble lady? What should be brought?

and desiring to take that very thing as well as something else, she should request something other than that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for that request; with the acquisition [of the item], it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, in the case of requesting one thing after having already requested another.
There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for three [offenses], and two offenses of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) when it is not another.

Furthermore, when it is not another and one perceives it as not another, if that [other] is not available, she asks for that very same thing again; or if there is need, she asks for another along with that [first] even though it is by another;
or if what was requested is something else and of greater value; or if she requests a pure other [item] after showing this benefit.
There is no offense for those who are insane and so forth. The three factors here are: the desire to take by means of a hint, the making known to another, and the obtaining [of the object].
The origins and other characteristics are similar to those of the *sañcaritta* (go-between) rule.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the making known to another is finished.

5. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Exchanging for Something Else In the fifth [rule], "having exchanged for something else" (*aññaṃ cetāpetvā*) means having bartered for something else by using one's own allowable goods (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*), saying, "Bring this.
"She should exchange for something else" (*aññaṃ cetāpeyya*) refers to one who, thinking, "By giving this to me, he will bring something else," says, "I have no need for this... [and so forth].
“Bring me such-and-such a thing,” and then she should cause something else to be bought for her. In the act of causing it to be bought, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
upon its acquisition, whether brought by that [original] price or by another, it becomes subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). The rest is exactly like the fourth [offense].
The commentary on the training rule concerning exchanging for something else is finished.

6. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning the Exchange of Property Belonging to the Sangha In the sixth [training rule], "with what is intended for another" (*aññadatthika*) means with that which has been given for the sake of another. "With what is designated for another" (*aññuddisika*) means with that which has been given after designating it for another.

"Belonging to the Sangha" (*saṅghika*) means that which has been relinquished to the Sangha. "Requisites" (*parikkhāra*) means allowable articles (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*). "Should exchange for something else" (*aññaṃ cetāpeyya*) means...
“Having designated and specified, ‘You may use this,’ if one causes another requisite to be exchanged for something other than that which was given,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of proposing it, and it is to be relinquished (*nissaggiya*) upon acquisition.
This was in reference to several bhikkhunīs at Sāvatthī, concerning the matter of exchanging one such requisite for another.”

It is laid down as a *pācittiya* offense for three [cases], and a *dukkaṭa* offense for two cases when it is not intended for another purpose. However, regarding that [offense], there is no offense for one who brings the remainder [of the robe] while perceiving it as not being for another purpose;
nor for one who brings it after having informed the owners, saying, "This was given by you for this specific purpose, and we have such-and-such a need for it";
nor in cases such as when the bhikkhunīs depart, even abandoning the monastery.
There is no offense for those who bring [the goods] during times of distress, nor for those who are insane and so forth. The remainder is exactly like the fourth [offense].
The commentary on the first training rule concerning the exchange of property belonging to the Saṅgha is concluded.
7. Commentary on the second training rule concerning the exchange of property belonging to the Saṅgha.
"In the seventh [offense], *saññācikenā* means even by what has been personally requested. This alone is the point of distinction here; the rest is exactly like the sixth [offense].
The commentary on the second training rule concerning exchanging for the Saṅgha is finished.
8. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Exchanging for a Group.
In the eighth [offense], it is "by what has been relinquished to a group"; this is the distinction from the sixth [offense] in this context.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning purchasing from a group is finished.
9. Commentary on the second training rule concerning purchasing from a group.
In the ninth [offense], "by means of a signal," this is distinct from the eighth; the remainder is exactly like the sixth training rule in both cases.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning the procurement of goods for a courtesan is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Procurement of Goods for an Individual.
"In the tenth [offense], ‘by what is given to an individual’ means by what has been relinquished to a single bhikkhunī. ‘By what is requested by herself’ means by what she has herself asked for.

‘Should exchange it for something else’: for the effort of one who exchanges for something other than that which was given with reference to a specific purpose, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
upon acquisition, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya)."
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā regarding the matter of exchanging one such requisite for another; the rest is exactly like the sixth [offense].
The commentary on the training rule concerning the exchange of personal requisites is finished.
The first chapter, the Chapter on Bowls, is concluded.
11. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Heavy Outer Garments (Garupāvuraṇasikkhāpada).
Regarding the first [offense] of the second [section], "heavy outer garment" refers to an outer garment worn during the cold season. "Not exceeding four kaṃsas": a *kaṃsa* is worth four *hāpaṇas*;
therefore, it is worth sixteen *hāpaṇas*. "Should be bartered for" means, except with those who share the same Dhamma (*sahadhammika*).

And in the case of one who has been invited by relatives, or when someone else, being satisfied with some particular quality [of hers], says, "Tell us, ladies, what you need," she may then request it.
Beyond that—that is, for her who requests more than that—it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), and what is obtained becomes subject to relinquishment (nissaggiya).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, in the matter of requesting a woolen blanket from a king.

There is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for [receiving] three [measures]; there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for two [measures] when it is less than four *kaṃsa* measures. Furthermore, there is no offense for one who perceives it as less; or for one who causes [the robe] to be purchased for up to four *kaṃsa* measures;
or for one who purchases it from a relative or one who has been invited; or for one who purchases it for the sake of another; or for one who purchases something of great value with her own wealth;

or for one who causes a valuable item to be purchased when it is of little value; and for those who are insane and so forth. [The factors constituting the offense are: being a heavy cloak and being more than four *kaṃsa* measures.

In this context, there are four factors: making a request in an improper place and the obtaining [of the robe]. The origins and other details are similar to those of the *sañcaritta* (mediating between men and women) offense.
The commentary on the training rule concerning heavy outer garments is finished.
12. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Light Outer Garments.

In the second [offense], "light covering" (*lahupāvuraṇa*) refers to a covering used during the hot season. "Not exceeding two and a half *kaṃsa*" means it is worth ten *kahāpaṇa*; the rest is exactly as in the first [offense].
The commentary on the training rule regarding light coverings is finished.

From here onwards, the eighteen training rules—eight in this chapter and ten in the third chapter—are to be understood according to the method already stated in the commentary on the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha.
The third chapter, on Gold.

"Venerable ladies, the thirty *nissaggiya pācittiya* rules have been recited. Eighteen are common, having been laid down with reference to monks; twelve are not common. Thus there are thirty. The rest is clear in every respect.
[End of] the Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*.
The commentary on the *Nissaggiya-pācittiya* rules is finished.
Chapter One of the *Pācittiya* Section:
The Garlic Sub-section.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Garlic (*lasuṇasikkhāpada*).

Regarding the first rule in the Garlic Chapter among the *pācittiya* offenses: "garlic" refers specifically to raw garlic of the *bhaṇḍika* variety grown in the kingdom of Magadha, and not that which has one, two, or three seeds.
For her who accepts it with the intention, "I shall eat it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); for every mouthful swallowed, there is a *pācittiya* offense.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā regarding the case of having garlic carried away; it is an offense of three *pācittiyas*.

For [other] garlic, there are two *dukkaṭas*. Furthermore, in the case of one who perceives it as garlic when it is actually onion, leek, green vegetable, chameleon-garlic, seasoning for soup, seasoning for meat, seasoning for oil, *sāḷava*, or *uttaribhaṅga*, and for those who are insane and so forth—
There is no offense. In this case, there are two factors: raw garlic itself and its being swallowed. The origin and other details are similar to those of the rule on wool.
The commentary on the training rule concerning garlic is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Hair of the Private Parts (*Sambādhaloma-sikkhāpada*).
In the second [rule], "in the private parts" (*sambādhe*) means in the concealed area, specifically in the armpits and the urinary organ.

"Should have it removed" (*saṃharāpeyya*): here, for one who has it removed by any means such as a razor, tweezers, scissors, and so forth, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the number of applications, not according to the number of hairs.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six bhikkhunīs regarding the matter of having hair removed from the private parts.
For one who commands another for her own sake, there is an offense entailing confession (*sāṇattika*); there is no division of offenses.
There is no offense in the case of an illness, nor for those who are insane and so forth. The two factors here are: the absence of illness and the removal of hair from the private parts.
The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors are similar to those of the training rule concerning traveling along a road together with a nun.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the pubic hair is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Slapping with the Palm.

Regarding "slapping with the palm" in the third [offense]: the meaning is that it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) when one slaps the opening of the urinary tract with even the tip of a lotus stalk, or strikes the urinary tract.
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning two bhikkhunīs on the basis of the incident of slapping with the palm;

it is a formal act of instruction (sāṇattika) in the same manner as the preceding rule, and there is no difference in the classification of the offense. Hereafter, however, we shall proceed without mentioning those cases where there is no difference.
There is no offense for one who strikes a boil or a wound due to illness, nor for those who are insane and so forth.
The three factors here are: the absence of illness, the striking of the urinary organ, and the relishing of the contact.
The origin and other characteristics are similar to the first *pārājika*.
The commentary on the training rule concerning striking the palms is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Lubricated Dildos:

Regarding the fourth rule, "a lubricated dildo" (*jatumaṭṭhaka*), this is stated by way of illustration; however, for one who inserts even a lotus filament out of lustful passion, there is an offense.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhunī, in connection with the incident of accepting a dildo made of wax; the rest is exactly like the third [offense].
The commentary on the training rule regarding the dildo is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Purification by Water.
In the fifth [offense], "cleansing with water" means the washing of the urinary organ. "Taking up" means performing it.
"To be taken up with two finger-joints as the maximum" means that by joining two fingers together, it should be taken up with no more than two finger-joints.
"One who exceeds that" means if, at the time of washing, out of lust, she exceeds [the limit] by the top joint of the third finger in width, or by even one [joint] in depth.
If one inserts the third joint of a finger, it is an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was prescribed regarding a certain bhikkhunī among the Sakyans, in the case of undertaking a very deep water-cleansing;

it is a *pācittiya* for three fingers, and there is a two-fold offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for less than two finger-joints. However, if one has the perception that it is less [than the required depth], [there is no offense].

For one who takes [it] with a maximum of two finger-joints, there is no offense even if it exceeds that amount when it is for the purpose of treating an illness; nor is there an offense for those who are insane and so forth.
The remainder is exactly like the third [training rule].
The commentary on the training rule concerning purification by water is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Attending Upon.
Regarding the sixth [rule]: "While he is eating" means while he is consuming any one of the five kinds of soft food.
"With drinking water" means with pure water or with any one of the liquids such as buttermilk and so forth. "With a fan" means with any kind of fan whatsoever. "He should attend upon" means...
If a woman stands within arm’s reach of someone who has taken either of these two [foods] and is eating, she incurs a *pācittiya* offense.
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning a certain nun, regarding the matter of standing thus while someone is eating;
it is a triple *pācittiya*. If she stands by while he eats solid food after he has left the arm’s reach, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

For one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each of the three [cases]. There is no offense for one who gives [the drink] saying, "Drink this," or "Chew with this," or for one who causes it to be given, or for one who commands a person not fully ordained to attend upon [the monk], nor for those who are insane and so forth.
Standing within arm's reach of the monk who is eating, or taking hold of the drinking water or the fan—these two [actions] constitute the offense here.
The factors, such as the origin and so forth, are similar to those in the case of the sheep’s wool [offense].
The commentary on the training rule concerning attending upon is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Raw Grain.
"Having requested," even down to requesting from one's own mother. "Should eat" means should swallow. In this case, both the request and the food are the measure;

therefore, whether one has requested it oneself and had another perform the roasting and so forth, or having requested it through another, one performs the roasting and so forth oneself—from the moment of receiving [the food] until it reaches the teeth—[it is an offense].
Regarding chewing: for the preliminary actions, there are *dukkaṭa* offenses; for each swallow, there is a *pācittiya*.
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhunīs, in the matter of requesting raw grain;
it applies to one who eats it herself or through another, whether obtained without being requested, or having had it roasted and so forth, or having had it prepared.

It is an *dukkaṭa* offense; however, for one who, having obtained [food] through a request made by another, eats it even after having herself roasted it or having had it prepared, it is likewise an *dukkaṭa*.

There is no offense for one who requests [food] for the purpose of treatments such as sudation when there is illness; for one who accepts what is being offered without a prior request for the purpose of new construction work;
or for one who requests non-staple foods such as mung beans or peas in a place where she is invited by relatives.
There is no offense for those who are insane and so forth. In this case, there are three factors: the requesting or causing another to request any one of the seven kinds of grain;
the acquisition thereof; and the swallowing after having roasted it or having caused it to be roasted.
The origin and other characteristics are the same as those of the training rule on the long journey.
The commentary on the training rule concerning raw grain is finished.
8. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning the Disposal of Excrement:
In the eighth [rule], "refuse" (*saṅkāra*) means rubbish; "scrapings" (*vighāsa*) means whatever remains after eating, including leftover water.
Even regarding a tooth-stick, there is nothing at all to be said concerning bones and hair.
"Beyond a wall or beyond a fence" means on the other side of any wall or any fence whatsoever. "Should discard or cause to be discarded":
for one who discards all these things together in a single act, it is a single offense; even if many items are discarded by a single command, it is likewise only one offense.
This rule was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhunī regarding the matter of discarding excrement over a wall;

it is an offense entailing an act of formal admonition (*sāṇattika*). It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for a bhikkhu. There is no offense for one who discards [it] after looking around or in a place where there is no passage, nor for those who are insane and so forth.
The factors constituting the offense are: the nature of being excrement and so forth, not looking around, a place of passage, being over a wall or over a rampart, and the act of discarding.

Or causing [it] to be discarded—these are the five factors here. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to those of the Sañcaritta [offense], but this is both an action and a non-action (kiriya-akiriya).
The commentary on the first training rule concerning the discarding of excrement is finished.
9. Commentary on the Second Training Rule Concerning the Disposal of Excrement Regarding the ninth [rule], "in green growth":
this refers to a field, or a coconut grove and so forth, or any place where cultivated plants are growing.
For one who disposes of such things herself or causes them to be disposed of, there is an offense according to the same method as before; having sat down in such a place...
Even for one who, having drunk water, discards even a coconut with its top cut off, there is indeed an offense.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhunīs regarding the matter of discarding excrement and so forth on green vegetation;
it is a rule involving an instruction, a triad of pācittiyas, a dukkaṭa for a bhikkhu, and also for a bhikkhunī in the case of a field where seeds have been sown.
As long as the sprout has not emerged, it is a *dukkaṭa*; if there is no green growth, it is two *dukkaṭas*.

However, there is no offense for one who discards [the refuse] in a field that she perceives to be devoid of green growth, or for one who discards it after having informed the owner, nor for those such as the insane and so forth. The remainder is exactly the same as in the eighth [offense].
The commentary on the second training rule concerning the disposal of excrement is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Dancing and Singing:
In the tenth [rule], "dancing" includes even the dancing of peacocks; "singing" includes even the chanting of Dharma-reciters; "instrumental music" [is defined as follows].
"Even as far as the sound of a water-drum. "For the purpose of seeing": for one who goes for the purpose of seeing any of these things, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) at every step;

where she stands and either sees or hears them, it is a single offense in that single act of going; for her looking toward each respective direction, there is an offense for each individual act of looking.
At Rājagaha, concerning the group of six bhikkhunīs, this was laid down regarding the matter of going to see dancing and so forth:

for one who herself performs those acts, or causes another to perform them, or speaks by such a means as saying, "Give an offering to the cetiya," or when it is said, "Let us make an offering to the cetiya," [responding] "Very well."
And for one who accepts [the offer], it is indeed a *pācittiya*; thus it is stated in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). For a monk, however, it is always a *dukkaṭa*.

But when someone says, "We shall perform service for your *cetiya*," and she speaks such an indirect phrase as, "Performing service is indeed excellent," while standing in the monastery or seeing or hearing [it being done], [it is a *dukkaṭa*].

Likewise, there is no offense for one who has come to her own dwelling place and, upon seeing or hearing [the nun] while she is engaged in necessary business such as receiving *salākabhatta* (ticket-food) and so forth, or while she is present on the road returning from that business;
nor is there an offense for one who has gone to a festival site during times of emergency, or for those who are insane and so forth.
[The offenses are: being engaged in any of the acts such as dancing, or going elsewhere except for a permitted reason.
"Seeing or hearing"—these are the three factors here. The origins and so forth are similar to those of the *eḷakaloma* (sheep's wool) rule;
however, this is a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), it is unwholesome consciousness, and it possesses three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule regarding dancing and singing is finished.
The First Chapter on Garlic. 2.
The Chapter on Darkness at Night.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Darkness at Night.
In the first [offense] of the *Andhakāravagga*, "in the darkness of night" means in the darkness of the night.
"Unlit" means not illuminated by even one among the lights of a lamp, the moon, the sun, or fire. "With a man" means with a wise human male capable of standing together or conversing.
"Should stand together" means that by merely being within arm's reach (*hatthapāsa*), there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). "Should converse" means therein...
If she stands and engages in talk concerning household matters, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī with reference to a certain bhikkhunī in the case of standing together;
it applies to one who stands together after leaving the reach of a man’s hand, even if she does not leave the reach of the hands of yakkhas and so forth, or while conversing.
Or there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who does so after taking any wise person as a companion;
there is no offense for one who expects privacy, for one whose mind is preoccupied with something else, or for those who are insane and so forth.

Herein, the four factors are: the state of darkness at night, the man being within arm’s reach, the absence of companions, and the expectation of privacy. This [offense] originates from a caravan of thieves.

It is a functional state (*kiriyā*), liberation through perception (*saññāvimokkha*), accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*), an offense against worldly convention (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and associated with three feelings (*tivedana*).
The commentary on the training rule regarding the dark of night is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding a Concealed Place (*paṭicchannokāsasikkhāpada*).
In the second [offense], "in a concealed place" means in a place concealed by anything such as a wall; this alone is the distinction here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning a concealed place is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Talking in the Open Air.
In the third [offense], there is ignorance regarding being under the open sky; the remainder is exactly the same as in the first case for both.
The commentary on the training rule concerning conversing under the open sky is finished.
4. Commentary on the second training rule concerning inciting a woman.
"In the fourth [offense], 'on a carriage road' means on a street. 'In a byway' means in a cul-de-sac. 'At a crossroads' means at a place where four roads meet.

'Or he should whisper into her ear' means he should say something into the root of her ear. 'He should dismiss her' means that, desiring to engage in improper conduct, he should dismiss his companion, saying, "Go away.
It is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) in the same manner as in the previous cases regarding standing together and so forth."

There are three *pācittiya* offenses. However, for one who is sending [a nun] away, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) both at the act of sending her away and when she has gone beyond the reach of hand; once she has gone beyond that reach, it is a *pācittiya*.

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā regarding the matter of staying together in this manner; the rest is exactly like the previous triad. Regarding non-offenses, however, the only addition is:
"if she does not wish to engage in improper conduct, she sends away a companion nun because there is business to be done."
The commentary on the second training rule concerning instigation is finished.
5. Commentary on the Fifth Training Rule:
Departing Without Informing "In the morning" means from the time of sunrise until midday. "In the seat" refers to the space occupied by the *pallaṅka* (couch).
"Without asking the owner" means without asking any sensible person belonging to that family. "Should depart" means:

having sat inside a covered place, for one who crosses the boundary of the open space (anovassaka) into the open air, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the first step, and an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the second step.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhunī regarding the matter of departing without having asked for permission;

it is an offense of threefold pācittiya, and a dukkaṭa for using a seat (pallaṅka) in an inappropriate place. Likewise, there is no offense when one has asked for permission but perceives that one has not, or when one is in doubt;
nor is there an offense when one perceives that one has asked, when the seat cannot be moved, when one is ill, in times of emergency, or for those who are insane and so forth.
There is no offense. The five factors here are: being before the meal; sitting in an inhabited area; making the seat a *pallaṅka* (cross-legged position);

not asking permission except for a permitted reason; and exceeding the stated limit. The origin and other characteristics are the same as those of the *kathina*, but this [offense] is both an action and a non-action.
The commentary on the training rule regarding departing without having asked permission is finished.
6. Commentary on the sixth training rule regarding sitting down without having asked permission:
"After the meal" means from when midday has passed until the sun sets. "Should sit down..."
For one who goes after sitting down at the beginning [of the journey], there is one offense; for one who goes without sitting down but lying down, there is also one offense;
for one who both sits down and lies down, there are two offenses.

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā regarding the matter of sitting down repeatedly on a seat; the rest is exactly like the fifth [offense]. However, just as in that case there was no offense regarding an immovable seat, so here there is no offense regarding a seat that is permanently established.
The commentary on the training rule regarding sitting down without asking permission is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule regarding spreading out [a seat] without asking permission:
Regarding the seventh [rule], "at the wrong time" means when the sun has set. "Bedding" includes even a spread of leaves; the rest is exactly like the sixth [training rule].
This, however, was laid down concerning a number of bhikkhunīs in Sāvatthī who, having approached families at an improper time and without asking the owners for permission,
spread out a bed and sat down; and herein, there is no such thing as a "permanent prescription" (*dhuvapaññatta*) among those that do not constitute an offense.
The commentary on the training rule regarding spreading out [a seat] without asking permission is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Causing Another to Be Reprimanded:
Regarding what was stated as "by what is wrongly grasped and wrongly judged," this refers to that which is grasped and judged otherwise [than it actually is].

*Ca*: Regarding "another," it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for one who complains against another who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), by way of such statements as, "I do not, it seems, attend upon the noble lady with proper care.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhunī, in this matter of complaining against another.
There is a *pācittiya* offense for one who is fully ordained; there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for one who is not fully ordained; and there is no offense for those who are insane and so forth.
The three factors here are: being wrongly grasped, the act of censuring, and the fact that the person being censured is fully ordained.
The origin and other characteristics are the same as those for taking what is not given, but this [offense] is associated with painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning inciting others [to commit offenses] is finished.
9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule Concerning Swearing Oaths:
"Should swear" means one should make an oath. In that context, examples such as "May I be reborn in hell; may he be reborn in hell," and so forth, [constitute the offense].
"Speaking" means cursing with reference to hell; that is to say, she reviles. Speaking such words as "May I become a householder! May she become a householder!
regarding her holy life (*brahmacariya*), for every such utterance, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning Caṇḍakāḷī, in this matter of cursing; it is a triad of offenses of expiation.

For one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each of the three [parts]; for cursing an animal, a hungry ghost, or one of inferior human status, there is an offense of wrong-doing. There is no offense for those whose primary intention is to instruct in the meaning and the Dhamma, nor for those who are insane and so forth.
Cursing by means of hell or the holy life, the state of being fully ordained, and having the instruction in the meaning and the Dhamma as one’s primary intention—[these are the factors involved].
"Non-existence"—these are the three factors here. The origins and so forth are exactly the same as in the eight [preceding] cases.
The commentary on the training rule concerning cursing others is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Weeping.
"Having struck her" means having struck her with the hands or other limbs; the *pācittiya* offense applies only to one who performs both actions.
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning Caṇḍakāḷī regarding the incident of striking herself and weeping.
For one who merely strikes or merely weeps, there is only a *dukkaṭa*. [This applies] to one who is afflicted by the misfortunes of relatives, illness, or loss of wealth. Only...
There is no offense for one who is merely weeping and not killing herself, nor for those who are insane and so forth.

Herein, there are two factors: both the act of killing oneself and the act of weeping. The origin and other characteristics are similar to those of the *samanubhāsana* (formal admonition) rule; however, this [present rule] is purely an action (*kiriyā*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning weeping is finished.
The second chapter: The Chapter on Darkness at Night.
3. The Chapter on Nakedness.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Nakedness.

In the first section of the *Naggavagga*, "naked" means either unclothed or uncovered. Thus, for one bathing in this manner, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for every movement, and at the conclusion of the bath, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was laid down with reference to several bhikkhunīs in Sāvatthī regarding the matter of bathing;
it applies in cases of emergency such as when the water-bath robe has been stolen or lost, or when [one thinks], "Seeing that this is of great value, even thieves might carry it off."
There is no offense for one who is bathing, nor for those who are insane and so forth. The three factors here are: being naked, the absence of an authorized reason, and the conclusion of the bath.
The origins and other characteristics are similar to those of the *eḷakaloma* (wool) rule.
The commentary on the training rule on nakedness is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Bathing Robe (Udakasāṭika-sikkhāpada).
Regarding the second [training rule], it was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six bhikkhunīs, in the matter of wearing bathing robes of unlimited size.
All else here should be understood according to the method already stated for the training rule on sitting mats in the Ratana-vagga.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the bathing-robe is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning sewing robes:
Regarding the third [rule], "having unpicked," this means having unpicked what was poorly sewn for the purpose of sewing it again. "One who has no obstacles" refers to [the ten]...
When not even one of the obstacles is present, except for the period of four or five days— meaning that after five days have passed from the day the robe was opened out— if one thinks,
"I will neither sew it myself nor make an effort to have it sewn," then by the mere fact of abandoning the task, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, regarding the matter of not sewing a robe after having opened it out.

There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for [giving] three items; there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for three items when giving to one who is not fully ordained (anupasampannā). Likewise, there is an offense for both [the giver and the receiver] regarding other requisites (parikkhāra).
However, there is no offense for one who is facing obstacles, or for one who, despite searching, receives nothing, or for one who, while making [the robe], exceeds the five-day limit.

There is also no offense for one who is ill, in cases of emergency (āpadā), or for those who are insane and so forth. [The definition of a robe is: being suitable as an undergarment (nivāsana) or an upper garment (pārupana).
The five factors here are: [the robe] belonging to one who is fully ordained; unsewing or having it unsewn for the purpose of sewing;
exceeding the five-day limit except for a permitted reason; and abandoning the task. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to those of the *samanubhāsana* [offense].
The commentary on the training rule concerning the sewing of robes is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Use of the Outer Robe (Saṅghāṭicāra-sikkhāpada).
In the fourth [training rule], "five days" (*pañcāha*) means five days; that which lasts for five days is "five-day" (*pañcāhika*).

The "use of the outer robe" (*saṅghāṭicāra*) refers to the movement of the outer robes. Alternatively, it is the triple robe (*ticīvara*) which has received the name "outer robe" (*saṅghāṭī*) in the sense of being sewn together, either by way of usage or by way of being dyed.
The meaning is: the exchange of these five robes, namely the *udakasāṭikā* (bathing robe) and the *saṃkaccikā* (bodice).

"Should she cause [the time] to pass, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)" means that at the rising of the sixth dawn, according to the method stated for a single robe when not exchanged, there is one offense; for five robes, there are five.
This was concerning many bhikkhunīs in Sāvatthī who, having deposited their robes, went on a journey through the country wearing only the inner and upper robes (*santaruttara*).
This was laid down in the context of the departure rule; it is a triad of *pācittiya* offenses. If five days have not elapsed, there are two *dukkaṭas*.

However, if she perceives that the period has not elapsed, or if on the fifth day she wears, puts on, or dries five robes, or if she is ill, or [if she thinks], "This robe of mine is of great value and cannot be kept during such a time of fear of thieves"—[in these cases, there is no offense].

In such emergencies, there is no offense for those who are insane and so forth. The four factors here are: being one of the five types of robes, the lapse of five days, the absence of an authorized reason, and not exchanging it.
The origin and other characteristics are the same as those for the *kathina* rule.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the use of the outer robe (*saṅghāṭicāra*) is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Transfer of Robes (*Cīvarasaṅkamanīya-sikkhāpada*).

Regarding the fifth [rule]: "Transferable robe" (*cīvarasaṅkamanīya*) means a robe that must be transferred; it refers to any one of the five robes taken from another's possession without asking permission, which must then be returned. "Should wear" (*dhāreyya*) means if she puts it on as an undergarment.
Or if she puts it on, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhunī, regarding the matter of putting on a robe after taking a bhikkhunī’s robe without asking permission;
it is a pācittiya for three cases, and a dukkaṭa for three cases involving one who is not fully ordained. Furthermore, [it applies] to whatever has been given by her.
Or, having asked permission, or being one whose robes have been stolen or lost, she wears it in such emergencies as thinking, "This robe of mine is of great value;
it is not possible to keep it during such a danger from thieves. For her, and for those who are insane and so forth, there is no offense.
[The factors for an offense are: the transferability of the robe, that it belongs to one who is fully ordained, the absence of any permitted reason, and the act of wearing it.
These are the four factors here. The origins and so forth are similar to those of the first *kaṭhina* rule; however, this is both an action and a non-action.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the transfer of robes is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Robes for a Group.
"In the sixth [offense], 'of a group' means of the community of bhikkhunīs. 'Acquisition of a robe' means a robe that is to be received, even one that has reached the stage of being assigned.
'Should create an obstacle' means she should strive in such a way that those who wish to give do not give. 'Pācittiya' means:
if they do not give because of her words, it is a pācittiya offense for the bhikkhunī."
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, regarding the act of creating an obstacle to a group’s acquisition of robes;

for other requisites, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Furthermore, even when there is an acquisition of a robe for many [monks] or for a single bhikkhunī, it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense for one who prevents [the giving] by pointing out benefits such as, “Give them when the price is lower,” nor for those who are insane, and so forth.

The three factors here are: the state of being the very last [robe] intended for distribution, the fact that it has been formally dedicated to the Saṅgha, and the act of creating an obstacle without seeing any benefit [in doing so].
The origin and other details are similar to those of the rule on taking what is not given.
The commentary on the training rule concerning robes for a group is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Obstructing.

Regarding the seventh rule: "A legitimate distribution of robes" refers to a distribution of robes being carried out by a complete Saṅgha having assembled. "Should obstruct" means she should prevent it; for her who prevents it in this way, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, in the case of obstructing a legitimate distribution of robes.

If it is a legitimate (*dhammika*) [distribution] but she is doubtful, or if it is illegitimate (*adhammika*) but she perceives it as legitimate and is also doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
There is no offense in both cases if she perceives it as illegitimate, or if she wards it off after pointing out the benefit, or in the case of those who are insane and so forth.
Here, the three factors are: the legitimacy of the distribution of robes (*cīvaravibhaṅga*), the perception of it as legitimate, and warding it off without pointing out the benefit.
The origins and other details are exactly the same as those for taking what is not given.
The commentary on the training rule concerning warding off is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Giving of Robes.
In the eighth [offense], "a monk’s robe" refers to one that has been made allowable and is suitable for use as an undergarment or upper garment;

having set aside such a robe, if she gives it away after dedicating it to any of the five fellow-followers of the Dhamma, or to her parents, or to any householder or person gone forth, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, in the case of giving a monk’s robe to a householder.

For a bhikkhunī, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense for one who gives [the robe] to others only for a temporary period even after having renounced it to her parents, nor for those who are insane and so forth.
Herein, there are three factors: the state of being a monastic robe; giving it to others—excluding fellow practitioners and parents; and not giving it for a temporary period only.
The origin and other characteristics are the same as those for matchmaking (sañcaritta).
The commentary on the training rule regarding the giving of robes is finished.
9. Commentary on the ninth training rule, concerning the transgression of the time limit:
"With a weak expectation of a robe" means with a feeble expectation of a robe, thinking, "If we are able, we shall give."
The meaning is: having generated hope by hearing only that much. "She should let the robe-season pass" means:

when the *kālacīvara* (timely robe-cloth) is being distributed among the nuns who have completed the rains residence, she says, "Wait, ladies, there is an expectation of robe-cloth for the Saṅgha," and thus lets that distribution of robe-cloth pass until the robe-season has ended; [this applies] for her, if the Kathina has not been spread, during the last month of the rainy season.
For one who lets the day for the suspension of the Kathina pass after the Kathina has been spread, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, regarding the matter of letting the robe-season pass while having only a weak expectation of obtaining a robe;
it applies to one who is uncertain about a weak robe, and to one who perceives a non-weak robe as a weak robe, or who is uncertain about it.

And there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). In both cases, if she perceives the robe-cloth as not being weak, even if they say, "We are not able," yet she prevents them by pointing out the advantage, thinking, "But now either cotton will arise for them, or a faithful man will come;
when he has arrived, they will certainly give it," there is no offense for one who is insane, and so forth. [The factor of] the robe-cloth being weak—

The perception of weakness and the prevention [of an action] without any benefit—these are the three factors here. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to those of the rule concerning taking what is not given.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the transgression of time is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule for the Suspension of the Kathina Regarding the tenth [rule], "the legitimate suspension of the Kathina":

when a lay follower (*upāsaka*), desiring to give out-of-season robe-cloth (*akālacīvara*) to all the bhikkhunīs, gives either more than or equal to the benefit derived from the formal spreading (*atthāra*), and having been requested by a unanimous assembly...

When the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs suspends the kaṭhina by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) during the [prescribed] period, that suspension is called "legitimate" (*dhammika*);
the meaning is that it is a suspension of the kaṭhina of such a kind. "Should prevent" means she should obstruct;
for her who obstructs such a suspension of the kaṭhina, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, regarding the matter of obstructing the suspension of the *kaṭhina*. The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated in the seventh [chapter].
The commentary on the training rule for the suspension of the *kaṭhina* is finished.
The third chapter, the Naked Chapter (*Naggavagga*), is concluded.

4. The Chapter on Rolling Over (Tuvaṭṭavagga) 1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Rolling Over on the Same Bed (Ekamañcatuvaṭṭanasikkhāpada) In the first [rule] of the Chapter on Rolling Over, "they should roll over" means they should lie down.
Among them, if one has already lain down and another lies down, or if both lie down together, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for both.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhunīs regarding the matter of two [women] lying down on one bed.
However, if one sits while the other is lying down, or if both sit, there is no offense for them, nor for those who are insane and so forth.
The two factors here are: being on one bed and the two of them lying down. The origins and so forth are similar to those of the wool-clipping rule.
The commentary on the training rule regarding lying down on a single bed is finished.
2. Commentary on the second training rule regarding lying down on a single covering:
In the second [rule], "a single covering and a single upper garment" refers to those which are portable.

This is a designation for those who lie down after spreading one end of a woolen rug (*pāvāra*), a blanket (*attharaṇa*), a mat (*kaṭasāraka*), or similar items, and covering themselves with the other.
It is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for those who lie down after spreading that very same thing and covering themselves with it.
This was prescribed regarding many bhikkhunīs in Sāvatthī concerning this matter of lying down; it is a triple offense of expiation.
If there is a single covering or a single upper garment, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); if there are different coverings or upper garments, it is two offenses of wrong-doing.
However, there is no offense for one who lies down after having established a boundary while perceiving those as different coverings or upper garments, nor for those who are insane and so forth.
The remainder is exactly like the first [offense].
The commentary on the training rule concerning lying on the same sheet is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Causing Discomfort:

Regarding the third rule, "causing discomfort" (*aphāsu*): without asking permission, thinking, "By this, she will find it uncomfortable," one performs such acts as walking in front of her, standing in front of her, or releasing [the body] in front of her.

For one who performs recitation, or causes it to be recited, or causes it to be pointed out, or asks questions, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) by counting the turns on the walking-path, by counting the applications in standing and so forth, or by counting the words in the recitations and so forth.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, in the case of intentionally causing discomfort; it is a triad-offense of expiation.

For one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing for each of the three [steps]. It is not an offense if it is not out of a desire to cause discomfort, if she does so after asking permission, if she performs walking meditation (*caṅkamana*) and other such acts in front [of the other], or in the case of those who are insane and so forth. Herein, the four factors are: the state of being fully ordained, the desire to cause discomfort, the act of causing discomfort, and the failure to ask permission.

The originators (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other characteristics are similar to those of taking what is not given; however, this is a "both-action-and-non-action" offense and is experienced as painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning causing discomfort is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Not Attending to the Sick:

In the fourth [rule], "afflicted" means one who is ill. "A co-resident" means a student (saddhivihārinī). "Neither attends to her" means that if she herself does not attend to her, or does not cause others to do so, the offense of expiation (pācittiya) occurs at the mere moment she abandons her duty.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, regarding a suffering co-resident who did not attend upon her;
it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the pupil or for one who is not fully ordained.

There is no offense if there is any one of the ten kinds of obstacles and she does not obtain [care] despite searching, or if she is ill, or in cases of emergency, or for those who are insane and so forth. [The factors are: being ill, and being a co-resident pupil.
The absence of an authorized reason and the relinquishing of one's responsibility in attending—these are the four factors here.
The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to those for the *samanubhāsana* [offense].
The commentary on the training rule concerning not attending is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule on Expelling (Nikkaḍḍhanasikkhāpada) Regarding the fifth [rule]:
"Having given a dwelling" means having given one's own private vihāra that is secured with a door. "Should expel" means:
for one who expels [them] through many doors by a single effort, there is one offense; for various efforts, there is an offense for each effort.

Regarding offenses, the same principle applies to commands as well. However, if one commands, "Pass through this and that door," there are as many offenses as there are doors counted in that single command.
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā in such a case; it is a triad of pācittiyas, [applying] from that which is not secured by a door-bolt.

It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); for one who is not fully ordained, it is three offenses of wrong-doing. Whether from a dwelling with a door-panel or one without a door-panel, in the case of both [monks and nuns] ejecting requisites, it is likewise only an offense of wrong-doing.
The remainder is exactly as explained in the training rule concerning the ejection of [requisites] from a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha.
The commentary on the training rule concerning ejection is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Socializing (*Saṃsaṭṭhasikkhāpada*).

The sixth [training rule] has its word-meaning already explained. It was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Caṇḍakāḷī, regarding the matter of living in social association; the rest here is exactly like the analysis stated for the first training rule concerning Ariṭṭha.
The commentary on the training rule on socializing is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Within One’s Own Kingdom (*Antoraṭṭha-sikkhāpada*) Regarding the seventh rule, "within one’s own kingdom" (*antoraṭṭhe*):

this refers to the kingdom of the one in whose domain she dwells. "A journey without a caravan" (*asatthikā cārikā*) means traveling without a caravan. For traveling from one village to another, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). In a forest devoid of villages, it is reckoned by half-yojanas.
This was spoken concerning several bhikkhunīs at Sāvatthī, in the same manner as the previous rule, regarding the occasion of setting out on a journey through the country.
It is thus laid down. There is no offense for one traveling with a man if it is in a secure place free from danger, in times of emergency, or for those who are insane and so forth.

The four factors here are: being within the same kingdom, the lack of security, the absence of any of the permitted reasons, and setting out on a journey. The origins and other characteristics are similar to those of the *eḷakaloma* (wool) rule.
The commentary on the training rule concerning another kingdom is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Another Kingdom:

Regarding the eighth [rule], "in another kingdom" (*tiroraṭṭha*) means in the kingdom of anyone other than the one whose realm he dwells in. The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated for the seventh [rule]; however, in this case, the city is Rājagaha.
The commentary on the training rule regarding Tiroraṭṭha is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule regarding the rains-retreat:
Regarding the ninth [rule], "during the rains" means having stayed for either the first three months or the last three months of that rainy season.

"Within [the rains retreat] itself. Here, there is no offense for one who goes on account of some seven-day business, or when constrained by something, or in cases of emergencies, or for those who are insane and so forth.
The remainder is exactly like the eighth rule.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the within-the-rains period is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Departure for Travel "Having completed the rains residence" means having completed either the first three months or the last three months.
"Five or six *yojanas*" means that after the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, it is permissible to travel five *yojanas*, but regarding six, there is simply nothing to be said [as it is not permitted]. If...
However, having gone three [yojanas], if she returns by that same path, it is not permissible; it is permissible to return by another way.
As soon as she has set out with the thought, "I will not go the distance specified," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This was in connection with a number of bhikkhunīs at Rājagaha, concerning the matter of departing on a journey after having spent the rains retreat.

It is thus prescribed. There is no offense in the case of an obstacle, for one who, having searched, does not find a second nun, for one who is ill, in times of distress, or for those such as the insane.

The three factors here are: having completed the rains-retreat, the absence of any permitted reason [for departure], and not exceeding five *yojanas*. The origin and other characteristics are similar to the first *pārājika*; however, this is a non-action offense and is experienced as painful.
The commentary on the training rule concerning departing while on alms-round is finished.
The fourth section, the *Tuvaṭṭa-vagga*, is concluded.
5. The *Cittāgāra-vagga*.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Royal Mansions (*Rājāgāra-sikkhāpada*).
Regarding the first [rule] of the Chapter on Painted Halls (*Cittāgāravagga*): "A royal mansion" (*rājāgāra*) is a king’s pleasure house.

"A painted hall" (*cittāgāra*) is a hall for paintings used for recreation. "A park" (*ārāma*) is a pleasure grove. "A garden" (*uyyāna*) is a pleasure garden. "A lotus pond" (*pokkharaṇī*) is a pleasure lotus pond.
"Regarding 'for the purpose of seeing' (*dassanāya*): for one who goes thinking, 'I shall see something among these,' there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at every step.
Wherever she stops and sees, even if she sees all five without lifting her foot from that spot, it is only a single offense.

However, if she sees by looking here and there, the offenses are according to the number of times the application of turning the neck occurs, not according to the number of times the eyes are opened."
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six bhikkhunīs regarding the matter of going to see a picture gallery;
for a bhikkhu, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in all cases, and the remaining analysis should be understood according to the method stated in the training rule on watching dancing.
The commentary on the training rule concerning royal residences is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Using High Seats (*āsandi*) In the second [rule], "high seat" (*āsandi*) refers to one that exceeds the prescribed dimensions.

"Couch" (*pallaṅka*) is said to be one made of woven hair and portable. Regarding the phrase "should use": here, an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) should be understood according to the number of instances of sitting or lying down.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhunīs regarding the use of high seats and couches;
there is no offense for one who uses them after cutting off the legs of a chair or breaking the legs of a couch, nor for those who are insane and so forth.
Herein, the two factors are: the nature of the chair or couch, and sitting upon it or lying down on it. As for the origin and other characteristics:
"Like the wool of a sheep.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the use of high beds is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule regarding spinning thread.

"Third, a thread" refers to any one of the six types [of fibers]. "Spun" (*kanteyya*): here, for as much as has been drawn out by hand, when that yarn is wound up, there is one offense. It is with reference to this that it is stated in the *Padabhājaniya*: "in winding and unwinding.
This rule was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six bhikkhunīs, regarding the matter of spinning;

starting from the initial act of separating the cotton before spinning, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for every application according to the number of times the hand is withdrawn. "Spun thread" (*kantitasutta*).
There is no offense for one who is ill, for one who is insane, and so forth. "Spinning" and "having spun"—these are the two factors here.
The origins and other characteristics are similar to those of the rule concerning wool.
The commentary on the training rule regarding spinning thread is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Service for Laypeople (*gihiveyyāvaccasikkhāpada*).
Regarding the fourth [rule], "service for laypeople" (*gihiveyyāvacca*) means service performed for householders.

For even if one’s mother or father, without having them perform any work themselves, prepares their conjee and so forth, there are offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) according to the number of preliminary efforts (*pubbappayoga*) involved.
Having committed [the offense], one incurs a *pācittiya* for each vessel in the case of rice-gruel and the like, and for each cake in the case of solid food and the like.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhunīs, regarding the matter of performing services for householders;
that is, when people were providing rice-gruel, meals, or offerings for the worship of a *cetiya*, acting as their assistants.
There is no offense for one who cooks gruel and so forth, or for one who performs those same services for her own attendant, or for those who are insane and so forth.

The two factors here are: performing domestic service for a layperson, and the absence of any permitted reason. As for the origin and other characteristics, they are exactly the same as those for the Eḷakaloma [offense].
The commentary on the training rule concerning service for householders is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*):

Regarding the fifth [rule], "legal issue" refers to any one of the four types. "Expiation" (*pācittiya*) means that here, as in the case of sewing a robe, the offense of expiation occurs merely by laying down the burden; there is no exemption even for a single day.

This training rule was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, regarding the matter of not settling a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*). The rest here should be understood according to the method already stated in the training rule on sewing robes.
The commentary on the training rule on legal disputes is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Giving Food.

In the sixth [offense], "with one's own hand" means: for one who gives any kind of edible food—excluding water and tooth-sticks—to anyone other than the five types of fellow practitioners (sahadhammika), whether by means of the body, what is connected to the body, or what is relinquished, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, regarding the instance of giving hard and soft food to a householder;

in the case of water and tooth-sticks, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, she who causes to be given but does not give herself, or gives after having set it aside, or gives an external ointment...
There is no offense for one who gives it, for her, or for those who are insane and so forth.
Apart from water and tooth-cleansing wood intended for swallowing, giving with one's own hand to anyone other than the five types of fellow practitioners—these are the two factors here.
The origin and other characteristics are similar to those of the Eḷakaloma [offense].
The commentary on the training rule regarding the gift of food is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule regarding lodgings and robes:
Regarding "lodgings and robes" (*āvasathacīvara*), this refers to robes given with the instruction, "Let the nuns who are in need of them use them. "Without having assigned them" (*anissajjitvā*)...
On the fourth day, having washed it, if she uses it without giving it to another—even if only to a female novice—who is menstruating, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Thus, for one who uses it without having relinquished it, there is an offense of expiation.
This was established at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, regarding the matter of using a lodging-cloth without having relinquished it.
It is prescribed as a *pācittiya* offense for three [days], and a *dukkaṭa* offense for two [days] regarding what has been forfeited.

However, there is no offense for one who uses it with the perception that it has been forfeited, or by way of another method, or because other women in their season are absent, or by one whose robes have been stolen or lost, or in times of distress, or for those who are insane and so forth. [The factors are: being a dwelling-robes [robe], and being on the fourth day.
Washing and not relinquishing [the robe], and the absence of an authorized reason—these are the four factors here. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to those of the Kathina [rules];
however, this is both an action and a non-action.
The commentary on the training rule regarding robes from a lodging is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Lodgings and Monasteries.

In the eighth [rule], "lodging" (*āvasatha*) refers to a monastery enclosed by doors. "Without having assigned" (*anissajjitvā*) means without giving it for the purpose of guarding, that is, without asking permission in this manner:
"Please keep watch over this. "Should set out on a journey, it is an offense of expiation" (*pācittiya*); here, from one's own village...

For one departing for another village even for the purpose of staying for a single night, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) as soon as she crosses the boundary of a walled lodging with her first foot, or the precincts of an unwalled one; with the second foot, it is an offense entailing confession (*pācittiya*).
This was in connection with Thullanandā at Sāvatthī, concerning the case of departing on a wandering tour without having formally relinquished the lodging.

It is laid down as an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the three cases; there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in a place not secured by a door; and there are two offenses of wrong-doing in the case of what has been relinquished.

However, there is no offense for one who perceives it as having been relinquished, or when there is an obstacle, or for one who, having sought a caretaker, does not find one, or for one who is ill, or in times of distress, or for those who are insane and so forth.
[The conditions for non-offense are: being secured by a door, departing according to the method already stated, and the absence of the permitted causes.
These are the three factors here. The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth are similar to those of the *kaṭhina* [rule]; however, this is both an action and a non-action (*kiriya-akiriya*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning dwellings and monasteries (*āvasatha-vihāra-sikkhāpada*) is concluded.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning the study of animal sciences (*tiracchānavijjā-pariyāpuṇana-sikkhāpada*).

In the ninth [offense], "animal sciences" (*tiracchānavijjā*) refers to any external knowledge that is unbeneficial, consisting of various types such as the arts of elephants, horses, chariots, archery, and swordsmanship;
the science of *āthabbaṇa*; spells for piercing, subjugating, and causing emaciation; and the application of mantras and medicinal herbs (*agada*).

Regarding the phrase "should master": for anyone who masters it by means of words and so forth, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the count of words and the count of syllables.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the mastery of animal sciences is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning the recitation of animal sciences:
In the tenth [rule], the word “should cause to recite” (*vāceyya*) is the specific distinction. Both [incidents] occurred at Sāvatthī, involving the group of six monks and several bhikkhunīs.
And it was laid down with reference to the incident of learning and reciting animal spells (*tiracchānavijjā*).

There is no offense for writing them, for memorizing them, for the purpose of protection, for any protective charms such as the *yakkha-paritta*, *nāga-maṇḍala*, and so forth, and for those who are insane and the like.
Herein, in both cases, there are three factors: the nature of being an animal spell, the learning and reciting, and the absence of an authorized reason.
The factors, such as their origination and so forth, are similar to those in the *Padasodhamma*.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the recitation of secular sciences (*tiracchānavijjā*) is finished.
The fifth chapter, the Section on Picture Galleries (*Cittāgāravagga*), is concluded.
6. Ārāma-vagga. 1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Entering a Monastery (Ārāma-pavisaṇa-sikkhāpada).
Regarding the first [rule] of the Ārāma-vagga: "A monastery with monks" (sabhikkhukaṃ ārāmaṃ) refers to a place where monks reside even at the foot of a tree.

To that place. Regarding "without having asked permission": here, if she crosses the boundary of an enclosed monastery or enters the precincts of an unenclosed one without having asked permission from anyone among the monks, novices, or monastery attendants, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the first step and an offense entailing confession (*pācittiya*) for the second step.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhunīs regarding the matter of entering a monastery without having asked permission:
“if there is a bhikkhu present,” and “knowing it to have bhikkhus. These are the two subsequent rules (anupaññatti) here.

For one who is in doubt when there are bhikkhus present, and for one who perceives there are bhikkhus when there are none, as well as for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
However, in both of these two cases—when one enters with the perception that there are no monks present; when one enters after having asked permission from a monk who is actually there;
when one follows behind the head of the nuns who have already entered first; when one has the perception, "I am going to where those nuns are assembled";
when the path lies through a monastery and she travels by it; in times of emergency; and for those who are insane and so forth.

There is no offense. The four factors here are: delighting in a place with monks, the perception that there are monks present, exceeding the prescribed limit, and the absence of any authorized reason.
It originates from formal admonition; it is an action; it is released through perception; it involves volition;
it is an offense of transgression against the rules of training; it consists of bodily and verbal action; it comprises three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule regarding entering a monastery is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Abusing a Monk:

In the second [rule], "should abuse" means that she should abuse him by means of any one of the ten grounds for abuse, either in his presence or in his absence. "Should revile" means that she should instill fear in him. "An offense of expiation" (pācittiya) means that for her who acts in this way, there is an offense of expiation.
This was laid down at Vesālī concerning the group of six bhikkhunīs in the matter of reviling the Venerable Upāli;

it is an offense of threefold pācittiya, and for one who has not received full ordination, it is an offense of threefold dukkaṭa. There is no offense for one whose primary intention is to provide instruction on the meaning or the Dhamma, nor for those who are insane and so forth. Herein, the factors are: the state of being fully ordained, the act of reviling or abusing, and the absence of the intention to provide instruction on the meaning and so forth.
There are three factors. The origins and so forth are similar to those for taking what is not given, but this [offense] is of painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the reviling of bhikkhus is concluded.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning censuring a group.
In the third [offense], "fierce" means angry. "The group" refers to the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs. "Should revile" means:

here, for one who reviles them anywhere with such words as, "These women are fools, these women are incompetent; they do not know the formal act (kamma), nor the defect in a formal act, nor the success of a formal act, nor the failure of a formal act," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, regarding the matter of reviling a group. For one who reviles several people, or a single person, or even one who is not fully ordained, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). The remainder is exactly like the second [offense].
The commentary on the training rule concerning reviling a group is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Being Invited to Eat.

In the fourth [offense], she should be understood as one who has been invited according to the method stated regarding eating in a group, and as one who has been invited according to the method stated in the training rule on *pavāraṇā*.
"Pācittiya" means that for her, having set aside the morning meal, if she accepts anything else whatsoever— whether rice-gruel or the other three types of timely food—

as well as any other kind of edible substance, for the purpose of consumption, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the moment of acceptance, and [an offense of pācittiya] at the moment of consumption.
An offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for swallowing.
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhunīs, regarding the matter of eating apart [from the Sangha].
There is an act of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) both for one who accepts the three types of meals for the purpose of food and for one who swallows them. However, for her who has been invited...

There is no offense for one who drinks conjey when not invited to do so, eats after having asked permission from the owners, or consumes the three types of food at the proper times when there is a requisite reason;
