this applies to her as well as to those who are insane and so forth. However, for one who is invited or has been invited to stop eating, or for both cases combined, the factors here are three:
the swallowing of solid food with the characteristics previously described before midday, and the failure to ask permission from the owners.
It is an offense arising from the journey; it may be both an act and a non-act, because an offense occurs for one who has been invited and eats without having asked permission;
it may be an act, because an offense occurs for one who eats—whether she has had something made allowable or not—after having been invited;

it is not to be cleared by confession, it is without mental concomitants, it is an offense of formal rule, it is bodily action and verbal action, it consists of three types of consciousness, and it consists of three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning *pavārita* (invitations) is finished.

5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Stinginess Regarding Families (*kulamaccharinī-sikkhāpada*) In the fifth [rule], stinginess regarding a family is *kulamacchara*. She has such stinginess regarding a family, or she is stingy toward a family; thus it is called *kulamaccharinī*.

"Envious of families" means one who might be such as this. "An offense entailing expiation" (pācittiya) refers to [the offense incurred] by a nun who, either in the presence of a family that wishes to provide requisites for the nuns, says, "How can the nuns not go there?", or in the presence of the nuns, says regarding a family, "How can they not give anything to them?
or in the presence of the family, says, "How can they not give anything to those [nuns]?"
There is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for one who speaks dispraise of the bhikkhunīs.
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhunī, in the case of being stingy regarding families.
There is no offense for one who, without being stingy, points out an existing danger, nor for those who are insane and so forth. [It arises from] a desire not to give gains to the bhikkhunīs.
Speaking dispraise of a family in the presence of nuns, or speaking dispraise of nuns in the presence of a family—these are the two factors here.
The origin and other characteristics are the same as those for taking what is not given; however, this [offense] is of painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning stinginess regarding families is concluded.

6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning a Residence Without Bhikkhus In the sixth [training rule], if there are no bhikkhus residing within half a yojana of the nuns' quarters to give them exhortation, or if the path is unsafe such that it is impossible to travel without hindrance, this is called a "residence without bhikkhus. In that case:
For one who, thinking "I shall dwell for the rains," performs such acts as preparing lodgings and providing drinking water, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
at the rising of the sun, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya). This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.
This [rule] was established concerning many bhikkhunīs at Sāvatthī, regarding the matter of dwelling for the rains in a residence where no monks are present.
It is prescribed that there is no offense for one who dwells where monks who have entered the rains residence have departed, left the order, died, or gone over to another faction;
nor is there an offense in cases of emergencies or for those who are insane, and so forth.

Herein, the three factors are: the state of being a residence without monks, the entering of the rains residence, and the rising of the dawn. As for the origin and other characteristics, they are exactly like those of the *eḷakaloma* (wool) offense.
The commentary on the training rule concerning a residence without monks is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Invitation (Apavāraṇā-sikkhāpada):
"In the seventh [case], 'having completed the rains' means having spent either the first or the last three months of the rains retreat. 'In both Saṅghas' means in the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha."
And also with the community of bhikkhus. Herein, however, is the detailed exposition:

on the fourteenth day itself, the bhikkhunīs, having assembled, should make either a motion encompassing the whole assembly thus, "Venerable ladies, let the Saṅgha hear me; today is the fourteenth-day invitation (pavāraṇā);
if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha invite," or they should make a threefold motion thus, "Let [the Saṅgha] invite by means of three statements."

Or, if there is an obstacle, having set aside a motion for a double invitation, a single invitation, or an invitation of equal seniority—thinking, "One should invite with a double invitation, etc."—and instead having set aside a motion that includes everyone, [she should say]:
"Venerable ladies, I invite the Saṅgha regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerable ladies speak to me out of compassion; seeing [my fault], I shall make amends."

In this way, having said either once, "Venerable lady, for a second time, I shall confess to the Saṅgha... [and so on]... for a third time, venerable lady, I shall confess to the Saṅgha," or having spoken thus two or three times, they should perform the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) in sequence.
In the case of a formal motion (*ñatti*) consisting of three statements (*tevācikā*), the wording must not be omitted;
in the case of those consisting of two statements (*dvevācikā*) and so forth, it is permissible to expand upon it, but it is not permissible to omit anything. Thus, in the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha...

Having performed the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), right there a single bhikkhunī should be appointed by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (*ñattidutiyakamma*) to invite the Saṅgha of bhikkhus on behalf of the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs, in accordance with what is stated in the Bhikkhunikkhandhaka. By that appointed bhikkhunī, on the fifteenth day,
having taken the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs, she should approach the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, arrange her upper robe over one shoulder, and extend her hands in reverential salutation (*añjali*).
He should be addressed thus: "Noble sir, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha invites the Bhikkhu Saṅgha regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the noble Bhikkhu Saṅgha speak to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha out of compassion;

seeing [the fault], she will make amends. For a second time, noble sir... [as before] ...for a third time, noble sir... [as before] ...seeing [the fault], she will make amends. Thus should the invitation be performed.

If the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs is not complete with five members, then having established a formal motion (*gaṇañatti*) with four or three, they should invite one another by means of a motion (*ñatti*) even with two, provided there is no deficiency. One [bhikkhunī] should resolve: "Today is my invitation day.
Having gone to the monastery, she should say: "Venerable sirs, the bhikkhunīs invite the Saṅgha of bhikkhus regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected;
let the Saṅgha of bhikkhus speak to the bhikkhunīs out of compassion for them, so that those who see [the faults] may [confess them]."

And one should speak thus three times: "I shall make amends," and "Venerable sir, I invite the Saṅgha of bhikkhus regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected; let the Saṅgha of bhikkhus speak to me out of compassion; seeing it, I shall make amends."
If the community of monks is not complete, [one should say]: "Noble sirs, the community of nuns invites you regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected;
may the noble ladies speak to the community of nuns out of compassion for them, so that seeing [the fault], they may make amends";
and: "Noble sirs, the community of nuns invites you regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected..."
“Venerable sirs, please speak to the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs out of compassion; seeing [the fault], they will make amends”—this should be said three times.
If both [Saṅghas] are incomplete, one should say: “Venerable sirs, the bhikkhunīs invite the venerable ones regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected;
may the venerable ones speak to the bhikkhunīs out of compassion; seeing [the fault], they will make amends. And: “Bhikkhunīs...”
“Venerable lady, they invite the venerable lady regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected;

may the venerable lady speak to the bhikkhunīs out of compassion, for those who see will make amends. And: “Venerable ladies, I invite the venerable ladies regarding what has been seen, heard, or [suspected]...
May the venerable ladies speak to me out of compassion, for I, seeing it, will make amends.”
And [she should say]: “Venerable lady, I invite you regarding what has been seen or heard... [as before] ...May the venerable lady speak to me out of compassion;
seeing it, I shall make amends. This should be said three times.

For by this method, she has indeed performed the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) before both Saṅghas. However, for one who has completed the rains residence and thinks, “I will not perform the invitation in this way before both Saṅghas,” [the procedure is as follows].
She lays down her burden; with the laying down of that burden, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhunīs who, having spent the rains residence, did not perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*).

However, it does not apply in the case of an obstacle, or for one who, despite searching, cannot find monks, or for one who is ill, or in cases of emergency, or for those who are insane, and so forth.

There is no offense. The three factors here are: having completed the rains residence, there being no invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) before both Saṅghas, and the absence of any authorized reason [for not inviting].
The origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other characteristics are the same as those for the instruction on formal admonition (*samanubhāsana*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning non-invitation (*apavāraṇā-sikkhāpada*) is finished.

8. Commentary on the Training Rule for Exhortation (Ovādasikkhāpada) In the eighth [rule], "for the exhortation" (*ovādāya*) means for the purpose of hearing the heavy rules (*garudhamma*). "For the communal living" (*saṃvāsāya*) means for the purpose of asking about the Uposatha day and for the purpose of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*). "A *pācittiya*" means that as soon as one has abandoned the duty by thinking, "I will not go for these purposes," it is a *pācittiya* offense.
This was laid down with reference to the group of six bhikkhunīs among the Sakyans, concerning the matter of not going for the exhortation. Regarding obstacles...

However, there is no offense for one who has mindfulness, or for one who, despite having searched, does not find a companion, or for one who is ill, or for one in cases of emergency, or for those who are insane, and so forth.
Not going for the sake of exhortation or communal residence—namely, the absence of the authorized reasons—these are the two factors here.
The origins and other characteristics are similar to the first *pārājika*; however, this is a non-action and involves painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning exhortation is finished.
9. Commentary on the ninth training rule concerning approaching for exhortation:
"Every half-month" means every fortnight. "Inquiring about the Uposatha" means the inquiry regarding the Uposatha day.
"Approaching for instruction" means approaching for the purpose of receiving instruction. Regarding the phrase "she who transgresses that":
on the thirteenth or fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, the bhikkhunīs should go to the monastery and ask, "Is this the Uposatha day of the fourteenth or the fifteenth?
On the Uposatha day, they should request the approach for instruction according to the method explained in the commentary on the Nidāna. Any bhikkhunī...
If she does not perform either of those two during the time specified, she is said to have "transgressed" it.
For her, the offense of *pācittiya* occurs the very moment she abandons the duty, thinking, "I will not even ask about the Uposatha, nor will I request the exhortation.
This was in reference to several bhikkhunīs at Sāvatthī, concerning the matter of not asking about the Uposatha and not requesting the exhortation.
It is laid down; there is no offense in the case of one who is exactly like the eighth [type of nun].

In this context, there are two factors: the laying down of the burden regarding the failure to request or ask for instruction on the Uposatha, and the absence of a permitted reason. The origins and other characteristics are the same as those for the *samanubhāsana* (formal admonition).
The commentary on the training rule concerning approaching for instruction is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Thighs (Pasākhejātasikkhāpada) In the tenth [rule], "in the thigh" (*pasākhe*) means in the region below the navel and above the kneecaps.
For it is because both thighs extend outwards like the branches of a tree that it is called a "thigh" (*pasākha*); [the act is committed] in that thigh.
"Boils" refers to any kind of boil. "Wounds" refers to a sore. Regarding the phrases "should cause to be lanced," etc.:
if he commands all of them, saying, "Lance it! Cut it open! and the other does exactly so, there are six *dukkaṭas* and six *pācittiyas*.
Or, if he commands, "Do whatever needs to be done here," and the other performs all the acts such as lancing and so forth, [the same penalty applies].
By a single utterance, there are six *dukkaṭas* and six *pācittiyas*.

However, if one commands only one among the acts such as splitting [the tumor] and so forth, saying, "Do this," and that person performs all of them, there is a *pācittiya* only for the performance of that which was commanded.
This was in connection with a certain nun at Sāvatthī, regarding the case of having a man split a tumor grown on her groin.
There is no offense for one who acts after having obtained permission, or after taking any wise person as a companion, nor for those who are insane and so forth.
Herein, the four factors are: being born in the groin, not obtaining permission, the absence of a companion, and causing a man to perform acts such as splitting [the hair] and so on.
The origin and other characteristics are similar to those of the *kathina* rule; however, this is a "non-action" (*akiriya*) offense.
The commentary on the training rule concerning one who has given birth is finished.
The sixth section, the Chapter on Monasteries (Ārāmavagga), is concluded.
7. The Chapter on Pregnant Women (Gabbhinīvagga).
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Pregnant Women (*Gabbhinīsikkhāpada*).

Regarding the first rule of the section on pregnant women: for one who, knowing [the candidate] is pregnant, ordains her as a preceptor, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) during the search for a formal group and so forth, and during the two proclamations of the motion (*ñatti-kammavācā*); at the conclusion of the final proclamation, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning several bhikkhunīs, based on the incident of ordaining a pregnant woman.

If she is pregnant, but one is doubtful; or if she is not pregnant, but one perceives her as such and is also doubtful—there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense if one perceives both as not pregnant, or in the case of those who are insane and so forth.

The three factors here are: her state of pregnancy, the knowledge that "she is pregnant," and the act of ordaining her. The origins and other characteristics are the same as for the offense of taking what is not given; however, this is an offense of formal rule (paṇṇattivajja).
"Three minds, three feelings.
The commentary on the training rule concerning pregnant women is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning women who have given birth.

"In the second [offense], 'one who is nursing' means one who is being nursed at the breast; the mother or the wet-nurse of the one who is nursing. This is merely the difference in the subject matter here; the rest is exactly the same as the first training rule.
The commentary on the training rule concerning one who is nursing is finished.
3. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning a Trainee Nun."
"In the third [offense], 'two years' means two years by way of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*).
'In six rules' refers to the six training precepts beginning with abstaining from taking life and ending with abstaining from eating at improper times.

'One who has not trained in the training' means, according to the method stated in the word-commentary, one who has not undertaken the training or one whose training has been broken. 'She should ordain a trainee'—in those six..."

Because of training in the teachings (*dhammas*), or because of honoring those very teachings designated as "training" (*sikkhā*), one might ordain a person who has received such a name but is not yet fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
It is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*); this is according to the same method stated in the first training rule, at the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhunīs, in the matter of the ordination of a trainee (*sikkhamānā*) of such a kind.
It is laid down that for a formal act in accordance with the Dhamma (*dhammakamma*), there is an offense of expiation involving three factors (*tikapācittiya*);

for a formal act not in accordance with the Dhamma (*adhammakamma*), there is an offense of wrong-doing involving three factors (*tikadukkaṭa*). There is no offense for one who ordains a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*) who has trained in the six rules for two years, nor for those who are insane and so forth. According to the method already stated, the three factors here are: the state of not having trained in the rules, the nature of the formal act being in accordance with the Dhamma, and the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*). As for the origin and other characteristics:
"In the first [case], the method is exactly as stated.
The commentary on the first training rule for a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*) is concluded.
4. Commentary on the second training rule for a trainee nun.

Regarding "not authorized by the Saṅgha" in the fourth [offense]: this refers to those for whom the Saṅgha has not granted authorization for ordination—even if only in the ordination hall—as stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).
These two types of trainees are called *mahāsikkhamānā*. Here, there is no offense for one who ordains her when she has been authorized by the Saṅgha, nor for those who are insane and so forth.
The remainder is exactly as stated in the third [offense].
This, however, is a case of neither-action-nor-non-action.
The commentary on the second training rule for a trainee nun is finished.
5. Commentary on the first training rule concerning one who has gone to a householder.
In the fifth [offense], "one who has gone to a house" means one who has gone to another man; here too, this is merely the basis for the offense, which is the only distinction.
Even though there is no offense for one who ordains a girl less than twelve years old while perceiving her to be full [of age], she nevertheless remains unordained.
The rest is exactly the same as the first training rule.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning one who has gone to a house is finished.
6–7. Commentary on the second and third training rules concerning one who has gone to a house:
In the sixth, everything is according to the method stated for the third; in the seventh as well, everything should be understood according to the very method stated for the fourth.
The commentary on the second and third training rules concerning one who has gone to a house is finished.
8. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning a Co-resident:
Regarding the term “co-resident” (*sahajīvinī*), it refers to a student (*saddhivihārinī*). “He should not support her” means he should not himself support her by means of recitation and so forth.
"Should not cause to assist" means: she should not cause another to assist her by saying, "Noble lady, give this woman instruction and so forth.
It is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) as soon as the responsibility is relinquished.

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā regarding such a case; the rest here is exactly the same as what was stated in the training rule on "the one who lives with the afflicted" in the Tuvaṭṭavagga.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning co-residents is finished.
9. Commentary on the ninth training rule concerning following after:
"A *pavattinī* who has been ordained" means that she by whom [the candidate] was ordained is her preceptor (*upajjhāyinī*).
Meaning: "Should not follow" means she should not attend upon her with various necessary services, such as with powder, clay, tooth-sticks, or water for rinsing the mouth.
"Pācittiya" means that as soon as she has abandoned her duty and does not follow, it is a Pācittiya offense.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhunīs regarding the matter of not following; [it concerns] one who is foolish.
However, there is no offense for one who does not follow a shameless woman, or for one who is ill, in times of distress, or for those who are insane and so forth.
The three factors here are: having been ordained, failing to follow for two years, and the absence of a permitted reason.
The origin and other characteristics are similar to the first *pārājika*; this, however, is a non-action and is experienced as painful.
The commentary on the training rule concerning following after is finished.
10. Commentary on the second training rule concerning co-residents:

"Neither shall she leave her behind" means she must not take her and go away. "Nor shall she cause her to be left behind" means she must not command another, saying, "Noble lady, take this one and go. It is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) as soon as the responsibility is relinquished.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, regarding the case of a co-resident nun not being sent away.
However, there is no offense if there is an obstacle; or if, after searching, one does not find a companion; or if one is ill; or in cases of emergency; or for those who are insane and so forth.

[The factors constituting an offense are: being a co-resident; the failure to send her away when she should be sent away; the laying down of the burden (i.e., giving up the duty); and the absence of any of the permitted reasons.
These are the three factors here. The origins and so forth are similar to those in the case of formal admonition (*samanubhāsana*).
The commentary on the second training rule concerning co-residents (*sahajīvinī*) is finished.
The seventh chapter, the Section on Pregnant Women (*Gabbhinīvagga*), is concluded.
8. The Chapter on the Maiden (Kumāribhūtavagga) 1–2–3.
Commentary on the First, Second, and Third Training Rules Concerning the Maiden.
The first, second, and third rules of this Chapter on the Maiden are identical to the three training rules concerning a married woman (gihigata). As for...
However, those two very first *mahāsikkhamānās* should be understood as having exceeded twenty years of age.
For whether they have gone forth to a husband or have not gone forth, in formal acts such as the granting of consent (*sammutikamma*), they are to be called simply "probationers" (*sikkhamānā*);

they are not to be called "those who have gone forth to a husband" (*gihigatā*) or "maidens" (*kumāribhūtā*). When one who has gone forth to a husband reaches ten years [of age], the granting of consent for training (*sikkhāsammuti*)—
Having granted [the training] at the age of twelve, the full ordination (upasampadā) should be performed; having granted it at the age of eleven, it should be performed at the age of thirteen;

having granted the authorization for training (sikkhāsammuti) at the ages of twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, or seventeen, the full ordination should be performed at the age of twenty. And from the age of eighteen onwards, this...
It is appropriate to call her either a "married woman" (*gihigatā*) or a "virgin" (*kumāribhūtā*).
However, that novice nun (*sāmaṇerī*) who is called a "virgin" should not be called a "married woman"; she should be called only a "virgin.
But by virtue of being granted permission for training (*sikkhāsammuti*), it is appropriate to call all of them "probationers" (*sikkhamānā*).
The commentary on the first training rule concerning those who have not yet reached maidenhood, etc., is concluded.

4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Those Under Twelve Years [of Ordination] In the fourth [rule], "under twelve years" means one whose twelve years of seniority are not yet complete by way of full ordination (*upasampadā*).

"An offense of expiation" (*pācittiya*) means that for one acting as a preceptor (*upajjhāyā*) and giving the full admission, there are offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the manner already described during the interval, and at the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*), it is an offense of expiation.
The commentary on the training rule concerning those less than twelve years [of standing] is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Those Fully Twelve Years [of Standing]:

Regarding the fifth [rule], "not authorized by the Saṅgha," this refers to one for whom the authorization to give the full admission (*vuṭṭhāpana-sammuti*) has not been granted by the Saṅgha, as stated in the word-analysis (*padabhājana*). The remainder is exactly the same in both cases as in the two training rules concerning the *mahāsikkhamānā*.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the completion of twelve years is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule regarding the grounds for censure:
Regarding the sixth [rule], "when she is told, 'Enough, noble lady, with ordaining for the time being,'" this refers to when permission to ordain has been requested.
Having been investigated by the Saṅgha, she was thus restrained with the words: “Since she is foolish, incompetent, and shameless, enough now with your full ordination.

Later, seeing that the authorization for other competent and conscientious women to give the higher ordination was being granted, she thought, “Surely I alone am foolish,” and so forth. This is what is meant by "the state of subsequent reproach."
"Wherever she may speak thus, she incurs [the offense]. *Pācittiya*: for one who falls into the state of censuring in this manner, it is a *pācittiya*.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Caṇḍakāḷī, regarding the matter of falling into such a state of censuring.

There is no offense for those who censure out of natural inclination toward approval (*chanda*) and so forth, nor for those who are insane and so on. [This applies] with regard to the formal authorization for ordination (*vuṭṭhāpanasammuti*).
The three factors here are: the request; the consent saying "It is well," after having investigated and not having rejected it out of favoritism or other such motives; and subsequent grumbling.
The origin and other characteristics are the same as those for taking what is not given; however, this [offense] is of painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the nature of grumbling is finished.
7–8. Commentary on the First and Second Training Rules concerning the Ordination of a Trainee Nun (Sikkhamānā).

Regarding the seventh [rule]: when a trainee nun has requested ordination (*upasampadā*), and that bhikkhunī, having spoken thus, subsequently obtains the robe-cloth—provided there is no obstacle—[she commits an offense] if she neither ordains her nor makes an effort toward her ordination.

If she were to lay down her burden, thinking, "I shall do it," then by that laying down of the burden, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). The same principle applies to the eighth [offense] as well.
Both of these were laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā on these grounds:
when there is an obstacle, when she has searched but cannot find [the necessary materials], when she is ill, in times of distress, and for those who are insane and so forth, there is no offense.
In both cases, there are four factors here: the promise, "I shall cause her to emerge [from training]"; the fulfillment of what was desired; the subsequent abandonment of responsibility;
and the absence of any authorized reason [for such abandonment]. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and other characteristics are the same as those for the formal admonition (samanubhāsana).
The commentary on the first and second training rules concerning the ordination of a trainee nun (sikkhamānā) is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Abode of Sorrow (*Sokāvāsa-sikkhāpada*).
Regarding the ninth [rule]: it is called "the abode of sorrow" because women who come having made an appointment cause internal sorrow to enter into men;
thus, it is "that abode of sorrow. Alternatively, just as a house is [the domain] of the householder, so too this [woman], not obtaining the company of men, [is like that].
“Sokāvāsā” means that she enters into sorrow; whatever she enters, that becomes her dwelling—thus they are called “dwellings of sorrow.

For this very reason, its word-commentary states the meaning in two ways: “Dwellings of sorrow means she causes suffering to arise for others, and she herself enters into sorrow. Regarding the term *pācittiya*:
for one who ordains such a person, at the conclusion of the formal ritual (*kammavācā*), the preceptor incurs a *pācittiya* offense according to the method already explained.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā regarding the matter of giving full admission to such a *sikkhamānā*.

There is no offense for one who does not know, nor for those who are insane and so forth. The three factors here are: being a dwelling place of sorrow, knowing [the girl’s condition], and giving her full admission.
The origin and other characteristics are exactly the same as in the case of giving full admission to a pregnant woman.
The commentary on the training rule concerning dwelling in fear is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning what is not permitted:
Regarding the tenth [rule], "by her mother and father" means by the biological mother and the biological father; "by her husband" means by him by whom she has been taken as his own.
"By him. "Without permission" means not having been permitted for the sake of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
For it must be requested twice by the nuns—both at the time of going forth (*pabbajjā*) and at the time of full ordination—whereas for the monks, it is permissible even if requested only once.
Therefore, for one who grants full ordination at the time of ordination without having requested permission, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the method already stated.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning Thullanandā, regarding the matter of giving the full admission (*vuṭṭhāpana*) without permission.
There is no offense for one who gives the full admission after having sought permission, for one who does not know that they exist, or for those who are insane and so forth.

In this case, there are three factors: the failure to seek permission, the knowledge that they exist, and the act of giving the full admission. It originates from what has not been permitted; it is both an action and a non-action.
It is without perception, a liberation, mindless, an offense by designation, bodily action, verbal action, consisting of three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning what is not permitted is finished.
11. Commentary on the training rule for those on probation (*pārivāsika*).

"By the giving of consent by one who has been sent away" (*pārivāsikachandadāna*) means by the giving of consent by one who has been dispatched. In this context, there are four kinds of being sent away: sending away from the assembly (*parisapārivāsiya*), sending away for the night (*rattipārivāsiya*), sending away by consent (*chandapārivāsiya*), and sending away by intention (*ajjhāsayapārivāsiya*).

Among these, "sending away from the assembly" refers to when monks have gathered for some business, and then either a cloud arises, a dispersal is made, or people arrive overwhelming [the space], and the monks...
If they rise up without relinquishing their consent, saying, “We have no time; let us go elsewhere,” this is called “leaving the assembly.
Even though it is leaving the assembly, because consent has not been relinquished, it is permissible to perform the formal act (*kamma*).
Furthermore, if monks gather at night, thinking, “We shall perform the Uposatha and other rites,” [and wait] until all have assembled...
They request one [monk], saying, “We shall listen to the Dhamma,” and while he is still delivering the Dhamma talk, the dawn breaks.
If they were seated intending to perform the Uposatha on the fourteenth day, it is permissible to perform it on the fifteenth.
If they were seated intending to perform it on the fifteenth, they may not perform the Uposatha on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pāṭipada), which is not an Uposatha day.
It is permissible. However, it is also permissible to perform other business of the Saṅgha; this is what is called "staying overnight.

Furthermore, when monks have sat down thinking, "We shall perform some business of the Saṅgha, such as a formal act of rehabilitation (abbhāna)," a monk who is an astrologer says there, "Today the constellation is ominous; do not perform this act."

Having relinquished their consent (*chanda*) at his word, they remain seated right there; then another person arrives and says, "While you wait for the auspicious moment (*nakkhatta*), a calamity has befallen this fool;
what do you achieve by waiting for the auspicious moment? This constitutes both the relinquishment of consent (*chandapārivāsiya*) and the relinquishment of intention (*ajjhāsayapārivāsiya*).
In this case of relinquishment, one need not bring forward the purity of consent (*chandapārisuddhi*) again for the formal act (*kamma*).
It is not permissible to do so; it is with reference to this that it was said, "by the giving of consent by one on probation.
Regarding the offense of *pācittiya*: for one who ordains in this manner, at the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*), there is a *pācittiya* offense according to the method already stated.
This was prescribed concerning Thullanandā at Rājagaha in the case of such an ordination. Without having relinquished her consent...
There is no offense for one who ordains when the assembly has not risen, nor for those who are insane and so forth.

Here, the two factors are: the giving of consent by one on probation (*pārivāsika*) and the act of ordaining. The origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other characteristics are exactly like those of the *Gambhīra* training rule.
The commentary on the training rule concerning those on probation is finished.
12. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Every Year (*Anuvassa-sikkhāpada*).
"Every year" (*anuvassa*) means annually. For one who ordains [a girl] in this manner, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the method already stated.
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhunīs, based on the occasion of ordaining [girls] every year.
There is no offense for one who ordains [a woman] every other year, nor for those who are insane and so forth.
Here, the two factors are: "every year" and "ordaining. The origins and other details are exactly as stated in the eleventh [offense].
The commentary on the training rule regarding "every year" is finished.
13. Commentary on the Training Rule for One Year (Ekavassasikkhāpada).
In the thirteenth [rule], there is no offense for one who ordains [a woman] with an interval of one year, nor for those who are insane and so forth. The remainder is exactly the same as the twelfth.
The commentary on the training rule for one year is finished.
The eighth chapter: The Chapter on Maidens.
9. The Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Umbrellas and Footwear.
In the first chapter of the *Chattavagga*, "umbrella and sandals" refers to the umbrella and the sandals as defined in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).
"Should carry" means that for one who carries them even for a whole day while traveling on the road by way of personal use, there is a single offense.
However, if, upon reaching such a place, she puts away the umbrella and takes off the sandals, and [carries them] again and again—
If she carries [them], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for each act of application.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six bhikkhunīs regarding the matter of carrying a sunshade and sandals;
"unless she is ill" is the subsequent rule (anupaññatti) here. There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the carrying of a sunshade alone, or sandals alone.

For one who is not ill, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for three [offenses]; for one who is ill, there are two offenses of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). However, there is no offense for one who perceives herself as ill, for one who wears [the robe] within the monastery or its precincts, in cases of emergency, or for those who are insane and so forth.

The two factors here are: the wearing by both [monks and nuns], and the absence of any authorized reason [for wearing it]. The origin and other characteristics are similar to those of the rule concerning wool (eḷakaloma).

The commentary on the training rule regarding sandals is finished. 2. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Vehicles (*Yāna-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā*) Regarding the second [rule], "by means of a vehicle" (*yānena*): this refers to a bullock cart and so forth.

Here too, for one who repeatedly mounts [the vehicle] after having dismounted, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the count of each individual act. In the section on non-offenses (*anāpatti*), the phrase "in a monastery or in the vicinity of a monastery" (*ārāme ārāmūpacāre*) does not apply; the remainder should be understood in the same manner as stated in the first [training rule].
The commentary on the training rule concerning vehicles is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning the hip-cord (saṅghāṇi).

Regarding the third [rule], "saṅghāṇi" refers to anything that serves as a hip-strap. "Should wear" means she should fasten it around her waist. Here too, for one who wears it by repeatedly taking it off and putting it back on, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) according to the number of applications.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhunī regarding the matter of wearing a hip-string.
There is no offense for one who wears a waist-cord due to illness, nor for those who are insane and so forth. The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated;
however, this [offense] is committed with an unwholesome state of mind.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the hip-belt is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning women’s ornaments:
“Women’s ornaments” refers to any kind of jewelry, such as those worn on the head and so forth. Here, the offense should be understood according to the number of items involved in each specific case.

This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six bhikkhunīs regarding the wearing of women’s ornaments. There is no offense for one who wears something [only] due to a medical condition, nor for those who are insane and so forth. The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the training rule on women’s ornaments is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule on Perfumes and Cosmetics.

Regarding "with perfume and colorant" in the fifth [offense]: this refers to any kind of perfume and any kind of colorant. Here, from the point of beginning the preliminary application by joining perfumes and so forth, there is an *dukkaṭa*;
at the conclusion of the bath, there is a *pācittiya*. There is no offense in the case of one who does so due to illness, nor for those who are insane and so forth.
The remainder is exactly the same as in the fourth [offense].
The commentary on the training rule concerning perfumes and colors is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Scented [Substances]:
Regarding the sixth rule, "scented" means scented with perfume. "Oil-cake" means sesame flour. The remainder is exactly like the fifth [training rule].
The commentary on the training rule concerning perfumes is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Having Oneself Massaged by a Nun:
"In the seventh [rule], ‘should have herself massaged’ means she should have herself rubbed with oil. ‘Should have herself rubbed’ means she should have herself stroked. And here, ‘hand’..."
If one rubs [the body] without releasing [the hand], it is a single offense; if one releases and then releases again while rubbing, there are as many offenses as there are acts.
The same principle applies to massaging.
This was concerning several bhikkhunīs in Sāvatthī, regarding the matter of having a bhikkhunī rubbed and massaged.
It is prescribed for one who is ill, in times of distress, and there is no offense for those who are insane and so forth.

Here, the fatigue from traveling on a journey is considered "illness," and trembling of the body due to fear of thieves and the like is considered "distress. The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated in the fourth [rule].
The commentary on the training rule concerning having a nun massage oneself is finished.
8–10. Commentary on the Training Rules concerning Having a Trainee Massaged, etc.

In the eighth, ninth, and tenth [rules] as well, the only difference is that [the subject] is a *sikkhamānā*, a female novice (*sāmaṇerī*), or a laywoman (*gihinī*). The remainder is exactly the same as the seventh.
The commentary on the training rules concerning having a trainee massaged, etc., is concluded.

11. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Not Asking Permission In the eleventh [rule], "in front of a bhikkhu" means not directly facing him; however, it should be understood that this is stated with reference to the *upacāra* (the vicinity).
Therefore, even if one is on the bare ground within the *upacāra* of a bhikkhu, one should say, "Venerable sir, I am sitting."
For one who sits down without having asked permission, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This was prescribed at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhunīs, regarding the matter of sitting down without asking permission;

it is a triple *pācittiya* offense, and if permission has been asked, it is a double offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*). In this case, if she perceives that permission has been asked, or if she is ill, or in cases of emergency, [there is no offense].

There is no offense for those who are insane and so forth. In this case, there are three factors: [the act being] done without having asked permission from a bhikkhu, sitting within the vicinity, and the absence of any authorized reason.
The origin and other characteristics are similar to those of the Kathina rules; however, this is a "non-volitional action" (kiriya-akiriya).
The commentary on the training rule regarding not asking permission is concluded.
12. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Asking Questions.
Regarding the twelfth rule, *anokāsakataṃ* means "not having made an opportunity" by saying, "I shall ask in such-and-such a place.

Therefore, for one who asks about the Vinaya or the Abhidhamma without first having requested an opportunity regarding the Suttanta, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). This applies to the remaining cases as well.
The same principle applies; however, in the case where [the formal act] has not been performed at all, there is simply nothing to be said.
This rule was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a number of bhikkhunīs who questioned a bhikkhu who had not granted them leave, regarding the matter of asking questions.
For one who asks after having obtained leave on each specific occasion, or for one who asks after having obtained leave in a general, unspecified manner—
There is no offense for one who asks anywhere at all, nor for those who are insane and so forth.

In this case, there are two factors: causing a bhikkhu not to grant an opportunity, and asking a question. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and other characteristics are similar to those of the *Padasodhamma* [offense], but this is classified as "action-and-non-action" (*kiriya-akiriya*).
The commentary on the training rule regarding asking questions is finished.
13. Commentary on the Thirteenth Training Rule:
Regarding "without a bodice" (*asaṃkaccika*), it refers to that which is for the purpose of covering the body, defined as the area from below the collarbone down to above the navel.

"Without the authorized *saṃkaccika*. "Should enter a village": here, for one who crosses or enters the enclosure of an enclosed village, or the vicinity of an unenclosed village, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) when the first foot [crosses], and an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) with the second.
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning a certain nun, on the occasion of entering a village without a *saṃkaccika*.
However, there is no offense for one whose *saṃkaccika* robe has been stolen or lost, nor for one who is ill, nor in cases of emergencies, nor for those who are insane and so forth.

The three factors here are: being without a *saṃkaccika*, exceeding the prescribed limits, and the absence of any authorized reason [for not wearing it]. The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other characteristics are similar to those of the *eḷakaloma* [offense].
The commentary on the training rule concerning the *asaṃkaccika* (not wearing a bodice) is finished.
The ninth section, the Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear, is concluded.
10… [etc. …16. The Chapter on False Speech and so forth.
Commentary on the Training Rules concerning False Speech, etc.:
In the seven chapters that follow, beginning with the Chapter on False Speech, the analysis should be understood according to the same method as stated in the commentary on the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha.
This is the sixteenth chapter.

"Venerable ladies, the one hundred and sixty-six *pācittiya* rules have been recited. Regarding these, seventy are common [to both monks and nuns], being prescribed with reference to monks; ninety-six are not common, being prescribed specifically for nuns. Thus, there are one hundred and sixty-six.
The remainder is clear in every respect. This concludes the commentary on the *Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha* within the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Pātimokkhavaṇṇanā*.
The commentary on the pure *pācittiya* offenses is finished.
Herein, this is the summary of the determination of origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) for the non-common training rules:

the training rule concerning mountaineering festivals, the training rule concerning picture galleries, the female waist-band, female ornaments, perfumes and ointments, and scented sesame oil—these [originate] with nuns and others.
"Ummaddana-parimaddana": these ten training rules (sikkhāpada) are unintentional (acittaka), offenses by worldly transgression (lokavajja), and involve unwholesome states of mind (akusalacitta).

This is the intended meaning here: they are "unintentional" because they can be committed even without a [specific] intention; however, since they must be committed with an unwholesome state of mind when such a mind is present, they are both "offenses by worldly transgression" and "involving unwholesome states of mind. The remaining [rules] are intentional (sacittaka).
These are indeed [the rules] excluding the mere formal injunctions (*paṇṇatti-vajja*). The nineteen training rules (*sikkhāpada*) consisting of intentional offenses (*sacittaka*) are as follows:

the rule on causing a thief to leave [the community], the seven rules beginning with the first of the section on pregnant women (*gabbhini-vagga*), the five rules beginning with the first of the section on unmarried girls (*kumāribhūta-vagga*), the rule on being in association with men and others, the giving of consent by one on probation (*pārivāsika-chanda-dāna*), the rule on ordaining every year, and the rule on ordaining every other year. These are the nineteen training rules that involve intention.

Those that are not prohibited by mere rule (paṇṇatti-vajja) are excluded. The remaining offenses committed with a conscious mind (sacittaka) are exclusively those prohibited by worldly convention (loka-vajja).
The Section on the Pāṭidesanīya Offenses: 1.
Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Solicitation of Ghee.
Regarding the first of the *pāṭidesanīya* rules, "ghee": this refers specifically to cow's ghee and so forth, as mentioned previously in the analysis found in the *pāḷi*.
Regarding the phrase "having requested it, one should eat": if one takes it with the thought, "I will eat what has been obtained through a request," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
for every swallow of what has been taken, there is an offense of confession (*pāṭidesanīya*).
This was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group of six bhikkhunīs regarding the matter of requesting ghee and eating it;
"one who is not ill" is the subsequent rule (anupaññatti) here. It is a triad of offenses entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya). For one who is ill, there is a twofold offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
However, for one who is ill and perceives herself as ill, or who requests it while ill but eats it after having become no longer ill—

There is no offense for one who is ill, or for one who eats what remains, or what was requested from a place where relatives have given permission, or what was requested for the sake of another, or what was taken with her own wealth. There is also no offense for those who are insane and so forth.

Herein, there are four factors: being afflicted by the aforementioned type of fever, the absence of any permitted reason, the act of requesting, and the swallowing [of the food]. The origin and other characteristics are the same as those for the *addhāna* (journey) offense.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the soliciting of ghee is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rules regarding the soliciting of oil, etc.:

In the second and subsequent rules as well, oils and so forth that have been previously explained and determined are already included in the Pāḷi; however, for all eight [substances] not mentioned in the Pāḷi, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). The remainder is in every respect exactly the same as what was stated for the first [rule].
The commentary on the training rules beginning with “intimating by gesture” is finished.
In the Commentary on the Pātimokkha for the Removal of Doubt, [this concludes] the section on the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha.
The commentary on the *Pāṭidesanīya* rules is finished.
1. Commentary on the training rules beginning with “all around” (*parimaṇḍala*).

From here onwards, however, the *Sekhiya* rules and the methods for settling legal issues (*adhikaraṇasamatha*) should be understood in their entirety according to the method already explained in the commentary on the *Bhikkhu-pātimokkha*.
The commentary on the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha within the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* Pātimokkhavaṇṇanā is completed.
The Concluding Statement.
And to this extent,
the commentary on the Pātimokkha has been composed at the request of the Elder Soṇa, who,
desiring the removal of doubts, sought to resolve the uncertainties regarding the Vinaya.
I have undertaken this entire work based on the method of the Sinhalese commentaries,
relying upon the oral tradition of the Mahāvihāra dwellers.
Having taken that completely, it has now reached its conclusion.
It contains the entire essence of the commentaries and the full meaning of the Pāḷi;
there is no word here that would conflict with the Pāḷi or with the ancient commentaries of the Mahāvihāravāsins.
Therefore, one who desires their own welfare should not entertain doubt regarding this matter,
but should indeed train themselves with diligence in this *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*.
And just as those who have reached the final conclusion [regarding] this *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*...
For this scripture, which consists of twenty-two recitation sections,
may all beings, having thus reached completion without obstacle and being supported by what is auspicious,
soon fulfill all their heart's desires.
Adorned with supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy; endowed with a multitude of virtues such as moral discipline, conduct, sincerity, and gentleness;
capable of plunging into the depths of both his own and other systems of tenets; possessed of analytical discernment;

a great grammarian whose unimpeded radiance of knowledge shone throughout the Teacher’s Dispensation—including the three Pitakas and their commentaries; and graced by the beauty of speech that was perfectly articulated, sweet, firm, noble, and eloquent, produced by the excellence of his craftsmanship.
By the one named Buddhaghosa—a title bestowed by his teachers—who was a speaker of the fitting and the ultimate, the most eminent of debaters, and a great poet;

who was adorned with virtues such as the six supernormal powers and the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā); whose intellect was firmly established in the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma);
and who served as an ornament to the lineage of the Elders residing at the Mahāvihāra, which is the lamp of the Theravāda succession.
This commentary on the Pātimokkha, called the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, has been composed by the Elder:
May it remain as long as there are in the world those seeking to cross over the world,
showing to sons of good family the method for the purification of virtue.
Even the name "Buddha" belongs only to that Pure-Minded One, the Peerless,
the Foremost in the World, the Great Seer— so it is proclaimed throughout the world.
The *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-ṭīkā* (Commentary on the Dispeller of Doubts) is completed.
